Preface The following interpretaƟon of Plato reﬂects an ongoing philosophical dialogue about who we are, or can be—at our best, our worst, and everything in between. As a parƟcipant in this dialogical exchange I have beneﬁted from various discussions with teachers, colleagues, and students, and I take this opportunity to express my graƟtude. One ﬁgure stands out in parƟcular, that of Jacob Klein, whose interpretaƟon of Plato was the starƟng point for my own. For all I know, Mr. Klein would have smiled indulgently on reading my interpretaƟon. But I feel safe in saying that he would have endorsed my view of engaged dialogue (dialegesthai) as having ontological signiﬁcance for Plato. I was a young student at St. John’s College many years ago by now, where Klein taught, though I should stress that my serious study of his interpretaƟon occurred only aŌer I had graduated. But both while I was there and ever more deeply since, Klein inﬂuenced me as a model for what it means to take teaching, learning, and dialogue seriously—both as a way of life and as an acƟvity having itself philosophical signiﬁcance. And the thesis of the present work is that these acƟviƟes have their ground in a platonic ontology. This ontology or metaphysics is traced out in my explicaƟon of two dialogues, primarily the Republic, with extended help from the Phaedo. It is oŌen remarked that each generaƟon, each epoch, has its Plato. While it has not been my goal to present a so-called modern Plato, some will ﬁnd it so, to the point of distorƟon or misrepresentaƟon. I ask only that they hear me out, that at least my reading is Ɵed to a careful explicaƟon of text. Concerning style, on the whole I have tried to sƟck with the language that has served me well in teaching young students. Some few passages in these two dialogues are dense enough without encumbering the interpretaƟon with too technical a vocabulary. I would also like to thank the following for their wriƩen and/or oral comments on earlier versions of the text and my reading of Plato: Eva Brann, David Lachterman, H.S. Harris, David Savan, Joe Gonda, and the publisher’s anonymous readers. At various Ɵmes along the way, others have oﬀered a criƟcal response, either to select secƟons in an exchange of

emails, or in conversaƟon, and while I have not always agreed with their comments I am grateful for their having taken the Ɵme to thoughƞully respond: among them I recall Drew Hyland, Bert Dreyfus, Nick Smith, Allan Silverman, Mary Margaret McCabe, and Verity Harte. A thank you as well to my kind and paƟent editor, Jana Hodges-Kluck. Finally, I thank my wife, YveƩe, for her encouragement and for puƫng up with the many hours that I spent hidden away in my study reading, wriƟng, and making long comments on student papers.

Introduction The main topic of this book is an examinaƟon of the interrelaƟon for Plato of soul, the world of its experience, and the Ideas. I explore this relaƟonship as developed in the Republic and Phaedo. But this exposiƟon also reveals that images and our capacity for image-making play a key role in that triadic interrelaƟonship. For it is in the exercise of this capacity that our world takes on its shape and meaning. In eﬀect, we interpret our experience by telling ourselves a story about it. And some stories are more successful than others—some are more conﬁning or limiƟng, some more illuminaƟng and liberaƟng. But these stories, these images, are not made out of whole cloth, as it were. They are not simply ﬁcƟons, however raƟonal, not simply subjecƟve, useful imposiƟons. For the world presents itself to us in its readability, it meets us halfway, so to speak. The quesƟon is which stories, which images, give a beƩer account and why. Note that I am not claiming that we construct reality, impose idenƟƟes. Rather, that idenƟƟes are a result of successive, ever improving, interacƟons between soul (the interpreƟve agent), the world(s) of its experience, and the Ideas that give it meaning (the acƟviƟes of dianoia and noēsis). The simple, and certainly true, view of what Plato thought about images, of course, is that they are “less real than their originals,” less real, less true, etc. This negaƟve view, I argue, needs to be supplemented by a posiƟve one. A recurrent theme in what follows is an aƩempt to look at what else Plato thought about images, and our capacity for image-making taken in a larger sense. I examine Plato’s use of speciﬁc images—looking at why and how in a given context he uses them, oﬀering interpretaƟons of the key images themselves—as well as Plato’s view of images per se. It will turn out (parƟcularly in the laƩer case) that the human capacity for interpreƟng images and for image-making of various sorts is rather diﬀerent—more complex and philosophically important to Plato’s ontology —than the simple view would suggest. Images, and image-making, in short, will be seen to play an unexpectedly posiƟve role in determining what is ontologically real. Paradoxically, the everyday version of the same acƟvity, carried out unaware, is the pervasive source of just what keeps us

from progressing towards knowledge, and changing the way we live. It keeps us in chains, as it were. Reading images is a basic acƟvity of the soul. Reading them correctly is what in a sense disƟnguishes the philosopher from the lover of sights and sounds, knowledge from opinion. Learning to read them correctly is what underlies the educaƟon of the philosopher. The ﬁrst and most important step in this, the fundamental ontological shiŌ, is learning to see the many kinds of images precisely as images. By images, of course, I do not mean simply the literally visible, as will become clear in the development of my argument. The noƟon of image that I will claim for Plato is as far removed from the sense of visible/visual image (though beginning with that) as sight is from insight, speech, and speech acts from discourse as dialegesthai—that is to say, the dialogue of the soul with others, and with itself, about the various objects of its varied experience. This is not as easy or as obvious as it sounds, as we shall see. The Republic takes us a good part of the way. To complete Plato’s story it is the Phaedo, ﬁlled as it is with images and talk about images, which will take us the rest of the way, before returning to the Republic. For the Phaedo deals in detail with the soul, and its reading of the presence or image of the Ideas in parƟculars. One consequence of my reading will be a rather diﬀerent sense of the eternality of the Ideas, the immortality of the soul, and the inƟmate relaƟon of the two. Finally, I should stress again that the study here of the meaning for Plato of image and image-making is not an end in itself, however interesƟng that might be. Rather, it is my claim that this is the way in to understanding the relaƟon of Soul, World, and Idea, and what makes it all work. Before beginning an analysis of text, I would like to comment on a methodological issue in the interpretaƟon of the dialogues. Much of the wriƟng about Plato in the past had focused on what might be called the proposiƟonal content of the dialogues, and oŌen in the logical analysis of isolated passages. The rest, the dramaƟc details and the use of the dialogue form in parƟcular, are in the extreme treated as so much literary window dressing (or worse sƟll, as an occasion for Platonic obfuscaƟon)— interesƟng, but not essenƟal to the assessment of the philosophical argument. There is, however, a conƟnuous tradiƟon (increasingly rich) for taking the form of Plato’s dialogues as inseparable from the philosophical content. The views of several modern Plato scholars so inclined are

instrucƟve, and will help to situate my own approach. This is all the more important given that I will argue for the philosophical signiﬁcance of images and image-making, an aspect of form, in the triadic relaƟon of soul, world and Idea. The excellent essay by Christopher Gill, “DialecƟc and the Dialogue Form,”[1] gives a clear summary of the variety of modern views “in which Plato’s use of [the dialogue] form is taken to be crucial for his philosophical objecƟves” (145). He then goes on to develop his own argument for exactly in what sense this is the case. His posiƟon is that there is conƟnuity in the corpus of philosophy understood as dialecƟc as a “shared” invesƟgaƟon that is “ongoing,” with “objecƟve knowledge of the essenƟal principles of reality as the ideal outcome, and proper target of dialecƟc.” What Gill insists is that each dialogue couches this project in its own terms. What each dialogue represents is a parƟcular take on a parƟcular subject, and a form of dialecƟc that is bound by the parƟcular immediate subject and the nature of the interlocutors—their interests, their strengths and weaknesses. Thus, the broader conƟnuity of dialecƟc conceived in terms of objecƟve and dialogical method is shaped and bound by the context of each individual dialogue. The ulƟmate result “if carried to compleƟon, would lead through shared enquiry to systemaƟc knowledge of the essenƟal principles of reality and method.” Given the conƟnuity of reader, each dialogue makes its parƟcular contribuƟon to the advance towards what remains an “ideal dialecƟc.” “The distance between represented and ideal dialecƟc is someƟmes underlined by couching the ideal version in the guise of myth.” As a result of this emphasis on each dialogue as a “dialecƟcal unit” that has to be understood in the contextuality that the dialogue form gives to it, Gill is wary of too ready an interpretaƟon of Plato “across dialogues”—and gives some criƟcal examples of this. He does not rule out looking to one dialogue for help in understanding another (as is indeed the case in my own reading) but rather insists that “our primary response should be to this piece of dramaƟzed dialecƟc” before moving to comparisons. So, for example, the role and funcƟon of an invocaƟon of anamnēsis, and its relaƟon to a theory of Forms, must ﬁrst be carefully parsed for the diﬀerences determined by the context of each instance, the individual

dialogue. Thus even Charles Kahn’s reading of the early dialogues as prolepƟc, in his Plato and the SocraƟc Dialogue; The Philosophical Use of a Literary Form[2] is faulted by Gill for not treaƟng each dialogue suﬃciently independently before any interpretaƟon across dialogues. “In responding to the aporia which is the outcome [of the Euthydemus] . . . it is crucial that we respond to this aporia, and do so in the terms in which it is framed,” rather than reading it prolepƟcally, as anƟcipaƟng a resoluƟon of the aporia oﬀered in the Republic. “It is not perhaps inconceivable that a Platonic dialogue could take up an aporia from another dialogue and resolve it. But Republic is very diﬀerent in the issues it addresses and in the kind of argument by which it addresses these issues” (156). In my own case, the aƩenƟon to just such a dramaƟc context in detail explains the length of my Phaedo chapters before returning to the Republic. (Considering passages in context however, including the context of the whole dialogue, does not in my case commit to a complete commentary on each of the two dialogues.) My text hopefully puts into pracƟce what he counsels, and for the same reasons regarding the dialogue form—as well as a similar concepƟon of dialecƟc and the disƟncƟon between dialecƟc as an ongoing dialogical praxis and an “ideal dialecƟc” that would be the compleƟon of the philosopher’s project (as contrasted to a synthesized platonic doctrine per Kahn). I would say that the laƩer is approached asymptoƟcally. By contrast, Michael Frede, in “Plato’s Arguments and the Dialogue Form,”[3] argues from the general formal characterisƟcs of the dialogue form itself, the use of quesƟon and answer, and from Plato’s parƟcular philosophical use of it. Frede rejects both “a merely literary use, a simple maƩer of presentaƟon . . . for the [mere] sake of clarity and vividness for the sake of drama, or in a sense at the other extreme, the doctrinal view, that the dialogue form represents in the quesƟon and answer format an unambiguous presentaƟon of what are closely knit, logically stringent arguments.” That is, on the doctrinal view, the dialogues present arguments the premises of which represent the actual views of either the historical Socrates, or whoever the quesƟoner happens to be, or ﬁnally the beliefs of Plato. On this characterizaƟon of the platonic dialogue form, which Frede rejects in parƟcular for the aporeƟc dialogues, the arguments

would always be “didacƟc dialecƟc,” that is, Socrates/Plato knows, the respondent learns. The alternaƟve is as follows: insofar as the elencƟc quesƟon and answer results in an aporia the respondent is not converted to a new belief or doctrine, that of the quesƟoner, but rather led by quesƟon and answer to see that his iniƟal starƟng point, the belief from which the conversaƟon begins, is itself contradicted by his other beliefs. As Frede points out, this belief or set of beliefs represents the contribuƟon, as it were, of the respondent. The argument proceeds from the respondent’s ”own assumpƟons” or “original thesis.” Or, on occasion, it proceeds from the interlocutor’s report of another person’s beliefs, to be tested—as is proposed by the interlocutors in the Phaedo and the Republic. And, I will argue, at least to some extent and in some cases, reﬂecƟng their own views, or those by which they are tempted. StarƟng from this view, by quesƟon and answer about the respondent’s other beliefs, or by examining unintended consequences, the contradicƟon is produced. From this aporeƟc conclusion, he might be led, but more oŌen rather the reader, to quesƟon which of two starƟng points, or another, is really preferable. That is, he is to start out on an exploraƟon of which of two starƟng points can be both logically consistent and consistent with experience, in contradisƟncƟon to being accepted on the recommendaƟon of experts or authority, whether that “of tradiƟon, of the many, or of self-styled experts”—including that of the quesƟoner, hence of Socrates, or of Plato. The literary form of quesƟon and answer is itself a protecƟon against, and represents an argument for, the epistemic rejecƟon of any blind acceptance of a parƟcular view. Thus Frede’s reasons for rejecƟng the”didacƟc dialecƟc’” view invoke not only the usual arguments about the literary form and authorial anonymity but the very formal supposiƟonal nature of quesƟon and answer itself. The point is for the reader/listener to be engaged in an examinaƟon of his own beliefs and their coherence, and their implicaƟons for how the belief system informs and shapes how one lives. ElencƟc dialecƟc is part of a search for a grounding of belief, and of acƟon, in knowledge. But since the kinds of subject under discussion (e.g., virtue, reality, jusƟce, evil) have a large potenƟal for eventual aporeƟc contradicƟon, one is commiƩed philosophically, not to epistemic skepƟcism, but rather to both modesty and conƟnued examinaƟon of the arguments presented dialecƟcally and

their implicaƟons for one’s own beliefs. What the dialogue form provides then is a way for Plato both to present and to develop his own beliefs but with an implicit rejecƟon of any claim to authority. This is reinforced by the drama, I myself would add, in those speciﬁc passages I examine here where the interlocutors are explicitly presented as either all too ready to hear Socrates opinion or belief on a parƟcular subject-maƩer, or as already adhering to it. It is also for this reason, as Frede points out in general terms, that the “ﬁcƟƟous context of the individual interlocutor’s character, social posiƟon, belief system, etc. is so important, and not a mere ‘literary device’. To know, we learn from the early dialogues, is not just a maƩer of having an argument, however good it may be, for a thesis. Knowledge also involves that the rest of one’s beliefs, and hence at least in some cases, one’s whole life, be in line with one’s argument.” Clearly, as we shall see, Frede’s descripƟon above is the case with Glaucon and Adeimantus, Simmias and Cebes. Frede concludes that Plato feared that the internal dialogue of the average soul with itself is prone to being self-saƟsﬁed and aƩached to its beliefs—and so he chose a form of wriƟng that, within the literary context, engages the reader in evaluaƟng the premises not only of the respondent but of the quesƟoner as well, and by implicaƟon the reader’s own. At least that is the ideal. I would add only and perhaps this is obvious, that this posiƟon applies not only to the more oﬃcial aporeƟc or so-called SocraƟc dialogues. It applies as well to those like the Phaedo and the Republic. These two dialogues contain elencƟc and aporeƟc porƟons (as contrasted to what appear as exposiƟonal). More importantly, it applies to the whole corpus, inasmuch as at least the form of a dialogue is preserved, and in parƟcular by Plato’s absence as a literary character (excepƟng the LeƩers, and even then). Perhaps the most extreme version of the claim that the dialogue form or method and its content are inseparable is that the method in some sense is the content. It is the claim that the contents of Plato’s philosophy rightly understood is expressed in dialogues because it can only be expressed that way—and this is so because any claim that Plato’s philosophy, in whole or in part, could be expressed in proposiƟons, or as a theory, is false. This view is defended by Francisco J. Gonzalez, in “Self- Knowledge, PracƟcal Knowledge and Insight: Plato’s DialecƟc and the

Dialogue Form.”[4] Gonzalez thus goes even further than Gill and Frede (whom he cites) in his claims for the strict necessity of the dialogue form. Plato had to write in dialogue form. He argues not simply, as others have, that the dialogue form itself has philosophical signiﬁcance, but that it is necessary to Plato’s view of what philosophy itself is—and not just philosophizing, but the very contents of philosophy. He argues that the dialogues have a necessary “reﬂexivity,” by which he means that they embody or exemplify what they argue for or about, and that therein lies their truth, all real knowledge and its jusƟﬁcaƟon. This embodied or “exhibited” truth is also in a culminaƟng insight — a kind of pracƟcal knowledge instrucƟng us about how to live that is a mode of “knowing what” (a special kind of epistemic knowing how as contrasted to mere knowing that [Ryle]) to be contrasted to any proposiƟonal formulaƟon. This, he claims, is what philosophy is for Plato (and tout court). Although later in the paper he backtracks to include argumentaƟon—and that “philosophy clearly has some theoreƟcal content” (183). Gonzalez is led to this in large measure by his view that any proposiƟonal interpretaƟon is “cogniƟvist,” hence dogmaƟc, hence not platonic (nor in even general terms truly philosophic)—philosophy “shows rather than proves, manifests rather than describes. It is primarily neither deducƟve nor analyƟc, but rather exhibiƟve” (162). This seems to me a simpliﬁcaƟon and a distorƟon of the alternaƟves. Boxing himself into a corner, it then turns out that there is no objecƟve knowledge but what is in the exempliﬁcaƟon. But then, one might well ask, of what is it an exempliﬁcaƟon, if all is in the “showing?” For Gonzalez actually says at one point that, This view makes philosophical method everything. The method is not simply a tool by means of which we arrive at some objecƟﬁable results which themselves consƟtute philosophical knowledge: instead the method is philosophical knowledge. . . . Philosophical knowledge is, accordingly, not a knowledge of facts that can be passed on to another, but rather a personal orientaƟon towards the truth in which this truth can make itself manifest. (161)

But given what he argues it is hard to see what the origin or status of the truth would be. To see and assent to the truth of something is in a sense beyond or behind the proposiƟons that formulate it. But this does not mean that that truth, of, for example, what learning is—of recollecƟon or anamnēsis (exhibited in the Meno and argued for in the Phaedo) is somehow inseparable from its presentaƟon in that context. The alternaƟve, I would argue, is that Plato wrote in the dialogue form because while presenƟng an argument the dialogue form best illustrates the diﬃculƟes in coming to it, the obstacles to understanding it and the signiﬁcance of assent (or denial). In short, it is not a necessity, as Gonzalez would have it, but a choice. That true knowledge, or we should say the most important knowledge (as contrasted to say, geometry per se), is life transforming should not have to commit us to rejecƟng all theory as somehow empty proposiƟonal formulaƟons—as long as we disƟnguish between the formulaƟons and what drives our assent. And that the dialogue form helps us to see more clearly surely should not be confused, let alone conﬂated, with what it is that we see. G. Press, in “Plato’s Dialogues as Enactments”[5] is not as extreme as Gonzalez, but is also out to reject the ostensible doctrinal interpretaƟon, at least understood as a ﬁnal posiƟon or “seƩled doctrines that could be wriƩen down or taught” (144). I support the noƟon that the dialogues are an invitaƟon to reﬂecƟon, an invitaƟon to dialogue, and that conclusions are in a sense oŌen, perhaps always, somewhat provisional, in that sense “open-ended” (Nails). Where I disagree is in the claim that undefended “recurrent principles” such as “that there is a soul, that it is more important than the body . . . the Ideas themselves . . . philosophy is the best way of life . . . there are such things as the virtues,” all serve as “general beliefs” that are the “premises of arguments and proposiƟons to which Socrates insists on geƫng his interlocutor’s agreement,” and that Socrates’s “certainty [about these] is moral rather than logical.” But the dialogues surely do not just suppose the existence of these—they examine just what these really are, their natures, and in that examinaƟon is an argument for their existence or truth. Press’ interpretaƟon does seem to me once again to take the doctrine of philosophers as meaning assertoric

proposiƟonal conclusions rather than the argument or system that they elaborate. As for Press’ sense of the dialogues as “enactments,” they are said to “embody” Plato’s “vision” of an ideal, of a life as lived—these are ﬁnal truths that are “glimpses” and obviously non-proposiƟonal. But while I too argue that the dialogues show the lived consequences of interpreƟng the world in such and such a way, I argue that this is in addiƟon to, and forms part of, an actual argument. Finally, Press seems to reduce philosophy to philosophizing, i.e., to the searching in authenƟc philosophical conversaƟon, rather than producing aƩempts at credible logoi. Press explicates Plato’s ﬁcƟve vision, (the enactments) as an appeal to our “feeling and imaginaƟon” as well as to our reason. But the rhetorical eﬀect of Plato’s images, the portrayals (and the myths) as convincing, hence as part of the argument is, at least for the philosophical parƟcipant/reader, based on and in our intellectual percepƟon of their veracity, as contrasted to the rhetorical eﬀect on those interlocutors or readers for whom their feelings, and their beliefs, play an important role, and whose feelings and beliefs precisely get in the way of any other appeal. This is as true of the metaphysical or ontological portrait of the lived in world of our experience in general, as we see in part in Socrates’s intellectual biography recounted by him in the Phaedo. Otherwise, we might as well sƟck with the poets. If the form and content are inseparable, as I too believe they are, our obligaƟon is carefully to unravel the text by applying an interpretaƟon of each speciﬁc dramaƟc feature to the logical or philosophical argument. The shortcomings of interpretaƟons that fail to do so serve on a case by case basis to help make the argument for the validity, indeed the necessity, of such an approach. This is not to say that the work of scholars working primarily in the analyƟcal tradiƟon does not contain much analysis that pays careful and rewarding aƩenƟon to the text, and from which we have much to learn. Rather, that where their insights and conclusions go astray (in my view) it can someƟmes be traced to a neglect of the dramaƟc features and their direct inﬂuence on an understanding of Plato’s argument as addressed to the reader. This holds as well on occasion for those whose interpretaƟve stance is closer to my own.[6]

The commitment to interpreƟng the form and the content as a unity is oŌen honored more in the breach than in the observance. Consider the following interesƟng and instrucƟve historical case of where a general commitment to the importance of the drama sƟll gives way to a philosophical preconcepƟon concerning Plato. Julius Stenzel, a scholar of an earlier generaƟon, was notable for having stressed the form-content relaƟonship. Stenzel also wished to fend oﬀ the view wherein the platonic Ideas are reduced to concepts, and he is right, in my view, to do so. Yet in its place he is keen to disƟnguish a SocraƟc skepƟcism regarding the achievement of an absolute knowledge from a Platonic home of absolute being. Thus for Stenzel,[7] The Pythagoreans had already given philosophical form to the religion of a world beyond. It was here that Plato found a home for his idea of absolute being. . . . It will be found to be an essenƟal moƟf in his philosophy that he calls in the assistance of religious faith in order to complete the SocraƟc ideal of an absolute knowledge; he gives to mere mythology the dignity of a religious metaphysic, and proves that it is the foundaƟon of that synopsis of the whole of knowledge for which he strives; or rather that it is the foundaƟon of all knowledge whatsoever. (Plato’s Method of DialecƟc, 13) According to Stenzel, the funcƟon of a Platonic portrait of SocraƟc irony regarding the mysteries is to render homage to his teacher’s original skepƟcism, skepƟcism of any literal interpretaƟon of the mysteries that Plato shares. But this same SocraƟc persona of the dialogues, Stenzel holds, is also in tension with a Platonic claim for an absolute knowledge that, in the early and middle dialogues, is sƟll a sort of faith, rather than arƟculated knowledge, albeit a faith in a rather diﬀerent otherworldliness than the convenƟonal one. The same disƟncƟon, between Socrates the wise moralist and Plato the over-zealous metaphysician, is ﬁrst suggested by Nietzsche, in Beyond Good and Evil (secƟon 191). This scenario explains for Stenzel, and many others since, why Plato drops the SocraƟc persona from those later dialogues which, for him, get down to the real business of sorƟng out “a clear view of the simpler discursive thought which ﬁnds relaƟons between concepts.” But is this view really jusƟﬁed by the text? Is

there an ironical Platonic mask behind which Plato would hide, or excuse, his “religious metaphysics,” or is the Platonic portrayal of a form of SocraƟc ontological skepƟcism actually consistent aŌer all with Plato’s view of the Ideas in these dialogues, and indeed poinƟng us in the right direcƟon. The answer, I maintain, is the laƩer. This claim can only be defended through the very reading of the text as a unity of form and content that Stenzel himself espouses but apparently did not implement.[8] More recent writers who also urge the unity of form and content, seem to me to be open to the same criƟcism, as I note in places below. It is only the general fact of the dialogue form, and such features as the absence of Socrates from certain dialogues, etc. that is taken as signiﬁcant. A close reading of the actual details of key passages of the dialogue does indeed present us with a parƟcular interpretaƟon of the reality of the Ideas, of their relaƟon to images, in parƟcular a thesis concerning the Ideas and a posiƟve view of image-making, and a resultant explicaƟon of Plato’s ontology (This is, of course, again in addiƟon and in contrast to the usual, and obvious, staple of Plato interpretaƟon that points to his standard contrast between original and image, or less real copy). It is only against the background of such an understanding derived from a reading that is both analyƟcal with regard to the arguments and takes account of the literary presentaƟon, that the Ideas make sense as precisely not a “religious metaphysic.” That is, I will argue that there is a more general epistemological and ontological need to see images as images rather than merely as “less real than originals,” and that this reading sheds light on the ontological argument. Furthermore, both the dialogue form, itself an image constructed of images, and the implicit reader-text relaƟon, act out the far more fundamental relaƟon of Ideas to human being. The method and content of the key images within the Republic and Phaedo provide insight into the relaƟon of knower and known in the everyday, habitual image-world, as well as paradigms of the correct producƟon and interpretaƟon of a noeƟc world of images of much greater clarity (saphēneia). Human discourse itself, I argue, is to be seen as the essenƟal, primary image-making, and revealed in these two dialogues as already metaphysical.

Some would even go so far as to deny that there is any other extra- dialogical correct noƟon of a platonic logos, or even of independent Ideas in any sense. They would claim that the dialogical form itself and the philosophical invitaƟon to dialogue about key issues in a constant process of searching for the truth, and the examinaƟon of proposals for a logos to see how they hold up both logically and as measured against experience, is all that there is in Plato’s serious philosophy. The claim would be that philosophy truly understood is just this and, as contrasted to actual possession of knowledge, is limited by human existence to the eroƟcized pursuit of knowledge. For this view, see for example David Roochnik, The Tragedy of Reason: Toward a Platonic ConcepƟon of Logos.[9] Roochnik tries to stake out a posiƟon for Plato seen as defending philosophy’s search for a logos as a truth—as a third posiƟon between the raƟonalism of truth as analyƟc, certain knowledge, proposiƟonal, and the anƟ-raƟonalism of relaƟvisƟc valuaƟons and/or emoƟve “poeƟcism” (Nietzsche, Heidegger, Derrida, Rorty). In so doing, he seeks to detach the real Plato from the Plato commonly imagined by philosophers and non-philosophers alike as the arch-raƟonalist, the impossible Realist, for whom there is in principle a science of knowledge, and whose model is best seen in the knowledge of science, underpinned by a theory of ﬁxed raƟonal enƟƟes (whether universals, concepts, or Ideas). While I agree in general with the opposiƟon that he sets up, I think Roochnik goes too far, runs the risk of subjecƟvizing, or historicizing Plato, and in ways that the texts will not support. As for myself, I urge in what follows rather that Plato requires that the world be given its due, that it meets us halfway, and truth and knowledge of more than the natural world is not just provisional but rather also cumulaƟve— which is not to deny the consƟtuƟve role of soul or consciousness. Jill Gordon, in Turning Toward Philosophy: Literary Device and DramaƟc Structure in Plato’s Dialogues[10] argues for the philosophical value of the platonic images themselves. See her introducƟon, the secƟon on Analysis and Argument-Focused Methods, pages 3-6, for a similar criƟque of method to my own above. “This approach tends to idenƟfy philosophical acƟvity with making and analyzing logico-deducƟve arguments. While this is certainly a part of philosophical acƟvity, and a part of Platonic dialogues, it cannot be the exclusive or even primary acƟvity of

philosophers” (3). Describing her own project, Gordon writes, “By focusing on the dialogues’ wriƩen style, wriƩen structure, content, and literary devices, I draw conclusions about how the wriƩen elements of the text engage the reader or audience in the acƟvity we call philosophy. The elements that are considered nonphilosophical by contemporary approaches — or, at the very least, extraphilosophical or extralogical—are the very elements of Plato’s dialogues that can turn a soul toward the philosophical life” (5). This is not to say that we reach the same conclusions about the meaning of even the dramaƟcal features of the text nor our respecƟve conclusions about what Plato intends by the philosophical life. Our take on the meaning and role of images for Plato has much in common, in parƟcular the importance of seeing the image as image. See her chapter 6, enƟtled Image. And yet, there is a fundamental diﬀerence. Gordon argues that images themselves can be an extralogical means of argument, that is to say, a complement to straight out “logico-deducƟve argumentaƟon.” And that it is the two taken together that eﬀecƟvely turn the soul towards a life of philosophy. I argue rather that the posiƟve role of Plato’s own images is to illustrate not to convince. Gordon does seem to say something like this when she says that “the richness of an image, and therefore its philosophical value, are appreciated only on reﬂecƟon” (164). Yet she believes also that the images themselves have philosophical content and that “images can lead to truth and philosophical insight” (165). As for their negaƟve role, it is oŌen to drive us to disƟnguish between the literal and the ﬁguraƟve, and someƟmes precisely what by contrast is not the case, or not Plato’s posiƟon, for example, around the meaning of the eternality of the soul and both the reality and the independence of the Ideas. (I reject, and Gordon accepts, a two worlds view. See her 168, n. 38. And our treatment of RecollecƟon and its implicaƟons, for instance, is diﬀerent.) Gordon tends to focus on the literary image, I do discuss these in detail, while I focus on the onto- epistemological arguments themselves, extending to the claim that to see the image as image is the ﬁrst step in philosophical ascent. Further, that this philosophical meaning of image is embedded in the use of discourse itself. In sum, Gordon stresses the human condiƟon as one of limitaƟon, cut oﬀ from a full insight into ulƟmate realiƟes, but that this gap can be bridged to an extent through extralogical means, that is, through images.

These are to serve not only as a bridge to the Ideas but to help us in turning towards the life of philosophy. I would argue that accepƟng this extralogical assistance is eﬀecƟvely turning away from philosophy, though indeed my own approach is certainly not to reduce the argumentaƟon of the dialogues to logico-deducƟve treaƟses. Concerning my analysis of Plato’s epistemological/ontological arguments, as contrasted to the dramaƟc elements, my exposiƟon is not of what is ostensibly meant behind the scenes, as it were, but rather in careful analysis of what Socrates actually says. OŌen enough the views of the interlocutors serve as a starƟng point, and ﬁnally a contrast. But such exchanges are seen to lead to the so-called metaphysical books of Republic V, VI and VII, thus to Socrates’s development of the Divided Line, etc. I devote a whole long chapter to this, returning to Glaucon and Adeimantus only for a few comments at the end. The same holds true for my exposiƟon of the diﬀerence between the true and the false philosopher, knowledge versus opinion, the cogniƟve faculƟes (dunameis) in chapter two, and the educaƟon of the philosopher in chapter ﬁve. Finally, it may be useful to make one more comment about my method of exposiƟon as compared to the so-called analyƟcal approach. In these two dialogues there is of course at certain points criƟcism of the posiƟons of the interlocutors, usually at a beginning of a new topic or transiƟon, leading to an aporeia, from which Socrates then takes oﬀ into new territory. But the Republic in parƟcular is in large measure descripƟve or illustraƟve—even when it comes to the Divided Line, which is really just a sketch or outline. Concerning method, Plato even tells us as much in turning to the development of the image of the soul writ large in the image of the city, and the menƟon of the “longer way.” In this sense, I think that it is fair to say that there just are few posiƟve, analyƟcal, proposiƟonal arguments in these and other ostensible middle period dialogues. The argument is, as it were, by analogy, by the development (and appeal of) images, which make sense or are explanatory of our experience. This is not to say that all are like that, or that there are not passages of logical argument in the early and middle dialogues, though these passages are, on the whole, (though not all) negaƟve or aporeƟc. For example, when it comes to Socrates’s discussion of the famous “three ﬁnger” illustraƟon etc., my discussion is an exposiƟon of the logical or analyƟcal moves in the

argument regarding conﬂicƟng percepƟons/judgments and contradictory predicates and/or qualiƟes. This is the ﬁrst move towards the argument for the hypothesis of the Ideas. Another example would be my analysis of the same issue and methodology in the Phaedo passage concerning the “ﬂight” of opposites when one approaches the ostensible presence of the other. The kind of exposiƟon that the analyƟcal school favors, and that some readers may ﬁnd lacking in my text, is perhaps appropriate to the later dialogues such as the Sophist, etc. My own method of exposiƟon for the two dialogues that are my texts, on the posiƟve side, is to try to make sense of what Socrates says in his descripƟons, including the ontological and epistemological claims, and the unpacking of the images, along with original examples. On the negaƟve side, I try to see just what metaphysical/ontological and epistemological assumpƟons are implicit in what the interlocutors say, as well as how they come a cropper. Further, I argue that a careful eliciƟng of these from the actual text (not ad hominem) can help us, by contrast, with an actual exposiƟon of posiƟve doctrines. But given the above, this exposiƟonal strategy has its limits— and so I turn for three whole chapters to the Phaedo, for a philosophical development of the concept of separaƟon or chōrismos (around which there is controversy in the literature) in order to ﬂesh out Plato’s claims (and my reading of them) about soul, and the Ideas. And with this I argue for a new and diﬀerent interpretaƟon of the immortality of the Platonic soul and the special kind of eternality of the Ideas. In the process of construcƟng Plato’s argument, a dramaƟcal reading of the dialogue is always aƩenƟve to the text to see in a passage that arƞul mimeƟc tone which will tell us just when, and how far, to take what is being said either literally or seriously—that is, the feature of Platonic irony. For, as has been pointed out each Ɵme by those who take the maƩer seriously, a conversaƟon between Socrates and the interlocutors is not the same as whatever is meant to pass between the various readers and Plato. Irony aside, the conversaƟon between a speciﬁc interlocutor and the platonic Socrates allows Plato to address speciﬁc subjects by engaging with the presupposiƟons (albeit oŌen enough implicit), the starƟng points, of a parƟcular point of view on the subject.[11] The characters, even when

corresponding to real people, are dramaƟc ﬁcƟons, oﬀered as types or kinds. It is a feature of the dialogue that the interlocutor has speciﬁc views and speciﬁc interacƟons with Socrates which are a funcƟon of these views —the characters are not interchangeable, abstract foils for Socrates. The reader/listener must always ask just why, philosophically, Plato employs images of just these speciﬁc individuals. It is only in taking such a quesƟon seriously in examining their image in the actual portrayal of their arguments, beliefs, emoƟons, and someƟmes acƟons, in short, in examining their souls—that an answer can be found.[12] But one thing is clear, it will not do to treat even agreement or consent by one of the interlocutors as equivalent to our own consent to the same proposiƟon, nor to assume that Plato wishes it—and all the more so for simply equaƟng what Socrates says in context, that is, in the presence of others, with Plato’s own address to the careful reader (nor for that maƩer to assume that all readers are addressed by the same text, as it were). I would argue that, given this caveat, the dramaƟc content (along with the analyƟcal content seen in context) is precisely what does give us Plato’s own presence, presents his own views and engages the reader.[13] Again, if there is a fairly obvious gross ﬂaw in an argument, for example the ﬁrst argument for immortality in the Phaedo, or the less obvious ones that I deal with in the Republic, it makes more sense to assume, at least as a working hypothesis, that an author who could write the dialogues was capable of not overlooking such ﬂaws, than the contrary, and that the dramaƟc nature of the dialogue is the reasonable explanaƟon (always with the proviso that any such parƟcular interpretaƟon is without strain). In other words, the arguments are well constructed precisely because of the supposed ﬂaw, and the reader is meant to ask just why this parƟcular feature is appropriate for this character and/or at this stage of the dialogue—what is it meant to say, and what are we meant to ask or conclude? I do not suggest that all cases are to be treated this way, rather that it is a useful principle of interpretaƟon. It is derived from premises concerning the author’s intelligence, the mimeƟc nature of dialogue, and most of all by consistent empirical observaƟon. Nor do I mean to suggest that Plato uses Socrates against his own (ﬁcƟve) will—rather quite the opposite. The Platonic irony is contained within the SocraƟc ﬁgure’s own

speeches and acƟons—in short, that Socrates himself is portrayed as knowing quite well who in parƟcular he is speaking with, and, while trying to move that person ahead in his understanding where possible (and in some cases it is conspicuously not), Socrates is acutely aware of the limitaƟons of that person, including those who are his own associates, personal friends and/or “friends of the Ideas” (I leave open whether or how this applies to certain of the so-called late dialogues in which Socrates is present). It is because the role of the interlocutors has philosophical signiﬁcance that they are never lost sight of in these two dialogues, and in my exposiƟon. Indeed, the ﬁrst chapter is devoted in large part to taking the exact measure of Glaucon and Adeimantus, to whom I return from Ɵme to Ɵme (as does Socrates) in order to posiƟon the argument of the text of the Republic. The same is true of Simmias and Cebes in my discussion of the Phaedo, and it is in chapter 7 that their views are a parƟcular focus. It is crucial that any such claims be worked out in a case by case interpretaƟon, and one not based on shadowy asserƟons about what is ironical and what is not, what is to be taken seriously or literally and what not, what is an intenƟonally ﬂawed argument or claim and what is seriously meant to be a sound argument. All of this can only be argued based on interpretaƟons of what is actually said at a given moment (and someƟmes what is done)—though this may also require seƫng the immediate text in the context of who is saying it to whom, and in the larger context of the progress and themes of the dialogue. The test is always whether there is suﬃcient evidence within the dialogue for the interpretaƟve case to be made, while at the same Ɵme subjecƟng the argument presented at a given point to rigorous analysis. The point is that such an analysis is usually not in and of itself the end of the task. Rather, it can only be part of the process of assessing the Platonic argument, to be complemented by a criƟcal reading of the context—before, during, and aŌer the passage in quesƟon. The program outlined above concerning the form/content issue and the philosophical signiﬁcance of the dramaƟc aspect of the dialogues, along with the substanƟve examinaƟon of image and image-making in these two dialogues, results in a reassessment of certain tradiƟonal views concerning the soul, the Ideas and their interrelaƟon. Much of my book is

an interpretaƟon of the Republic. But in order to develop and support my reading of soul and of the Ideas as interdependent, I do turn for three chapters to the Phaedo. Chapter 6 deals with the crucial noƟon of separaƟon and our capacity for separaƟng, as a special kind of image- making. Chapter 7 deals with image-making gone astray, or the problem of misreading the world. Chapter 8 deals with Socrates’s responses to Simmias and Cebes and his own “second sailing,” his own image-making. The famous hypotheƟcal method and the Ideas as explanatory are read as dealing with the reality of the images of the Ideas in speech, hence with the relaƟon of soul, knowledge and existence. I argue that both behind and through the myths and literary images (in the descripƟon of the dynamic of parƟcipaƟon) there is another, diﬀerent, and more serious argument—one in which the soul is indeed immortal, but has a form of immortality that is present in everyday life as an atemporality rather than a literal deathlessness—hence consistent with the soul ceasing to exist. Parallel is a noƟon of the Ideas that requires that they be eﬃcacious and separate only within the context of lived human experience. It is this down to earth noƟon of soul and the Ideas that is both reﬂected in and a precondiƟon of, language and inquiry. These acƟviƟes are carried out in the producƟon and response to images. The nature and signiﬁcance of images per se, of the human capacity to read images and for image-making are interpreted as the key to Plato’s ontology as seen in these two dialogues, hence key to the nature of the soul, the Ideas and their interrelaƟon in the world they inhabit. (I reject then a simple two worlds interpretaƟon.) The various images in the Phaedo and the Republic are to be read as serious muthologia, disƟnguishing between the literal-mindedness dictated by the natures of the interlocutors in both dialogues, and the argument addressed to the reader. Read in this way, I argue, the Ideas are not to be conceived as independent substanƟal existences—in essence defending Plato, as does Gadamer, against Aristotle’s charge of reiﬁcaƟon (Meta, 1086a, 1087a). It is with these interpretaƟons that I return to the Republic to explicate the noƟons of soul and Idea found in the closing books. Perhaps the seemingly most radical or challenging suggesƟon in my interpretaƟon is that the Ideas have something of a quasi-temporal dimension. This is not, of course, to deny or ignore those passages where the Ideas are explicitly said to be eternal, unchanging, stable—most oŌen

in contrast and over and against the aisthēta, the sensible, the changing, the context relaƟve, etc. Ideas are invoked as causes and/or explanaƟons in a wide variety of contexts over the corpus, an Idea “corresponding to each grouping of parƟculars to which we give the same name” (Rep. 596a). It would seem that a variety of Ideas are considered, corresponding to the variety of objects and contexts (see Peters, 48)—including ethical (Parm. 130b, Phaedrus 250d), natural (Tim. 51b, Soph. 266b), mathemaƟcal (Phaedo 101b-c), trivial (Parm. 130c), man-made objects (Rep. 596a, 597d, Soph. 265b) relaƟons (Phaedo 74a-77a, Rep. 479b, Parm. 133c), and even negaƟons (Rep. 476a, Theat. 186a, Soph. 257e). In most if not all of these domains, in addiƟon to parƟculars being a plurality, a many as opposed to a one, it is “context relaƟvity” that poses an obstacle to certain knowledge, and by contrast it is “invariance across context,” (Burnyeat, 2000) within a given domain that has been suggested as the feature that characterizes the Ideas. But what else do these various kinds of eidē corresponding to kinds of discourse have in common, and how is the search for stable knowledge to be understood in each context, and/or for the whole? What is the topos noētos (Rep.508c, 517b) where they are all to be located? What understanding of “parƟcipaƟon” (methexis) can encompass or accommodate all these various sorts of experience—far more than merely sensible parƟculars? What is their relaƟon to the various logoi of ongoing discourse in which we search out their right names? What account must we give for their presence even in everyday discourse? These are large and complex, if related, issues. What I will argue is that the realm in which the Ideas all have their being is revealed as inextricably embedded in the acƟvity of discourse about these various worlds, and that the key to understanding how it all works, the common epistemic and ontological thread, is in our primary image-making. This linkage results in a certain necessary and permanent temporal horizon for being and our knowledge of it. From the analysis of the meaning and role of image and image- making in the intertwining of soul, world and Idea, it would seem that the content of an Idea must be conceived as both stable and ﬂexible for knowledge to be possible. That is, it has to be ﬂexible enough to embody and explain the evolving meanings of logoi, of the naming itself, while at

the same Ɵme serving human discourse as a point of stability for interpreƟng our world as it presents itself to us in its various facets.[14] NOTES 1. For an approach similar to mine concerning the necessity of a contextual reading and its implicaƟons, see Norbert Blossner’s detailed remarks on methodology (SecƟon IX) in his “The City-Soul Analogy,” in The Cambridge Companion to Plato’s Republic, ed. G. R. F. Ferrari (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2007), 345-385. “What is said . . . [in addiƟon to “certain argumentaƟve goals”] . . . is also directed at the interlocutor’s level of understanding, since it is he whom the argument must convince, and convince in such a way that the argument conƟnues to look realisƟc. But given that the argument develops and the level of the interlocutor’s understanding varies as the dialogue progresses, a correct understanding of what is said in the dialogue must aƩend at every point to the context of these uƩerances and to the argumentaƟve goal at which they aim” (378). “Remarkably, many of these passages not only contain rhetorical ploys, but also are scripted in a way that makes the arbitrary and fallacious elements of Socrates’ argument leap to the eye—at least, to the eye of the viewer who does not insist on treaƟng Plato’s text as authoritaƟve on its surface and on seeking to protect it from all criƟque” (380-81).
