Chapter 1 The Interlocutors’ Request THE PROBLEM SET BY GLAUCON AND ADEIMANTUS Book I of the Republic has the air of a self-contained dialogue, and it has been suggested that it was originally just that. It is called by Socrates a “prelude” to the rest. Yet it is so in a strange sense. Rather than a smooth introductory prelude to the whole, the discussion conƟnues based on an ironic discord. From a dramaƟc point of view, the conversaƟon conƟnues not because of Socrates but more importantly because of one of the interlocutors. As we shall see, the necessity of conƟnuing, and in what manner, is understood very diﬀerently by Socrates and by his interlocutors, Glaucon and Adeimantus. And it is this iniƟal diﬀerence, contained in the dramaƟc aspect, that will lead us in to the interpretaƟon of the dialogue. At the beginning of Book II, Socrates says that he “had supposed that [he] was done with the subject, but it all turned out to be only a prelude,” (357a) because Glaucon would not “acquiesce in Thrasymachus’s abandonment of his case.” Thrasymachus’s case, it will be recalled, was that injusƟce was more desirable, more proﬁtable, than jusƟce. But what is the “subject” that they supposedly had “done with”? That is less clear. It could be the immediate subject just referred to—the disagreement with Thrasymachus over whether jusƟce or injusƟce is preferable—or the quesƟon as to whether jusƟce or injusƟce should rightly lay claim to wisdom and is a virtue, and the other, its opposite, vice and ignorance. But this vagueness about the “subject” is appropriate since, as Socrates himself notes at the end of Book I, the discussion had moved from one subject to another “as gluƩons snatch at every dish that is handed along and taste it before they have properly enjoyed the preceding” (354b). Thus, not only has there not been one subject discussed but the outcome is, for Socrates himself, far from saƟsfactory.[1] As Socrates says, he has not “dined well” and “for me the present outcome of the discussion is that I know nothing, and this especially because if I do not know what the just is, I shall hardly know whether it is a virtue or not, and whether its possessor is or is not happy” (354c). Thus,

the sense even in which he has supposed that he had “done with the subject” is ambiguous. We must then understand that he has “had done” with it in an ironic sense. In narraƟng the event to his listener, we are told that Glaucon’s tenacity would not let a sleeping, if bloated, dog lie. He would have “been done with it” in the sense of having quelled Thrasymachus—the argument had temporarily “ﬁnished” in the sense that Thrasymachus had withdrawn into silent contempt. And yet, more importantly, the argument had not been ﬁnished, had barely been begun, in the philosophical sense of being adequate to the “subject.” We must then, look at Glaucon and Adeimantus and see what it is that they themselves require for the “subject to be done with,” and then what methods Socrates actually adopts to further examine the subject. Glaucon and Adeimantus, Plato’s half-brothers, are presented as young men with whom Socrates oŌen converses. The very ﬁrst sentence of the Republic presents Socrates as being accompanied by Glaucon. They are both returning from the Piraeus, where they had “said their prayers and seen the spectacle” (327b). Socrates says he had gone in order to “pay my devoƟons to the Goddess, and also because I wished to see how they would conduct the fesƟval since this was its inauguraƟon.” Their relaƟonship to Socrates and to the argument is further expressed in two signiﬁcant ways. First, both present themselves as friends of virtue, in this case of jusƟce. In Book II, it is they who insist that Socrates conƟnue and present an adequate defense of jusƟce. Secondly, Glaucon is presented iniƟally as employing what might be called Platonic methods and disƟncƟons. He begins by invoking a familiar disƟncƟon, and one that will later play a crucial role, that between seeming and being, though signiﬁcantly here at 357a it is not applied to objects but to convicƟon or opinion, to whether Socrates wishes merely to appear to have persuaded them or “really” to have done so. Next, he proceeds to a division and classiﬁcaƟon of kinds of good—as regards whether they are desirable merely for their own sake (e.g., joy), or for their own sake and for the consequences (e.g., health), or only for the consequences or beneﬁts (e.g., healing and the “art of making money,” etc.). Here again, we have something familiar, the method of division. (Whether it is adequately employed is another quesƟon.) Finally, we have the employment of myth, more or less skillfully, in the adaptaƟon of the story of the ring of Gyges. All

of this takes from 357a to approximately 361d, a rather long passage for an interlocutor. It even prompts Socrates to exclaim, “Bless me, my dear Glaucon, how strenuously you polish oﬀ [clean] each of your two men for the compeƟƟon for the prize, as if it were a statue.” Its purpose is to “clearly separate” the just man from the unjust, and presumably jusƟce from injusƟce, in order that each may be seen and evaluated for what it is in itself. But why does Socrates use the image of polishing (cleaning, scouring) a statue? Because, while the iniƟal divisions have some merit, as does the goal of seeing the desirability of jusƟce or injusƟce “in itself,” separated from the “beneﬁts” of appearing just, sƟll, uncovering what each is, is not the same as elaboraƟng the desirability of each. Now though the knowledge of what each is in itself would be prerequisite to deciding on the desirability of each, as Glaucon on the one hand appears to see, sƟll, he, and Adeimantus aŌer him, devote much eﬀort to presenƟng the just man in as painful and undesirable a way as possible, and the unjust man as in the most enviable posiƟon. Each is said to have been portrayed as having aƩained the limit (361d) of jusƟce and injusƟce “so that we may pass judgment which of the two is the happier,” and if happier then more desirable. The just man has been stripped of what might be called material beneﬁts, in order to be sure that he chooses jusƟce for its own sake alone, thus indicaƟng its desirability in spite of all other consideraƟons. But let us note that the kind of life prescribed for each has been presented in each case in terms of either pleasure and pain or honor, or of what we might call material condiƟons. Thus, while Glaucon’s intenƟon was to set up a model in which we could see whether the just man could be truly happy with nothing leŌ but his jusƟce, his choice of aƩendant circumstances to force the test is revealing. First of all, if we are to judge only the happiness provided by jusƟce itself, then why go to such lengths to dress out the just man’s life as miserable (the rack, his eyes burned out, etc.). It might be argued that this is done only to be sure that we have isolated the just man from any other possible raƟonale for being just—and this is of course the raƟonale for the set-up that Glaucon oﬀers. But it is also an extreme version of the common opinion that jusƟce does not pay, that in fact, as Thrasymachus iniƟally had suggested, the just usually suﬀer. Perhaps Glaucon is not altogether convinced that the common opinion is wrong? AŌer all, he is asking,

exactly how or why is the just life more desirable? Secondly, by describing their respecƟve lives in such extremes is one not precisely inﬂuencing the listener to consider factors other than jusƟce and injusƟce themselves, Glaucon thus having lapsed back into exactly what he had intended to avoid? One might argue that Glaucon wishes the good or desirability of jusƟce in itself to be produced precisely to counterbalance these “evils.” But surely the meaning and value of jusƟce could be produced without this perverse seƫng and it would sƟll ostensibly be seen as its own reward, that is, precisely as separated from its consequences. Finally, the descripƟon of each life in terms of material condiƟons alone, reveals something about Glaucon. For although he had said that he wished to hear “what each of them is, and what potency (dunamis) and eﬀect it has in and of itself dwelling in the soul” (358b), yet the noƟon of in what area the life of jusƟce and injusƟce would reveal its value and/or be of beneﬁt or harm, that of the well-being of the soul, seems to be not too clearly envisioned in contrast to the material condiƟons. This leads to a limitaƟon of Glaucon’s seƫng out of the condiƟons of analysis. In the case of jusƟce, and other virtues, Glaucon seems to be contrasƟng condiƟons of soul and external beneﬁts. In other words, what Glaucon would like to have demonstrated is that even if there is no “beneﬁt” from being just, if jusƟce is stripped of its desirable consequences, that it remains desirable “in itself.” But why is the cost of being just conceived in external terms? If the eﬀect on the soul is relevant, how relevant is it? Or how relevant are these externals in spite of their seeming importance for happiness?[2] JusƟce as a quality of the soul, is a good and beneﬁt to that of which it is a quality, the soul. Thus, the original apparently sound disƟncƟon that Glaucon had made between that which is desirable in itself and that which is desirable for the beneﬁts it brings, will not serve. This is not surprising, since the concepƟon of beneﬁt that was operaƟng there was of something other, goƩen in the external world. But this important point aside, what is at issue here is that Glaucon, in polishing the image, does not seem able or willing at this point to idenƟfy the area of concern. He knows that Socrates says that it has something to do with soul. But he has liƩle idea of what that might be, either with regard to the nature of the soul, or consequently of what arises from its condiƟon or what soul itself is aﬀected by. Put another way, to

defend jusƟce requires not only the exploraƟon of what jusƟce is but what soul is—and Glaucon does not see that his knowledge of the laƩer is lacking. This vagueness will be persistent and signiﬁcant—it corresponds to a literal-mindedness to which we shall return when we consider the issue of possibility for the ideal city. It is easy to lose sight of the fact that the soul is the over-arching topic of the Republic—its nature, its relaƟon to its world, and its well-being. A primary task of my discussion is never to allow us to lose sight of this, and to see in the text itself the suggesƟons as to why and how Glaucon and Adeimantus might so easily do so. There are further, related reasons for suggesƟng that all is not as it seems with regard to the moƟves and/or state of soul of both Glaucon and Adeimantus.[3] At the very least we can say that while Glaucon does feel he ought to desire virtue—and that he is in general a good person, one who is well disposed towards virtue; sƟll, he does not know why it is desirable, cannot give an account of it. That is, in spite of his associaƟon with Socrates, he sƟll operates at the level of opinion, albeit of perhaps right opinion. And this lack of ground for his virtue renders him vulnerable to the rhetorical inﬂuence of such as Thrasymachus. How does such a rhetoric work? Precisely by dressing up opinions in such a way as to have a certain desired eﬀect on the emoƟons, manipulaƟng them so as in turn to manipulate the opinions, and ulƟmately the acƟons of those under its inﬂuence. Now the means of manipulaƟng the emoƟons is by creaƟng images in words of the desirable or undesirable, of that which will either repel or aƩract the listener, and this almost always in terms of material advantage or disadvantage, as we see in the example of Thrasymachus at work. That it would be in terms of material advantage or disadvantage is not surprising, since this is the area where the emoƟons are most vulnerable and most open to manipulaƟon. This nexus, of material/external sƟmulus and the responsiveness of the emoƟons in terms of desire and fear, and the producƟon of corresponding opinions, is precisely what Plato will describe and analyze in detail later. It is then this nexus which is aƩacked and to an extent reorganized. The educaƟon of the guardians consists of a reformaƟon, a redirecƟon of the emoƟons with regard to the objects of desire and of fear, away from the convenƟonal ones, those Ɵed to the body and in other respects unworthy, and towards those objects, i.e., situaƟons,

conducive to virtue and thus the health of the soul. For the majority of guardians, this reformaƟon consists in a change of opinion as to the objects worthy of desire and fear. For a few, the potenƟal rulers, this reformaƟon and redirecƟon, this re-educaƟon of the emoƟons, is further grounded in insight and understanding as to why certain experiences are to be feared and others desired. Let us note in passing that these few are selected from among the guardians as a whole for further educaƟon, i.e., they are not conceived as having bypassed this ﬁrst kind of retraining, the training of one’s emoƟons and corresponding opinions about virtue, but as possessing the potenƟal for superseding or grounding it. I suggest that Glaucon, and sƟll more Adeimantus, belong to the former group, those governed by opinion—whether and to what extent they are eligible for the second group remains to be seen. But this sort of rhetoric, or dressing up of the life of the just and the unjust man, is precisely what Glaucon, and then Adeimantus, engage in. Being lovers of virtue does not prevent them from being tempted by vice. In both the method and content of the test, as it were, they reveal in what they say the inﬂuence of Thrasymachus as much as that of Socrates—and perhaps for the moment somewhat more of the former than the laƩer, as we shall soon see. Socrates says of Glaucon and Adeimantus’s rephrasing of “what they [the many] will say,” “I believe that you are really not convinced. I infer this from your general character, since from your words alone I should have distrusted you” (368b). Now their words had included a disclaimer—they were presenƟng merely the words of what “those others” who defend injusƟce as the more desirable would say. If these truly were merely an imitaƟon, an image of the words of those who defend injusƟce and aƩack jusƟce, then Socrates’s statement would be a straighƞorward reference to this fact, and to Glaucon and Adeimantus’s imitaƟve or rhetorical skill. But the speech is spoken with a polish and convicƟon that perhaps bespeaks more than just art. That they are “really not convinced” by Thrasymachus is evidenced only by the knowledge of their character that weighs against it. Socrates’s statement may thus be deeply ironic, implying that it is not only jusƟce to which he must “come to the rescue,” but the souls of his friends as well, to the extent and in the manner possible. If I am right, the admiraƟon for them which he had just voiced upon hearing their discourse is likewise cast in doubt, and is at the least

ambiguous. What they desire to be shown is commendable: “Do not then merely prove to us in argument the superiority of jusƟce to injusƟce, but show us what it is that each inherently does to its possessor—whether he does or does not escape the eyes of gods and men—whereby the one is good and the other evil” (367b). And the method that they have used in seƫng up the case to be decided is also in part desirable, as is the demonstraƟon of some dialecƟcal skill. But their moƟves, skills, and general state of soul are, I would suggest, portrayed as ambivalent or mixed, as is suggested in the ironic tone of Socrates’s statement that, “there must indeed be a touch of the god-like in your disposiƟon if you are not convinced that injusƟce is preferable to jusƟce though you can plead its case in such fashion” (368b). Thus when Plato in the following passage has Adeimantus refer to “certain young men,” the passage may with at least some dramaƟc irony in this case, refer to Glaucon and Adeimantus themselves: What, Socrates, do we suppose is the eﬀect of all such sayings about the esteem in which men and gods hold virtue and vice upon the souls that hear them, the souls of young men who are quick-wiƩed and capable of ﬂiƫng, as it were, from one expression of opinion to another and inferring from them all the character and the path whereby a man would lead the best life? Such a youth would most likely put to himself the quesƟon Pindar asks, ‘Is it by jusƟce or by crooked deceit that I the higher tower shall scale and so live my life out in fenced and guarded security? (368e) As for Adeimantus, as disƟnguished from Glaucon, he is concerned to elaborate the “reasoning and the language” (more about this below) and especially the “kind of language about jusƟce and injusƟce employed by both laymen and poets,” about the reputaƟon of each, and about the possible virtues of seeming, that is to say, appearing, as opposed to being just, thus the rhetoric of injusƟce. As for his reasoning, it consists for the most part in a rather cynical use of the poets, etc., to build the case for the advantages, again, of seeming, or for the prospect of buying oﬀ the gods with sacriﬁces and rites, should that be necessary, all this skepƟcal pragmaƟsm albeit in the name of describing at second hand what “our

calculaƟng friend will say” (366b). It is relevant here to note that while we are introduced to Glaucon at the beginning of the Republic as in the company of Socrates, having returned from the Piraeus together, we ﬁrst meet Adeimantus in the company of Polemarchus, the iniƟal opposing party both in the ﬁrst encounter on the way and in the discussion at his father’s house (i.e., aŌer Cephalus hands over the argument to him). Note as well that in the (rather signiﬁcant) banter of the opening encounter on the road from Piraeus to town, Polemarchus playfully threatens to force Socrates to their will to come along with them by force of numbers, taunƟng, “But you see how many we are?” It is then Adeimantus who interposes with the suggesƟon that surely Socrates will want to see the “torchlight race this evening on horseback in honor of the Goddess.” This is to say, Adeimantus is a parƟsan of spectacle, in this case physical, in the case of rhetoric, verbal.[4] But there is more evidence to look at concerning the nature of Glaucon and Adeimantus’s request and the problem it poses for the task of the rest of the dialogue, and what we learn about their souls from the language that Plato has them use. What image of their souls is painted? And what is the philosophical point made through the image? Let us now return to a closer examinaƟon of what exactly it is that Adeimantus and Glaucon ask Socrates to do. We will then be able to address ourselves to that ﬁrst and overriding metaphor, that of the City-Soul analogy, and examine its iniƟaƟon in context. First, let us look at Glaucon. He begins, as we have already noted, by asking, ”Socrates, is it your desire to seem to have persuaded us or really to persuade us that it is without excepƟon beƩer to be just than unjust?” (357a). To which Socrates replies, “Really, if the choice rested with me.” But one can only persuade someone of that of which they are capable, both intellectually and morally. Then too, but more importantly, the whole noƟon of the agency of learning is to be considered. Glaucon is asking to be persuaded by Socrates, to be acted upon, in other words. Further, consider the verb that Glaucon uses, peithō, and the use that he puts it to. This verb does indeed mean “to persuade,” but with the primary connotaƟon of “to win over” (So, according to Liddell and ScoƩ, when used in “a bad sense,” “to mislead, over-persuade, cheat”). This is all the more

so with the perfect inﬁniƟve, as is used here—pepeikenai means to have won us over or persuaded us to comply. Again, the choice between “seeming” (dokein) and “really” (aleithōs) or “truly,” applies to having been persuaded “that it is without excepƟon beƩer to be just than unjust,” and not to the “seeming” or “truth” of the argument.[5] The means of this “persuading” is not menƟoned, and, if we take Glaucon at his word here, he would be content to be merely “really persuaded” that it is more desirable to be just than unjust, even if this were not truly the case! Glaucon, above all, is asking to be reassured in his shaken faith. Recall that I have already given him some credit for asking for a reasoned account, and for seƫng up in the following passage a sort of test case for the examinaƟon of jusƟce in itself and its desirability. There is, however, some ambiguity, or lack of clarity, as to what he is asking for and why. Let us further pursue this ambiguity. Let us look again at the passage referred to above. Just before seƫng up his case, or rather represenƟng that of Thrasymachus, Glaucon says that “Thrasymachus seems to me to have given up to you too soon, as if he were a serpent that you had charmed, but I am not yet saƟsﬁed with the proof (apodeixis) that has been oﬀered about jusƟce and injusƟce. For what I desire is to hear what each of them is and what potency and eﬀect it has in and of itself dwelling in the soul, but to dismiss the rewards and consequences” (358b). So far, well and good. Glaucon here is asking for a seƫng forth, a demonstraƟon, or a proof. He says that the apodeixis just given by Socrates to Thrasymachus and the others was not saƟsfying, not saƟsfactory (nor was it in Socrates’s own eyes, as we have noted). But again, what sort of apodeixis does Glaucon have in mind? Part of what he asks for sounds promising, i.e., apparently a request for a reasoned account, an examinaƟon, of “what each of them is.” “Dismissing their rewards and consequences” seems like a good idea. However, as we have noted above, the desire to hear “what potency and eﬀect it [each] has in and of itself dwelling in the soul” seems to contradict this, since surely this is considering a “consequence,” though not of the external, material kind. And how is this eﬀect to be “demonstrated”? Glaucon proposes to restate Thrasymachus’s argument, in the following way. He will, “ﬁrst state what men say is the nature and origin of

jusƟce; secondly, that those who pracƟce it do so reluctantly, regarding it as something necessary and not as a good; and thirdly, that they have plausible grounds for thus acƟng, since certainly the life of the unjust man is far beƩer than that of the just man” (358c). To which he adds immediately, “as they say; though I, Socrates, don’t believe it.” Note that this third step is conceived in terms of the very “rewards and consequences” which Glaucon had just said at 358b we were to dismiss. Granted, he is proposing here to restate Thrasymachus’s argument so that Socrates can refute it to their saƟsfacƟon, by discarding and discounƟng “rewards and consequences” and showing that virtue is its own reward. But exactly how sensiƟve is Glaucon to these “rewards and consequences”? He tells us in the next phrase; “Yet I am disconcerted when my ears are dinned by the arguments of Thrasymachus and innumerable others”—that there are “plausible grounds” for preferring injusƟce. And what do these “arguments” point to? To the “life of the unjust man,” which is “far beƩer than that of the just man”—that is to say, to the image in speech that we are given of such a life. The verb for “disconcerted” here is aporō, he is reduced to confusion—ironically the very verb used so oŌen in connecƟon with that aporia induced by Socrates as a prelude to learning. He then tells us that he has never heard a “defense of jusƟce” as he would like to have heard it. Here, Shorey and Grube both use “prove” by inference from the preceding passage—but the text simply says that up to now he has not heard (akēkoa—perfect middle of akouō) the speech for jusƟce as beƩer (ameinon—beƩer, stronger) than injusƟce as he would like to hear it. He has not heard it in a convincing way, to counteract the others. “But the case for jusƟce, to prove that it is beƩer than injusƟce, I have never yet heard stated by any as I desire to hear it” (358d). However, it is the second, following line that is revealing– that gives what it is exactly that Glaucon wants from Socrates, what he means by an “argument,” or “demonstraƟon,” what it is that he wants Socrates to do for him, or rather to him. “What I desire is to hear an encomium [enkōmiazomenon] on jusƟce in and by itself.” He wishes, then, not a demonstraƟon (apodeixis) in the sense of reasoned argument, but to be convinced, be won over by a convincing speech in praise of jusƟce. Thus he himself will give a demonstraƟon of the manner (tropon) in which he wishes Socrates to speak—by giving, as he says, a speech “in praise of the

life of injusƟce” and asking the same of Socrates. Socrates responds that “Nothing could please me more,” than to hear and speak about such things. But obviously they have rather diﬀerent noƟons of what such a discourse should be. Socrates’s own speech, the Republic itself, is a demonstraƟon, the raƟonal construcƟon in words of the true image of jusƟce, as opposed to an encomium. What is at stake is just the kind of image in words that will serve, and even more so, the kind of image- making. Returning to Adeimantus, we had noted earlier his emphasis on “language,” on the language of the poets, and praise and blame for jusƟce and injusƟce. Now while Adeimantus has been poinƟng out the contradictory nature of what the poets say, or rather that they can be used by either those who praise jusƟce or those who denigrate it, his overall cynical conclusion, in the name of those who praise injusƟce, is that the authority of the poets can be invoked on the side of the advantage of injusƟce, provided that we are careful to use a smoke screen of counterfeit decorum to deceive men, and are ready to bribe the gods with the appropriate propiƟatory sacriﬁces and vows. Needless to say, the aƫtude towards the gods in the laƩer case is rather demeaning. But the whole of the argument is based on the examinaƟon of the possibiliƟes of the unjust gaining advantage under various cynical hypotheses concerning the gods— from the possibility that there are none, to that of their being either uncaring or selﬁsh and/or suscepƟble to inﬂuence. That the gods might love jusƟce more than sacriﬁces is not even considered. And the basis and support for these hypotheses is again no more than a cynical appeal to authority, primarily of the poets. Thus Adeimantus concludes, “If we combine this with a counterfeit decorum we shall prosper to our heart’s desire, with gods and men, in life and death, as the words of the mulƟtude and of men of the highest authority declare” (366b). In the end, Adeimantus, like Glaucon, says that such speeches are such as “Thrasymachus and haply another might say in pleas against jusƟce and for injusƟce” but that in his view they are “inverƟng their true potencies.” And perhaps one might think it true that he has “ . . . no reason to hide anything from you [and] I am laying myself out to the utmost on the theory, because I wish to hear its refutaƟon from you” (267b). One wonders, however, which other Adeimantus has in mind above?

Let us look at a few indicaƟons that Adeimantus is in fact, in part, speaking for himself, voicing his own doubts just as Glaucon had, while denying vehemently that such is the case. Adeimantus returns to the theme that jusƟce has never been defended in its own right. But always, among “you self-styled advocates of jusƟce,” including “the men of the present day,” thus including Socrates himself it would seem, “not one has ever censured injusƟce or commended jusƟce otherwise than in respect of the repute, the honors, the giŌs that accrue from each . . . neither in poetry or prose . . . For if you had all spoken in this way [that is, giving an explanaƟon of what each is in itself, etc.] . . . from the beginning and from our youth up had sought to convince us, we should not now be guarding against one another’s injusƟce, but each would be his own best guardian” (367a). Here Adeimantus is again clearly speaking for himself, and yet it is at this point that he concludes as we have quoted above, that “this, Socrates, and perhaps even more than this, Thrasymachus and haply another might say . . . ” Once again, I am not casƟng doubt on the ulƟmate sincerity of Adeimantus’s desire to see jusƟce vindicated. But rather, that this not so veiled hide-and-seek points to an ambivalence in his senƟments, and an even stronger one than in the case of Glaucon. It is almost as if while Glaucon is asking to be saved from the temptaƟons of both injusƟce’s “beneﬁts” and from Thrasymachus’s rhetoric, Adeimantus (who had, I repeat, arrived with Polemarchus) is rather much more in the middle—and in his concern for “language” and liberal if cynical use of the poets, reveals himself as much closer to Thrasymachus’s camp; his aƫtude is, "Show me." He needs to be convinced, persuaded in the sense of won over. One might even go so far as to say that he himself is an example of someone who puts on the appearance of being a ﬁrm friend of jusƟce, when this is not quite the case. He would then be hiding behind two masks—the one that he tells us he is puƫng on in order to beƩer present Glaucon’s argument/request, which is in turn Thrasymachus’s posiƟon, and a second, which masks his own ambivalence. Thus while he may indeed, as he says, “wish to hear its refutaƟon” from Socrates it is not quite the case that he has “no reason to hide anything from [him].” Finally, we return to the quesƟon of just what, again, it is that he is requesƟng in the way of a refutaƟon. Adeimantus concludes: “Do not then,

I repeat, merely prove to us in argument the superiority of jusƟce to injusƟce, but show us what it is that each inherently does to its possessor —whether he does or does not escape the eyes of gods and men— whereby the one is good and the other is evil” (367e). We ﬁnd that Adeimantus, like Glaucon, refers both to proof that jusƟce is superior and to showing of the eﬀect that jusƟce and injusƟce has on the soul. But it is apparent that what Adeimantus means by “to show what each does” is once again to give a speech that adequately praises the just man. In the comments just preceding his concluding request, the verb used several Ɵmes is epaineō, to praise, paralleling Glaucon’s request for an “encomium.” “This is what I would have you praise about jusƟce—the beneﬁt which it and the harm which injusƟce inherently works upon it possessor. But the rewards and honors that depend on opinion, leave others to praise” (367d). From the way that his concluding request at 367e is phrased—“Do not merely (mēmonon) prove to us in argument . . . ” it is clearly this “praise” that he sees as the most important task, perhaps even more so than Glaucon. Once again, but more emphaƟcally, Adeimantus repeats the two part request that Glaucon had made, for a proof that jusƟce is superior to injusƟce (a demonstraƟon in words) and showing what jusƟce and injusƟce do respecƟvely to those that possess it (that have it in their souls) i.e., such that we can say that the one is a good and the other is an evil. Yet this clarity is rendered somewhat paradoxical by the method which he favors for the second of these tasks, that of “praise.” But this should not surprise us, since in his own speeches it is this very predilecƟon for the methods of rhetoric that we have seen. Adeimantus appears to scorn “opinion” and “reputaƟon,” and ask that these be discarded as being merely producƟve of “rewards and honors” and thus external to the consideraƟon of jusƟce and injusƟce in themselves. We are rather to consider “goods that are producƟve by their very nature and not by opinion” (367d). Thus Adeimantus seems to be asking to really know what each is. Yet clearly the method of praise, as we have noted in the earlier discussion concerning Glaucon, is allied to the producƟon (reproducing) of opinion, not to that of knowledge.[6] In the end, Adeimantus has the clearer, if limited, noƟon of the diﬀerence between erisƟc rhetoric and dialecƟc, but he sƟll prefers the

former. Both of them, then, are in actuality asking Socrates not to examine jusƟce but to defend it, to praise it in a convincing or moving way, though the one, I suggest, with more sincerity than the other.[7] Their aƫtude, and their request, is appropriate to the auxiliary class of the ideal city, those who defend the city based not on knowledge but opinion, habituaƟon, or training.[8] The task and goal, to understand jusƟce in itself as a prerequisite to deciding whether or not it is more desirable than injusƟce, is indeed SocraƟc, but the method suggested is emphaƟcally not so, and is indeed in contradicƟon to it. Further, in spite of the apparent separaƟon or disƟncƟon between proof of superiority in itself and the showing of eﬀect, in the end, both are required as a means of demonstraƟon, and they cannot, as Adeimantus apparently thinks, be separated (cf.367e). Moreover, myth and metaphor or image and image-making (a part of showing) will provide the necessary link between a philosophical and a certain form of rhetorical truth.[9] THE CITY/SOUL ANALOGY: FINDING JUSTICE Part of coming to know what jusƟce in itself is, is coming to know the disƟncƟon between knowledge and opinion, and their relaƟon to the soul —that is, one must not only know that jusƟce is best, but also know that one knows, and not merely opines. It is thus that an examinaƟon of the just life and of jusƟce itself, must entail an examinaƟon of knowledge itself, and of the knower and the known, hence the necessity of the middle books of the Republic. But clearly such disƟncƟons are not available to Glaucon and Adeimantus, as revealed in the very nature of their request. To what extent they can be moved forwards towards comprehension of it remains to be seen. Let us not forget, however, that the Republic exists not only for them but for the reader as well—and their limitaƟons may not be ours. Their limitaƟons may serve expressly to show us the way beyond them.[10] The nature of the arguments, and of the means of persuasion may be mulƟple, reﬂecƟng the various persons addressed. It is to the diﬀerence between Socrates’s means and that of Thrasymachus that we now turn. The discussion has already been begun in the above, but only in its negaƟve aspect—i.e., we have examined Glaucon and Adeimantus, their

expectaƟons, needs and suscepƟbiliƟes as the context within which the Republic unfolds. What then is the diﬀerence between the erisƟc of a Thrasymachus and the methods employed in the Republic?[11] Appropriately enough, this disƟncƟon is explicitly discussed (at 454ﬀ) not too long aŌer the moment when Polemarchus intervenes at the beginning of Book V. This problem, or task, brings us back to the issue of the role of imagery in the diﬀerence between erisƟc and dialecƟc. Having completed the construcƟon of the city that is to serve as the image of the soul writ large, Socrates says that “This then is the kind of city and government which I call good and right [orthos], and so too this kind of man. And if indeed [eiper] this is the right kind, then the others are bad and wrong, both in the management of the ciƟes and the manner of life of the individual soul. Their badness is of four kinds” (449a).[12] Socrates is about to conƟnue, to discuss these, when the interlocutors then raise their objecƟon. Had Socrates been allowed to conƟnue, the project was to examine in detail the forms of bad, evil or sick souls by conƟnuing the soul-city analogy and examining the consƟtuƟons that correspond to them. The purpose is to see the kinds of evil writ large and at work, unjust acts to be seen producing (praƩein) injusƟce,[13] as unhealthy things produce illness, and thus we would “see more clearly” that jusƟce is more proﬁtable than injusƟce. The interrupƟon, at a turning point in the dialogue, is iniƟated by Polemarchus, who is “siƫng a liƩle further away,” and who “extended his hand and took hold of [Adeimantus’s] cloak from above at the shoulder.” This dramaƟc detail echoes the very beginning of the Republic, where it is Polemarchus’s slave who runs ahead and “caught hold of [Socrates’s] cloak from behind,” (327b) and Polemarchus’s joking threat of force: “Do you see how many we are? . . . You must either be stronger than we are, or you must stay here.” And Socrates’s response there: “Is there not another alternaƟve, said I, namely that we may persuade you to let us go?” But Polemarchus replies, “Could you persuade men who do not listen?” Have they been listening? Are they going to listen now? The objecƟon raised regards the ostensible lack of completeness of the model—Socrates had not detailed the manner in which women and children would live. It had been implied that “the possessions of friends [the ciƟzens] will be in common” (423e). Socrates

assents—then what of women and children? Will they too be held in common, and what are the “details”? But it is clear from the manner in which this request is introduced that their intenƟon and hope is to catch Socrates up, to ﬁnd something objecƟonable in his ideal city. Polemarchus —“Shall we let him oﬀ, then. . . . ” Adeimantus—“Don’t then pass over the one [the manner] that you have in mind. For we have been lying in wait for you.” Rather than a mere request for more detail it is a just faintly disguised aƩack. One in which Thrasymachus, who we must note has remained silent unƟl this point, happily joins in, adding his support. It will iniƟate the discussion of the three waves of paradox concerning the possibility of such a city, as contrasted to its mere desirability, and serves as the transiƟon to the so-called digression of the middle books. What the interlocutors raise is the specter—given that the guardians are to have “all things in common”—of common wives and children. They ask that Socrates “say something both of the procreaƟon of children and their bringing up,” hoping to be able to sully the reputaƟon of the city, and thus hold Socrates and his city up to ridicule. This will issue in the challenge as to the possibility of such a city, but these interlocutors, as contrasted to Glaucon, are more interested in seeing how well Socrates can hold up in the baƩle of words than in the actual issue of possibility. Thus they are concerned to ﬁnd a ﬂaw in the “city in words” which would prevent its actualizaƟon were such a city to be aƩempted. And it would be suﬃcient for this that the community at large be anƟcipated to hold the opinion that the community of women, etc. would be scandalous etc. Socrates would then have lost! Thus, as we shall see in more detail, the demand for a further discussion is ﬂawed in several ways. First, because possibility in the external poliƟcal world is of minor importance as compared to its funcƟon and or realizaƟon a) in words as model b) in the city within the soul. Second, because the moƟve for the discussion of possibility is an erisƟc one, victory. And ﬁnally, because the means of the challenge itself, relying as it does on the imagined emoƟon and opinions of the community is at this point concerned only about possibility as disƟnct from rightness. Thus it is highly ironic that Adeimantus should stress that “ . . . this word ‘right’ like other things, requires deﬁning as to the way and manner of such a community. There may be many ways” (449c). As Adeimantus uses it, we

are only required to look at the “ways,” to decide which of the many is the right one—thus the request for a more detailed look at Socrates’s city. But how will we evaluate it, with what will we measure its rightness? Right can only mean here convenƟonally acceptable or possible. The sentence itself contains the ambiguity; it begins by saying that what needs deﬁning is “this word ‘right’” (orthos—correct) and ends by focusing on the types of community, etc. But it is the former, the deﬁning of “right,” which is needed, i.e., the principle by which the right way can be measured. Again, Adeimantus says that “We think that the right or wrong management of this makes a great diﬀerence, all the diﬀerence in the world” (449d). Yet the measure of rightness or wrongness is not to be examined—or rather, the measure is to be the possibility, as determined by the unexamined moral response of the community. Glaucon’s response is easily disƟnguishable from that of the others, though he himself believes, apparently, that they are all friendly listeners; “Do not shrink, for your hearers will not be inconsiderate nor distrusƞul nor hosƟle” (450d). Glaucon is good-natured (in more senses than one) and somewhat blind, apparently, to the natures of others. He is all too willing to be led, and thus poses quite another problem for Socrates. For as Socrates says, he is wary lest he “drag my friends with me in maƩers where it most imports not to stumble, and not to mislead opinion about the honorable, the good, and the just,” and he avers that he fears “to speak when one doubts oneself and is seeking while he talks, as I am doing.” That is, that he will be speaking in his reply not with knowledge, where there would be “safety and boldness.” But this cannot apply to the later parts of the digression, those concerning precisely the nature of knowledge and reality. There, Socrates speaks with certainty, if cauƟously. Rather, it is applicable here, where their quesƟons concerning the supposed possibility of the “city that is good and right” force Socrates to lead Glaucon through the perils of the skepƟcism that might be induced by doubts about the possibility of the city. Socrates, then, is “unsure” about how successfully and with what means he can reassure Glaucon, successfully meet the objecƟons of the others, and not be reduced to the level of conﬂict that has its realm in opinion, that of erisƟc dispute. And so, instead of a) objecƟng to the analogy itself, or the method, or b) examining the relaƟve proﬁt or disadvantage of jusƟce versus injusƟce, they insist rather that

Socrates further elaborate the “consƟtuƟon” of the just polity, at the point at which they consider it to be the most vulnerable—aƩacking at the level of literal possibility, they thus remain at that level of discourse. They should, or could, object that the hypothesis, the city-soul analogy, is in need of a ground. In actual fact, at best, they can be said to object to the hypothesis by asking that its possibility be shown, i.e., to ground the hypothesis empirically. But what needs to be done is to ground it epistemologically and ontologically. The good city is developed by the use of the principle that each thing, person, quality, part funcƟons best when it pursues its own funcƟon and that alone—that when it does so, it is most itself, and most achieves both its own excellence and contribuƟon to that of which it is a part. But this noƟon was never thoroughly examined; its use rested on an early equivocaƟon concerning the term good, where good at or for was equated with good in itself. There are then, two noƟons which have been operaƟng as hypotheses, that of idenƟty of funcƟon and that of the best, or of excellence (of nature). These can be expressed as two principles that have been used to construct the city and guide the discussion. The one is what one might call existenƟal or concrete idenƟty—this is the supposiƟon that a thing has an essence or funcƟon that can be isolated. The other principle is that excellence or good in some sense is achieved when a thing pursues, and is limited to, the end contained in its proper idenƟty. The two coalesce in the principle that the excellence of the city is achieved by each part pursuing well its proper funcƟon. But they are separable, and each is in need of a ground. In parƟcular, the noƟon of what is best needs qualiﬁcaƟon and explanaƟon since the desiring and spirited parts of the soul, if leŌ to pursue their own natural ends know no limits and are liable to excess, they are not self- limiƟng. The principle of the perfecƟon of idenƟty of funcƟon will not suﬃce, and is certainly not self-jusƟfying. (The analogy with health rests on acceptance of an explicaƟon of the natural relaƟon ruler-ruled at 444c-e.)[14] Thus while from a dramaƟc point of view Socrates is interrupted when he was about to go on and describe the “four forms of badness,” for Plato and for the perspicacious reader the hypotheƟcal nature of the discussion up unƟl this point is in need of at least the outline of the higher level that would ground these principles.

This then is the necessity of the so-called digression. Books II-V (to about 475e) consƟtute the movement from hypothesis to construcƟon, and the aƩempt with respect to Glaucon at both inculcaƟng the acceptance of the principles and exercising him in the method. Books VI and VII aƩempt an outline of the ground for the two concepts employed in the principles and an argument for their reality. (The full and adequate argument for their reality would be accessible only through the actual educaƟon proposed for the philosopher.) As the conversaƟon picks up again, Socrates begins with the noƟon that the educaƟon (music and gymnasƟc) of men and women would have to be the same if, as a community of friends having “all things in common,” the women are to share in the watchdog/guardian funcƟon. Since this would be a great change in the established custom, it would likely provoke the mockery and scorn of the many, but he urges Glaucon, “Since we have set out to speak our minds, we must not fear all the jibes with which the wits would greet such a revoluƟon, and to hold fast to that which . . . reason revealed to be the best.” Thus Glaucon is being educated, as is said of the guardians, as to the proper objects of fear, or rather what is worthy of fear and what is not—i.e., that he must not fear ridicule for something which reason has led him to, and that “he talks idly who deems anything else ridiculous but evil, and who tries to raise a laugh by looking to any other paƩern or absurdity than that of folly and wrong or sets up any other standard of the beauƟful as a mark for his seriousness than the good” (425d). These are remarks that are clearly made with those others present in mind. (Note here the emphasis on “looking to . . . ” “paƩern,” “standard of the beauƟful . . . ” regarding the noƟon of image, to be discussed in the following; as well, the contrast with the appearance of physical absurdity presented by women in the palaestra, etc.) But Glaucon had, in fact, spoken too soon in assigning to women the same funcƟon as men— Socrates had even suggested in passing that perhaps they would be too busy childbearing and raising. Glaucon had forged ahead by restaƟng the accepted plaƟtude that since they are a city of friends, they “have all things in common,” and an apparent contradicƟon has been produced, as follows. The supposed contradicƟon in the argument (435b-c) is that Socrates had taken as his beginning and foundaƟon of the city that “each one ought to mind as his own business the one thing for which he was ﬁƩed by nature,”

he cannot deny that there is “by nature a great diﬀerence between men and women,” who then should have a diﬀerence of funcƟon. But he has just aﬃrmed that the “females of watchdogs” ought to “join in guarding what the males guard . . . ” Note that while the original interrupƟon or objecƟon that had begun Book V is the acƟon of others, here it is internalized, so to speak, so that the argument may be given its due. “Shall we then conduct the debate with ourselves on behalf of those others so that the case of the other side may not be taken as defenseless and go by default?” (453a) But giving the argument its due will mean giving Glaucon a chance to reassess the beginnings or foundaƟon of the argument (as well as its method) a task that is characterisƟc of philosophy. And so, as contrasted to erisƟc, Socrates must make him backtrack to examine the basis of an idenƟty of funcƟon, and consequent idenƟty of educaƟon—namely, idenƟty of nature. Socrates says: We must throw open the debate to anyone who wishes either in jest or earnest to raise the quesƟon whether female human nature is capable of sharing with the male all tasks or none at all. . . Would not this be that best beginning which naturally and proverbially lead to the best end?” (453a) It is then to these proposals concerning equality of the mode of educaƟon in parƟcular that he is returning, and for the purpose of making a beƩer beginning, or rather that Glaucon should have the experience of making a beƩer beginning. And further, for the reader to note the diﬀerence between the two beginnings, will be crucial to understanding the transiƟon to the middle books. The ﬁrst beginning, at 451d, was based on a return to the early analogy of the guardian with a watchdog (a rather comic one at the Ɵme, involving philosophical dogs possessed of wisdom). Extending the analogy, Socrates suggests that they “preserve the analogy, then, and assign them a generaƟon and breeding answering to it. Do we expect the females of watchdogs to join in guarding what the males guard and to hunt with them . . . ?” Such an analogy or image is inadequate not simply for its humorousness—Glaucon takes it rather seriously—but the very physicality of its imagery (generaƟon, etc.) is crucial to its

shortcoming. What needs to be shown, and is the basis of the second discussion, is that men and women may have the same natures with respect to the funcƟon of guardian. That Glaucon had replied so readily with his formula “they have all things in common” is of a piece with his insensiƟvity to the inadequacy of the imagery and the argument. The second beginning starts with the quesƟon “whether female human nature is capable of sharing with the male all tasks or none at all, or some but not others. . . .” That is, Glaucon must start to make disƟncƟons, and ﬁnd a basis for assigning women to one category or another. The ensuing discussion is an analysis of tasks and requisite capaciƟes, and just how women are suited to one or another. But just as the physical nature of the dog analogy was limited or misleading, so here Socrates points to the need to disƟnguish between a diﬀerence in physical nature between men and women and a general sameness of their nature with respect to the requirements for guardians, or, more generally sameness of structure and capaciƟes of soul. Yet Socrates is careful not to argue that empirically they are actually enƟrely the same (there is much jockeying with the noƟon of men being on the whole more giŌed), but rather, what is more important, that what Glaucon must learn is to be able to disƟnguish diﬀerence and sameness of nature with respect to idenƟty of quality or funcƟon, where and when such does exist. “We did not then posit likeness and diﬀerence of nature in any and every sense, but were paying heed solely to the kind of diversity and homogeneity that was perƟnent to the pursuits themselves? We meant, for example, that a man and a woman who have a physician’s mind have the same nature” (454c). That this concept is a diﬃculty for him is evident from the comment Glaucon makes when Socrates has ﬁnished paraphrasing his now silent adversaries. The paraphrased objecƟon is once again, that, according to his own principle of a diﬀerence of funcƟon accorded to a diﬀerence of nature, and men and women being so manifestly diﬀerent in nature, they cannot be rightly assigned the same funcƟon. Socrates then asks Glaucon “Can you surprise me with an answer to that quesƟon?” (about relevant sameness and diﬀerence). To which Glaucon replies, “Not easily on this sudden challenge, but I will and do beg you to lend your voice to the plea in our behalf, whatever it may be.” Socrates adds, “These and many similar diﬃculƟes I foresaw and feared.” Again, what is crucial here, is not the

quesƟon of whether men and women are actually equal, or whether it is actually possible that they will in fact perform the same funcƟon of guardian in the city, etc., but rather the principle that it is the relevant quality or capacity that determines the funcƟon, and that sameness and diﬀerence of nature are determined by this and not by physical characterisƟcs. Thus sameness of nature is an expression of, or is ulƟmately equivalent to, idenƟty of quality or essence not of existence.[15] Secondly, in the movement of the dialogue, it is at this point that Glaucon, and the reader, are iniƟally brought to the beginning of a clariﬁcaƟon of the ontology that is its basis.[16] For Glaucon, what has been “demonstrated” is that the proposed city is “possible,” but this has been done by shiŌing the argument from the recepƟon such features as the community of women and children would get, the pracƟcal poliƟcal possibility, to the natural possibility, i.e., that such an arrangement would not be contrary to nature.[17] Secondly, the nature of nature has been redeﬁned so as to connote not physical sameness but sameness of the non-visible capacity of our understanding. Thirdly, the actual possession of the same qualiƟes (as also the degree of sameness) is formulated as (or relegated to) the hypotheƟcal. But such judgments, it would appear, are never so certain as the idenƟty of the concepts themselves. We note in this connecƟon that at the end of Book V, and before the discussion of the Divided Line, Cave etc. the reality of the soul and parƟcularly its structure and parts is expressly deﬁned in terms of funcƟons or capaciƟes and processes corresponding to degrees of knowledge and of reality.[18] Chapter two, to follow, is expressly devoted to the relaƟon between capaciƟes (dunameis) and their objects, and their role in the relaƟon of discourse and image-making. Let us now backtrack a bit and see just how jusƟce was found. Now prior to proceeding to the obstacle of the “third wave,” concerning the possibility of the ideal city constructed in words, Socrates reminds us of the iniƟal and sƟll unconcluded object of the search. “The ﬁrst thing to recall, then, is that it was the inquiry into the nature of jusƟce and injusƟce that brought us to this pass. . . . if we do discover what jusƟce is . . . ” (472b) Then, at 472e, Socrates likens the image of jusƟce that they have created to the painter’s beauƟful portrait of a man. Neither a painted portrait nor

the “city in words” would be judged the less beauƟful, the less well spoken, were that of which it is an image not to exist, or be possible as it is depicted. Glaucon, of course, already has a noƟon of what is meant by well spoken. Since Socrates elsewhere derides painƟng as an art (597d), in fact denies that strictly speaking it is an art at all, how are we to understand the use of this metaphor here and at several other points, as well as the constant use of vocabulary related to seeing, looking, the good use of the eyes, etc.? What is, exactly, “portraying a paƩern”? True, the painƟng is in words, but how do the images in the Republic, parƟcularly the “paƩern” of the just city, diﬀer in kind from those of Thrasymachus etc.? We are closer to being able to disƟnguish, in other words, between the imagery of dialecƟc and that of erisƟc. Near the close of Book IV the parts of the city had been found to be congruent with those of the soul, and the virtues of the former have been found in the laƩer. Had this not been so, we were to have returned with whatever concepƟon of jusƟce we had found at the level of the soul to compare it to the previous one at the level of the city and, in the manner of rubbing two sƟcks together, somehow the truth about jusƟce would shine forth. But this method, of comparison and contrast, has somehow not turned out to be necessary. Socrates: Finished, then, is our dream and perfected—the surmise we spoke of, that by Providence [kata theon] at the very beginning of our foundaƟon of the state, we chanced to hit upon [kinduneumenon] the original principle and a sort of type of jusƟce. Glaucon: Most assuredly. Socrates: It really was, it seems, Glaucon, which is why it helps, a sort of adumbraƟon [eidōlon, an image] of jusƟce [dikaiosunēs] this principle that it is right for the cobbler to cobble and occupy himself with nothing else, and the carpenter to pracƟce carpentry, and similarly all others. But the truth of the maƩer was, as it seems, that jusƟce is indeed something of this kind, yet not in regard to doing one’s business externally, but with regard to that which is within and in the true sense concerns oneself. (443b-d)

The guiding providenƟal hand was of course not some god, but Socrates. We did not chance to hit upon a type of jusƟce that would be present both in the city and the individual. Let me sketch in broad strokes how this was done. A geneƟc/historical account is oﬀered for the origin of the character of the larger in the smaller, but this is only to assuage the literal minded. The procedure was, in fact, to begin with the city as it exists, the “fevered” city, and to purify it to achieve the good city. But how was this puriﬁcaƟon carried out? Socrates starts with the tradiƟonal virtues and, in applicaƟon to the city, signiﬁcantly redeﬁnes each of them in just such a way that while they resemble somewhat the tradiƟonal virtues (and are hence easily accepted by the interlocutors) they are in actuality the virtues of the individual soul as Socrates conceives it. The transformaƟon of the virtues is as follows: Wisdom Wisdom (sophia) tradiƟonally would be taken to be knowledge connected with craŌsmanship, or a theoreƟcal knowledge (phronēsis). As poliƟcal wisdom it would be the craŌ of ruling the city (as it is for Thrasymachus). But poliƟcal wisdom here is speciﬁcally shaped to underwrite stability and unity, and opposiƟon to pointless change. The stress is parƟcularly on city preserving and exemplifying the harmonious unity out of many (422e-424b). Unlike a poliƟcal technē, it is given a speciﬁc telos. It is sound judgement about legislaƟon that will “maintain good relaƟons both internally and with other ciƟes” and secure the true happiness of each element by direcƟng each member to the one task for which he is suited (through legislaƟon and educaƟon). The poliƟcal conservaƟsm is mandated by the raƟonality of the organizaƟon of the whole. The virtue of wisdom is here rule over those who cannot rule themselves (a rule that is administered through legislaƟon and educaƟon). Examples of the non-raƟonal abuse of poliƟcal power and other excesses are included for contrast. The stress on the achieving and preserving of unity, and idenƟty of natural funcƟon, is autocraƟc, but not totalitarian if one takes this not as a poliƟcal prescripƟon but suitable when transcribed

to the rule of the soul. (There are also speciﬁc features of the ideal city that are democraƟc, but as this is not the issue here I pass over that debate.) Courage Courage (andreia) convenƟonally would mean a character disposiƟon, steadfastness in the face of danger, etc. The soldier guardians or auxiliaries are to protect the city from its enemies without and within. But the descripƟon of the dangers changes this virtue into something of another sort. Here (429b-c) the auxiliaries are to be educated in, and have as their deﬁning task, to “preserve [the city’s] beliefs about things to be feared” as taught them by the guardians and the laws. And their enemies—from whose aƩack they are to preserve the beneﬁcial beliefs “inculcated by the law through one’s educaƟon as to what things and what kinds of things are to be feared,” and against which they are to be steadfast, like dyed wool— are “pleasure and pain, fear and desire.” Courage, rather than an aggressive acƟon (cf. Laches 178a-184; 199c, d, e) is “a kind of preservaƟon.” And the most potent of these dangers, which to this moral dye is one that is “much more potent than any soda or soap or powder,” is “pleasure.” That this is a redeﬁniƟon of bravery or courage is stressed by Socrates concluding, “I call and deﬁne [this] as courage, unless you say otherwise.” And “accept also that it is civic courage (poliƟkēn) and your acceptance will be sound. We shall discuss the subject more fully some other Ɵme, if you want to . . . ” (430c). Clearly by this point this courage is not at all civic courage in the normal sense of the word. Here, even more than with wisdom, the virtue of the city has been tailored to exemplify the principles that will suit the soul and to already express in a working model the ontological claim for “what is to be feared” and what not. (This is reiterated in Book X, and examined in my analysis of the Phaedo.) Moderation ModeraƟon or temperance (sōphrosunē). The tradiƟonal Greek concept is diﬃcult to deﬁne, covering a variety of traits or behaviors. It obviously has something to do with a self-eﬀacing restraint in various

contexts. If Charmides is represenƟng the tradiƟonal view, it is “doing all things orderly and quietly . . . temperance is a kind of quietness” (Charm. 159b, JoweƩ transl.). Not that this is at all an adequate deﬁniƟon, as Socrates’s elenchus there quickly shows. But it does, perhaps for that very reason, capture something of just that aspect which the redeﬁniƟon will go beyond. The change here consists of two aspects. First, the tradiƟonal virtue is a descripƟon of the behavior of the single individual, while the SocraƟc version immediately divides the individual into ruler and ruled: “the expression seems to want to indicate that in the soul of the man himself there is a beƩer and a worse part,” (431a) and one in which a disposiƟon of character is replaced by an acƟvity—passions “directed by reasoning with intelligence and right belief.” Second, and even more of a change, moderaƟon is a step towards jusƟce in that it too is a virtue “spread through the whole . . . both in the city and in each individual.” And ﬁnally, this is a diﬀusion of the inﬂuence or rule of reason, in the agreement of each part “as to who should rule.” The result then is that the moderaƟon that before was only a certain quiet orderliness has now quickly become something acƟve that “resembles a kind of harmony” or concord. In this last descripƟon, it is not merely a disposiƟon but an acƟve virtue that reﬂects a belief or opinion of the parƟcipants. For all three virtues, wisdom, courage, moderaƟon, there has been a transformaƟon of their content and of their form, each has become the exercise of a kind of belief. This transformaƟon has prepared the way for the image of this parƟcular virtuous city to resemble that of the virtuous soul as no poliƟcal model city would, and in a way parƟcular to the principles that will give the form or image to jusƟce that Socrates wishes to represent.[19] Following the generaƟon of the virtues of the city, the descripƟon of the virtues of the soul (436-444) is arrived at by beginning with human capaciƟes as inferred from behaviors, by classifying the laƩer into three groups and then applying the principle of idenƟty of funcƟon to each, and to the whole, such that each is a disƟnguishable part of a whole or unity, and the dedicaƟon of each part to its funcƟon and the harmony of the whole is the sought for jusƟce. But this descripƟon of the soul’s virtues had already been implanted in the city that preceded it. Since the larger,

the city, has in fact been modeled with regard to the smaller, it is no wonder that there is a congruence, nor that jusƟce turns out to be the same in each. That the number of parts is the same is solely a consequence of insisƟng, at the point of the pairing of analogous parts, on the noƟon of consistently applying the principle of idenƟty, that is, that it is more intelligible and hence more real to assign a separate part to each form of behavior, and of course arbitrarily limiƟng the number to four virtues and three parts in both cases.[20] Thus the progression of the dialogue itself at this point, the order of presentaƟon, is the reverse of the order of importance, and of the knowledge of the arƟst painƟng the city in words. And the forming of each of these models, that of the city and that of the individual soul, is dependent on knowledge of the principles that form them, and notably of jusƟce, the very thing sought. The noƟon of each thing having and preserving its own task and hence idenƟty, and yet of each being harmonized with, subservient to, the unity of the whole, and that both of these are best, all funcƟon as principles, as hypotheses, with which the two models are given form. In sum, it is the Idea of jusƟce that serves as, which funcƟons as, the fundamental hypothesis which forms the two models. Or rather, it is a certain ontology that takes the form, in the Republic, of a hypothesis as to the nature of jusƟce. In the ﬁrst ﬁve books of the Republic it funcƟons as a hypothesis for the construcƟon of the two models which give it concrete, if ideal, form. This construcƟon corresponds to the descent from hypothesis to image in the Divided Line. In the chapters on the dynamic of the Line and Cave I will trace the parallel of the meaning, structure, and dynamic moƟon of the Line and Cave. We return now to the passage at 443 quoted directly above. In what sense, we ask again, has the original principle of jusƟce been “chanced upon”? Clearly it is Glaucon (and Adeimantus) who have been handed the principle, have “chanced upon it.” In what sense could they be said to actually know it? Recall that the original worry that Socrates raises at the end of Book I was that they had let the original quesƟon as to the nature of jusƟce pass, and had been discussing whether it was vice and ignorance or virtue and wisdom. What they can be said to know, or to have experienced at this point, is the embodiment of the principle in models or images of the

good city and the good soul, the principle in acƟon, so to speak. But do they know the principle, or jusƟce itself, that is to say as other than a hypothesis? The answer, clearly, is no. For only were they to pass by the “longer way” and the higher educaƟon would this be the case. Nor will the middle books provide that, since whatever they do provide they are not that educaƟon or that vision itself. Note that in the passage under consideraƟon it is because of the ostensible chance nature of the way jusƟce has been found that Socrates says that that “is why it really helps, a sort of adumbraƟon of jusƟce, this principle. . . . ” Shorey’s word “adumbraƟon” stands for the Greek eidōlon, the standard word for an image, a shape, an image in the mind, or a portrait. This is to be disƟnguished from eidos, both starƟng from the same root; it is the laƩer that is used for the noƟon of kind, and for the Forms or Ideas. But what is the eidōlon here? Not the images of the soul and city that are developed, though the word certainly could be used of them as well, but the word is applied here to the principle itself. The principle is itself an image of jusƟce, or, I would suggest, is jusƟce expressed as a hypothesis or complex of hypotheses (see above) with which to form those images which are the models for the life worth living. But if such eidōla[21] can be principles as hypotheses, then Glaucon’s soul can be formed by the principles via acceptance of the images that are formed on their basis—as is the case at the end of Book IV, the eﬀect of philosophical rhetoric—Socrates’s elaboraƟon of the respecƟve virtues of the good city and soul. Note that the true home of the living principle, the principle actually at work, as an image of jusƟce, is within the individual soul, for as Socrates adds, jusƟce is indeed something of this kind, [that is to say, to ta heautou praƩein] yet not in regard to doing one’s own business externally, but with regard to that which is within and in the true sense concerns oneself and the things of one’s self—it means that a man must not suﬀer the principles in his soul to do each the work of some other . . . (443d) It is only aŌer and as a consequence of the achieved harmony of these parts, aŌer “having linked and bound all three together and made of himself a unit, one man instead of many, self-controlled and in unison,

[that] he should then and then only turn to pracƟce, if he ﬁnd ought to do either in the geƫng of wealth or the tendance of the body or it may be in poliƟcal acƟon.” And even then, such acƟons are treated here not as ends but as means: “ . . . believing and naming the just and honorable acƟon to be that which preserves and helps to produce this condiƟon of soul, and wisdom, the science that presides over such conduct . . . ” (443e). We note also that wisdom seems to be limited here to the pracƟce of virtue, in accord with belief in the principle that forges this unity of the soul, and belief in that unity itself, as being the image of jusƟce. How then does such a noƟon of image relate to the disƟncƟon between erisƟc and dialecƟc, or philosophical rhetoric? ErisƟc is described at 454a as the making of “purely verbal disƟncƟons” reﬂecƟng and resulƟng from an “inability to apply the proper divisions and disƟncƟons to the subject under consideraƟon.” One ends up then “confusing wrangling with arguing.” In the case of Thrasymachus, since the end is not truth but power or victory, the moƟve itself may be described as an erisƟc one: to win or control the argument by the manipulaƟon of merely verbal disƟncƟons, either in one’s own argument, or by producing ostensible contradicƟons in the opponent’s arguments, is suﬃcient. The former is exempliﬁed by Thrasymachus’s shiŌing, in fact reversing, of the terms of his argument in Book I with regard to jusƟce being the advantage of the stronger, in order to maintain his thesis—arguing ﬁrst that jusƟce is the word of the ruler, and then that it is the convenƟonal virtue (and fear) of the ruled, so that jusƟce shiŌs from ruler to ruled but advantage remains always with the stronger. The producƟon of contradicƟon in the argument of one’s opponent, is seen in the paraphrased objecƟon that Socrates produces with regard to the argument concerning female guardians, an ironical SocraƟc image of erisƟc. Thus even when in this case the moƟve itself is not an erisƟc one, one may ﬁnd oneself “slipping unawares into contenƟousness,” “even against their wills,” as Socrates avows they (Glaucon and himself) have done. This is aƩributed to “the power of the art of contradicƟon” and its aƩracƟon. Now the results in such a case are believed valuable and true, and the method valid, only because one supposes oneself to be “not wrangling but arguing,” and this is so because of one’s “inability to apply the proper divisions and disƟncƟons,” that is to say, because of one’s ignorance of the proper method and of its results.

That is, one is aƩracted and impressed by the method and results of the “art of contradicƟon” because one literally does not know any beƩer. But this ignorance could, as well, be said to be that of the person whose moƟve is erisƟcal. Thus with regard to knowledge the iniƟal disƟncƟon between method and moƟve is a tenuous one, as is the disƟncƟon between the two diﬀerent moƟves of Glaucon and Thrasymachus. True, one pursues truth while the other pursues victory, but as long as ignorance of method prevails, the danger exists that (apparent) victory itself may be taken for truth. Furthermore, why would the “art of contradicƟon” be so aƩracƟve? Partly, as just suggested, for some it would appear to be the road to truth, in the absence of an alternaƟve. But partly also, again in the absence of an alternaƟve, because it appears desirable as an end in itself— it is seducƟve as a human endeavor. Adeimantus, and possibly Glaucon, are tempted to admire Thrasymachus’s (and Socrates’s) “way with words,” both with respect to style or eloquence and agility in argument (thus the complaint of various interlocutors in the dialogues with regard to Socrates’s tricks). But the choice of method is in part linked to the choice of goal. One chooses the method of erisƟc because one desires and loves power and erisƟc promises the sweet taste of victory, hence the language of trial and the courtroom, and of physical trials (453-454). But one chooses this end as best and its method as the right one partly because one is ignorant not only of an alternaƟve method, but of the alternaƟve end to which it conduces.[22] What then does the alternaƟve, “making proper disƟncƟons,” here entail? It is not enough to start with “the principle that natures not the same ought not to share in the same pursuits” for this could itself be pursued as had just been the case in their ﬁrst eﬀort “most manfully and erisƟcally,” that is, contenƟously, analyzing the applicaƟons of the principle to produce a contradicƟon, and thus supposedly invalidate the principle. Rather, one ought to “consider . . . what parƟcular kind of diversity and idenƟty of nature we had in mind and with reference to what we were trying to deﬁne it when we assigned diﬀerent pursuits to diﬀerent natures and the same to the same” (454b). We are thus brought back again to a consideraƟon of nature, this Ɵme in relaƟon to correctly sorƟng out sameness and diﬀerence. One cannot talk sensibly of diﬀerence and

sameness of nature unless one speciﬁes with respect to what. Thus nature is deﬁned as the same or diﬀerent depending on what one is looking at: this is carefully expressed in the passage under consideraƟon: “What form (eidos) of diﬀerence and sameness of nature and referring to what, do we deﬁne it when we grant as due or allow that we assign the same pursuits to certain natures as being the same and others diﬀerent pursuits as being diﬀerent by nature” (454b, my translaƟon). It is thus not enough to be able to disƟnguish sameness and diﬀerence, as the example of the bald versus longhaired cobbler shows. Thus “we did not then posit diﬀerence of nature in any and every sense, but were paying heed solely to the kind of diversity and homogeneity that was perƟnent to the pursuits themselves” (454d). It is then, a quesƟon of relevant diﬀerence and sameness, and this cannot be got from the mulƟtude of qualiƟes. To advance the argument, Socrates makes two changes, the ﬁrst being tacƟcal, directed at Glaucon (and the others), the second, more fundamentally methodological, for us. Socrates shiŌs ﬁrst from the posiƟve to the negaƟve—in the absence of any relevant diﬀerence, women should be allowed the same guardian roles. “But if it appears that they diﬀer only in this respect, that the female bears and the male begets, we shall say that no proof has as yet been produced that the woman diﬀers from the man for our purposes . . . ” (454e) Secondly, and more crucially, rather than looking for a supposed diﬀerence in nature that could accord with an exclusion or limitaƟon with regard to the conduct of the city, the argument is shiŌed to looking for a pursuit in which being a woman would make a signiﬁcant diﬀerence. We argue then, not as before from diﬀerence and sameness of nature to appropriate diﬀerence and sameness of pursuits, but rather from deﬁniƟon of the pursuit as a test for potenƟal capacity, that is, from pursuits to natures. Those that can fulﬁll it may be said to have demonstrated their sameness—thus the hypotheƟcal discussed earlier. So, for example, the disƟncƟon between “the man naturally giŌed for anything and the one not so giŌed” is based on the results of observing in the relevant images that in fact “the one learned easily, the other with diﬃculty; that the one with slight instrucƟon could discover much for himself in the maƩer studied . . . ” (454b). Note again that Glaucon does not really follow the argument, and falls back, with Socrates’s complicity, on the noƟon that while most men are beƩer than most women in most

things, excepƟons must be allowed. Thus the ﬂaw in the case of the watchdog/guardian of the polis image of 375a is repaired, for the reader, in that instead of moving from sameness of nature to same pursuits, here we move from the deﬁning pursuit or funcƟon to the relevant diﬀerence or sameness. The images projected in the Republic are constructed as an elaboraƟon of principles; they are images that are in a sense natural products of principles—principles made visible. The principles themselves, and the model of the funcƟoning soul/city developed on their foundaƟon, are intellectual images, both in their basis and in their appeal, while erisƟc by contrast, in both its methods and its ends, is based in the seducƟveness of the image, and the experience, of power. The rhetoric of reason, as contrasted to the images of erisƟc, is 1) pracƟce in applicaƟon of hypotheses or principles, which is achieved through 2) parƟcipaƟon in the construcƟon of models, that is, images, which are the expression of those principles, and ulƟmately of the concepts that are their basis, 3) reﬂecƟon on the divisions that are the basis of the images. Thus the soul-city analogy and the experience of both its construcƟon and its dynamic consƟtute itself the iniƟal educaƟon of potenƟal guardians of the good soul, in Glaucon and the reader. It is a movement towards a Platonic redeﬁniƟon of happiness and its relaƟon to a revised understanding both of virtue and of the soul that will meet the threat posed by Thrasymachus. And it will do so in resolving the problem posed by Glaucon and Adeimantus. The construcƟon of this analogy corresponds, I suggest, to that movement in the Divided Line (510b) which consists in the applicaƟon of epistemic images taken as hypotheses to the construcƟon of ideal visible images in the existent world—in this case that of imaginaƟon and discourse. The move to a higher level of discourse, where images are of a rather diﬀerent kind, is reserved for the middle books (as suggested above). As noted earlier, the noƟon of pursuits as deﬁning natures, is elaborated in some detail at the end of Book V where the discussion of the reality of capaciƟes (dunameis) is the prelude to the discussion of the middle books, and it is to this that we now turn in the next chapter. Plato’s noƟon of capaciƟes, as sketched schemaƟcally in the secƟons of the Divided Line and its objects, is key to understanding how the soul and its world interrelate. These capaciƟes, I will argue, can each be seen as a kind of image-making. The resultant dynamic reveals how the Ideas are

implicated at each stage, how they are imaged, in the interrelaƟon of soul, world, and Idea.[23] NOTES 1. See Gerasimos Santas, “The SocraƟc Method in Republic I,” Skepsis 20 (2009): 222-37.
