In this essay, on the method of book one of the Republic, Smith opts for “opening up quesƟons” in “talking things through,” by placing a given assumpƟon in quesƟon, e.g., that jusƟce is the self-interest of the stronger, through examining the meaning of jusƟce in situaƟons where a variant of the opposite assumpƟon would apply. This allows for a Heideggerian working back to a lost fundamental meaning/name—a “forgoƩen, primary, communal understanding” (of e.g., true jusƟce as rooted in philia, as contrasted to the Thrasymachean sense of jusƟce as self-interested pleonexia, cf. 123). Smith sees in the development of book one a method that “deviates radically from single- strand linear logic of demonstraƟon” (pace Reeve and Annas) As contrasted to a reading of Plato that seeks a platonic apodeicƟc argument, Smith sees a “layered” method of exploraƟon that proceeds to ﬁnding, deﬁning, searching out in discourse, the right name for a certain acƟvity— to ﬁnd the being of jusƟce we must search out the true meaning of being just, that is of acƟng, justly. It is clear that his approach to the method of book one would give Glaucon and Adeimantus intellectual credit, where I ﬁnd them to be foils for the real philosophical dialogue (to dialegesthai)

between reader and author—hence my stress on the nature of what they request here. 7. See Roslyn Weiss “Wise Guys and Smart Alecks in Republic 1 and 2,” in The Cambridge Companion to Plato’s Republic, ed. G. R. F. Ferrari (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2007), 90-115. Weiss argues that what Socrates spells out in the ﬁrst two books is all that is essenƟal in the defense of jusƟce, both in itself and for its consequences, to be simply ﬂeshed out in the rest of the dialogue—in parƟcular, the missing piece, the details of the nature of the soul. But truly the devil is in the details of that development. Glaucon and Adeimantus’s sense of what is needed to come to the rescue of jusƟce, I have argued, is crucially encomium rather than apodeixis. Secondly, what is needed for Socrates to actually argue that the compulsion to return to the Cave and to rule is not an injusƟce, a second best? Weiss thinks that the essenƟal elements of an answer are already implicitly given, in the noƟon of harmony (inner for soul and outer for city), though this is in need of being ﬂeshed out in book seven. The just soul, Weiss argues, rather than being compelled in any negaƟve sense, actually rules in response to the express desire of the reformed souls of the ciƟzens of the polis (and the reformed spirited and desiring parts of the soul), who now want the true philosopher to rule. Being just, hence refraining from unjust acts, “changes a man’s desires,” and while ruling may sƟll be onerous in itself, the consequences, for both ciƟzens and philosopher ruler, are “desirable.” Again, Weiss does say in conclusion that “Socrates’s argument for the superiority of jusƟce to injusƟce in Book I is not complete, however, unƟl the soul is introduced” (114). But just what does it mean for the soul to be introduced into the argument? I would argue much more than is implied in her argument concerning Books I and II and the reply to the challenge posed by Glaucon and Adeimantus. For the nature of jusƟce, and of the soul to be explained rather than “praised” one needs not just a diﬀerent method but crucially a diﬀerent ontology—and for that one needs the argument of the middle books, and the detailed outline of the philosopher’s educaƟon. 8. See also Annas “What Are Plato’s ‘Middle’ Dialogues in the Middle Of?” in New PerspecƟves,1-23. “(T)he reader should accept Plato’s claims, not because of Plato’s authority but on the basis of the understanding of Plato she has achieved as the result of her own use of reason and argument” (4-

5). Annas argues that for the philosophical reader the earlier aporeƟc dialogues are a necessary complement to the middle ones. “Seen in this light, Book I of the Republic rather than a remnant of an earlier style (some having argued on this basis that was originally a separate dialogue), serves to both stress the conƟnuity of the dialogues, but also ﬁnds its place in the dramaƟc and philosophical unity of the Republic.” This is just the point of my explicaƟon of the refutaƟon of Thrasymachus, and the dramaƟc role of Glaucon as a friend of the Ideas. Thus the Republic is both aporeƟc and elencƟc. With regard to Thrasymachus, the dialogue is so not only in the obvious sense of the refutaƟon of Book I, but also in that the rest of the Republic, parƟcularly the middle books, give an alternaƟve to the implicit ontology of a Thrasymachus as a basis for refutaƟon. This is what might be called a posiƟve elencƟc, developing an argument about soul, happiness and jusƟce that will save Glaucon at one level, and the reader at another— so, aporeƟc for Thrasymachus etc. elencƟc for us. 9. For the argument that Glaucon’s request for a defense of “jusƟce itself” is sƟll regarding this as an instrumental good, see Laszlo Versenyi, “Plato and His Liberal Opponents.” Philosophy 46 (1971): 222-237, esp. 237, n.2. Versenyi argues that there is always a teleological subtext to any request for a raƟonal jusƟﬁcaƟon, parƟcularly of a human virtue. Compare Reeve, whose argument is similar in a way, an argument that shows that jusƟce itself is a homoiomerous essenƟal component of happiness. If Reeve’s argument holds up, and I think that it does, to appeal to happiness in the defense of jusƟce is not to appeal to a consequence. “Happiness will not, then, be a mere G-consequence (Glauconic consequence) of being just, and it will be possible to defend jusƟce by showing that it pays oﬀ in terms of happiness, without thereby violaƟng the condiƟons for its defense set by Glaucon” (31). Cf. Terence Irwin, Plato’s Moral Theory, (Oxford: Clarendon Press.1977) 184-91, also 325, n.8. 10. See Guthrie, Greek Philosophy, vol. IV. (1957), 554 and especially note 3. For a more sympatheƟc view of Glaucon and Adeimantus, see for example Ruby Blondell, “Leƫng Plato Speak for Himself: Character and Method in the Republic,” in Who Speaks for Plato, ed. G.Press (Lanham, MD: Rowman and LiƩleﬁeld, 1995), 127-46. The diﬀerence between our approaches (and that of similar interpretaƟons of the literary-philosophical role of character) is that I take the serious philosophical conversaƟon to be

between the reader and Plato about the interlocutors. Blondell takes Glaucon and Adeimantus as showing some of the requisite intellectual skills, at least as philosophers-in-training. Blondell refers at one point to the discussion of the “propaedeuƟc studies in mathemaƟcs and astronomy” (at 533a), where Blondell says that “we can see, in Glaucon in parƟcular, some sign of ability to follow the curriculum that will eventually lead to knowledge of the Good. (cf. 528d).” But the whole passage shows instead Glaucon’s limited, that is, convenƟonal, understanding of these studies as concerns their true propaedeuƟc value, culminaƟng in Glaucon’s revealing claim about the true value of astronomy, actually quite funny: “I think it is obvious to anyone that it compels the soul to look upward and leads it from things here to things yonder” (528e-529a). Finally, the noƟon that the books other than book one address the arguments rather than the union of belief and soul that is addressed by elencƟc, I ﬁnd odd in that the dialogue with the reader over the whole of the Republic concerns precisely the consequences for how we live in the light of a reformed analysis of the nature of soul and its interpretaƟon of reality, hence of what would make it truly happy. 11. The purpose of conƟnuing on in the middle books for Shorey is apparently solely to provide a philosopher-ruler: “the necessity of securing the perpetuity of the reformed state by the superior intelligence of the rulers” (Vol. I introducƟon, xvi). But this is to put the ontological cart before the horse!

This is consistent with Shorey’s view of the Good, which is essenƟally limited for him to the moral or poliƟcal viewpoint. (Cf. his introducƟon to vol. II. xxiii ﬀ.) 15. White thus misses the disƟncƟon between the two beginnings, the important contrast of methods (doxa vs. dialecƟc) and the ontological signiﬁcance of the issue concerning nature and natures. 17. On the relaƟonship between the meanings of nature, having a nature and the meaning of being, see the suggesƟve comments of Klein, in “On the Nature of Nature,” a lecture given at St. John’s College, Annapolis, MD, Feb. 28, 1964: 1-21, esp. 9, 16-17. Republished in The Independent Journal of Philosophy, vol. III, 1979. To apply his remarks to the present context, ritualized, convenƟonal descripƟons of male and female, which would correspond to the physical natural division, are the basis of Glaucon’s iniƟal assessment. 18. I am concerned here primarily with the basis of the construcƟon and the ostensible analogy, not with a detailed analysis of the contents of the reformed virtues as contrasted to the tradiƟonal ones, that is, with the issues that Irwin deals with in detail—their jusƟﬁcaƟon, relaƟon to SocraƟc problems of deﬁniƟon and the issue of the value of these virtues, whether good for the agent or the beneﬁciary. See Bernard Williams, “The Analogy of City and Soul in Plato’s Republic,” in Gail Fine (ed.) Plato: Ethics, PoliƟcs, Religion and Soul, (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1999), 255-64. Williams’ arƟcle argues that there are “grave obstacles to Plato’s reading back into the city what he needs for his poliƟcal conclusions, obstacles to some extent concealed by his use of the triparƟte analogy” (264). I have argued rather that the elaboraƟon of the “larger,” the city, is carefully designed to accommodate the “smaller,” the triparƟte soul, so as to allow the analogy to work—in short, reversing the

announced strategy of ﬁnding jusƟce in the larger to enable seeing it more clearly in the smaller. Contrast also Kenneth Dorter, The TransformaƟon of Plato’s Republic (Lanham, MD: Rowman & LiƩleﬁeld, 2006), 131 n. 15, on Williams : “The whole-part argument explains how the three characterisƟcs (appeƟƟveness, spiritedness, and raƟonality) get into the city, but the presence of the four virtues and the ﬁve consƟtuƟons is explained by the internal relaƟonship of the three characterisƟcs (parallel accounts for the city and the individual) not by addiƟonal whole-part arguments,” (131) though this is not my soluƟon. 20. Contrast the diﬃculƟes that Annas ﬁnds, IntroducƟon, 146-151. “If each class corresponds exactly to some funcƟon in the soul, then in an important way the ciƟzens of the state will not share a common human nature, or conversely, if arguing from city to soul, each part will be a homunculus. But if the city-soul as analogy is strictly adhered to, one will not insist on complete individuals for the parts of soul, nor ﬁnd the representaƟve classes as each lacking a human nature because they epitomize or take their idenƟty from the funcƟon which it is their task to symbolically represent as image.” Compare Blossner, City-Soul Analogy, 345-85. Blossner stresses the rhetorical funcƟon of the analogy and hence the diﬃculty if one takes the various ciƟes as corresponding to poliƟcal enƟƟes and respecƟve virtues. Like myself, he argues that the ciƟes and the virtues (and vices) are so described as to apply to the ciƟzens’ values, the states of their souls, rather than the city as a funcƟoning poliƟcal enƟty, and that this is done to set up, to facilitate, the analogy. For example, “members of [an actual] city can change their allegiance, but parts of the soul cannot. Those designated for the military class can become producers, (415b-c) ƟmocraƟc types can become oligarchic (551a), but within the soul, spirit never becomes appeƟte” (358). etc. “In the context of this thought-experiment, names become ciphers for mistaken ways of life, led by mistaken ideas of happiness. What Socrates gives us here is no poliƟcal criƟque but rather a criƟque of four ways of life that compete for aƩenƟon with the just way of life that he recommends” (371). In sum, the analogy is craŌed as a rhetorical device speciﬁcally to illuminate what human jusƟce, and happiness for the individual soul, are and are not.

21. The very relaƟon and terms of the Cave objects and their eﬀect or percepƟon by eikasia—but here as the formaƟon of right opinion. 22. Note that I am not evaluaƟng the argument of Thrasymachus concerning jusƟce, as interesƟng as that may be, but rather his moƟve and method, as seƫng the stage for a contrast of rhetorics in Books II-IV, and the relaƟon of Plato’s image in words to the metaphysics on which it is based, outlined in the middle books, and explored by me in the Phaedo analysis. For Thrasymachus’s argument itself, compare for example, Irwin (1977) 30, 179-183, Henderson (1970), SparshoƩ (1957), Reeve, (1988) 9- 13, and Blondell (2000) 127-129. 23. The complicated issue of whether Plato holds either an instrumentalist or a deontological posiƟon with regard to virtue, hence the relaƟon of jusƟce to happiness, hinges in part on just how the craŌ analogy is parsed. This in turn will aﬀect how we interpret the argument of the rest of the Republic. There is an illuminaƟng dispute in the exchange of leƩers in the Times Literary Supplement following Vlastos’s review of Irwin, commencing Feb. 24, 1978 . (Gregory Vlastos, Times Literary Supplement, Feb. 24 to Sept. 22, 1978). For Irwin, Socrates’s use of the CraŌ Analogy points to virtue as instrumental, a craŌ-like means to happiness, while the suﬃciency of virtue thesis suggests that virtues are either the whole of, or components of happiness. (Cf. 100, 281) Vlastos holds that Irwin is right about Plato but wrong about Socrates regarding the suﬃciency of virtue thesis, i.e., that Socrates is not an instrumentalist any more than Plato is, and that there is no irreconcilable tension between the CraŌ Analogy and a suﬃciency of virtue thesis, at least when these are properly understood. In other words, that happiness is in both cases a ﬁnal good of which virtue (hence jusƟce) is an integral part, a component. See also Myles Burnyeat, “The Virtues of Plato,” in The New York Review of Books, Sept. 27, 1979. In his review of Irwin, Burnyeat, like Irwin, rejects use of the craŌ analogy to support an instrumentalist view. He links this rejecƟon, and a diﬀerent (Platonic) view of happiness than that of Socrates, to the doctrine of recollecƟon, for its asserƟon of the independent existence that will resolve the problem of the relaƟvity of predicates. In this case, “that jusƟce and goodness exist on their own separately from the sensible things which are concrete instances of jusƟce

and goodness,” must be linked to an interpretaƟon of separaƟon, since good and other value predicates cannot be given in value-neutral terms. Because of the relaƟvism of empirically based comparisons and judgments about happiness, etc., any instrumentalist version of the craŌ analogy must be abandoned, in which disagreements are about diﬀerences of means. Thus it cannot be that an “evil-doer is mistaken only about means to [happiness]” but rather that “his desire is misdirected or corrupt not only his belief” (59). The independent existence of forms, based on a doctrine of separaƟon, will provide the necessary objecƟvity. The point is generally correct, but Burnyeat slips it seems to me—concrete instances of jusƟce and moral goodness are obviously not concretely in sensible things (as immanent) and need not be separated from them, rather they need to be separated from concrete instances of virtue or virtuous acts, and the road to this form of separateness is complex. For this kind of separaƟon, a diﬀerent noƟon of independent existence is required. The doctrine of recollecƟon must be interpreted, I argue, in conjuncƟon with an interpretaƟon of the doctrine of separaƟon, and both of them demythologized, all of which forms part of my own interpretaƟon to follow.

Chapter 2 Discourse THE THIRD WAVE AND THE POSSIBILITY ISSUE In the previous chapter, we dealt with the nature of the soul-city analogy. But we did not deal with why an analogy in the form of an image is employed at all. At 473a, aŌer the city has been sketched out, Plato has Glaucon’s agreement that it is “natural for pracƟce or acƟon (praxin) to grasp less of truth than speech (lexeōs).” But how much less, and what is meant by praxis and lexis? The immediate reference is to the image of the just city that has been “created in words” as a type or model (paradeigmatos) by or against which we may measure actual just men and ciƟes, and from which we can see what jusƟce itself is, which is really the measure. Hence in the larger sense it might be expected that this same statement about pracƟce and speech could apply to the Ideas themselves, since the Ideas are referred to as being more substanƟal in Plato’s scheme of things than their actual instances, which in turn would then be termed pracƟce. It is with this extended meaning of the contrast in mind, and perhaps looking forward to dianoia, that Grube, otherwise fairly literal in his translaƟon, translates lexis in this sentence as “theory”—which is strictly speaking not in the text. AcƟon and speech, pracƟce and theory, being acƟviƟes of a consciousness in relaƟon to truth, theory would then be something having to do with the percepƟon of the Ideas, and pracƟce would be the applicaƟon of, say, the Idea of jusƟce, in the world of experience, for example in the guardian’s wriƟng of laws. The laws would then be, in relaƟon to theory (formed around a percepƟon of the Ideas), themselves a kind of pracƟce. Yet the laws are in a sense also a kind of theory, and speech its embodiment, lexis in contrast to the praxis of parƟcular instances of their applicaƟon. But parƟcular instances of jusƟce are not made just by theory since it is said (in the Phaedo, for example) that the instances are the occasion through which we are able to mount to, and perceive that which is just in itself. Finally, the immediate context for this phrase, the “model of a good city in our argument,” is compared to the

work of a good painter, and contrasted to its possible existence in pracƟce. The laƩer, if it can be shown to be possible at all, will have only a “measure of success”—it is the nature of “pracƟce,” because it involves more than words, because it is involved with acƟon and maƩer, not to “exist precisely.” Thus the examinaƟon that follows 473 will be of what is now badly done in the ciƟes which prevents them from being governed in this way, and what is the smallest change which would enable a city to reach our type of government” (473b), that is, to the degree possible. As to the former, the model, the picture painted in words, what at the end of Book IX is called a “model laid up in heaven,” though it is closer to the truth than is pracƟce of its applicaƟon, yet it too is a construcƟon—it too is an image. The ideal city constructed in Books II-IV is on the one hand a theoreƟcal construcƟon, a theory in lexis in relaƟon to its use as a model or paradigm for the poliƟcs of the soul, the life of the just man (which inevitably falls short of jusƟce itself)—but it is also in a sense a pracƟce, the image-making of the philosopher, in relaƟon to the Idea of jusƟce—thus a construcƟon, an ideal, not an Idea. And the purpose of these images, of both jusƟce and injusƟce it should be noted, was “with these models before us, to see how they turned out as regards happiness and its opposite” (472c). Thus, using these images as if they were indeed lived, that is, imagined as living pracƟce and not as theory, “we would be forced to come to an agreement about ourselves, that he who was as like them as possible would also have a life most like theirs.” But if then even what is “formulated in words” is in a sense a pracƟce, albeit as an ideal a more perfect one than any government we may actually set up in imitaƟon of it (whether amongst the city of many souls or the one soul that is a city within), what is it that is truer than it, and that on which it is based? To what extent might even this basis, the Ideas, itself be regarded as a kind of theōria and itself a kind of pracƟce, though the ground of all other pracƟce, including lexis. What is the relaƟon of lexis and pracƟce for Plato and their relaƟon to the Idea? Is the Idea too in some sense an Ideal? What is the status of the painted image of the ideal city as image, as paradigm or model, and its relaƟon to what is above it, the Idea, and below it, the “possible city”? What is a philosophical image of an Idea? Might even the Idea or Form, in some sense, be seen not only as an

original but also itself funcƟoning in certain respects as a pracƟce at the highest level?[1] Now it is agreed that the discussion will not have been “less worthwhile if we cannot prove that it is possible to found a city such as we have described”—i.e., that with “such models before us” even if unrealizable, we will sƟll be able to complete our purpose, which was to “see how they turned out as regards happiness and its opposite,” etc. and this would seem to be enough to fulﬁll the original purpose. Then too, the beauƟful painƟng of the completely just man or city would nonetheless be beauƟful for its being a mere ideal, and its painter nonetheless a good painter, or so it would seem. Thus, the conversaƟon is to conƟnue apparently not by some necessity, but “if we must, to please you” to discuss the quesƟon of possibility, and then only with the agreement beforehand that “to realize anything in pracƟce as it can be formulated in words” is not possible, and that, again “it is natural for pracƟce to have a lesser grip on truth than speech.” But that the conversaƟon conƟnues simply to “please” the interlocutors is absurd. To show “how and in what respect” this city “might best be possible” must have a greater necessity than that; the “to please you” is clearly ironic (just as the task of deﬁning jusƟce cannot really be completed by the end of Book IV, leaving the larger part of the Republic as so much icing on the cake). But clearly the construcƟon of the just city, while a detailed exposiƟon, requires the jusƟﬁcaƟon and compleƟon of its ground—the principles of its construcƟon.[2] Since this issue of the possibility of the ideal city, the one which in its administraƟon “can come closest to our theories” is to introduce for the ﬁrst Ɵme the person of the philosopher-ruler, and philosophy itself, both in its pracƟce and its theory—in the discussion of the middle books—it would be rather too trivial to make such serious maƩer a gratuitous excursion, and render the Republic as lacking any organic structure or necessity. Nor would much of the discussion and imagery of the Sun/Line/Cave be needed even to meet the minimum needs of a simple-minded noƟon of possibility—one in which all one would need to do is simply posit a philosopher-ruler as in charge of the wise law- making and administraƟon of the then truly just city, or a reasonable

approximaƟon thereof. No need to go into detail about just what truth the philosopher-painter has his eye on, and how it is possible! The possibility issue as concerns the ideal city is played out again at the level of the individual soul, concerning here too its jusƟce, happiness and moral conduct. Terry Penner, in “The Historical Socrates and Plato’s Early Dialogues: Some Philosophical QuesƟons,”[3] argues that strictly speaking it is not the desires that diﬀer but the beliefs that x is desirable (will make me truly happy). But I would suggest that it is in the iniƟal split between belief and desire that he goes astray, and in aƩribuƟng this to the historical Socrates as well. To begin with, it seems contrary to common sense that Socrates would not see many cases where the passions determine what one raƟonalizes in a belief. What has happened I think is that given a preference for a certain desire-belief acƟon theory, Penner keeps the primary desires as general and ﬁxes the locus of the objects of desire in the belief part of the formula. But my desire for x is surely visceral, and disƟnguishable from the belief that x will make me truly happy. In a sense, desires are already beliefs. And it is likely that Socrates appreciated that many if not most acƟons implied that it is good because I want it, rather than the contrary. If this is right, then rather than a deep split between a SocraƟc teleological determinism and a Platonic irraƟonalism, it would seem simpler, and consistent, to read Socrates (an historical Socrates reﬂected in the early dialogues if one wishes) as arguing what would be the case if only we saw more clearly, and Plato compleƟng the argument by an analysis of the soul that shows why we don’t. In both cases the locus of the obstacles to virtue, hence again the possibility issue, are in the moƟve force of desires and the resistance of desire’s own beliefs —which are cashed out in ignorance and false beliefs, as contrasted to knowledge. What Plato supplies is an analysis of the source of the soul’s blindness, and on my account this requires both a developed psychology (perforce diﬀerent than Penner’s) and an ontological argument that will ground the soul’s moral conduct and the true context of real possibility— which is what we get in the Republic (and elsewhere). Let us then take another look at this issue of possibility, with an eye to ﬁnding some more serious inner necessity for the ensuing discussion and imagery and a more careful noƟon of possibility. At an earlier point, the

objecƟon had been raised that we were possibly making the guardians unhappy by depriving them of certain luxuries, etc. to which the reply was that we were not looking to make any one part of the city well oﬀ—happy or content—but rather the whole. And yet it is aŌer all the happiness of the individual just man that is to be in the end measured against that of the unjust individual to see which is the greater, or which more truly happy. The city constructed was to serve as a model wherein one could read jusƟce and then see if, were jusƟce found to be the same in the individual, such an individual would indeed be truly happier because of it. Yet at this stage in the Republic it is the city itself that is foremost in the minds of both the reader and the interlocutors. It is this city of many souls, the possibility of which is that third and “greatest wave” of objecƟon. The model that we have constructed is of the ideally just city, yet the judgment, which we must make, is of the ideally just man (and the ideally unjust man). Why then did we not construct the laƩer, that is, an image of him? Because it was argued at the transiƟon of Book II that the image of jusƟce and injusƟce could not be seen clearly, or rather, that jusƟce within it could not be so seen. This is so not, as it is ﬁrst presented, because of their relaƟve size—the non-visible, e.g., jusƟce, is not any larger in the city nor any smaller in the man, but rather, I suggest, precisely because our aƩachment to the visible world makes it diﬃcult to see beyond the apparent simple unity of the one individual, represented by the body which we experience and idenƟfy with, that which is imaged in reﬂecƟons of the mirror and in the images of the painter. And which we also represent to ourselves as that psychological unity of the individual idenƟﬁed with sensaƟon, feelings and memory—in short, with all that is collected under the term self-awareness or consciousness of self. This false image, of the apparent unity of the self—a simple oneness whether of the body or the soul—is to be replaced by a many that is potenƟally one. And this is best done, best illustrated, in a context where it is readily accepted, that is to say a visible, experienced many—the many souls of the city. For in this context, not only will the manyness be readily apparent, but also the idea of a unity of a non-visible, not individually subjecƟve unity, yet one that is Ɵed to the manyness of the collecƟon of ciƟzens, hence more imaginable, and already familiar in the ideal and pracƟce of the polis. Then, too, the causes of a lack of unity can be

analogized and studied in the pracƟces which we call war when considering one city in conﬂict with another, and which Plato applies to the conﬂict within the polis itself. JusƟce then, is not more apparent because it is “writ larger” but because in the images of the Idea it is in a form that is more recognizable—nor is it found, as it were, but rather deﬁned and created, or recreated. The precondiƟon for understanding not only what jusƟce is but how it is, and how it is possible, is the heurisƟc movement from the simple apparent unity of the existent one to the created or formed unity of the non-visible many.[4] The apparent one must ﬁrst be accepted, seen, in its actual disparate manyness before a unity can be imagined or sought both in theory and in pracƟce. An image or paradigm of the just man needs to be mediated through an image of the just city because we have an ontological bias, an ontological opinion with regard to what is real, hence what is really one, which stands in our way—we take ourselves to be already one, and hence a natural unity. This noƟon needs to be destroyed, deconstructed, before a new one can be constructed in its place. Plato’s method is ﬁrst to do the reconstrucƟon at the level of analogy, while the ontological deconstrucƟon goes on sub rosa in the principles and method of construcƟon—the pracƟce of the building of the image—and then to return to an explicit examinaƟon of the ground of the new image of the city and person in a new image of the ontology that lies behind it. There is another way to see the same necessity of method and content. The ulƟmate goal was to be in a posiƟon to judge of jusƟce and injusƟce as to which life would give the greater happiness. By carrying out the argument through the analogy of the city not only is the unity of a many issue able to be raised but that of the nature of happiness itself— and this, not only when the happiness of the whole is supported over against that of any one part. Plato does not exclude the happiness of the parƟcular part or individual but only points out that such is not the objecƟve in forming the image in order to ﬁnd jusƟce in the city “happy with itself.” But in turning to the image of the city as the appropriate analogy the very kind of happiness has altered.[5] A city, ideal or otherwise, is not an individual consciousness, and thus cannot be said to experience happiness. At the beginning of the forming of the image of the city we

have Socrates replying to the objecƟons that the model is lacking in luxuries, in condiments for the meals, etc., that it is a “city of pigs” not of men. Socrates responds by suggesƟng that the original image seems a good one to him as an image of jusƟce, and that what they are suggesƟng is a construcƟon and consideraƟon of what he characterizes as a “fevered city.” The laƩer is of course more realisƟc, corresponds to the city and the individual as we actually are, and allows us to examine the actual condiƟon that poses the problem to which Plato’s noƟon of jusƟce corresponds as proﬀered soluƟon; jusƟce as the curing of the fever and the taming of the beast. But for the point at hand, of more interest is that the city is characterized in quite human terms, as “fevered”—so much so that it is unmistakable that a metaphor is at work, it is inescapable, and thus the image, while serviceable, at the same Ɵme stands out in its diﬀerence—a city cannot feel “fevered” as an individual can; they are, on this score, diﬀerent kinds of beings. But what if the analogy is worked in the other direcƟon? That is, not looking upward from the standpoint of the individual to the city, but rather downward from the paradigm of the ideal city to the individual (bearing in mind that the city is shaped expressly to mirror the soul). The quesƟon then becomes, looking now not just at fever but at happiness, whether the happiness of a city, a happiness which by its very nature is not a feeling, and which by its very nature is a created thing, whether, on both scores, human being can imitate such a model. In other words, what is a signiﬁcant diﬀerence between the two elements of the comparison serves as the basis for a shiŌing of the ground of the discussion. Which is not to say that the painƟng of the image of a diﬀerent noƟon of happiness, in however beauƟful colors, is self-jusƟfying. Quite the contrary. To shiŌ from the natural noƟon or image of human happiness as a feeling to the constructed image of human happiness as a condiƟon or state is a shiŌ in ontology that is in much need of a ground. Or at least it is in need of an imagery that is speciﬁcally directed at explicaƟng the larger ontological claims on which the parƟcular images of human being are based (the city of many souls and the soul of many inner ciƟes). And such is the necessary task of the ontology and imagery of the middle books. In the previous chapter, I have already suggested that the image of the polis and its virtues is formed with the soul and its virtues in view, thus

that the relaƟonship of social jusƟce to psychic jusƟce is to be seen strictly in this light. The happiness of the ideal polis need not result from other than the psychic jusƟce ideal of inner harmony because there are no real complete individuals represented within the image (see below). SƟll, one may ask what the relaƟonship would be of social or relaƟonal jusƟce to the newly deﬁned jusƟce of inner harmony, and also with what jusƟﬁcaƟon the term jusƟce can be applied to the laƩer at all. Is it recognizable as what is commonly called jusƟce, or, does it have anything in common with vulgar jusƟce to jusƟfy the subsƟtuƟon of the one for the other as real jusƟce?[6] Choosing to construct an image of the just city rather than one of the ideally just man has not so much to do with the ontological shiŌ as with the form of the argument and more directly with the quesƟon of possibility. The original goal was to be able to judge of jusƟce and injusƟce as to which life would give happiness and which unhappiness, that is, as Adeimantus asks, “So do not merely give us a theoreƟcal proof that jusƟce is beƩer than injusƟce, but tell us how each, in and by itself, aﬀects a man . . . ” (367b). Now we have given above the reasons why the image is that of an ideal city and not that of an ideally just individual (note that when it comes to the ideally unjust, an image is constructed at the level of the individual—that of the tyrannical soul, but then this is aŌer the ontological air has been cleared). Apart from these reasons for the argument being carried out through the image of the ideal city one might be tempted to regret the absence of such an image of the ideally just individual as precisely something that might then serve pracƟcally, as that painter’s model. Or, to put it negaƟvely, if the city constructed is only an ideal and the rest conƟnued “to please you” (albeit this is meant ironically, so I have argued), is this equally so of the possibility of the just man—is this only an ideal? The answer must be no—for the city to exist only in the heavens might indeed be thought beauƟful—nonetheless, for the just man to exist only so would be shameful, or in the context of the argument, laughable, and not a true defense of jusƟce. Now any actuality is to fall short of its ideal image, and as Plato says at one point, even by a liƩle is an incommensurable gap—yet in some sense the quesƟon of by how much is crucial, and even more so, in what manner does it fall short.

For the city to come as close as possible requires either luck (chance) or the gods (cf. 592a), which emphasizes how far this is unlikely—one would need either luck or the gods to 1) get a philosopher-king to start out with 2) get a populace who would accept one. How unlikely it is that, for example, the pre-ideal city will agree to give up their children over ten years of age to “send into the country … away from their parents” and way of life. It is enough possibility to saƟsfy Glaucon that the whole construcƟon is not merely wishful thinking, but the possibility hangs by a rather slim and unphilosophical thread. “You agree then that what we have said about the city and its consƟtuƟon is not altogether wishful thinking, that these things are diﬃcult, but somehow possible, though only in the way indicated, whenever true philosophers, be it one or more, become rulers in a city” (540d). That Glaucon and Adeimantus have their feet a liƩle too ﬁrmly planted on the ground, in their suscepƟbility to Thrasymachus, has been argued in chapter one. It is of a piece with their being arrested at the level of concern for the possibility of the ideal city of many souls, rather than the consƟtuƟon of the soul that must seek the unity of its own mulƟplicity. When they say that “the more you speak like this the less we shall let you oﬀ from telling us how this city is possible” (472a), it is the realizaƟon of the paradigm literally transported to earth as a city which they wish to see defended and explained—at this point seemingly having forgoƩen the original task (recalling what had been said of memory as one of the requirements for the philosophical personality). But the case for the possibility of realizaƟon of the individual as just and hence happy is far graver—and far more relevant to the Republic, as we have not failed to stress, since “to come as close as we can” would be needed as a real possibility if the argument regarding happiness is to be both convincing and viable. If a just city cannot be founded, if it is possible but not likely, well, at least the individual man might be approximately just, and there would be a more or less demonstrable reason for his being so, if jusƟce were shown to be a condiƟon of his happiness. But if not only the just city is unlikely but the just man equally so, then we are leŌ with nothing, with an empty ideal, and eﬀecƟvely, Thrasymachus gains the day. It must be shown then not only that the individual would be living the best life, if he were to approximate the jusƟce of the ideal, but that his life is suﬃciently possible,

unlike the city—i.e., that its actualizaƟon does not depend on chance or the gods. About the realizaƟon of public happiness in the public city Plato can aﬀord to be skepƟcal, pessimisƟc to the point of irony, but about the realizaƟon of private happiness in the private city he dare not be so. As well, it will turn out that the private city, the soul, is itself public, in its relaƟon to lexis and truth, and the public or social nature of images and image-making. The sense for this is developed in our discussion of the Cave and the Divided Line, in the chapters to follow. That it is solely in the laƩer that the true consƟtuƟon is actualized in imitaƟon of the ideal, is corroborated by the discussion at the end of Book IX, where it is the government within that is ﬁnally at issue. “The man of sense will direct all his eﬀorts to this end [the inner condiƟon of jusƟce] even of his own body . . . he will culƟvate harmony in his body for the sake of consonance in his soul” (592a). As regards honors, that most precious of Greek commodiƟes, “He will share in and willingly taste those which he believes will make him a beƩer man but he will avoid both public and private honors which he believes will destroy the exisƟng condiƟon of his soul.” Then immediately, the response by the interlocutors, “He will not then, if that is his concern, be willing to go into poliƟcs.” To which Socrates replies, “Yes, by the dog, he will, at least in his own kind of city, but not in his fatherland perhaps, unless divine luck should be his.” Now clearly the fatherland is the naƟve city—the public one—and here it would be unlikely, it would take divine luck, a dubious commodity for a philosopher. But if this skepƟcal irony is felt, then the emphasis is all the more posiƟve, and emphaƟc—that is, emphaƟcally on the one city where there is a real possibility—the philosopher’s “own kind of city,” the private city.[7] Hence the poliƟcs of the soul is the only one where the “model laid up in heaven” can in fact serve[8] —”our city of words” as Glaucon calls it. But there is no poliƟcs there, in heaven, only in the actual applicaƟon of the model, only “as he looks” then to “set up the government of his soul” (592a). We look upon that model/image, and it is in the aƩempt to take it as the original, to form ourselves aŌer it, that poliƟcs is engaged in, in the government of our own souls here, in the creaƟve, Ɵme-bound aƩempt to “set up the government or consƟtuƟon (politeia) of the soul.” “He would take part in the public aﬀairs of that city only, not of any other.” This would also allow for just

acƟons as an eﬀect, indeed as the ﬁeld in which the mortal just soul would express its inner jusƟce as convenƟonal social jusƟce. Thus there are not two images provided, one of the ideal city and one of the ideal man; the paradigm constructed serves for both, and in its applicaƟon has its end (telos) or purpose only as the visible image of the laƩer. It is because the soul is invisible, though our real being, that we need a visible image of it in the city. It is in eﬀect a visible paradigm of non- visible jusƟce (see the discussion of the Divided Line to follow).[9] But if we are right thus to stress the primacy of the individual soul as the true (good/just) city, the means to this end is contained in the image of the philosopher who is also a ruler, albeit ulƟmately only of himself. The response to the “third wave” is the Philosopher-Ruler. And thus it is that the nature of philosophy itself and the nature of the philosopher, that is, the philosophical nature, is raised. The quesƟon of philosophy is raised for the ﬁrst Ɵme at Book V, 472a, and is followed by the ﬁrst explicitly philosophical discussion, in the aƩempt to disƟnguish the true from the false philosophers. This discussion serves as a rough introducƟon to the middle books, where the maƩer of philosophy and the philosophical life is given its proper constructed image. In eﬀect, the disƟncƟon between the apparent philosophical life and the true one, as outlined in the discussion of the “lovers of the spectacle of sights and sounds” versus the “lover of the spectacle of truth,” inherent in the nature of that spectacle. But this sort of anƟcipaƟon, or circularity, is characterisƟc of the structure of the Republic in general. Thus, before turning to an analysis of the imagery of the middle books we shall look at this preliminary discussion (with a brief look at the educaƟon of the true philosopher, from Book VII). We note too, what is rather obvious, that the philosopher, and philosophy itself, at least in the Republic, is presented as a means to the truly just life, ulƟmately, to happiness truly deﬁned, and not an end in itself. This life is combined in the person (and so represented in the image) who has both knowledge, has “learned to know the ideal reality,” and who does “not fall short of others in experience.” And further, that while he is to be “enamored of that kind of knowledge that is eternal, and is not wandering between the poles of generaƟon and decay,” the context of the argument requires that this knowledge be put to work. The philosopher’s soul is the site of the true

city and its poliƟcs, and it is the philosopher who is responsible for its consƟtuƟon. KNOWLEDGE AND OPINION: THE PHILOSOPHER VERSUS THE SIGHT- LOVER The philosopher is said to be the “lover of all kinds of knowledge” and not just of one, nor of each kind would he pursue “only a part” but the whole of it. This rather general noƟon could of course be generously treated as a tribute to the philosophical spirit’s intellectual curiosity. Then too, if we look at it when it is a quesƟon of detailing the educaƟon of the philosopher somewhat later in Book VII aŌer the Line, there are a broad range of subjects to be studied. Yet, when at that point the subjects are set out (521c ﬀ.) they are not so broad as to encompass any and every kind of knowledge—and are in fact not so much chosen for their content, as objects of intellectual curiosity, but rather speciﬁcally as suitable, if studied with a speciﬁc perspecƟve, for their eﬀect on the soul of the learner. They are, it should be recalled, not an end in themselves but serve simply as the means by which the philosopher’s soul may be prepared for that higher insight which is the knowledge of the Ideas in and of themselves. To the extent that each study has a content that is amenable to establishing a habit of thought that is appropriate to the percepƟon of the Ideas, it may serve. Thus, astronomy is mere star-gazing if it is just looking into the sky, and not at all, as Glaucon suggests, a way of turning the soul from concern with earthly things to concern with the higher, heavenly things. In fact, even the study of mathemaƟcal moƟons of the heavens, while an improvement on the mere idealisƟc romanƟcism of the “star gazer,” is sƟll the study of the changeable, of an irregular moƟon no maƩer how beauƟful the stars; and no maƩer how assiduously one aƩempts to contain their moƟon with the applicaƟon of geometry etc., the material nature of the object remains stubbornly visible, that is to the eye of the “true astronomer.” Ironically, the real astronomer gazes not upward but downward—to the piece of paper and the penciled calculaƟons and diagram.[10] For while that to which it is applied, and from which it is drawn in a sense, is variable and inexact, the diagram etc. is not so (which is not to say that one does not need to compare the two, and adjust or

change the diagram). Thus it is geometry which is the most important part of the study, and is contrasted to the study of the moƟons themselves as the non-visible to the visible. And it is in this aspect that the study is part of the preparaƟon of the philosopher for higher things. But even that study of the “true existences” is once again said to have its end, in the context of the Republic, in reconstrucƟng the soul that will be capable of poliƟcal rule. —Let us then study astronomy by means of problems as we do geometry (itself) and let the things in the sky go, if the study of astronomy is to be to make the naturally intelligent part of the soul useful instead of useless. You are prescribing a task that is many Ɵmes harder than the present pracƟce of astronomy. —I think that our other prescripƟons will be of the same kind if we are to be of any beneﬁt as lawgivers. (530c) Thus, “astronomy must be studied in a diﬀerent way, if the study is to be useful for our purpose” (529c). The study is to serve as both a reinforcement for, and an example of, the diﬀerence between the visible and the non-visible, accessible within our experience. The “ornaments which brighten the sky,” though “the most beauƟful and most exact of visible things . . . fall far short of the true existences, of the moƟons by which true speed and true slowness are carried along in true number and true shapes, both in relaƟon to each other and carrying along what these true shapes contain.” But these “true existences” are not the Forms or Ideas: here, the “moƟons,” however perfect, are in turn only the raƟonalized moƟons, raƟonal construcƟons, at least as compared to the elements applied to their descripƟon, e.g., “true speed” and “true number.” The raƟonal images are used to explain the visible, and they in turn rest on that which is more truly called the unchanging Ideas. The passage distances Plato from the convenƟonal eternality of the Greek heavens. For the studies of the moƟon of the stars, the mathemaƟcal works which we design are, as is the model of the ideal city, construcƟons that uƟlize and presuppose the reality of the principles and elements on

which they are constructed. Such models are, as Socrates says, like the plans of Daedalus (for his famous automata, for example). On coming upon them, “A man versed in geometry, on seeing these, would think them beauƟfully worked out, but that it was absurd to examine them with any hope of ﬁnding the truth there about the equal, or the double, or any other raƟo” (529e). Now note that Plato does not speak of an astronomer coming upon these plans, not even a real astronomer, but rather a geometer. And what this geometer says about Daedalus’ plans is as true of his own ﬁeld, of geometry—“for neither will the truth about the equal, or the double, or any other raƟo” be found there; these are precisely the elements which are assumed as known, uƟlized in the study and construcƟon of geometrical space, and studied in themselves only insofar as they are seen in applicaƟon, i.e., at work—as are jusƟce and the ontological principles at work in the construcƟon of the ideal city. Hence the “real moƟons” of the stars (planets), while they “can only be perceived by reason and thought,” and are thus closer to the invisible realm than the visible, bringing those who study them in turn closer to the non-visible world, sƟll, such moƟons, whether in the sky or on paper, are themselves only images of the truly non-visible elements—in the example of astronomical moƟon, of the ideas of speed and slowness and regularity, without which the account of moƟon would be unintelligible. The advantage of the geometer is that the essenƟality of such elements is not obscured by the ﬂux and inexactness of the material world. Thus, for the sake of ontological clarity geometry is the example chosen in the discussion of the Divided Line. But, again, it is in the realm of images of the mixed kind of existence that the separaƟon of the visible and the non- visible has its most important applicaƟon. Thus, ﬁnally, of the real astronomer, it may be said that he looks upon the “embroidery of the sky as models in the study of those other things.” Even as the stars are reduced to examples or subjects for paradigms in the diagrams on his paper, so these diagrams are images containing, re-presenƟng, the elements of intelligibility appropriate to the subject at hand. The geometer, the astronomer, or the constructor of the ideal city, each must ask of his image whether it in fact works, whether it contains, in both senses of the word, the phenomenon sought to be brought under control and/or into the light of intelligibility. But as to the very means which are employed, though

insight is gained into their nature through their very use, and some sense of their reality in the experience of their eﬃcacy, yet to ask speciﬁcally for knowledge of these elements, for insight into their own reality, is to pass beyond being a geometer, and beyond being a poliƟcal philosopher in the sense of a craŌsman of the ideal city, and to have posed quesƟons that have answers, if at all, in the realm of ontology. From that vantage point one would “consider it strange” to consider the “relaƟon of night to day, of these to month, and month to year, and of the other stars to these and to each other” and to “believe that they are ever the same and do not deviate anywhere.” He will undertake rather to “understand the real truth of these things,” that is, that general ontological view on which any understanding of them is predicated. But this discussion of astronomy and the astronomer is part of the discussion of the educaƟon of the true philosopher, and, signiﬁcantly, follows the discussion of the Divided Line, etc. which is that very ontological descripƟon needed. By giving us a dramaƟc image of just how not to take images, it advances the reader’s noƟon of just how Plato understands the noƟon of image, and ulƟmately of the Platonic Ideas. The astronomy discussion is, in eﬀect, an image in words of that very understanding (and here Glaucon’s humorous misunderstanding) of the concept of paradigm or image suggested in the Divided Line discussion. Glaucon, in his taking astronomy in precisely the wrong way, in looking physically upward rather than downward (at the diagram) and inward, reveals that his sincerity surpasses his understanding, and that the preceding explicaƟon of the Sun/Cave and especially of the Divided Line, went by only half understood, if at all. Though immediately concerned with astronomy, the passage is instrucƟve for the reader as precisely how not to take the Ideas: Glaucon’s error is a parody and a warning. AŌer geƫng it wrong twice—astronomy is praised by him ﬁrst as useful for pracƟcal maƩers like navigaƟon, secondly as in a way which he hopes is “less vulgar” because it “compels the soul to look upward and it leads from things here to things yonder”—he admits that Socrates’ “rebuke is deserved,” and he takes his punishment in the form of a rather sarcasƟc comment. “If someone were contemplaƟng ornaments on a ceiling and learned something with his head bent back you probably would say that he is not looking with his eyes but with his intelligence” (529b). It is in this

context that Plato has Socrates make the rather extreme sounding asserƟon that, “If anyone tries to acquire knowledge about any object of sense, whether gaping upward with his mouth open or looking down with his mouth shut, I say he cannot learn anything, for there is no knowledge of such things, and his soul is not looking upward but downward, even if he is lying on his back on land or in the sea” (529c). We have jumped ahead to this discussion in Book VII because the disƟncƟon between the true and the false philosopher (474ﬀ.), which precedes the discussion of the Line, is rather like the disƟncƟon between the true and the false astronomer which follows it. The false philosopher is described as the lover of spectacles indiscriminately, Glaucon speaks of those who “always want to hear some new thing,” while the true philosopher is described as the lover of the “spectacle of truth,” and in both discussions we are confronted with the contrasƟng images of those who gaze at diﬀerent kinds of images.[11] Why should Plato have used the characterizaƟon of lovers of “spectacle” (philotheamōn), to contrast the lovers of spectacular sights with the philosopher’s love of the spectacle of truth? The image of the eye, of what is seen or appears before one, and of deceiving appearances, etc. is so conspicuous in the Republic that it merits further explicaƟon, beyond the obvious that one could say about appearances versus reality and the visible and the invisible—as Glaucon’s blind adherence to the doctrine of the Ideas shows. The key, I will suggest, is in the proper interpretaƟon of the noƟon of image and our relaƟon to it, and this can be seen in an explicaƟon of the Divided Line (as well as the Cave image) in the next chapters. But we must ﬁrst ﬁnish our remarks on that iniƟal introducƟon to philosophy and philosophers. The argument begins, as we have said, with a characterizaƟon of the philosopher as a collector, as one “willing to learn every kind of knowledge,” and who is compared, somewhat tongue in cheek, to a “lover of boys,” such as Glaucon, who praises each for a diﬀerent quality, seeing beauty in each, and again, with wine lovers, who love every kind of wine. The images are half-mocking, half-serious, when contrasted with the later discussion. It recalls the very boƩom of DioƟma’s ladder of ascent in the Symposium to the idea of the beauƟful. SƟll, it does require, and illustrate at a base level, the acƟvity of collecƟng, and at least potenƟally of seeing

the one amongst the many. It has a certain resemblance to true enquiry. But even Glaucon is able to see that this is rather too general to be adequate and he objects that this would seem to “include lovers of spectacles” and of “sights and sounds,” those who “run around to all the Dionysiac fesƟvals, omiƫng none.” Yet he seems at the outset to have missed the point about perceiving the common factor, etc. and is seemingly only upset by the reference to wine and beauƟful boys, hence his reference to Dionysiac fesƟvals. But this confusion, or rather obtuseness, allows and requires Socrates to make the disƟncƟon between the lovers of such spectacles, who are the false philosophers, noƟceably aƩached to the spectacles of the visible, physical, and here sensual world, as well as the random “sampling of every study” voraciously, and those true philosophers who are the “lovers of the spectacle of truth.” This in turn leads to a discussion of just what that spectacle of truth might be. The analysis revolves at ﬁrst around the discriminaƟon of opposites (a theme to which we shall return in chapter ﬁve). “Since the beauƟful is the opposite of the ugly they are two . . . and each is one,” (476a) while each one appears as many. So here, the philosopher is he who can discriminate correctly opposites, and as well, see the many grouped under each one, e.g., the many beauƟful as one in possessing Beauty, and the many ugly as one in possessing Ugliness. But this is rather facile, and confusing. The “lover of sights and sounds” is “unable to see and welcome the nature of Beauty itself.” Rather, he “believes in beauƟful things but not in Beauty itself . . . his life is like a dream.” And this is contrasted to the philosopher, who is “awake” and sees “both it and the things that share in it, and does not confuse the two.” Now this is fair enough as an image in words of what Glaucon already accepts as the theory of Forms, and the image of the one as dreaming, without being aware of this, while the other is awake, is a vivid one. But there is a rather large hole, or leap if one wishes, in Socrates’ argument. One might be willing to admit that if “the beauƟful is the opposite of the ugly they are two” and that if two, each is one, yet the sense of one in this case, one as deﬁniƟonally self-idenƟcal, is rather diﬀerent than the sense of one as meaning that one thing which all beauƟful things share. And it is precisely this laƩer sense that is denied by the lover of sights and sounds, of “many beauƟful things,” who yet does not admit of “beauty in itself.” Now it is true that the two senses are in a

special relaƟonship to one another in Plato’s ontology, but they are disƟnct, would need to be explicated in their relaƟon, and Socrates is made to blithely pass from one to the other without pausing.[12] The problem is that while there are what one might call philosophical principles at work here (collecƟon, discriminaƟon of opposites, unity in mulƟplicity), they are more invoked than pracƟced with care, intenƟonally so, I have suggested, since this is a pre- or proto-philosophical passage. In eﬀect, it assumes, as dogma (and one that Glaucon is ostensibly pracƟced in), the very thing supposedly being disƟnguished—that which disƟnguishes the philosopher from the non-philosopher, that is, that parƟcular knowledge of the nature of things which is accounted for by the noƟon of parƟcipaƟon such that the philosopher who knows beauty “sees both it and things that share in it, and does not confuse the two. . . . ” In other words, the basis of the disƟncƟon between knowledge and opinion which Plato upholds. For the lover of beauƟful things, of the spectacle of the many, there is no such disƟncƟon, since all opinion, in its diversity, mirroring the diversity of experience, is for him knowledge. And so, the argument, in disƟnguishing between knowledge and opinion as the respecƟve objects of the true and false philosopher, assumes this disƟncƟon as the hypothesis on which the argument is based. Or more properly, the hypothesis is the self-idenƟty of the Forms and its presence (parousia) as the unexplicated basis for collecƟon, hence the possibility of disƟnguishing knowledge from opinion. (In other words, the relaƟon between parousia and methexis.) “The same is true of the just and the unjust, the good and the bad, and all the Forms, each is itself one, but because they appear everywhere in associaƟon with acƟons, and bodies, and each other, each appears to be many” (476a). They then pass to a discussion in which the disƟncƟon between the respecƟve objects (knowledge and opinion) is further defended against “an objecƟon from one who has opinion . . . if he is angry with us” for so beliƩling his claims to legiƟmacy. Glaucon is solicited as a stand-in for the would-be angry objector. But indeed he is potenƟally this very person, since his adherence to the doctrine of Ideas is, I have suggested, rather blind—and insecure at that. We are confronted here with the relaƟonship of a certain kind of praxis and lexis.

We are ﬁrst asked to consider, “Does the knower know something?”— to which the answer is obviously, if casually, yes.[13] Then “Is it something that is or is not?” The reply is, something that is, “for how could something that is not, be known.” This is, of course, to move ambiguously from the object as knowledge to the object of knowledge. It is to shiŌ from what I may be said to have in mind, or even to know about x (quite apart from whether or not x exists), to know, as in to be acquainted with that which exists—and about which I might have various degrees of knowledge. The respondent, Glaucon in this case, sensibly assumes that the quesƟon applies to that which is before me in consciousness, this is obviously something, i.e., it has a content, is the thought of something, and then, reasonably, that if this thought were not, it could clearly not be (even) known. But the sense of is and is not taken by Socrates in what immediately follows is not of the thoughts or knowledge itself as object, but rather as the being of the thing known, the object of knowledge, since his conclusion is that “In how ever many ways we examine the quesƟon, we can hold this to be certain: what fully is, is fully knowable and what in no way is, is altogether unknowable” (477a). As we shall see, this move, or intenƟonal ambiguity, is both necessary and consistent with the stage of the discussion. That it is neither an error, nor a trick or permanent manipulaƟon, is clear from the fact that it is recƟﬁed later in this dialogue and discussed explicitly as a problem elsewhere. Also, that slip is too carefully worked out in this passage. For, once again, what is oﬀered as the ﬁrst conclusion, is really part of the hypothesis on which the elaboraƟon of knowledge and opinion, and their objects, is based, as follows. “Knowledge is directed to what is while ignorance is of necessity directed to what is not,” which would also make ignorance into a capacity with its own proper object; both are somewhat dubious—but the statement that ignorance is in some way “directed to what is not,” or about nothing, when it takes itself to be about something, seems plausible. It is the same confusion to call a speech about nothing as if it were non-being, and to speak as if there were a capacity governing ignorance. Note that in the Divided Line, where the capaciƟes and their proper objects are spelled out in detail, there is no such capacity of ignorance, nor an ostensible object for it. Its purpose here is to provide a quasi-visual

symmetry such that we can search for an “intermediate” between ignorance and knowledge both with respect to the capaciƟes and their respecƟve objects; this intermediate is “opinion.” “Do we say that opinion is something?” One could not say no; here it is not clear whether in admiƫng to this one is referring to the statements or the capacity though in a few lines we will be looking for the “opinable” as the object of the capacity of opinion. Referring again to the objects, we are asked to agree that “if anything is in such a state as to be and not to be, will it not be intermediate between that which purely is and that which in no way is?— Yes it will be between them” (477a). Now we note two things—ﬁrst, that the statement is put hypotheƟcally, and second, that there is no reason why anything should be “intermediate,” nor any sense to the term; that is, its acceptance hangs heavily on the visual metaphor, on the image of something between the two extremes of the two other pairs. Thus it is, that “knowledge is directed to what is, while ignorance is of necessity directed to what is not,” and “we must ﬁnd something intermediate between ignorance and knowledge for that which lies between them, if there is such a thing”(477b), ambiguously the capacity or the proper object. Now opinion “is something,” and it is then asked whether it is “a diﬀerent capacity from knowledge or the same.” To which Glaucon answers, “A diﬀerent one.” But this is precisely what is at issue, whether opining and knowing are in fact disƟnguishable. Socrates then conƟnues, “Opinion then is directed to one object, and knowledge to another, according to the capacity of each?” “That is so.” “Knowledge then is by its nature directed to what is, to know it as it is,” and Socrates then breaks oﬀ, to introduce the discussion of capaciƟes. The conclusion of the sentence would have had to have been something like, “and opinion then is by its nature directed to what is fallible, what is and is not, to opine about it someƟmes as it is and someƟmes as it is not.” To turn to a discussion of capaciƟes (dunameis) at this point, and so abruptly, in mid-sentence as it were, “but I think it necessary ﬁrst to make this disƟncƟon”—means that the argument, the disƟncƟon between knowledge and opinion, cannot stand without some prior disƟncƟon being made and accepted. As we shall see, the disƟncƟon of diﬀerent capaciƟes does no more than spell out the hypotheses which are necessary and implicit in the argument between the lover of spectacles and the lover of the spectacle of truth, and then too, as

only the iniƟal arƟculaƟon of the maƩer qua hypothesis, not the grounding of its validity, not the explicaƟon of the ground on which it stands.[14] DUNAMIS AND ITS OBJECTS The disƟncƟon which Socrates introduces as a necessary preliminary step in the disƟnguishing between knowledge and opinion (and hence the philosopher from the sight-lover) is really rather extraordinary. “We shall say that capaciƟes are a certain class of realiƟes that enable us to do what we are capable of doing, and so with anything else which is capable of doing anything. I mean sight for example, or hearing, are among the capaciƟes, if you understand the class of things to which I want to refer” (477c). Now the ﬁrst thing to note is that the sentence is framed quite explicitly as a hypothesis that needs to be accepted as such; not, as Shorey’s translaƟon would have it,[15] as a quesƟon, but as an asserƟon —“we shall say” etc., as Grube correctly translates it. I have also adopted Grube’s term capaciƟes and avoided Shorey`s faculƟes. Shorey asserts that “Plato makes his simple meaning here quite plain, and it would be irrelevant to bring in modern denunciaƟons of the old faculty psychology.”[16] This does not face the problem—to call Plato’s meaning “simple” and let it go at that is rather too simple—what Plato intends by the term dunamis and what kind of level of reality dunameis are to have, are not issues to be resolved by a phrase such as “his simple meaning here is quite plain.” ParƟcularly given the sober metaphysical role given to dunameis and pathēmata (Rep.511d-e, 580d, 581a) in the discussion of the Divided Line, the asserƟon here that such capaciƟes are to be taken as a class of realiƟes, as a genos Ɵ tōn ontōn, must be seriously considered. It is apparently necessary if the disƟncƟons between knowledge and opinion and their objects are to hold.[17] The ﬁrst thing that is stressed in the development of the asserƟon of the soul’s capaciƟes is that whenever I speak of hearing or sight or some such, it is of something which I cannot directly perceive with the senses. “I cannot see any color or shape of a capacity, or any such aƩribute as I see in many other things” (477c). Thus, to the extent that I am willing to say that such things exist, that they are in some sense real, Socrates suggests that it is as an inference from what is indeed observed directly, and this is not an

observed thing or quality but a behavior or pracƟce. “In the case of a capacity I can only look to this: to what it is directed and what it achieves, and in this way I called it a capacity. . . . ” (477d) Now in what sense is it an inference, and in what sense is it necessary? This is not discussed here. All we are given is that this way of speaking is in some sense descripƟve of what “enables us to do what we are capable of doing,” e.g., of hearing and seeing. Hearing is not in the ear, nor sight in the eye; it is rather with their aid that we carry out these acƟviƟes, of which we have the capacity (Cf. 507c-e).[18] An ear by itself hears nothing. But to put it this way is not to explain really what this something is. Even though dressing the explanaƟon out with the proper details about the central nervous system, the psychology and physiology of percepƟon as we know it today is a help, the asserƟon that processes, and capaciƟes for them, are kinds of being is not rendered thus much less radical, it is sƟll in other words in need of philosophical jusƟﬁcaƟon. Socrates is presenƟng, as he says to Glaucon, “what he thinks about them.” And what is signiﬁcant for him here is that, ﬁrstly, they are supposed as having some sort of being, as a “class of realiƟes”; they are not visible, but rather inferred from the visible or experienƟal, as in some sense giving an account for how the visible as intelligible is possible, e.g., the collecƟon of sounds and sights perceived. Thus the asserƟon is in a sense an acknowledgement that we do these things, hearing, seeing, etc., and that collecƟng the visible, etc. is an act of consciousness, in other words of percepƟon—hence, “I can look only to this; to what it is directed and to what it achieves.” Thus capaciƟes are oﬀered as, are asserted as, hypotheses which account for the acƟvity of percepƟon. This is not to say that this accounƟng for is at all clear, or grounded in itself, which is why it is posited as a hypothesis at this point. Why call an acƟvity (or process) a reality? It seems as if the disƟncƟon between knowledge and opinion, and even more importantly between their respecƟve objects, is in some way made to depend on the acceptance of the disƟncƟon here made, that “capaciƟes are a certain class of realiƟes.” How and why this is so is not made clear unƟl the discussion of the Divided Line etc. and even then, will require some help from the Phaedo.

But an even more signiﬁcant detail is contained in the next phrase, poinƟng sƟll further in this direcƟon. For Socrates conƟnues that, “I called it a capacity; if it is related to the same object and achieves the same result I call it the same, while that which is related to a diﬀerent object and achieves a diﬀerent result I call a diﬀerent capacity” (477d).[19] Here, in disƟnguishing diﬀerent capaciƟes according to the diﬀerence in their objects, and in doing so by ﬁat, “I call” etc., it is clear that what is taken as the primary datum, so to speak, is the diﬀerence in the objects; i.e., that there are such diﬀerences, that they can be disƟnguished and grouped accordingly. If [20] the capacity is related to the same object then we can call it the same capacity at work. One would have thought that it would be the other way around, starƟng with the capacity and concluding with its relevant objects. But put in this way we see that what is at stake is disƟnguishing the kinds of being, or in this case the disƟncƟve objects of percepƟon, and that the capaciƟes serve as theoreƟcal enƟƟes (hypotheses at this point) which reﬂect our relaƟon to the phenomena, as classiﬁable, as well as reﬂecƟng our pracƟcal connecƟon to them, i.e., in our acƟviƟes as perceivers. (But again, that such construcƟons be called a species of realiƟes is sƟll at issue.) Having then made these disƟncƟons, or rather gained Glaucon’s assent to calling them in the same way, to “call it the same, if it is related to the same object” etc., Socrates then says, “let us go back,” that is, to the discussion of knowledge and opinion, noƟng that what has been accepted by Glaucon (and by us very provisionally) is the existence, in some mode, of non-visible being inferred from visible, and taken as in the nature of a hypotheƟcal, as theories for the pracƟce of percepƟon, and in general “anything else which is capable of doing anything.” Glaucon is then ﬁrst asked if he accepts knowledge as a capacity, then if opinion is one, and he agrees that both are such. He is reminded that he had “agreed that knowledge and opinion are not the same,” that is, the content, not the capacity. And he again says they are not the same, adding that, “how can any intelligent man say that a fallible thing is the same as an infallible one.” Socrates then adds, “each of these two is by its nature directed to a diﬀerent object and achieves a diﬀerent result.” Glaucon easily agrees, the diﬀering results being fallibility and infallibility.

Knowledge then is “directed to what is, to know it as it is,” and opinion is taken to be a diﬀerent acƟvity directed to a diﬀerent object. “And we say that opinion opines?” “Yes.” “[i] Does it opine on the same subject which knowledge knows; [ii] are the knowable and the opinable the same, or is this impossible?” (478a) But note here that Socrates is presenƟng two rather diﬀerent proposiƟons (labeled i. and ii. above) as if they were the same. Glaucon, not seeing this, replies negaƟvely to the concluding formulaƟon, i.e., that “the knowable and the opinable” are not the same, and in so doing commits himself to the formulaƟon immediately preceding it, which is in fact not at all the same; namely, he again is brought to assert that opinion does not “opine on the same subject which knowledge knows,” and hence that they have diﬀerent objects. Now clearly this is not at all the case without some further explanaƟon, since I may have one person with opinion and another with knowledge about the same item, e.g., whether the exterior angle of a triangle is equal to the sum of the interior opposite angles, or whether jusƟce is indeed “paying one’s debts,” and if so in what sense (i.e., to whom, and what do I owe). Thus it is not so much, or not always or only, what one is talking about, but rather how and in what regard. Consider the discussion of the objects of the true and false astronomer, where it is not simply a quesƟon of what one looks at, the same literal object, but rather what in this one takes as important, what one takes under consideraƟon. Thus, if opinion has as its proper objects the things of generaƟon and decay, that which is as changeable as opinion itself, it is not so because opinion looks at one object while knowledge looks at another, elsewhere located, as it were. Rather, that knowledge searches for the ﬁxed that is the knowable in the changeable, while opinion aƩaches itself to that which is changeable, believing it ﬁxed: either materially changeable, when this is taken for the truth, or subject to generaƟon and decay because of the weak way that opinion is aƩached to its object, as in an opinion about the relaƟon of the angles of a triangle which it cannot demonstrate to be so, and hence which opinion might as easily assert to be otherwise. To return to the text here, opinion can indeed “opine on the same subject which knowledge knows” but its relaƟon to it is a diﬀerent one. Or, one might express it by saying that they have a diﬀerent object regarding the content of each; the object qua subject maƩer (e.g., virtue) can be the same though radically diﬀerent in

our relaƟon to it. Knowledge and opinion behave diﬀerently in relaƟon to the same phenomenon, and produce a diﬀerent object. Further, and more to the point here, given what Socrates is up to, the objects can be diﬀerent only if we admit of Ideas as the object of knowledge, as contrasted to opinion, which has change or the intermediate between knowledge and ignorance as its object. But if this is what is required, then this needs an explanaƟon from the side of the object, (as the jusƟﬁcaƟon for disƟnct capaciƟes already discussed) and an exposiƟon of capaciƟes. Gail Fine gives a detailed analysis of the same passages, in her oŌen- cited arƟcle “Knowledge and Belief in Republic V.”[21] This is not the place for a detailed discussion of her argument and my objecƟons. Fine’s main point in interpreƟng the text is to oppose an interpretaƟon of the disƟncƟon between knowledge and belief as based on a claim for diﬀerent objects of knowledge and belief (opinion) and the resultant “two worlds (TW)” interpretaƟon. In TW knowledge would have radically diﬀerent objects, the Forms, than belief or opinion, which would have as its objects, sensibles. She argues rather that “knowledge and belief are disƟnguished not by their diﬀerent sets of objects, but by their truth implicaƟons” (139). “Note that by the ‘two worlds theory’ I do not mean only the theory that there are Forms as well as sensibles (a theory I do not dispute), but especially the epistemological claim that there is only knowledge of Forms and only belief about sensibles, a claim I shall dispute” (121). Fine also acknowledges that at 478e-480a (132 ﬀ. steps 28-36.) Plato starts from the non-controversial agreements that are garnered in the imagined elencƟc with the sight-lovers, then “shiŌs away from is-v” (veridical). But, Fine argues that this is sƟll compaƟble with the view that the capacity of belief is set over the set of true and false beliefs (T) (contra degrees of truth interpretaƟon)—and allows that the shiŌ is only to is-p (predicaƟve), not to is-e (existenƟal). She notes that the arguments “menƟon the availability of content, not just the truth or falsity of parƟcular contents” (131). While I see that the text will sustain a “veridical/contents” analysis, as contrasted to an objects analysis, in some places this appears strained. It seems to me rather that the play on the meanings of esƟ is intenƟonal ambiguity etc. as is the complement of epi as object versus content—that this is linked to the use of dunamis in the argument, and that this is to point forward to the

metaphysics of the Line etc. I reject TW insofar as it posits an otherworldly realm of Forms, and as exclusive objects of knowledge, but rather on the basis of a reinterpretaƟon of “is-e” (existenƟal), one that preserves a variant of an objects reading over against Fine’s contents reading (T, for is- v). Fine is out to show that there is an interpretaƟon of the passage that is “plausible,” hence saving Plato from either mistakes in the argument or violaƟng the “dialecƟcal requirement” of a non-controversial starƟng point. My interpretaƟon, by contrast, sees the argument as intenƟonally playing on ambiguiƟes. I think the diﬀerence also is that Fine is concerned with the applicaƟon of knowledge and belief, especially of belief, and to deny that each is limited to its own supposed domain, respecƟvely of Forms and sensibles, and here I would agree. But my concern is with the enƟƟes/objects that populate the world (more than merely the sensible), and Plato’s ontological arguments for them. It may well be, as she argues, that “knowledge and belief are disƟnguished not by their diﬀerent sets of objects, but by their truth implicaƟons,” and in parƟcular in this passage, that is, that they can be. But one wants to know what enƟƟes/objects of the world these dunameis pick out when they make their claims. Fine says as she concludes that while “all knowledge begins with knowledge of Forms, but it need not end with them too” (137).
