And so the issue of parƟcipaƟon is implicitly raised—but this is I take it primarily an ontological rather than a merely epistemological issue. The “two worlds” account that she eﬀecƟvely argues against is a rather limited, and limiƟng, one. In the end one that does not make much sense. But some version of a two worlds interpretaƟon is eventually going to be required if Forms are going to be more than meanings etc. How does Fine’s veridical or contents analysis rather than an objects analysis help us (and I think to an extent that it does) relate to sorƟng out the ontological issues? But the quesƟon of whether and how there are two objects or one, and whether two capaciƟes or one, is resolved in a most peculiar way by Glaucon. For his actual response to the quesƟon posed at 478a, as quoted above, is as follows: “It is impossible [to have the same object for knowledge and opinion] following from our agreement. If a diﬀerent capacity is directed to a diﬀerent object, and opinion and knowledge are capaciƟes but diﬀerent, it follows that the knowable and the opinable cannot be the same” (478a). Now what is odd here is that this formulaƟon reverses the procedure that

had been iniƟally proposed—here we are going from capaciƟes to their objects, rather than from the pracƟces and objects to the supposiƟon of capaciƟes. “If a diﬀerent capacity is directed to a diﬀerent object . . . and opinion and knowledge are capaciƟes but diﬀerent, it follows that the knowable and the opinable cannot be the same” (Cf. 477d). Thus, rather than looking for intermediate being (between ignorance and knowledge) and then inferring the capacity, as was proposed, we end up taking the capaciƟes as hypotheses, as casual supposiƟons, parƟcularly the existence of an intermediate capacity, opinion, and then looking for the opinable, intermediate being. On the grounds that “opinion must be something” (but without disƟnguishing between the opinion as statement and that about which it is made, the opinable), it is assumed as corresponding to the changeable by nature: “If anything is in such a state as to be and not to be . . . then it is intermediate. . . . ” But this also assumes the existence of (the disƟncƟon between) opinion and knowledge. Both intermediates are assumed, i) that of an object that is and is not at the same Ɵme, assuming the extremes of being and non-being between which it lies, and ii) the intermediate of opinion, as the corresponding capacity, found, as it were, between knowledge and ignorance. The method, of “applying the extreme terms to the extremes and intermediate to intermediate” simply maps out the area of cogniƟon and object without jusƟfying it—as is reﬂected in the physicality of the ostensible argument, ﬁnding the intermediate as somehow rightly between. While even for knowledge we cannot truly assert it as a capacity unƟl we know its object, yet the discussion proceeds on the basis of this; on the basis, for example, of accepƟng that knowledge and opinion are “not one but two” and disƟnguishable as the “fallible” versus “infallible” (477e). The result as well of this exchange is that in a discussion that has shiŌed to quesƟons of epistemology and ontology, we have moved from the visible to the non-visible, at least as concerns human being, through the introducƟon of the noƟon of capaciƟes and their corresponding noeƟc objects.[22] But this model is no more than that, a model, introduced somewhat covertly as the hypotheses needed if we are to be able to disƟnguish between the philosopher and the lover of spectacles of the non-philosophical sort.

Let us turn again for a moment to the relaƟon of Glaucon, our interlocutor, and “those others,” the sight-lovers. Michael Stokes, in “Plato and the Sight-lovers of the Republic,”[23] noƟng Glaucon’s “too ready agreement with Socrates,” (109, 117 and following) takes him as conƟnuing the discussion as an honest, if not too swiŌ, representaƟve of the sight- lovers to fulﬁll the “dialecƟcal requirement” (that is, an elenƟc beginning in agreement) on their behalf. On the other hand a true sight-lover, he thinks, perhaps might have done beƩer, but only if he were clever enough—a riposte is available. Stokes tries to ﬂesh this out, though the eventual result would sƟll be elencƟc. Now Glaucon in Book V has not yet been exposed to the exposiƟon of the Line and Cave etc. to follow, much less passed through the educaƟonal journey itself. Then too, I claim that Glaucon is in part tempted by the posiƟon of Thrasymachus, or at the very least is in need of being persuaded that it is wrong. For these two reasons, when Socrates asks that Glaucon “answer for” the sight-lovers, rather than responding as a too compliant stand-in as Stokes would suggest, he is indeed answering for himself. Further, Plato is fully aware that the development of the argument is not altogether philosophically sound, convincing or suﬃcient. This is why the conƟnuaƟon in Book VI, in discussing “how men [the philosophers] can be qualiﬁed in both knowledge and experience” (485a) to rule in the just city must include an ontological dimension (and even then), a needed dimension of which Glaucon is on the whole unaware. Stokes argues that an “internal incoherence” is developed in the posiƟon of the sight-lovers. “The desired eﬀect of the whole elenchus appears to be the showing up, or at least the manufacture, of an internal incoherence in the posiƟon of those who deny in their confusion the existence of ‘the beauƟful by itself,’ ‘beauty by itself’ and the like.” IniƟally they hold the manifold objects of sights and sounds actually to be the only object of knowledge—the beauƟful simply can only mean the collecƟon of beauƟful things, and is all there is to know—while they eventually are forced in the elenchus to idenƟfy those objects with the object of opinion, hence leŌ without an object of knowledge, to be ﬁlled in, as it were, by the Forms. “The objects of the philosopher’s knowledge are taken for granted in that their existence is not directly proved and their properƟes are

entered without argument. Book Five aƩempts rather to prove or persuade us that the dwellers in what will become Plato’s Cave are incoherent. At best, it uses that incoherence to point the way out of the Cave” (131). Stokes holds that the “separaƟon of the provinces [my emphasis] of belief and knowledge in the Republic need not be accepted as an item of Plato’s own stock of philosophical beliefs on the basis of Republic 5, whatever may go on in other parts of the Republic” (132). Stokes goes on: The elencƟc nature of the argument and the dialecƟcal requirement issue in a disƟncƟon that refers to ‘objects’ for belief and knowledge based in an existenƟal reading of esƟ/einai. But there is ambiguity at 477b10 and, crucially, at 478a6, where Socrates, in discussing ‘opposites’ slips ‘from the ‘being’ of predicaƟon . . . to a conclusion . . . about existence. (129) And Stokes traces the dialecƟcal success of the argument to the ready acceptance by any sight-lover of at least a dunamis for objects of sight and sound. (Contrast Fine’s aƩempted veridical reading throughout.) I would argue rather that there is a repeated intenƟonal play on the various meanings of einai, and other slights of hand. (Cf. Stokes, 117) Stokes does not appear to note, or at least to make as much of, the reversal of the direcƟon in the argument—beginning in objects to capaciƟes, then from capaciƟes to looking for a suitable object—a move that I take to be crucial. The result of all this, is that while Stokes’ analysis is on the whole appealing, it is precisely the image of Glaucon’s character in relaƟon to the limitaƟons and manipulaƟons of the argument at this stage, and the need for further development, that are necessary to point the way out for the reader, if not altogether for Glaucon. Further, even the middle books do not do more than sketch this out. The knowledge—opinion disƟncƟon, and the sense of capaciƟes for each kind of object can be more fully explicated only by turning to the discussion and images of the Phaedo (chapters six, seven and eight below). The capaciƟes will receive further elaboraƟon, and further jusƟﬁcaƟon, in the discussion of the Divided Line, etc. We note here the following points: i. that they are the ﬁrst introducƟon of the non-visible; ii. that they are inferred from, or rather support, the comprehensibility of the

visible; iii. that they are covert hypotheses, and that being such is appropriate to the level of the argument (cf. Socrates’ comment regarding method and level concerning the divisions of the soul at 434d ﬀ.); iv. that the discussion is introduced abruptly, in mid-thought, to stress the noƟon of a necessary hypothesis; v. ﬁnally, that such a mapping of a structure which holds the world of knower and known together is in some sense an image, a model in words, in thought, which proposes to present, or rather re-present, a hypothesis of how knowing and being are possible. Yet this image or paradigmaƟc model is sƟll rooted to an extent in the physical mode, in imagining rather than its noeƟc counterpart. Thus opinion, like the opinable, is located with the rhetorical help of the language of physical metaphor, the use of “between” and “assigning.” So Socrates asks, “Is it outside these, exceeding either knowledge in clarity or ignorance in obscurity?” “Neither.” Opinion is ﬁnally described as “more shadowy than knowledge but clearer than ignorance,” the conclusion being that it then “lies between the two (478c). It remained, however, to say more about that x which was supposed as the object of the new found capacity of opinion which has now “appeared between these two [knowledge and ignorance].” “It is now leŌ to us to ﬁnd that which partakes of both being and non-being . . . in order that, if it appears, we can rightly call it the opinable, thus applying the extreme terms to the extremes, and the intermediate to the intermediate” (NoƟng again the visual, pseudo-logical methodology). And thus “these things being established [the acceptance of the capaciƟes and at least two of their objects], I shall say, I want a word with, and an answer from, the good fellow who does not believe there is a BeauƟful itself, or any Form of Beauty itself, which remains eternally the same in all respects, but who believes that many beauƟful things exist, that lover of spectacles who would not allow anyone to say that the BeauƟful is one, and so with the just and all the rest” (479a). In the ensuing discussion there is more philosophizing, but once again, as we shall see, it is both intenƟonally ambiguous and, for those who see behind the scenes, really another statement of the hypotheses which underlie the disƟncƟon between knowledge and opinion, hence underlies that form of seeing which properly disƟnguishes the lover of the spectacle of truth from the one

who, loving appearances, himself appears, resembles, or seems like the philosopher. The discussion will invoke again the noƟon of opposites—having located an intermediate capacity, with regard to the objects of cogniƟon, the beauƟful being the prime example. Looking ﬁrst at the dramaƟc form, we note that, once again, the capacity has been found ﬁrst, and we are now to look for the corresponding object “if it appears”; we have, as noted before, reversed the original procedure, which was to have been to infer capaciƟes from the existence of the respecƟve object. Socrates then asks whether “there is one of those just acƟons which does not also appear unjust” and so with the many beauƟful things, as also with the many double, “are they any less half than double?” Glaucon then agrees that, in his words, “each of these things partakes of both opposites.” And as he says about the beauƟful, a few lines earlier, “beauƟful things will appear ugly under certain circumstances.” The conclusion to which we are supposedly driven is then put: “Is then” Socrates asks, “each of the many things, more than it is not, that which anyone might call it?” To which Glaucon, somewhat huﬃng and puﬃng over the meaning of this riddle, seƩles nicely for an ambiguity in the new found object such as he recalls concerning such riddling conundrums: “Those things too are ambiguous and one cannot know for certain either that they are or that they are not, or that they are both or neither,” thus covering all bases, as it were. To this, Socrates adds, “Well, have you any beƩer way of dealing with them? Can you put them in a beƩer place than between being and nonbeing?” Once again the physical imagery is invoked, the opinable has been found in its place between being and nonbeing, to be “not more obscure” than the object of ignorance, nor is it “clearer” than the object of knowledge (479c). And then the ﬁnal image of “The many convenƟonal opinions of the majority about Beauty and the other things [which] are rolling around between being and nonbeing,” “the wandering intermediate, grasped by the intermediate capacity” (479d). Note that it is the very opinions themselves, and not the opinable qua objects about which opinion opines, which are characterized as “rolling around.” One supposes that the changeable which is its object is to be tarred with the same brush, but it is

interesƟng that here the opinions themselves have been subsƟtuted for the objects. The opinions have in eﬀect been made into objects.[24] But let us look more closely at the argument itself. “BeauƟful things will appear ugly under certain circumstances.” What exactly does this mean? (It is Glaucon’s statement.) Does this mean that a beauƟful statue is only so subjecƟvely, relaƟve to the viewer? And what of a just act? Plato would certainly not accept such an ethical or aestheƟc relaƟvity. The only relaƟvity permissible would be an objecƟve relaƟvity: so, in the famous example used with Cephalus in Book I, whether returning a weapon held in trust was to be just or not would depend on the circumstances, but for a given situaƟon the judgment ought to be the same. But Glaucon clearly has in mind the coexistence in the object of opposite qualiƟes, hence the applicability of opposite predicates. Socrates: “So with things big and small, light and heavy, does any predicate we apply to them apply to them any more than it’s opposite?” Glaucon: “No, each of these things partakes of both opposites” (479b). In the Phaedo, in order to avoid this and preserve the intelligibility of each quality, each opposite is described as “ﬂeeing” at the approach of the other. But for Glaucon, not only are the opposites said to coexist in the object somehow, but it would seem that the many opposite opinions about the same object are a puzzle to him—for when Socrates had asked “Is then, each of the many things, more than it is not, that which anyone might call it,” (479b) his response is, as we have said, “This is like those double meanings one is entertained with at banquets . . . ” and his puzzlement may be as much at the fact that diﬀerent people make opposite judgments about the same object, “that which anyone might call it,” as it is puzzlement over the ambiguity of the object itself. That he is so willing to agree with Socrates that knowledge is so diﬀerent from opinion, and that the former is somehow linked to “that which remains eternally the same in all respects” does not mean that he in fact knows the diﬀerence, and understands the nature of opinion and the opinable! Socrates’ formulaƟon to Glaucon is revealing; “And is there one of those just acƟons which will not also appear unjust? And of pious acƟons, one that will not appear impious? And of all those beauƟful things, is there one which will not also appear ugly?” (479a) This is rather close to precisely that relaƟvism that Socrates is at pains in fact to avoid—for the

reader, it is saved from that by the signal in the choice of the word “appears (phanēsetai)”—the beauƟful can appear ugly, the just unjust, and be judged so, while for Glaucon, the object is, for the moment, paradoxically, both. Finally, we note that the opponent of a beauƟful itself need not even posit the many beauƟful things, in order for the many beauƟful things each to be subject to the appropriate relaƟvity. It is not that they are many beauƟful things versus one Beauty which is crucial to their being subject to opposite qualiƟes, but rather the diﬀerence in changing circumstances; and yet the conﬂict is precisely with those who defend the existence of the many with no unifying one. Thus the argument concerning opposites here will not serve to convince the more perspicacious lover of spectacles that there are in fact two kinds of object, and a diﬀerence between opinion and knowledge. The contrast is between the many which change with circumstances, and the BeauƟful one “which remains eternally the same in all respects.” The “good fellow who does not believe” in the laƩer is called a “lover of spectacles” precisely because what passes in its mulƟtude, the many beauƟful things, are his sole object. Now for Plato as well, the world in which the BeauƟful is manifest is also a world of many beauƟful things; this is then accounted for by reference to the BeauƟful itself which, in itself is claimed to be “eternally the same in all respects.” But it is in fact not the manyness of the appearances of beauƟful things that is then brought forth in the argument with “this fellow,” rather the fact that the same thing (existent) can appear beauƟful and then ugly (either at the same Ɵme to diﬀerent viewers, or the same object at diﬀerent epochs, etc.)—which is then generalized to a theory of opposites. That is to say, it is not so much Beauty and how it works, but rather the change or ﬂux of the world subject to such diverse predicates—it is judgment that is focused on, not parƟcipaƟon—the manyness as seen from the perspecƟve of percepƟon rather than Being, although this is in fact the aspect that needs to be supplied if the intermediate of judgment is to be legiƟmately founded. And yet this cannot be done without a thorough exploraƟon of the relaƟon of Being and Knowing as provided in the following passages describing the Cave and Line. And, I have suggested, a further elaboraƟon of dunamis to be found in the Phaedo. [25]

The theoreƟcal base provided by the middle books is an ontological response to a Thrasymachus, as an archetypal lover of sights and sounds, but one that is addressed to the reader—and the abstract dryness of the Line is matched by the wetness, so to speak, of the Cave. Then too, this is primordially self-rule, hence addressed to the struggle within ourselves that mistakes a sensual dream-world for what is more real, and of more real value—hence an ontological error at root. Thrasymachus will never be convinced, only silenced, and his appeal to others present can be diminished according to their lights, and by diﬀerent means—while the Thrasymachus within the philosophically inclined reader is to be tamed rather with a philosophical, ontological muthos. In sum, the discussion that produces the knowledge—opinion disƟncƟon of capaciƟes in correlaƟon with the disƟncƟon of their objects is then, I suggest, intenƟonally provisional. This is reﬂected in the very structure of the Republic, and gives a real philosophical jusƟﬁcaƟon to the digression of the middle books. For these books will spell out in greater detail, in detailed images, just how these disƟncƟons are mapped out in the worlds of discourse and experience. This mapping, or what serves as Plato’s own explicaƟon, sƟll remains a sketch. We will need to turn to the Phaedo in search of further support for Plato’s ontology of images (and my own version of TW). That the BeauƟful (or the Just) is one, is “always the same,” is presented as a saving hypothesis—it too, at this point, exists like the image of the ideal city. Each presents an “image in words” at the level of the hypotheses of the Line. As a supposiƟon, it is oﬀered as an account for the appearances of the many just things, etc. but is itself in need of a ground. The image of the ideal city, whether taken as the poliƟcal polis or the soul, is constructed with an eye to jusƟce, which in turn exists only as a hypothesis or image thus far. Moreover, this would be true as well of the claim that the philosopher and not the sight-lovers should rule the city and, its analogue, that reason should rule the soul. When asked whether the imagined clamoring voices of the many are now tamed, Glaucon’s posiƟve reply, and the way Plato has him phrase it, is perhaps signiﬁcant. It might be taken to reﬂect the level of the argument, as well as Glaucon’s own place in it. Socrates: “Will they be very angry with us for calling them that? [lovers of the spectacle of the many]” Glaucon: “Not if they take my advice [that is, my opinion], for it is not lawful with

those who speak the truth” (480a). In what is to follow, the linear and physically vague images of “rolling around,” of “shadows” and “dreams,” of the “intermediate” which is “between,” will at least be made analogically precise and ﬂeshed out, if schemaƟcally, in the descripƟon of the dynamic of the Divided Line and the assignment there of pathēmata, as more speciﬁcally technical epistemic powers (dunameis). This world of shadows will be even more vividly outlined in the Cave image, where the dynamic and the psychological dimension ﬂesh out the raƟonal dynamic of the Line. Taken together, the Cave and Divided Line images introduce us to Plato’s vision of just how the soul as image-maker at various levels elaborates, reads out, its world of experience. The two images produce a portrait of the dynamic of soul, world and Idea. Opinion as disƟnguishable from knowledge is not laid to rest so easily, any more than the deﬁniƟon of jusƟce of the end of Book IV is to be taken as complete.[26] A more exact, a clearer, more precise image or paradigm (paradeigma) is needed for both. That is, the image of jusƟce of Books I through IV is indeed quite detailed but, to use a Cartesian disƟncƟon, the image we have there developed, while certainly clear enough (i.e., vivid), is not yet what Descartes would call disƟnct.[27] NOTES 1. At the very least, as Irwin suggests (Plato ’ s Moral Theory, 321 n.47) the Forms in applicaƟon do not produce a permanent Platonic deﬁniƟonal absolute standard for moral conduct, though they are also said to be that by which we measure the parƟcular judgment. This points, in eﬀect, to the subject of separaƟon to be dealt with below, the relaƟon of separaƟon to the Platonic method of hypothesis, and the metaphysical aspect of these two noƟons—in contrast (at least per Irwin, 158, pace Vlastos regarding Socrates) to the SocraƟc elencƟc. I will argue, though on diﬀerent grounds, that Irwin is right in rejecƟng the view that “Forms are known by some kind of direct acquaintance issuing in greater certainty about morals than an elencƟc deﬁniƟon could provide. There is no reason to ascribe such a view to Plato” (Ibid. cf. 225-26). 2. Pace Shorey. “Our problem is apparently solved” (Republic, vol. I, pg. xvi). Taking the possibility issue to apply to the literal city contributes to

not seeing the ontological necessity to conƟnue, i.e., the search for a ground for the implicit ontology of the image in words of the just city (the jusƟﬁcaƟon of the principles of its construcƟon). 3. Terry Penner, “The Historical Socrates and Plato's Early Dialogues: Some Philosophical QuesƟons,” in Annas and Rowe, eds. New PerspecƟves, 189- 212. 4. Though a unity or one only as a normaƟve ideal. See Hans Gadamer, The Idea of the Good in Platonic-Aristotelian Philosophy (New Haven: Yale University Press, 1986) and P. Christopher Smith's introducƟon. Unity as an ideal goal in this life is to accept a perpetual falling short or breakdown both in pracƟce and in principle. 5. This is not to say that non-moral potenƟal sources of eudaimonia, such as health, wealth, etc., just those candidates that would interest a Thrasymachus, etc., are not to be considered. Deﬁning their relaƟonship to virtue and happiness is in fact crucial to understanding the laƩer. As previously indicated, I agree with Vlastos' ﬁnal posiƟon, that neither Plato nor Socrates hold either an IdenƟty Thesis or an instrumentalist view of the relaƟon of virtue to happiness, that consequently non-moral goods, while high on the list for a eudaemonist, are not maƩers of indiﬀerence, as they would have to be for the IdenƟty thesis, and that they are condiƟonally good, dependent for their contribuƟon to eudaimonia on their right use, their connecƟon to wisdom. 6. See Gregory Vlastos, “JusƟce and Happiness in the Republic” in Platonic Studies, ed. Gregory Vlastos (Princeton: Princeton University Press, 1969), 111-39. Vlastos thinks that Plato requires that the truly just man (possessed of inner harmony) be also socially just—that “to do one's own” applied to the whole man, as opposed to the parts within him, must be taken in more than just the sense of fulﬁlling the appropriate role within the ideal polis. The larger sense must be one that includes a self-imposed having one's own, the limitaƟon of pleonecƟc desires, etc., which has perforce a social dimension but that this is not fully developed in argument, and Vlastos aƩempts to complete the logical picture. For Vlastos, Plato has established only that if the just man is just in the way that the ideal polis is just, and this is by each doing his own, then more argument is needed (and one that is available within the Platonic framework). But what if a man who does his own is not to be construed at

all as fulﬁlling even a special form of relaƟonal jusƟce (Vlastos' just-1) but rather as sƟll only an image of psychic jusƟce (just-2)? If the polis is designed to mirror the soul in its virtues, and that is all, then rather than needing a repair of the argument (133), social jusƟce exists, at least in the image of the ideal polis, only as an incidental consequence—and this is as true of the happiness of the individuals within it, as Plato expressly says in reply to the query about the happiness even of the guardians (419a, 466a, cf. 472c). The temporal sequence in the image of the educaƟon of the guardians describes the replacement of a revised virtue sƟll based on habit and training with the moƟvaƟons of raƟonal desire, and if this is the case I do not see that Vlastos' repair is needed by the Ɵme the end, in both senses, is reached, if indeed doing one's own is living appropriately for the whole soul as a unity.(Cf. Irwin on 441c-e, 201, 204 ﬀ. and Vlastos 331-32 n.29, n.30.) 7. I do not say that Plato does not have a poliƟcal philosophy, nor that the Republic does not in part and in places express it, simply that both dramaƟcally and philosophically the understanding of the soul and its fate is ontologically prior. 8. For the interpreter who misses this playful irony, who does not see at what level possibility is being discussed and the image of the city as image, Plato is “pessimisƟc” (Cross and Woozley, 199) and/or anƟ-democraƟc (Popper), since few are called and even fewer chosen, and divine inspiraƟon is a poliƟcal deus ex machina. This is not to deny that Plato may indeed at some point have been pessimisƟc about insƟtuƟng a just city, but it is not this possibility that is the subject of the Republic unless the funcƟon of image is lost, as per Glaucon and Adeimantus (and commentators). That they do so and hence raise the issue of real possibility in the Third Wave, is precisely what we are meant to see—and to ask just why they do so. The result of asking why they are stuck at the literal level, why they have diﬃculty seeing the image as image, is that we are led to see the ontological predisposiƟon of the human psyche as an obstacle to knowledge of reality, and to point us in the right direcƟon, a direcƟon which is also contained within the everyday experience of the psyche. For the importance and the signiﬁcance of seeing the “image as image,” see Jacob Klein, Meno, 113-15.

And there we may once again disƟnguish between a saƟsﬁed interlocutor and the real argument of the text, which points ahead. Both authors menƟoned have Plato assuming the knowledge-opinion, fallible-infallible disƟncƟon. See J.C. Gosling, “Doxa and Dunamis in Plato’s Republic,” Phronesis, vol. 13 (1968): 119-30. Gosling, in an otherwise interesƟng arƟcle, does not disƟnguish between the admissions of Glaucon and the paciﬁcaƟon of the lovers of spectacles. The argument is not directed, as he says, to them, but carried on, such as it is, by Glaucon, “You may reply for them,” Socrates says, that is, Glaucon is made to assume, diﬀerent objects, Beauty itself etc. (476d) Gosling would like 479b5-d1 to refer to answers not to objects, but it ambiguously refers to both. His conclusion, that dunameis are diﬀerent “abiliƟes” and not faculƟes avoids the issue. His statement that “applicaƟons of diﬀerent abiliƟes . . . [imply] applicaƟons of the same faculty” sƟll leaves the relaƟon of subject to object unclariﬁed. The issue is how the process is structured, and what is concluded about objects and their image in the knowing soul. (Cf. nn.13, 25.) 23. Michael C. Stokes, “Plato and the Sight-lovers of the Republic,” Apeiron, The Language of the Cave, vol.25/4 (1992): 266-89. 24. Cf. I. M. Crombie, An ExaminaƟon of Plato’s Doctrines. (London: Routledge and Kegan Paul, 1963). Crombie aƩempts to transform a clearly troublesome ontological claim into a harmless epistemological one. For the sentence, “That which is altogether existent is altogether knowable, that

which is in no way existent is altogether unknowable,” (477a3-4) Crombie suggests as the meaning, “That which is without qualiﬁcaƟon a fact is without qualiﬁcaƟon a proper object of knowledge, whereas that which is without qualiﬁcaƟon a ﬁgment is in no way a proper object of knowledge” (66). If I am right about the dramaƟc play here, then there would be no necessity to avoid the usual interpretaƟon, which as Crombie points out has as its result that “we should have to ﬁnd a place for the objects of doxa 'between existence and non- existence'—and that means nothing.” It is for this reason that Crombie rejects it; the very reason which leads to my accepƟng it as what is intended at this stage, I have argued. 25. Contrast Eugenio Benitez, “Republic 476d6-e2: Plato’s dialecƟcal requirement,” The Review of Metaphysics, vol. 49, No. 3 (March 1996): 516-46. Contrary to Benitez, I argue that the shiŌs in the meaning of esƟ are intenƟonal and aporeƟc with regard to the sight-lovers. That is, that it begins in easy agreement, exercising the ostensible dialecƟcal requirement, but exploits the ambiguity of esƟ to make for what for them would be an uncomfortable conclusion. For the philosophical reader, the argument for diﬀerent objects, and in what sense, requires the elaboraƟon of Books VI and VII to follow, an elaboraƟon not strictly required by Glaucon, who, at the end of Book V, already accepts a Beauty in itself, etc., paradoxically as a belief. Benitez insists that the knowledge-belief (opinion) disƟncƟon at 473c11- 480a13 be read in the context of the Third Wave paradox, which concerns the actual possibility of the ideal city. He holds that posiƟng a philosopher- ruler leads directly to disƟnguishing the lover of sights from the philosopher, and that these are disƟnguished by the diﬀering objects of their sight—the laƩer having access to the Forms while the former is bound to opinion. He thus supports a version of the two worlds theory (TW) as a consequence of beliefs being Ɵed to the unstable, changeable sensible world, and defending an objects over a contents version for the complement of esƟ on the basis of his analysis of what the text will support. He holds that Fine is wrong to subsƟtute is-v (veridical reading) contents for objects—hence that some version of TW is required. Generally, I would agree that the knowledge-opinion disƟncƟons in the text are based on quesƟons that Socrates asks that require an ontological rather a logical response, hence are of “ontological import” (the content

versus object dispute.) But the presence (parousia) of the Forms, along with a diﬀerent interpretaƟon of both dunameis and logoi in a sense closer to Fine, would not require even Benitez’s version of TW. 26. Compare Rowe, Philosophical WriƟng, 200-213, who also stresses the two diﬀerent audiences, and the “persuasive funcƟon” and “immediate rhetorical purpose.” Rowe argues as follows. The sight-lovers believe that the various beauƟful objects are beauƟful—and see no need to go looking for a beauƟful itself beyond this, while the philosophers believe that beauƟful objects have beauty (when they do), and point to the need to account for the acƟvity and success of the collecƟon that we make. The sight-lovers err in “misidenƟfying one thing with another, namely parƟcular beauƟful things with beauty, and indeed with beauty itself (since that is what beauty is)” (206). So the problem is not with the objects as with what the sight-lovers believe, and believe they know. In other words, unbeknownst to themselves, when the sight-lovers “run eagerly to see them, as beauƟful things, they must already be idenƟfying them as beauƟful, rather than as ugly, and so be separaƟng oﬀ their beauty from their ugliness. So beauty is something that beauƟful things have, not what they are” (208). For Glaucon, speaking for the sight-lovers, what Socrates needs to do for the moment is to “persuade the sight-lovers that their state of mind (their dianoia, 476d5-6) is one of belief,” (205) i.e., that their knowledge claim is inadequate or unworkable, while the philosopher’s account, in appealing to a beauƟful-itself, has explanatory force. For the reader, the work of jusƟfying this diﬀerence remains to be done, to explore just what the objects of knowledge need to be, if knowledge is to be possible, and accounted for, as well as accounƟng for the even “parƟal truth” that the sight-lovers have in picking out beauƟful parƟculars. Thus the following elaboraƟon of the three similes. Note that according to Rowe, in terms again of the “immediate rhetorical purpose,” Plato does not strictly speaking argue for two sets of objects and two faculƟes or capaciƟes, rather “we have two states of mind—knowledge and mere belief—that ulƟmately ‘deal with’ [are ‘set over’] the same set of objects [parƟculars], only with one of them doing it more successfully that the other” (213). 27. The image of the ideal of jusƟce is not yet of something that, in Descartes's sense, is a real possibility—it is not yet philosophically

grounded. Descartes says that though the images of fantasy are vivid enough, and in some sense clear, for example griﬃns, they do not merit the disƟncƟon of existence as they are not also raƟonally disƟnct. See The Principles of Philosophy, Part I. Principle LX, 243-44 (cf. Principle XLV) in The Philosophical Works of Descartes, in two volumes, edited and translated by Elizabeth Haldane and G.R.T. Ross. (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1967). This cannot really be understood without clariﬁcaƟon of the concept of a “real disƟncƟon,” in Descartes a technical term. See the seventh reply to ObjecƟons II (vol. II. 52-59), especially on the relaƟon of objecƟve to formal reality. Compare the conclusion of Prop. IV “Hence, at least through the instrumentality of the Divine Power, mind can exist apart from body, and body apart from mind,” and DeﬁniƟon X, “But now, substances that can exist apart from each other, are really disƟnct.”

Chapter 3 The Cave: Education and the Lack of It BELIEF, KNOWLEDGE, AND THE GOOD Book VI begins with the asserƟon that “aŌer a somewhat lengthy discussion,[1] the philosophers, and those who are not, have each of them with some diﬃculty revealed who they are” (484a). They are then to move on to the “next topic,” while Socrates, in passing, notes that the diﬀerence would have been “seen more clearly if we had only this topic to discuss, and not the many other topics which are necessary if one is to realize the diﬀerence between the just and the unjust life.” The next topic is supposed to be “who is competent to guard the laws and ways of the city,” who shall be “established as ruler” in the city that they have just created in words. The irony is that, as the preceding chapter has shown, a valid disƟncƟon between the philosopher and the lover of sights and sounds, or opinion, cannot be said really to have been completed without a clearer picture of the disƟncƟon between the objects of knowledge and the objects of opinion. Thus, “the philosophers and those who are not,” have not in fact “each of them . . . revealed who they are,” while truly disƟnguishing “between the just and the unjust life” will be made to depend on the reality of the one as contrasted to the other, and this on the arƟculaƟon of the diﬀerence in ontologies. Thus going on to the “other topics” ought to be really conƟnuing the same topic, and crucially and necessarily so. What is Glaucon’s relaƟon to the argument at this stage? The brief exchange at the beginning of Book VI tells the story. The choice for a ruler in their city is to be between those who “are not philosophers but wander among the many phenomena which exist in mulƟfarious ways,” that is, the lovers of sights and sounds, and the true philosopher, the one “who can apprehend that which remains in all respects ever the same.” It is Glaucon who then asks, “How shall we proceed to deal with this quesƟon at a suitable length? [metriōs legoimen]” (484b). Moments before, as we noted, it is Socrates who had quipped that the disƟncƟon of the previous discussion had been rather “lengthy,” while it had taken up in actuality only a few pages, and was, Socrates had suggested, hardly adequate. But

Glaucon, ready to move on, asks Socrates what is the “next topic.” Socrates’ reply is, “that which follows,” (Grube) or the “next in order” (Shorey). The contrast is between what, for Glaucon, is a random next topic, and what is next “in order.” The brief exchange presents Glaucon himself as the image of wandering amongst the many phenomena, here the many topics. That is, unless he is led by Socrates, who in turn leads by following the logos, and is aƩempƟng to bring Glaucon along the same path. Thus the very disƟncƟon between the non-philosopher and the philosopher that is at issue at this point, is itself presented graphically in the discursive images of the two men. Moreover, the language suggests right measure and calculaƟon, measuring rightly, integral to the Cave and the Line. Glaucon’s sense of either “suitable length” or of what is next in the discussion is arbitrary, as contrasted to the philosopher’s sense of true measure—the length of conversaƟon and the order of topics being determined by the necessity of truth and of method. The noƟon of taking the “right measure” and of “measure” in general, will be examined in more speciﬁc detail in the discussion of the Divided Line. Nor is this the only image that anƟcipates later discussion and imagery. The false philosophers here are said to “wander” among the phenomena, without direcƟon, as do the minds of the souls chained in the Cave, aimlessly pursuing discussions about the ﬂickering shadows before them. As well, the complex of images around sight and the eye is here introduced. For, as concerns the choice of leaders, the philosopher and the lover of the many sights and sounds are contrasted as the blind man and the one with “keen eyesight,” while the acƟvity of the one with sight is again compared to that of the painter looking at his model: Do you really think that there is any diﬀerence between the blind and those who are really deprived of the knowledge of every reality, who have no clear model of it in their soul and cannot as painters can, look to that which is most true, always refer to it, contemplate it as exactly as possible, and so establish here on earth lawful noƟons about things beauƟful, just and good where they need establishing, or guard and preserve them once established? —No, by Zeus, these are not very diﬀerent from the blind. (484c-d)

Now this elaborate descripƟon and comparison, so clearly anƟcipaƟng the discussions of the Sun, Line and Cave, and one might add the myth of Er as well, is here just so much rhetoric—and somewhat too rich at that. It serves its purpose, however, and so when Glaucon is asked, “Should we then make these people [the blind] our guardians rather than those who have knowledge of every reality and are not inferior to the others in experience, or indeed in other aspect of excellence?” he replies that, “It would be absurd to choose others if these are not inferior in other respects, for in this respect they are superior in what is probably the most important maƩer.” I say just so much rhetoric for, as I suggested in the previous secƟon, the quesƟon of just what is meant by a “knowledge of every reality,” what the original object is that is true and to which the philosopher must “always refer,” and ﬁnally, what a “clear model of it in their soul” is, how it gets there, and what use the philosopher makes of whatever the “beauƟful, just and good” are . . . all of that remains precisely not clear yet. Glaucon’s faith in the philosophers needs some jusƟﬁcaƟon, and what seems to Glaucon a “clear choice” is rather empty and unclear unƟl these images are explicated—for how would Glaucon or the reader know just who ﬁts these descripƟons, just who can be rightly said to be “keen-sighted” and who “blind”? And yet, the noƟons of sight, the eye, and a “clear model” of “that which remains the same” will turn out to be more than just casual praise. Socrates turns to the quesƟon of just “how men can be qualiﬁed in both knowledge and experience.” That is to say, the quesƟon of just what consƟtutes the philosophical nature, for “it is ﬁrst necessary to understand their nature. I think that, if we can reach adequate agreement on their nature, we shall also agree that the same men can possess both qualiﬁcaƟons, and that none but they must be leaders in our ciƟes” (485a). But what does Socrates have in mind by “knowledge and experience”? Note that this resembles the quesƟon discussed before with regard to the “possibility” of the city constructed in words. There, at issue was the possibility of an actual polis that would resemble the one constructed in speech, while here we are discussing the condiƟons for the possibility of the philosopher-ruler, which is the condiƟon for the coming into being of that other possibility both in speech and in existence. And so, at issue is his nature, as well as his recepƟon in the world of the polis, hence the ship

metaphor and the quesƟon of the bad reputaƟon of the philosopher (Cf. 488a-489d). But just as earlier the quesƟon of possibility was revealed to be somewhat limiƟng if taken only at the literal poliƟcal level of the city’s existence—the city of the many as contrasted to the personal city of the soul—so here, too, we must disƟnguish between the sociological view of the philosopher as potenƟal ruler of the many, and the philosopher as the soul that is capable of intelligent self-rule (as well as the philosopher as model-maker, in speech, and actual legislator-ruler). When taken in this laƩer sense, of self-rule, the quesƟon of “how men can be qualiﬁed in both knowledge and experience” (485a) or, as it is then formulated, “what [we] must look to when [we] are about to decide which is the philosophical nature and which is not” takes on a diﬀerent signiﬁcance.[2] The focus is necessarily shiŌed from the person of the philosopher-ruler to the object of his sight and his relaƟon to it, from the nature of the philosopher to the nature of philosophy. Seen in this light, the discussion preceding and leading up to that of the Line is seen as a prologue, giving the requirements for a philosophical nature, the qualiƟes of character and intellect that make for a good candidate as well as the public life of the profession. What follows this prologue, the Sun, Line and Cave, deal increasingly with the nature of objects and the task of knowing them (which is not to deny the social level and component of the imagery, especially of the Cave). The part before the Line, etc., deals with the ethical qualiƟes and the psychological nature of the philosopher, at the same Ɵme announcing some of the philosophical themes as well: knowledge versus opinion, appearing versus being, are with us from the very beginning, when in Book I the great debate about the just life had been begun. The very opening lines of the Republic have Socrates recounƟng his returning from the fesƟval down in the Piraeus, where he had oﬀered up a prayer to “the goddess” and now wonders aloud about how the fesƟval is to be carried out—thus about rightly speaking and rightly acƟng. Now we are midway along that journey. The part aŌer the central images deals with the intellectual training of the philosophical mind, its immersion in the analysis of the experience of that to which it is akin. I do not mean to suggest that this intellectual experience, that of the philosophical training, and of the ascent of the Line, is all that is meant by

suﬃcient “knowledge and experience” when considering the individual person as his own philosopher-ruler. If anything, the noƟon of the personal city that is at peace with itself and is in that sense one, a uniﬁed plurality, suggests an intelligent experience of the world and one’s self, an interpretaƟon or right measure of this public or social world—the counterpart of the guardians’ experience, through which in fact the philosophical soul must also pass. But intellectual experience is sƟll a special kind of experience, and one that can be said to condiƟon the way one sees the world, hence consƟtuƟng at least one element in determining the way that one lives in it (in Plato’s case in parƟcular). Nor is there a clear division between what one sees, the way that one sees it, and even the ways of preparaƟon for seeing, since this last is described as a kind of unknowing pracƟce for what is a later insight into its essence. But the relaƟonship between these two kinds of experience, that of the intellect and that of the sensual and social self, each in relaƟon to its world and to each other, must also be worked out. Each has its objects, someƟmes overlapping, and each has its inner world of subjecƟve experience. It is in the saƟsfactory relaƟonship between these two kinds of experience that the condiƟons for the true philosophical nature, and hence the right candidates for the ruler of the true city, must be sought. It is with this relaƟonship in mind that we shall eventually turn in this chapter to an exposiƟon of that central group of images. But ﬁrst we must conƟnue to look at the clues for interpreƟng these images rightly. For this, we must look at two things: the passage at the end of Book VII where Plato interprets the soul’s acƟve relaƟonship to the educaƟon that is represented in the form of these images, including ﬁnally the use of dialecƟc, and secondly, some comments on the Good, that is, on the capstone of the objects represented. If, as Plato says in his own brief interpretaƟon at the end of Book VII (532 ﬀ.), the purpose of dialecƟc is to “gently draw the eye of the soul” “which is really buried in a kind of barbaric mire, and lead it upwards,” (533c-d) then whatever “knowledge and experience” we are concerned with must be eﬀecƟve in whatever this “turning” of the whole soul is. From this point of view, the preliminary studies, which we normally call science (geometry and astronomy or celesƟal physics, for example), are called so only “through force of habit” (533d), and it is only “dialecƟc” which

deserves the name of science, since the laƩer alone “travels this road, doing away with hypotheses and proceeding to the ﬁrst principle where it will ﬁnd certainty” (533c). There is nothing wrong with regarding these as sciences in themselves as long as one is concerned with their use as models or systems that explain or make intelligible the range of phenomena to which they are directed. As long as we do not ask either how it is possible that they do so, or what it means that it is possible; as long as we simply construct and use them, the normal name for them as science is more than adequate. But dialecƟc is in part the search for the answers to just such meta-scienƟﬁc quesƟons, and from this vantage point, the former, while they may be said to “grasp at reality to some extent” on account of their content, is seen as “dreaming about reality, unable to have a waking view of it so long as they make use of hypotheses and leave them undisturbed and cannot give a reasoned account of them” (553c). Just what a reasoned account is and what is meant by hypothesis, much less doing away with them, is controversial. But this level of meaning, which might be called the epistemological, would limit the “turning of the eye of the soul” to the turning of the intellecƟve part alone. However, it is the whole soul that must be turned around, as the ﬁrst menƟon of this turning at 518c ﬀ. shows. It is true that the virtues of the body “really do not exist before and are added later by habit and pracƟce,” while the intellect possesses its own virtue as something that by contrast “belongs above all to something more divine,” something in some sense prior to and beyond it. However, the right or ﬁƫng use of this divine capacity is, I suggest, in the service of the whole soul: “It is as if it were not possible to turn the eye from darkness to light without turning the whole body; so one must turn one’s whole soul from the world of becoming unƟl it can endure to contemplate reality, and the brightest of realiƟes, which we say is the Good” (518c). That this “service” relaƟonship is true at the epistemological level, seems clear enough from the descripƟon of the misuse of intelligence below it, hence the requisite turning of the whole soul and its moral-ethical implicaƟons: we must turn in order to be able to know. But the ﬁnal and highest relaƟonship of knower and known, or rather of beings and the source of being, is also in the service of the whole soul and hence the turning in its own interest: we must know in order that we may turn. This is a much deeper claim. It is to say, in eﬀect, that the

vision of the Good is not an end in itself and the jusƟﬁcaƟon for the turning. The experience represented in this capacity to know, even in its use, can be well or ill used. In the laƩer case “its capacity for sight is not inferior, but it is compelled to serve evil ends, so that the more sharply it looks the more evil it works” (519a).[3] Now this descripƟon of the misuse of intelligence is clearly with the poliƟcal or social realm in mind: “have you never noƟced in men who are said to be wicked but clever, how sharply their liƩle soul looks into things to which it turns its aƩenƟon.” Thrasymachus (or Alcibiades) would be an example. But while this is misuse or abuse (and convenƟonal science would be not an abuse but rather a limited use, albeit the one most frequent), there is a higher use from which perspecƟve these sciences serve as “assistants and helpers in the process of turning the soul around” (533d). That is, while individually and internally so to speak, they are sƟll funcƟoning epistemologically, the results of this, given that one raises the right quesƟons about the acƟvity and gives the right account of it, are not epistemological but rather ontological. The ﬁrst suggesƟons of this, close to the present discussion, are at 485b-e where the philosopher’s passion for knowledge and truth results in a canalized direcƟon of the passions—towards the one object of the intellect—and as a result, “withdrawal of the energy and interest of the passions for pleasures of the body.” The qualiﬁcaƟon of the philosopher- ruler is reﬂected in this complex turning. It is the interrelaƟonship of these two senses of turning, the epistemological and the ethical-ontological, that is contained in the images we are about to study, and which contain Plato’s answer to the original quesƟon and quest for the meaning of happiness in reply to the challenge of Thrasymachus. This might make it seem as if the turning of the eye of the soul per intellect would be enough to morally condiƟon and reform the soul. But this is not the intent, for clearly the educaƟon of the appeƟtes, as with the guardians, is in some sense a pre- condiƟon for the ascent of the philosopher. In this sense, the eye of the soul would seem to have been already turned, at least at the level of habit, while the descripƟon here might seem to indicate that it is insight into the Good which in turn turns the rest of the soul. As well, the image of the man who returns to the Cave aŌer his vision seems to follow this line of

development. However, the philosopher is selected from among those whose souls have already undergone a turning towards the non- visible in their training, hence already a moral and an epistemological change. As regards the epistemological quesƟon, the everyday experience in meaning is also already a turning to the non-visible, and this without any special philosophical educaƟon. This is an important lesson of the analysis of the Line, which seeks to explain the condiƟon of the possibility of everyday experience of discourse as signiﬁcant. Very liƩle is said about the Idea of the Good, but there is no way to avoid talking about it. For example, when discussing the studies the philosopher will be required to pursue, the measure of to what extent they are to be studied, to what extent they are useful in preparing the philosopher to be both a true philosopher and a true ruler of the true city, is the extent to which such a study can lead one to the vision of the Idea of the Good: But for those purposes [pracƟcal applicaƟon of geometry in warfare, e.g., encampments, troop formaƟon, etc.] even a small amount of geometry and calculaƟon would suﬃce. We must examine whether the greater porƟon of it which is more advanced tends to make it easier to see the Idea of the Good. All things tend in that direcƟon which compels the soul to turn itself toward the place in which the most blessed part of reality exists, which the soul must see at any cost. (527e) Now the discussion of the Idea of the Good is extremely brief, admiƩedly dogmaƟc—Socrates says that he will give only his “opinion” (506e) about it, and that, under duress—and the image of the Sun, etc., is oﬀered as second best, a look at the “oﬀspring” rather than the “parent.” It is Adeimantus who urges him to give his “posiƟon” on whether the Good is “knowledge or pleasure or something else.” To which Socrates replies, ironically, “What a man! It has been clear for some Ɵme that the opinion of others on this subject would not saƟsfy you.” That is, he will accept, or at least desires, the mere opinion of Socrates on the subject. When Socrates asks, “Do you think that it is right to talk about things one does not know as if one knew them?” Adeimantus does not hesitate to reply, “Not as if

one knew them, but for a man who has an opinion to say what that opinion is.” And when Socrates asks whether “those who express a true opinion without knowledge are any diﬀerent from blind people who follow the right road?” Adeimantus agrees, and presumably is silenced. But this does not prevent Glaucon, and one assumes with Adeimantus’ silent consent, from urging Socrates to conƟnue: “Do not stand oﬀ as if you had come to the end. We shall be saƟsﬁed if you discuss the Good in the same fashion as you did jusƟce, moderaƟon and the other things” (506d). That is, from their point of view, this would mean that Socrates merely give his opinion on the issue at hand, and on the Good itself presumably. However, what would discussing it in “the same fashion” mean? Clearly not the mere giving of his opinion about it that they intend. Socrates says that to do so would “also quite saƟsfy” him, but that he fears that he “shall not be able to do so, and that in my eagerness I shall disgrace myself and make myself ridiculous.” But is this because the nature of the discussion of the Good is of necessity diﬀerent than that of the virtues (for example, because the laƩer have been examined through the use of hypotheses), or rather perhaps because the interlocutors are not capable of following? At any rate, Socrates does not say that he absolutely could not give such an account, and begs oﬀ, on the grounds that the nature of the Good itself is a “larger quesƟon than what we started on, which was to ascertain my present opinion about it” (506e). And it is in this context that the analogy of the Sun is introduced. It then appears that what Socrates is doing is acquiescing in their desire to hear his opinion about such things, and that what will be provided is a mere appearance—thus, “I am willing to tell you what appears to be the oﬀspring of the Good and most like it [homoiotatos], if that is agreeable to you. If not, we must let the quesƟon drop.” Now given what he has just said about mere true opinion being like the expression of “blind people”—the taunt that they thus would want “to contemplate ugly, blind and crooked things when you can hear bright and beauƟful things from others,” from those who have knowledge—we, at least, ought to feel rather uncomfortable, and at least be forewarned about how we are to read the images about to be presented. In fact, much more is given than the mere opinion which Glaucon and Adeimantus are willing to seƩle for. For the following elaboraƟon includes not only the sketch of the Good through its acƟvity in analogy with the Sun image, but the

elaboraƟon of the Line and the Cave as well—since the laƩer are expressly oﬀered as a further explicaƟon of the former (cf. 517b). However, there is a certain degree of dogmaƟsm in the elaboraƟon of all these images: the Line is an account of the relaƟon of the knower, knowing and the known, but that it indeed works as an account would need further examinaƟon, or beƩer, the experience of its truth. SƟll, it is all a far cry from the simple response that Glaucon and Adeimantus requested, which was only Socrates’ opinion as to whether he considered the Good to be “knowledge, or pleasure, or something else.” They would have been happy with the simple reply as to which it was. They take it that the contents of a simple reply, in the form of an idenƟﬁcaƟon, can saƟsfactorily be given, and that the form of such a reply in a simple dogmaƟc answer is acceptable. Neither is the case. As in the Meno, the nature of an appropriate answer is related to the proper understanding of the quesƟon, and as in the Meno, the interlocutors are seen to be operaƟng at a diﬀerent level than the reader is meant to operate. The blindness of the interlocutors when perceived by the reader points the reader to the real issues and the development of the argument. At the very beginning of the dialogue, Glaucon and Adeimantus had asked not for insight and knowledge about the nature of jusƟce, but for an adequate defense of it against the claims of injusƟce. (It is, in fact, speciﬁcally Adeimantus who asks for Socrates’ “opinion” at this point, while it is Glaucon who asks for further elaboraƟon of the image—but it was Glaucon who had asked for an “encomium” of jusƟce at the very beginning (358d), to be “persuaded” that jusƟce is preferable to injusƟce, as noted in some detail in chapter one.) There, and now again here, Glaucon and Adeimantus are asking that Socrates give his opinions—that will saƟsfy them. Now in some sense the disƟncƟon between knowledge and opinion has already been made at 479c-e and it has been illustrated by the image of the city as a ship and the discussion of the one who truly has the knowledge requisite to guiding the crew. This is contrasted with the one who is simply good at convincing the owner of the ship that he, the rhetorician, can manipulate them. Or, again, it was implicit in the thesis that each of the divisions of the city should funcƟon in accord with what it does best, that is, according to what it knows. But the nature of what it means to know per se has not been examined; hence even an adequate

doxa concerning the Good must be spelled out in some measure— concerning its rule over knowing and being. But why is it parƟcularly appropriate to raise this issue of the method of discourse once again at just this point in the dialogue, and what is its connecƟon with the Idea of the Good, and knowledge of it? When disƟnguishing the three parts of the soul earlier, they had discussed, “with reference to these parts the nature of each of jusƟce, moderaƟon, courage and wisdom” (504a). “We spoke as best we could at the Ɵme, and we said that to see these things most clearly there was a longer way” (509b) and it is this way that the “guardian of a city and its laws” must endure, and “put as much eﬀort into his studies as into physical training; otherwise he will never reach the end of the most important and most appropriate study.” This study is, or culminates in, the study of the Good (note that it is not said to be the study of how to aƩain a vision of the Good, but a study of the Idea of the Good—and its relaƟons—itself). Now Glaucon and Adeimantus are presented by Socrates as being already familiar with at least the existence of such a study, and of the controversies around it: “You have certainly heard it [what the study is] oŌen enough, but now you are either not thinking, or you intend again to make trouble for me by your intervenƟon. I rather think that the laƩer is the case, for you have oŌen heard it said that the Form of the Good is the greatest object of study . . . ”(504e-505a). And yet, as familiar as they are with its existence as a doctrine, its connecƟon with the present discussion of the nature of the philosopher who must lead the city (beginning at 503b) and the soul that must be “exercised in many kinds of studies to see whether it can tolerate the greatest studies,” (503e) is, apparently, far from obvious to them. And so when Socrates ﬁrst speaks of a “most important and most appropriate study,” Adeimantus responds by asking, “Are these virtues then [jusƟce, moderaƟon, courage, and wisdom], not the most important subject of study? Is there anything sƟll more important than jusƟce and the things we discussed?”(504d). Thus while the subject of the nature of the Good is “a subject of great and frequent controversies” it is unrelated for them to the quesƟon of the nature of virtues, say of jusƟce, and moreover to the knowledge of such. One has the impression that for them, as for some commentators, the argument could have been declared concluded at the

end of Book IV (at 445a), which indeed it was, of course, dogmaƟcally, hence ironically so. It is Socrates who ﬁrst menƟons, in connecƟon with the study of the Good, the “current controversies” as to whether the Good is knowledge or pleasure or something else, and then he points to a diﬃculty for those who would idenƟfy knowledge as the Good, namely that when asked knowledge of what, they can only reply “knowledge of the Good” (508b). The Divided Line aƩempts to indicate where kinds of knowledge stand in relaƟon to the Good, which is not “another knowledge.” Those who taunt anyone with either a lack of knowledge of the Good or being unable to arƟculate it, are themselves no beƩer; “For they say it is the ‘knowledge of the Good’ [when asked knowledge of what] as if we understood their meaning when they uƩer the word good.” In spite of this diﬃculty for those who merely mouth a noble plaƟtude about the object of the study, Glaucon and Adeimantus, a few lines later (506b), sƟll want to know what Socrates’ “choice” is and his opinion in the controversy. But having made the disƟncƟon between knowledge and opinion, between appearance and reality at the end of Book V, is not suﬃcient unƟl such disƟncƟons are made more than doctrine, more than philosophical doxai, and are related to the real natures of the objects of knowledge. And that requires an examinaƟon of their actual structure and acƟvity in relaƟon to the human subject, which will suggest their relaƟon to the Good and what a study of the Good would possibly mean. For the discussion concluding at the end of Book IV, and that dealing with the problem of possibility in the books that follow, are sƟll fundamentally under the gun as ex hypothesi: though more than bald opinion, since they are the philosophical elaboraƟon of an image, a demonstraƟon of sorts, yet they sƟll are not suﬃciently developed to lay claim to being knowledge. Socrates’ statement at the beginning of Book V sƟll holds: “This then is the kind of city and government which I call good and right, and so too this kind of man. And if this is the right kind, then the others are bad and wrong” (449a). In the intervening books, I have argued, the issue of possibility is seriously discussed, “lest our discussion should seem to be mere wishful thinking,” only by shiŌing the ground from the model of the outer image of the ideal city back to its original purpose, the descripƟon of the just city of the inner soul in harmony with itself. But while this shiŌ focuses the careful reader

on where true jusƟce is possible if at all, and begins to give us a beƩer picture of what jusƟce is, sƟll, it does not explain the reality of jusƟce itself, and its integraƟon with the rest of reality. Books I-V present the embodiment of principles used in construcƟon of the city in acƟon, construcƟng images of deﬁniƟons of virtue and posiƟng diﬀerent objects for knowledge versus opinion, with the suggesƟon of permanence and stability versus change as essenƟal characterisƟc of the knowledge/opinion disƟncƟon and built into the city and its parts. The discussion of the Line and of the educaƟon of the philosopher will replace visible images of the imaginaƟon with a raƟonal image of the non-visible. This raƟonal image represents to us, in schemaƟc form, the underlying structures of the arƟculated whole, the actual world of experience. The Line is a schemaƟc raƟonal image of the raƟonality of the world as it actually is, while the model of the soul in acƟon constructed in imaginaƟon in the Republic, in the drawing of the details of the city/soul analogy, is an image of how the soul ought to be in relaƟon to that raƟonal actual world to which it is akin (and which it in some sense helps produce, both individually and publicly). As I have indicated, the need for this shiŌ from the constructed image in imaginaƟon of the city/soul, to its ground, the raƟonal or reﬂected image of the actual, intelligible world, is not seen by the interlocutors. Hence, for them, the virtues are independent of knowledge, are convenƟonal, even if in a newly deﬁned set of convenƟons which they have just worked out to their saƟsfacƟon in the development of the image of the ideally just city.[4] It is for this reason that the theoreƟcal knowledge of the Good would not occur to them as in any way germane to the present discussion, although they are aware of it as an object of intellectual controversy. Thus it is rather ironic that they agree that “many men would choose to do, possess and enjoy the reputaƟon for things that are opined to be just and fair even if they aren’t, while when it comes to good things no one is saƟsﬁed with what is opined to be so but each seeks the things that are, and from here on out everyone despises opinion” (505d, Bloom transl.). Ironic, for they themselves, in just a few lines, are quite content, as we have pointed out, to have Socrates give his private opinion about the Good, and to do so through what “appears to be the oﬀspring of the Good.” The dictum that every man seeks what he truly believes to be good

for himself needs to be taken up as an image in words, and then puriﬁed into its proper end—the pursuit through knowledge, that is, through dialecƟc, of the authenƟc idea of Good which can order the personal city of human being morally and does order the epistemological and ontological relaƟons. The diﬀerence between the rude state of the truth of the dictum: things that are seen as good, that is, appear so, because we call them so, hence the level of opinion or convenƟon (if even personal convenƟon)—and the contrast with an intuited higher state, at which things are seen to be good because we know them to be so, is reinforced in the next line: “This every soul pursues, and all its acƟons are done for its sake. It divines that it is something but is perplexed and cannot adequately grasp what it is . . . ” (505e). Finally, for just acƟons to be more than simply called good, even when so transformed as they have been up unƟl now, and thus to meet the ulƟmate and original challenge of Thrasymachus, such just acƟons need to be seen in the light of their relaƟon to the Idea of the Good. For not only is it the case that the studies of the philosopher result in insight into what is the just ordering, the “preserving and ordering” of the city, but also insight into in what sense just acƟons are useful and beneﬁcial suﬃciently to answer the debate concerning which man is happier, the just or the unjust: “ . . . that the Form of the Good is the greatest object of study, and that it is by their relaƟon to it that just acƟons and the other things become useful and beneﬁcial” (505a) and consƟtuƟve of human happiness. In this way, knowledge of the Good will be seen to be beyond the merely moral ideal (pace Shorey)[5] and linked to the necessity for a more detailed disƟncƟon between knowledge and opinion in general. The “best men in the city to whom we entrust everything” must have not just moral knowledge—in fact, to have just this would seem to be impossible, since “when it is not known how just and beauƟful things come to be good, these things will not ﬁnd it much use to secure a guardian over themselves who does not have this knowledge. And I surmise that no one will understand those just and beauƟful things adequately before he knows this” (506a). THE IDOLS OF THE CAVE: SHADOW IMAGES, PUPPETS, AND PUPPETEERS

Having made some brief remarks about the introducƟon of the Good,[6] I now propose to look at the Cave and the Line in detail. For reasons that shall become apparent, my exposiƟon reverses the order of the text, and deals with the Cave allegory ﬁrst, in the present chapter, and the Line in the following chapter. We have seen the signiﬁcance of Glaucon and Adeimantus’s parƟcipaƟon in the search for the best ruler, in the disƟnguishing of the true from the false philosopher. This has been done in a preliminary but also a rather doctrinaire way, as has the disƟnguishing of their methods and objects, knowledge and opinion. Once the issue of whether such a law-maker is possible, and what the nature of such a one must be like, has been seƩled, or at least laid to rest to the saƟsfacƟon of the discussants, it remains to take up “how the saviors of our consƟtuƟon will develop, what studies and pursuits they must follow [as compared to that outlined for the guardians] and at what age they must severally take up each of these” (502d). They are to be evaluated as to their suitability for the pursuit, and then “tested by pleasure and pain” (503a) and that “neither in toil nor in fear, nor in any change in circumstances must they lose that love,” the “love for their city.” And he who comes through this “like gold tested in ﬁre” is then ﬁt to be “established as ruler” (503a). This tesƟng of his nature is in “those toils, fears and pleasures that we menƟoned before” but now to be added are the tests of intellectual studies, conceived in a certain way, with the goal of turning the soul in such a way that it is led towards a vision that will equip it for its ulƟmate task, that of ruling justly. (The ﬁrst tests are external tests of the meƩle of the soul, while the intellectual tests both accomplish the turning of the soul and take place internally.) It is in response and dismay that there are sƟll greater studies, greater heights to be scaled, that the quesƟon of just what these studies are calls forth the discussion of the idea of the Good, the Sun-Good analogy, and the images of the Line and the Cave. “We must test this nature in those toils . . . it must be exercised in many kind of studies to see whether it can tolerate the greatest studies, or whether it will shrink from them, like those who fail other tests” (503e). But in addiƟon to noƟng this prolepƟc language of an arduous uphill climb we must also recall the context of the whole of the discussion, namely the quesƟon of the nature of jusƟce (and injusƟce) and the just life, and the

ﬁnal quesƟon which had called forth the whole discussion of the Republic, whether the life of the just man or that of the unjust man is happier. I recall this especially now as we are about to look at some rather unhappy ﬁgures, the chained inhabitants of the Cave. It is natural to think of men in chains as being rather unhappy, though clearly they would not say so themselves—in fact, quite the opposite. But these are so in a rather special sense, for they are unaware of their chains, or at least of what it would be like without them, they have always been in chains. They are not unwilling and/or psychologically unhappy slaves. Also, although the journey upwards is ﬁlled with pain, yet in the end we are, one supposes, meant to judge the one who makes it as somehow truly happier or beƩer oﬀ than those in chains, including those who return to the cave, but are to remain unbound (but to point to the issue as it is reﬂected in the image is not to resolve it). We must recall, then, what perspecƟve on jusƟce is being assumed in the discussion, having been developed up to this point, as we are about to enter the Cave, as it were. What stage in the reinterpretaƟon of the original quesƟon regarding jusƟce and the just life has been reached? JusƟce is tradiƟonally, then as now, thought of as external, as a social relaƟon. Plato argues that it is rather a state of soul, and just acƟons a secondary, though necessary, consequence or result, of which jusƟce is the cause. Further jusƟﬁcaƟon of this view is of course one of the purposes of the rest of the argument of the Republic, as is its correlate, the nature of happiness. And yet the grand analogy of the city that consƟtutes one half of the Republic is jusƟce in its external, social sense, at least as a visible analogy. Why should an external, social model (as more visible) be appropriate as an image? The suggesƟon of a full answer will have to wait upon a discussion of the Divided Line. The tension of the paradox is felt by those who see the image as image. Those like Glaucon and Adeimantus who remain at the literal level, sƟll see only ordinary external jusƟce, the jusƟce of acts. Another way of puƫng it, even within the terms of the image at the social or literal level, is that there is a diﬀerence between the jusƟce of the whole society in the relaƟons and aƫtudes of the ciƟzens, versus the individual consequences of these relaƟons and aƫtudes. But the one who sees the image as image, the analogical level, who sees the purpose and necessity of the analogy, at least sees more clearly the non- visible nature of social relaƟons and aƫtudes in tracing even these to their

non-visible cause, the human soul. Part of the answer to this paradox is that the appropriateness of the analogy is in part explained by its purpose, to make visible the true jusƟce—ironically to make the invisible visible through the making of an image—thus we turn the soul around, and at the same Ɵme turn it inside out, 1) to make it look upward in order to turn and look inward, and 2) to look inward in order to look upward. The ﬁrst concerns psychology, morality and epistemology, while the second concerns epistemology and ontology. The allegory of the Cave must be understood not only epistemologically but also poliƟcally, or more broadly speaking socially—and ulƟmately brought back down to the journey of the individual soul.[7] That this is so, is, as I have said above, in the ﬁrst instance simply because of the larger context of the objecƟve of the Republic as a whole; secondly, because it is pointless to separate the educaƟon of the philosopher, and hence the image of its beginnings in the Cave, from its proper use, the end towards which it is directed—the vision of the Good, which in its turn must be useful, put to use as the highest educaƟon of the philosopher.[8] The temptaƟon to read the image only epistemologically is due, ironically, to the physicality of the image—the models or manufactured things and their shadows—as if only the natural world were being talked about.[9] And yet that journey upward of the Cave and the Line—the studies which “draw the soul from the world of that which becomes to the world of that which is”—provides precisely “those who have the best knowledge of the principles that make for the best government of a city,” even though these are said to “also know honor of a diﬀerent kind, and a beƩer life than that of the poliƟcal” (521b). The two images, that of the Cave and that of the Line, are of course presented separately, and are disƟnct for good reason, as we shall see. AŌer the Line, Plato presents the parable of the Cave proper, then, at 517b ﬀ. he talks about it; “This whole image must be related to what we said before [the Line]” and then, “Come then, share with me this thought also: do not be surprised that those who have reached this part are unwilling to occupy themselves with human aﬀairs” (517c). Then, in the discussion of the compelling of the philosopher to take on the task of ruling the city, we are told that the law which “binds together” the city, making it one instead of many, is the principal task of the philosopher, and

that “we must not allow them to stay behind” in the realm of mere thinking. But who are we and they here? The descripƟon of the unwelcome recepƟon of the one who has “returned from his upward journey” is in clearly poliƟcal terms: “Would it not be said that he had returned from his upward journey with his eyesight spoiled, and that it was not worthwhile even to aƩempt to travel upward? As for the man who tried to free them and lead them upwards, if they could somehow lay their hands on him and kill him, they would do so” (517a). This is said outside of the Cave image passage proper—all the more reason to take it as poinƟng us towards a poliƟcal level of interpretaƟon of the goings on within the Cave. Here, as oŌen noted, we have a certain reference to the death of Socrates.[10] As well, we might remember a similar recepƟon of the navigator in the case of the sailors and the ship parable, there an explicitly poliƟcal image (488ﬀ). But we shall see that behind the poliƟcal language and imagery lays a more fundamental, epistemological, and ulƟmately ontological, theme. Next, consider the passage at 517c, the sole explicit descripƟon of the Idea of the Good; it is “the cause of all that is right and beauƟful, to have produced in the visible world both light and the fount of light, while in the intelligible world it is itself that which produces and controls truth and intelligence.” Yet, for all its ontological cast, the sentence ends with “and he who is to act intelligently in public or in private must see it.” Hence ﬁnally it is public acƟons in the polis, and the private ones, both in relaƟon to other souls, and private intending in relaƟon to ourselves, inner jusƟce —which are the consequence and the purpose or end of such vision, in the context of the Republic at least.
