At 517d there is another implied comparison with the ship parable; in the laƩer, it had been said that the one with knowledge of navigaƟon might not be good at arguing his case, might not even get a chance to apply his knowledge in navigaƟng, that is, in ruling, but that this would not negate the superior insight of the navigator into both the principles that would issue in the best rules for the craŌ of navigaƟon, and even insights into how best, with that end in view, the crew should then be ruled. Both the true navigator and here the person returned from his upward journey are pointedly described as behaving “awkwardly” and as subject to the “ridicule” of others. In the case of the Cave he is described as both “behaving awkwardly” and

“appearing ridiculous” while he is sƟll dazzled, and before he is suﬃciently adjusted to the darkness around him, that is, if he were “compelled to contend in court or some other place about the shadows of jusƟce or the objects of which they are shadows, and to carry through the contest about these in the way that these things are understood by those who have never seen jusƟce itself . . . ”(517d-e) It should be clear from this passage alone that among the objects carried along the wall casƟng shadows below are made images of jusƟce. The problem is how to integrate this with the Cave descripƟon as a whole; what is a made image of jusƟce such that it casts decepƟve shadows of jusƟce etc. and how does this compare to the other more material sense of objects. Here “the darkness around him” is not just epistemological but a moral and poliƟcal one as well, as the menƟon of contending in a court, etc. implies. Nor should we pass over the second reference to the trial and death of Socrates in one hundred lines. The image of violently contending, is used both within the Cave image along with the other poliƟcal signs just menƟoned and right following this, outside the image proper, when Socrates is interpreƟng the parable (cf. 516e; 517d), and recalls the contending (the same word is used) in the case of the navigator and crew. And so in the end we are led to examine the image of the Cave to see more exactly in what sense the shadows described, and the whole dynamic of the Cave story, is suscepƟble to a poliƟcal, ethical, but ulƟmately ontological interpretaƟon, especially of the nature of images and image- making.[11] Socrates concludes when addressing vive voce the philosopher- ruler himself in convincing him to return to the cave: What we shall say to compel [him] . . . When you are used to it you will see inﬁnitely beƩer than the dwellers below; you will know what each image is and of what it is an image, because you have seen the truth of things beauƟful and just and good, and so, for you as for us, the city will be governed as a waking reality and not as in a dream, as the majority of ciƟes are now governed by men who are ﬁghƟng shadows and striving against each other in order to rule as if this were a great good. (520c)

The task is to maintain both sides of the primary analogy in one’s interpretaƟon—in the metaphysical books, to see the conƟnuity with the rest of the inquiry of the Republic, and the necessity of the digression, while in the poliƟcal books, as it were, to see the epistemological and ontological level. Let me suggest then, that we consider the Cave myth as if the cave itself were the city, and not merely the sensible world, an epistemological story, as it is someƟmes taken to be (though of course it is that as well). Secondly, that the cave is itself as well an image of the individual soul, in other words, that it is to be treated just as that image of the city originally generated for comparison with the soul in Books I-V. This passage at 520c, again occurring outside of the cave image proper, speaking as it does of “men who are ﬁghƟng shadows and striving against each other to rule as if this were a great good,” and the earlier ones at 517a and especially 517d, “contending in court or some other place about shadows of jusƟce or the objects of shadows . . . by those who have never seen jusƟce itself,” all make it clear that the shadows of the cave are, in context, in the ﬁrst instance to be interpreted poliƟcally, but that we are to see the deeper sources of poliƟcal blindness and injusƟce. If the Cave is to represent the whole of human experience, as does the Divided Line, then the image should depict the whole range of dialogical experience, hence a variety of subject types of discourse. Thus the poliƟcal must be understood in both its more literal restricted sense, but also the priority of the more general sense as the poliƟcs of the soul. This priority is reﬂected in the epistemological and ontological divisions of the Line. Socrates tells us as much about the Cave image himself. We are to compare the Cave to the enƟre realm of the visible; “the realm of the visible should be compared to the prison dwelling” (517b). But we must ask what aspects of the visible versus the non-visible are relevant to the central quesƟon of the just versus the unjust life and the issue of happiness. Having looked at some of the indicaƟons of context which suggest what to bear in mind, let us look at the details of the image proper. The general disposiƟon of the cave is well known. I will comment only on certain dramaƟc features. The Cave parable begins, likely enough, with the physical seƫng. It is an “underground cave-like dwelling.” Why underground? Various suggesƟons have been made. It will present a ready

contrast between the light of the ﬁre and the light of the sun, between the visible world and that of the intelligible, hence analogous to the major divisions of the Line, which had been already presented. The actual physical sun of our visible world, while its virtues are extolled in the analogizing of it to the Good in the intelligible world, is sƟll as ﬁre in the cave when compared to the Good itself. Hence the light of the actual Sun when outside the cave (the parable) is not the physical sun but the Good— thus the visible world is expressly inside the cave. But what is this visible world of the cave? As I have suggested, it is not merely our epistemic world in the narrow sense; rather, it is our whole world, our lived in, poliƟcal/social world. Darkness, of course, is suggesƟve of ignorance, and the purpose of this parable is given at the outset as illustraƟng “the eﬀect of educaƟon or the lack of it upon our human nature” (514a). Again, this darkness is not just epistemological but moral and poliƟcal darkness—that is, we are to look at the eﬀect of having or lacking educaƟon, and one of these eﬀects is the posiƟon in which it puts us in relaƟon to others, for it is signiﬁcant that there are others in the cave itself—there need not have been, aŌer all. (Recalling as well the relaƟon of Glaucon and Adeimantus to Thrasymachus and Socrates, as studied earlier.) The men at the very boƩom of the cave are in feƩers. One may see this as simply symbolic of their ignorance, from which they must be freed, and this certainly is what happens later. But being in feƩers is certainly evocaƟve of the condiƟon of being a slave. Further, others in the cave play an important role in keeping them in chains, as we shall see. Next we note that they have been there since childhood (those who carry the ﬁgures as well, it is presumed). This stresses that a) they are in ignorance from the beginning of their educaƟon, having no equipment with which they might free themselves (unƟl the parts of the image are considered as parts of one soul’s struggle) and b) since they are now grown men, they have been habituated to the life of the cave and are somewhat rigid in its games, accounƟng for the pain of release, and the resistance encountered when one of them returns with a radically diﬀerent interpretaƟon of their world. Behind and above those in chains is a path across the cave, and running the length of this is a low wall. This wall is then compared to the screen at a show. Such a screen would normally prevent the viewers of a puppet show from seeing the puppeteers, the real source of the voices and

movements, the animaƟon of the puppets. Since in the version [12] of a theater being constructed in the cave the puppets are being used to cast shadows on the wall in front, here the eﬀect of this wall separaƟng the puppeteers from those enchained would be to prevent the shadows of those carrying the puppets from being cast as well. This feature adds to the decepƟon—the shadows appear to be original sources and to be alive. Behind a ramp, and sƟll higher up, is a ﬁre, which is used to cast shadows on the wall before the enchained. It is along this ramp that men are carrying puppet like ﬁgures, which in turn cast shadows on the wall. Though those in chains presumably are able to see their own shadows they would not be able to idenƟfy them as such, that is, as shadows, anymore than they are able to idenƟfy correctly any other shadow. Socrates asks, “Do you think, in the ﬁrst place, that such men could see anything of themselves and each other except the shadows which the ﬁre on the wall casts in front of them?” to which the reply is, “How could they, if they have to keep their heads sƟll throughout life?”(515a). Nor of course can they see their own bodies; they are ﬁxed so as to be able to regard only the shadows on the wall. This ﬁts nicely with their ignorance of their own souls and of their condiƟon; for they do not in fact know that they are enchained and ignorant, as this has been all that they have known during their lives. Note that there is no pain coming from their present condiƟon—the only one who experiences pain is said to do so aŌer being freed, or in the process thereof. Next let us note the variety of the objects carried. They are “all kinds of arƟfacts, statues of men, reproducƟons of other animals in stone or wood . . . ” and they are carried by men, some of whom are talking while others are silent. We thus have representaƟves of the whole visible world —manufactured objects, human beings and that of “other animals,” represenƟng nature. The most interesƟng part of the story is the dynamic of what happens, the drama of images. The shadows, as the only things known to the enchained, are taken to be the real things. “If they could converse with one another, do you not think that they would consider these shadows to be the real things?—Certainly.” But further, these objects, or rather their shadows, are animated, and in a special way. For Socrates suggests that there could as well be an echo in the cave, and that

sounds made from behind them would be reproduced as echoes, as images of the original sound, seeming to come from in front of them, that is, from the direcƟon of the wall and its shadows. Thus, “whenever one of the carriers passing behind the wall spoke, would they not think that it was the shadows passing in front of them which were talking?”(515b) And most signiﬁcantly, the ﬁgures casƟng shadows include the “statues of men.” Now it seems reasonable to ask just who these puppeteers are, what their relaƟon is to the ﬁgures that they are carrying, and thus to those below them, the enchained. For not only do they give the ﬁgures they carry moƟon, but speech as well. Would it not be plausible to suppose to begin with, that they are in fact the arƟﬁcers of the ﬁgures that they each carry? And further, that the voices that echo from the wall each in some sense go with the respecƟve ﬁgures and the puppeteer behind them, much as would be the case in a real puppet show. Again, not that those in chains would know which echo properly goes with which shadow—they in fact spend much idle Ɵme debaƟng just this, which has a signiﬁcance of its own, as we shall see in a moment. It is said of those carrying the ﬁgures that “some of the carriers are talking while others are silent.” This added bit of animaƟon is likely for some dramaƟc reason. Could it perhaps be that they either talk about the ﬁgure they carry or else even consciously animate their parƟcular ﬁgure, in the case of statues of men? It is parƟcularly the statues of men that are animated, their shadows which are taken to be talking, and the real things. What I am suggesƟng is that since the topic here is “the eﬀect of educaƟon and the lack of it,” and given the language of the context already pointed out, perhaps it is appropriate to think of those carrying the puppets as acƟvely being a cause of the ignorance of those enchained—of misleading them, perhaps consciously. Why, if not, have singled out so conspicuously, in the list of things carried along the wall, “images of men,” and then have stressed their speech; and what, aŌer all, are the images of men? Perhaps it is their speech itself, and the word is the image of the deed, or the word is the shaping of the deed. And if, then, the puppets were to be thought of as manufactured by those carrying them, perhaps it would complete the meaning of the Cave image to conceive of the puppets themselves as the doctrines of those who made them, and the shadows as the public images of the doctrines. The doctrines or opinions would be images formed about the nature of reality,

but as doxai they are self-consƟtuƟng in a sense, hence reﬂexive discourse about the images themselves, whether of things in nature or the world of manufactured things, or ﬁnally, about human things, i.e., poliƟcal and moral reality. UlƟmately, various implicit compeƟng ontologies would be likely candidates, it is parƟcularly the compeƟng views of jusƟce (as in Book I) which would be the most relevant, for it is ﬁnally this vision which the one who has made the journey and returned must impart to those sƟll enchained. InteresƟngly enough, the acƟviƟes of those enchained ﬁt very well with this explanaƟon of the shadows and those who make them. First, at 515b, Socrates asks, “if they were able to talk to one another, do you not think that they would suppose that in naming the things that they saw they were naming passing objects?” and there is nothing in the descripƟon of their enchainment that suggests that they could not, in fact, talk to one another, albeit they cannot turn their heads, thus see one another. Then, a bit later, Socrates suggests the following as a potenƟal recollecƟon of one who has been freed, of life back in the cave, “if he recalled to mind what passed for wisdom there, and his fellow bondsmen” (516c). The prisoners are imagined as busying themselves arguing about the shadows, “the men below had praise and honor from each other,” again a poliƟcal or public overtone, “and prizes for the man who saw most clearly the shadows that passed before them” (516c-d). They study the order of the shadows and “which came earlier and which came later, and which came together,” clearly a mock, erisƟc study in contrast to that of dialecƟc. One might then suppose that they are aided in this acƟvity by the voices of the puppeteers. The most likely group of candidates for those who teach such a skill of disƟnguishing or classifying dependent on mere arbitrary perceived sequence, etc. would be the sophists, who are said to be expert in a decepƟon “by words that cheat the ear,” in “exhibiƟng images of all things in a shadow play of discourse” (Sophist, 234c). This image of erisƟcal and arbitrary idenƟfying or naming is in contrast to the method of examinaƟon by successive hypotheses (or in the Sophist’s descent by classiﬁcaƟon—the division and collecƟon of a dialecƟc) in search of reality. The governance of such an examinaƟon reﬂects the rule of the Good, and is its image—as is that of the Sun, also discussed in its rule “in its own place” in the same passage at 516c. The shadowy presence of the sophists is also suggested

by the goal of this study of the shadows, which is that those who carry it on believe that they thus “could most ably predict the future,” that is, win out over their compeƟtors in this pseudo-skill—as well as by the contrast between the philosopher and those who “desire those rewards and envy those who were honored and held power among the prisoners.” But as Socrates says when discussing those who give philosophy a bad name, the true sophists are not those who formally teach sophisƟc but those who use it in the manipulaƟon of the polis, whether having studied it or in their own cleverness.[13] The philosopher and the sophist are contrasted with an image borrowed from the Underworld of the Odyssey but altered ironically and given an expressly poliƟcal turn in this context. (We see elsewhere that Plato subtly changes a story or passage to suit his own needs.) Socrates says, “As Homer put it, that he [Achilles] certainly wished to be ‘serf to another man without possessions upon the earth,’ and go through any suﬀering, rather than share their opinions and live as they do,” (516d) as the inhabitants of the underworld. Achilles is an honored and respected warrior-ruler in the Underworld. Homer has Odysseus say to Achilles that while he, Odysseus, has been “dogged by misfortune,” Achilles has been fortunate, “the most fortunate man that ever was or will be. For in the old days when you were on earth, we Argives honored you as though you were a god: and now, down here, you are a mighty prince among the dead.” Achilles does indeed object, but for reasons quite other than that suggested by Socrates; he prefers life at its most penurious to being a pale bloodless shade, and Homer ﬁnishes the phrase, rather “than king of all these dead men.” Plato ﬁnishes it rather to suit his own purposes, with “ . . . rather than share their opinions and live as they do,” that is, live as those who are “honored and held power among the prisoners” for their speech about the shadows. Homer’s Achilles, the man of acƟon, is leŌ in Hades to contemplate a realm where, as he says, “the dead live on without their wits as disembodied ghosts,” and where all the decisions worth making are made by the Three Judges of the Underworld. Achilles, a warrior-prince in the Underworld, has liƩle to do there.[14] But Plato’s Achilles is repulsed not by the shadowiness of the acƟve life there but by the shadowiness of their opinions and the life it breeds—as the philosopher-ruler of the

Cave/polis he would have lots to do, but the rewards are not such as the Sophists oﬀer to provide, honors and power. And again by contrast, this passage in Plato is followed by those stressing the honorable “contending” etc. of he who returns to debate with those “who never see JusƟce itself,” (517d) thus providing the honorable baƩle of the philosopher-warrior. What more can be said about the speciﬁc nature of the producƟons of the puppeteers and its recepƟon? An answer will help us to understand further just what those chains are and the nature and signiﬁcance of seeing images as images. Those who carry the ﬁgures are not, of course, explicitly menƟoned again. What role do they play in relaƟon to those enchained? The language of the immediate context, as well as the larger purposes of the Republic, combine to suggest the nature of such an answer. If they are, as I have suggested, the makers and molders of doxa, there are at least several parƟes who suggest themselves as fulﬁlling the role of sophists in relaƟon to those in chains below them.[15] Firstly, there are the professional Sophists, those who teach interpretaƟon as a self- contained art, unrelated to truth (or rather, denying it altogether). Secondly, there are the professional philosophers, but as the source of doxai, of opinions overheard by those whose access is limited to either blind acceptance or, at most, blind debate over shadows (and those philosophers, themselves, those of them whose philosophies are actually so much doxa). Thirdly, there are the poliƟcians or social theoreƟcians, whose pronouncements are taken not as personal value judgments but as the truths of poliƟcal and social life. Fourthly, there are views of nature, or natural philosophy, and generally science itself (including what we would call the social sciences) in its popularizaƟons and public recepƟon, that is, again, as doxa—especially in its poliƟcized form. This is not to suggest that all such popularizaƟons are misleading, or worse, intenƟonally decepƟve. Rather, that while they can be informaƟve, and contain to varying degree an actual summary of the arguments and evidence, they are qualitaƟvely disƟnguishable from science that they are summarizing. Of course this is on a conƟnuum. Also, the interpretaƟons, and misinterpretaƟons, of those in chains below are not necessarily the result of conscious manipulaƟons of the puppeteers above them. Rather, it is that their interpretaƟons are limited to what they can see, that is actually know, which can be not much.

Finally, there is the tradiƟon, itself a subject of interpretaƟon, consisƟng of the Poets (e.g., Simonides and Homer) and the society's collecƟve memory of great men. All these forms of doxai are related, as are their correlates in epistēmē—and this relaƟon will be brought out in the discussion of the Line. Crucial to the dynamic of the Cave is that the objects carried are fabricated. Now all of the above groups can be seen as makers of doxa.[16] And further, it is crucial that those in chains do not see that the very shadows and the echoes that they take for reality are eﬀecƟvely the producƟons of images that are merely made by human beings. This is in fact what the potenƟal philosopher sees on his ﬁrst release, and only fully understands returning to the cave, the aƩempted revelaƟon of which provokes such a violent reacƟon. So, as in the case of the Line, the dynamic requires that only from a higher posiƟon can one see the sense in which the lower posiƟon consists of shadows or images. Though with this diﬀerence: it is iniƟally from within a given secƟon of the Line that one ﬁrst begins to be dissaƟsﬁed—and this is equivalent to seeing that the truths of that secƟon are inadequate accounts, thus forcing one upward to a higher secƟon. The dynamic of the Cave requires an outside source of revelaƟon. But this diﬀerence is dissolved once one returns from the image and allegory to the level of the individual soul’s experience—or to the unity of the community of human discourse as a whole. If, then, those enchained are ignorant of the true nature of both the shadows and their causes, the puppets or objects, what about the puppeteers themselves? Surely they know what is going on? The answer is both yes and no. They know that they are responsible for having made the icons and the unreality of the shadows. They know that the bickering of those in chains is folly, and that the laƩer take mere images for real things, and misinterpret them at that. But we must not forget that they too are in the cave, and have never leŌ it. We must then ask what their aƫtude is to the objects (as opposed to the shadows these cast). Clearly, for them, more parƟcularly for the sophists,[17] they are merely made, and this is, for them, the only way that objects can have being. In other words, there is no other truth than that made by them, by man. And either each believes blindly in the truth of his own, simply because it is his, or else he sees that all have an equal claim to being man-made and reality is simply a quesƟon

of individual interpretaƟon. Yet, we ourselves must observe, their man- made images are not made out of whole cloth, they spring from somewhere—they are thus models of, are patched together from, something—a something or somethings that the puppet makers got from somewhere, though they do not know, and do not ask, from where. It then remains to ask from whence the raw material comes, what is the source and dynamic of their image-making itself and of the image-making capacity. And ﬁnally, is there a more intelligent, more raƟonal image- making possible in contrast to the personalisƟc and somewhat arbitrary image-making of the Cave and the interpretaƟon of the order or sequence of the shadows and echoes—a more raƟonal discourse to replace the hollow echoes of the cave. In sum, the makers of the puppet-images are clearer about the situaƟon within the cave than those in chains are, but only to a certain extent. Both those enchained and the puppet makers, each in their own way, deal with images, and each cannot see them as such, though their noƟons of truth are rather diﬀerent. Those in chains, the slaves as it were, are both deceived by the shadow-images and are unaware of their slavery (again, speaking metaphorically). Their masters are aware of the master- slave relaƟon, that the slaves are deceived by the images which the masters make and unaware of it—but the masters are unaware of the limits of their own mastery (of discourse and of meaning), which they take as absolute. That is, they take their image-making as creaƟng and, being themselves denizens of the cave, do not, and cannot, know any higher cause—thus they too are unaware of their slavery. They are perhaps not so foolish as to take their images, which are said to be “in stone or wood, fashioned in all sorts of ways” as the truth, while those in chains, by contrast, cannot see “anything of themselves or each other” and “believe the truth [to] be nothing else than the shadows of the arƟfacts.” Yet the masters of the show believe in this very arbitrariness, having seen nothing else. Or, of those who are untainted by sophists, believe in a higher source for their image-making, whether the gods, or Nature, but since they can give no account of it, their beliefs and systems of Nature remain doxai, while for the ethical, poliƟcal, and religious, their authority and sancƟons remain external and dogmaƟc. Note that the puppets are carried above the low wall behind which the puppeteers walk. It would thus appear that

the ﬁre does not cast the shadows of the puppeteers themselves on the wall in front of the prisoners, thus adding to the decepƟon—the shadows themselves appear to be the sources, and to be alive. The way in which the puppeteers hold on to the doxai which they produce corresponds in this reading of the epistemological image to pisƟs or trust, while those in chains, wholly concerned with discourse about ﬂiƫng images operate within the most basic form of eikasia—though this includes the images in speech of the echoes thrown by the puppeteers and their own speech as well, presumably. It is perhaps for this reason that the puppeteers are not heard from again—and that the philosopher who returns to the Cave speaks not to them but to those enchained. The allegory of the ship earlier had the contrast between the true navigator and the one who appealed to those who owned the ship, who oﬀered a way to rule and subdue the rebellious sailors, not in the laƩer’s interest but in that of the rulers. (In the above interpretaƟon of the objects fabricated I do not mean to ignore the more obvious, and literal, interpretaƟon, that the objects are sensible models of sensible originals in the natural world, including diagrams, etc., which are themselves copies of more real originals. But rather to bring out what I deem to be more relevant in the context of the dialogue’s main topic.) As for the ﬁre itself, not much is actually said about it, other than that, when someone is at ﬁrst freed from his chains, having to “stand up suddenly, turn his head, walk, and look upward toward the light, doing all this would give him pain, the ﬂash of the ﬁre would make it impossible for him to see the objects of which he had earlier seen the shadows” (514c). Thus the ﬁre, far from being a source of vision, at ﬁrst is itself blinding. The puppeteers, of course, do not consider the ﬁre itself at all, though presumably their eyes are beƩer adjusted to it, as it is closer to them, and, in the context of the image, they have not been prevented from looking at it, as have those in chains. Yet, if it is not going too far in looking into the details of the image, the ﬁre is also behind them, and further up. The result is that, though they are aware of the images which they themselves make, they are much less aware of, nor concerned about, the following: how it is that the shadows are cast; how it is that doxa comes to have its appeal and success; how it is that pisƟs actually funcƟons (again, to anƟcipate the Line) epistemologically both at the level of formed speech and the

elemental pisƟs in the elements or units that make discourse possible at all. Next, we should consider that the “deliverance from their bonds” (515c) of those in chains is eﬀected not by themselves, and the iniƟal reacƟon to release is to be blinded—they must in fact be led by another to see more clearly the actual situaƟon, to see “that what he saw then was foolishness, that he was now somewhat closer to reality and turned to things that existed more fully, that he saw more correctly.” It is somewhat pointless to ask for literally how, and even more so for when, the ﬁrst person was freed, who this guide is and where he comes from. Rather more relevant is the stress on the need for interrogaƟon and a sort of force as the necessary process. “If one pointed to each of the objects passing by, asked what each was, and forced him to answer [anankazoi erō tōn apokrinesthai]. And if he were compelled to look at the light . . . ” (515d, and see Shorey’s note in the Loeb ediƟon). The reacƟon at ﬁrst is recalcitrance and a retreat to the certainty of the former experience—the shadows are truer (alēthestera), less painful, more reliable. But the guide is persistent. First when asked “what each thing was,” looking for the ﬁrst Ɵme at the objects that cast the shadows—the subject resists; he “would be at a loss, and believe that the things he saw earlier were truer than the things now pointed out to him.” Confused by what he now sees for the ﬁrst Ɵme, and more importantly, having new criteria by which to judge between the shadow-images and the objects, he retreats to that with which he is most familiar. This aƩempt at geƫng him to say “what it is” before him is in contrast to his behavior when in chains; then, in another sort of conversing, that amongst themselves, he had been occupied with “naming the things that they saw” thinking that in so doing “they were naming (nomizein onomazein) the passing objects” (Shorey). The contrast is between discerning what a thing is and arguing blindly about the arbitrary naming of things. The issue of rightly naming something had been stressed earlier, parƟcularly in connecƟon with the idenƟﬁcaƟon of the virtues and the pairing up of the acƟviƟes of the city—its parts and the civic virtues—with the virtues and the parts of the individual in relaƟon to himself (Cf. 435b). Finding the correct name is, of course, tantamount to ﬁnding out exactly what jusƟce (for example) is, that is, as it is put by Socrates, what acƟvity “deserves the name.” This is contrasted to the

naming of the shadows, which would correspond to mere arbitrary deﬁniƟons. In the earlier text, the “sudden appearance” in a place that is “dark and hard to hunt in” of jusƟce, which “surprisingly had been with us from the very beginning” (432d) points with ironic humor to the fact that, although the method being used at that point is superior to mere blind debate, it is sƟll somewhat hypotheƟcal, as it were, and ﬂawed—and to be replaced by a superior method. The next step is for the subject to be forced to look at the source and cause of the very shadow-images to which he clings, to look at the ﬁre itself, as opposed to the puppet-images. The ﬁre is analogous to the Sun outside the Cave, as an image of an image (ﬁre:sun :: sun:Good). That is to say, it illuminates in the way that doxa can, a kind of inspiraƟon whose real source is hidden. But just as the Sun is the brighter and more real cause of illuminaƟon, so the ﬁre only seems to make things clear—the puppeteers are not inclined to ask how light and seeing are possible, how they are yoked even within the Cave, is the condiƟon for their decepƟon of others. But this too results in a fearful ﬂight, and the same claim that “those things which he could see [formerly] . . . were in fact clearer than those now shown to him.” And so it conƟnues; “as if one were to drag him thence by force up the rough and steep path, and did not let him go before he was dragged into the sunlight, in physical pain and angry as he was being dragged along.” That he must be forced, compelled, and dragged is not without signiﬁcance—stressing the dialogical nature of authenƟc enquiry. This can be contrasted with the ease and naturalness of common sense, of doxa and pisƟs, as well as with the suggested use of external physical force in the poliƟcal methods of a Thrasymachus as contrasted to that of the Republic and its own polis. The image of physical force is seen in the very opening passages of the dialogue (327a-328b), from the moment when the slave boy, sent ahead to have Socrates wait up, grabs hold of Socrates’ himaton, and then in the contrast between physical force, “we are more than you,” “see how many we are,” and the eroƟc compulsion that Socrates experiences in the lure of a good conversaƟon with young men, “unless they were to refuse to listen” (though the decision to stay is shiŌed onto Glaucon—“If you think so, said I, then we must”). And the theme of conversaƟon is soon conƟnued in Cephalus’ musings about the ostensible advantages of old age. Ironically, the shiŌ is from Socrates using persuasion

to convince them to let him leave, to being seduced to stay by the spectacle of the fesƟval of Bendis down in the Piraeus, and more so of course of the promise of aŌer dinner conversaƟon at the house of Cephalus/Polemarcus. As for the rest of the Cave story, the brief descripƟon of what takes place outside the cave proper when in the light of the sun itself, we note only that the released prisoner goes through the same stages again; iniƟally blinded by the light, then able to see “shadows,” then “images of reﬂecƟons of men and other things in water” (the above world’s counterpart of the made objects of the cave), then the “things themselves,” then, interesƟngly, “objects in the sky and the sky itself, the light of the stars and moon more easily than the sun and the light of the sun during the day,” and ﬁnally, “he would be able to see the sun itself, not images of it in water or in some alien place” (516b). The presence of the celesƟal objects, apart from leading up from the “lesser light to the greater light,” is interesƟng because of the later discussion of the role of astronomy in the speciﬁc educaƟon of the philosopher. (The disƟncƟon between outside the cave and the object world within it requires that we work out the knowledge-opinion disƟncƟon in the discussion of the Line proper. Brieﬂy, the iniƟal stage outside the Cave would correspond, I suggest, to dianoia, then a vision of the things themselves, to noēsis.) TURNING OF THE SOUL: ONTOLOGY, SIGHT, AND INSIGHT We can see now, on such an interpretaƟon of the cave and its denizens and dynamic, why the passage concludes with the two references to the trial of Socrates (517a; 517d), and why a contrast is made between those who “say that knowledge is not present in the soul and that they put it in, like puƫng sight into blind eyes” (518b), and the view of “our present argument,” which claims that the “capacity to learn is in every person’s soul” (518c). But further, we see that educaƟon is a turning not merely of the mind, the epistemological sense of the Cave parable, but ontological, a turning of the whole soul. In fact, there is a mutuality of the aspects. The contemplaƟng of the highest reality is not achievable without the precondiƟon and preparaƟon of the whole soul—hence the image of the training of the guardian as applicable to the individual in preparaƟon for

the higher educaƟon of the soul, the image of which is presented in the educaƟon of the philosopher proper. But the vision at the end of the upward journey is also of use; it is put to use in the perpetual turning of the soul from things visible to those not visible, in this visible /poliƟcal world, as well as a guiding vision in the turning of the souls of others. We turn again to the passage at 518b: It is as if it were not possible to turn the eye from darkness to light without turning the whole body. So one must turn one’s whole soul [not just the intellect] from the world of becoming unƟl it can endure to contemplate reality . . . educaƟon is then the act of doing this very thing, this turning around, the knowledge of how the soul can most usefully and eﬀecƟvely be turned around . . . the virtue of intelligence . . . according to which way it is turned, becomes useful and beneﬁcial or useless and harmful . . . liƩle souls [have] a capacity for sight [which is] not inferior, but is compelled to serve evil ends. (518b-519a, Grube transl.) Thus, again, clearly more than just epistemic insight is at stake. Within the Cave the iniƟal condiƟon of those in chains is also described as “prevent[ing] them from turning their heads” and then, “Whenever one of them was freed . . . [he would] . . . turn his head . . . ” and ﬁnally, when compelled to look at “the ﬁre itself, his eyes would hurt, [and] he would turn around and ﬂee towards those things which he could see.” The turning of the head, an image in which the eye/mind is stressed, is to be set in the larger context of the struggles, turning to and away, of the whole person up the “rough and steep path.” Thus “educaƟon and the lack of it” is seen as a social, and ulƟmately intrapersonal conﬂict, ﬁnally as struggle with oneself and the obstacles to ascent, self rule and freedom. The “anger and physical pain” is a result “as he was dragged along” (516a).[18] Seeing images as images, the fruits of the journey as well as its method, has consequences in the lived world in which the soul has learned the habit and value of turning itself around. We turn in the next chapter to the image of the Divided Line, in which the world of images and their measurement is described. The details of the dynamic of that image will give in schemaƟc form the interrelaƟon of soul, its world and the Ideas that is our theme.

But before that let us look brieﬂy at a famous essay that also takes this dynamic seriously—Heidegger’s interpretaƟon of the allegory of the Cave in his insighƞul essay, “Plato’s Doctrine of Truth.”18 There are iniƟal similariƟes to my own interpretaƟon, but it is rather the contrast that will help make my point, and ulƟmately defend Plato against Heidegger’s criƟcal conclusion. Heidegger sees that the signiﬁcance of the Cave allegory is in its dynamic, in its “incidents” and “transiƟons,” from the dark of the cave to the light of day, and from day back down into the night world. The hiddenness of truth is in the very directness of the appearance of the shadow images, while their origins and possibility are unseen, and this hiddenness reﬂects the essence of truth as unhiddenness, as a shining out, hence the importance of the ﬁre, and the sun image. Heidegger rightly stresses, in my view, that the Republic is about the link, the “essenƟal unity,” between educaƟon and truth, that is, on Heidegger’s interpretaƟon, between the new educaƟon and the new concept of truth. “The essence of educaƟon is founded in the essence of truth” (260). True freedom from one’s chains is achieved in a progressive turning of the whole soul, and “the narraƟve of the freed man’s return to those sƟll enchained in the cave also belongs to the allegory.” But the Platonic disclosure of the truth and the very meaning of truth, can only be carried out by a re-interpretaƟon of the basis of shining out, phenomenal truth, of the phenomenon. “Consciousness properly speaking, has to do with the way outward appearance manifests itself and is preserved in the brightness of its steady appearance” (261). Appearance here is not the mere appearance oŌen contrasted with the real, but rather the manifesƟng of the Idea, its shining forth or parousia, the truth disclosing itself as the What it is of things. “Thus . . . the Idea achieves presence, namely the presence of every being as what it is” (my emphasis). For Heidegger, the key shiŌ in the meaning of Truth is from the supposiƟon of a pre-Platonic direct presencing of beings and of Being, to a truth that is ‘permiƩed’ or facilitated through the Idea, a process energized by the Good, and through which beings are uniﬁed. “The Good preserves the manifestaƟon of outward appearance, wherein what is present as what is has duraƟon. Through this preservaƟon beings are held together in Being and ‘delivered’” (264). Now, “the idea becomes master of alētheia,” “alētheia comes under the yoke of the idea. The essence of truth

relinquishes the basic feature of unhiddenness.” That is, insight becomes sight, and truth becomes seeing. The stages in the Cave analogy are thus advances guided by a new noƟon of truth. “The transiƟon from one situaƟon into another consists in making one’s glance more correct. Everything depends on orthotes the correctness of the glance” (265). EducaƟon thus must become an educaƟon in seeing correctly—that is, seeing through the Ideas in their showing forth, to the Ideas. The essence of beings becomes the essence of truth as the dynamics of the disclosedness of the Ideas. “Truth becomes orthotes, correctness of the ability to perceive and to declare something” (265). “As unhiddenness, truth is sƟll a basic feature of beings themselves. But as correctness of ‘looking,’ truth has become the label of the human aƫtude towards beings.” This shiŌ for Heidegger is the beginning of Western metaphysics. He laments that this shiŌ is in a sense away from Being, sƟll present in the unhiddenness of beings, and “at the same Ɵme the inquiry into unhiddenness [truth] is shiŌed to the way outward appearance manifests itself and with that to the associated ability to see: to what is right and the correctness of seeing.” We come then to the crux of his argument. Heidegger observes what he claims is a ﬂawed “ambiguity of the deﬁniƟon of the essence of truth,”—truth as “a characterisƟc of beings,” versus truth as the “way outward appearance manifests itself [the ‘what it is’ manifested in the parousia of the idea] and with that to the associated ability to see; to what is right and the correctness of seeing,” (H265) evident in Plato’s own interpretaƟon of the allegory of the cave (at 517 b7-c5). The “yoke between recognizing and what is recognized” which is forged by the Good, is explicated, he claims ambiguously, in a “twofold manner.” The idea of the Good is both “the cause of correctness and of all that is beauƟful,” but also then as “master dispensing unhiddenness and perceiving.” Heidegger says that the two expressions are “not parallel,” and that by making them so, the rule of the Good is so explicated in such a way that “truth no longer is, as unhiddenness, the basic feature of being itself, but is, in consequence of having become correctness by being yoked under the Idea, from this Ɵme forth the label of the recognizing of beings.” “Unhiddenness now refers to the unhidden always as that which is accessible thanks to the Idea’s ability to shine. But insofar as the access is necessarily carried out through

‘seeing’ unhiddenness is yoked into a ‘relaƟon’ with seeing. It becomes ‘relaƟve’ to seeing” (H226/ Sheehan transl.). “. . . [I]dea gains dominance over alētheia” . . . The idea of the Good, “ . . . is mistress in that she bestows unhiddenness (on what shows itself) and at the same Ɵme imparts apprehension (of what is hidden). Alētheia comes under the yoke of the idea . . . henceforth the essence of truth does not, as the essence of unhiddenness, unfold from its proper and essenƟal fullness but rather shiŌs to the essence of the Idea. The essence of truth gives up its fundamental unhiddenness” (H230, my emphasis). His argument is rather dense, not to say ellipƟcal, so let us look at it again, spelling out the details. The sequence ortha-kala is followed by the sequence alētheia-nous and Heidegger observes that Plato “criss-crosses” the correspondence (that is, relates the two outer terms to the two inner terms)—nous or ‘correct perceiving,’ to ortha, the ‘correctly perceived,’ and alētheia, or ‘unhiddenness’ or ‘truth’ to kala, or ‘the beauƟful’—the shining out of the outward appearance of the Idea. The result is that “both sentences [in Plato’s text] tell of the precedence of the Idea of the Good as the possibility of correctly recognizing something [what it is] and the possibility of what is recognized becoming unhidden” (H266). This is the consequence, according to Heidegger, of the “intenƟonal fusing of alētheia, and orthotes as a standard—all in the same train of thought.” Thus even while for Plato “truth is both unhiddenness and correctness here,” the directness of the shining forth has receded, given place to truth as necessarily mediated—and thus educaƟon (paideia) becomes ontological necessity; and truth becomes a property of asserƟons. “Where the understanding makes an asserƟon in order to pass judgment is the place of truth and falsity and their diﬀerence.” Truth is thus understood as the opposite of falsity, the incorrect, rather than the disclosure and unhiddenness of beings and of Being as a consequence. The result is to deﬁne the Being of beings as Idea. “The essence of unhiddenness . . . shiŌs its abode [from beings] to the essence of the idea” (H265) as “alētheia comes under the yoke of the idea.” “In this change of the essence of truth a shiŌ of the place of truth takes place at the same Ɵme. As unhiddenness truth is sƟll a basic feature of beings themselves. But as correctness of ‘looking’ truth becomes the label of the human aƫtude towards beings” (H265).

But I would suggest that Plato’s “criss-crossing” and the “ambiguity” makes philosophical sense. That is, the Good is intenƟonally conceived in two ways, as “cause of correctness and all that is beauƟful,” but also as “master dispensing unhiddenness and apprehension (nous).” What Heidegger takes as an ambiguity regarding the explicaƟon of the Idea of the Good, hence the place of Truth (alētheia/ H’s ‘unhiddenness’), I take as two perspecƟves that make a whole (the world of the Line and Cave), and just because “alētheia comes under the yoke of the Idea.” Plato saw that direct insight into the Being of beings was not possible, indeed an illusion that he describes in the Phaedo (parƟcularly in Socrate’s own intellectual autobiography there). And he saw that beings could disclose their essence only to and through what they shared both with one another, and pre- eminently with human being or soul through the medium or prism of image-making—primarily within discourse. Truth does not become proposiƟonal (or predicaƟonal) for Plato, as Heidegger claims, if the Ideas are shared amongst soul and world. If the dynamic of paideia requires both correctness and unhiddenness in equal measure—the ability to see, but equally the ability to be seen—then to be “under the yoke of the eidē” is not a burden but the only source of freedom, not only for the perceiver but for the perceived. The shimmering presence that Heidegger thinks once shone forth, and that we ought to seek again, beyond metaphysics, is chimerical—risks being a retreat to poetry and myth rather than an advance through images. Heidegger condemns as “humanism,” the “process bound up with the beginning, unfolding, and end of metaphysics” in which educaƟon as metaphysical is a “concern for human being and for the posiƟon of man in the midst of beings [which] dominates throughout metaphysics.” Plato’s claim is to have found where beings and Being truly meet. For Heidegger, it is a tragedy and a cul-de-sac that “the real is expounded according to ‘ideas’ [and] that the ‘world’ is weighed according to ‘values,’ limiƟng unhiddenness to sighƟng, perceiving, thinking, staƟng. To pursue this relaƟonship means to give up the essence of unhiddenness” (H270). This is as opposed, Heidegger claims, to learning to live fully aware in the “clearing” in which Being unfolds itself to Dasein, “ex-staƟcally” showing itself, appearing through beings to the being that has a primordial acƟve relaƟon to it, and most tellingly in discourse. “No aƩempt to found the essence of unhiddenness in ‘reason’, in ‘spirit’, in ‘thinking’, in the logos

in any kind of ‘subjecƟvity’ can ever deliver the essence of unhiddenness. . . . [T]he most that they can accomplish is only a steady ‘explanaƟon’ of an essenƟal consequence of the ungrasped essence of unhiddenness” (H270). But this is to assume that there is such an “ungrasped essence” that is beyond such discourse. Is unhiddenness available to be grasped any other way than in the discourse of the dialogical community? Are Heidegger’s own aƩempts not subject to the standard of correctness in at least some sense, if that is, they are discursive? ExplanaƟon is indeed a consequence— and it is because it is so (aƩempts to be so) that the essence of beings does not remain ungrasped. Heidegger, one supposes, objects that in so grasping them they are transformed, deformed. But suppose that it is only in this transformaƟon in discourse that beings were understood to achieve Being. Not all transformaƟons/explanaƟons are equally successful and the provocaƟon of successes and failures reﬂects in image a dynamic that is more than subjecƟvity. This, I would say, is the very lesson of the Cave. (See also Heidegger, Being and Time H28-29. Heidegger later decided that even the Pre-SocraƟcs were in the grip of this general turning away from truth as unhiddenness, etc. See “The End of Philosophy and the Task of Thinking” [386 ﬀ.] Thus the task has always been, and remains, for him, to go beyond the Greeks.) That Plato’s concepƟon of alētheia ﬁnally goes beyond a correspondence with ortha “what is correct and its correctness” to the kala, is for Heidegger a last fatal move in which “the essence of unhiddenness [alētheia, /truth] shiŌs its abode [from beings] to the essence of the idea.” But it is precisely this primary linking of truth and the beauƟful, rather than with the correct (that is with proposiƟons), that makes for a platonic ontological as opposed to an epistemological claim, as is the duality, or ostensible “ambiguity” of the Idea of the Good. This diﬀerence will prepare us for the discussion of the Line and its ontology of images in the next chapter. It should now be clear why in my presentaƟon I have reversed the order in Plato’s text, considering the Cave before explicaƟng the Line. My claim has been that Glaucon and Adeimantus operate at the literal level of the city/soul analogy, and correspondingly at the level of opinion as contrasted to knowledge. This is understandable if they have not in fact been through the educaƟon that would help them rise above it, something

oŌen overlooked, though the signs are embedded in the text.[19] But that they are somewhat stuck at the level of doxa about the very knowledge- opinion disƟncƟon, itself receives both an explanaƟon and an illustraƟon in the dialogical image of them that has been unfolding before us. Since Socrates’s plan is to deal with the “eﬀects of educaƟon and the lack of it” in the Cave image, and my having already pointed out the limitaƟons of Glaucon and Adeimantus in several earlier passages, I thought it useful to deal ﬁrst with the image of the eﬀect of the lack of educaƟon, or of mis- educaƟon, as imaged in the Cave. AŌer all, the sequence of the Good, the Sun, the Line, the Cave and the educaƟon of the philosopher-ruler—the downward, then the upward, moƟon of the text—is schemaƟc, while the willingness of Glaucon and Adeimantus to hear what they are warned are Socrates’ “mere opinions” about the oﬀspring of the Good is as much a warning for us, and renders the Cave image somewhat ironical with reference to these friends of the Ideas.[20] NOTES 1. dia makrou. Aiken (New York: Random House, 1962), 251-69. Also in Pathmarks, ed. William McNeill, translated by Thomas Sheehan, Cambridge University Press, 1998. Barlow is used throughout, except where noted. Page numbers refer to Barlow (H. refers to the page in Wegmarken in the Gesamtausgabe, Band 9). Contrast my interpretaƟon with Drew Hyland, Finitude and Transcendence in the Platonic Dialogues (Albany: State University of New York Press, 1995) 139-63. Hyland does not, it seems to me, see the force of Heidegger's criƟque of “correctness” as the standard for truth and the tension between direct, ulƟmately non-discursive insight into beings and a platonic mediated knowledge. (I would, however, agree that for Plato alētheia has a dimension of ﬁnitude.) Thus, while as he notes, the Form of the Good is said to be “beyond being” at 509c, his explicaƟon of the relaƟon of the ethical to the ontological sense of the Good remains problemaƟc. I also disagree with his characterizaƟon of noēsis as intuiƟve and non-discursive insight (see my criƟque of a similar posiƟon by Sayre in chapter eight

below). For one thing, it is hard to see how a ﬁnally non-discursive insight as noēsis (Hyland acknowledges the role of discourse as leading towards it) would be of any help in explaining, of giving greater clarity and precision to, the objects of dianoia, as it is said to do. Furthermore, the objects of noēsis themselves are said to be a subject of study for at least an ongoing aƩempt at greater clarity. Thus, while it is true that “neither the originaƟng nor the culminaƟng noēsis is reducible to dianoeƟc speech itself,” (182) taken in the sense of reducing the eidē to meanings or predicaƟons, neither is noēsis intelligible as a transcendent (albeit ﬁnite) direct vision cut oﬀ from that discourse. Indeed it is that search and its discursive means in dialegesthai that Heidegger rejects, and opposes with his own direct methods, parƟcularly in the later wriƟngs. 19. For the general noƟon of compulsion or being “forced” (necessity - anankē) and in parƟcular with regard to the original ascent out of the Cave, see Rachel Barney, “Eros and Necessity in the Ascent from the Cave,” Ancient Philosophy 28 (2008) 1-15. Barney parses the diﬀerent meanings of “necessity” in Plato, disƟnguishing, for one, external compulsion from internal or self-imposed compulsion. There is, then, the “curricular” compulsion of the educaƟon of the guardian/philosopher. Here the potenƟal student is not forced to remain in the program, as it were, (and certainly not forced to learn) but the studies themselves are “necessary” given the desired end. While for those who respond posiƟvely and stay the course, the studies force the student in the sense of the turning the soul. “ArithmeƟc is to be the ﬁrst compulsory subject (522e1, 525b2) precisely because (like the sight of the great and small mixed up together, 542c) it compels a reorientaƟon of thought from the visible to the intellectual world” (4). Secondly, there is the SocraƟc reading of the forcing of the individual soul inherent in the engagement of dialegesthai. Finally, an eroƟc sense (a term not explicitly used in the Cave passage) conspicuous in the Symposium, the eros experienced as an implacable human desire for the beauƟful and the good, eventually an increasingly irresisƟble aƩracƟon for the truly beauƟful and the really good, albeit iniƟally an “ascent to the realm of reason” (15) that one’s other self resists, ﬁnds painful. But perhaps stressing that the whole image be ﬁnally brought down to the individual soul’s internal struggles, the descripƟons of external compulsion are less problemaƟc: evolving inner debates over ethical/poliƟcal cruxes,

pracƟcing Liszt in pain and ending in pleasure in the beauƟful, studying a diﬃcult text unƟl late into the night and ﬁnding myself both caught up, yet also Ɵred and hungry, or hearing my partner’s pleas to come to bed for heaven’s sake. 20. See E. T. H. Brann, “The Music of the Republic,” The Saint John’s Review vol. 39, nos. 1and 2 (1989-90): 1-103 (reprinted in Brann, 2004). Brann thinks Glaucon is treated as a student in the dialogical community that is the “fourth city” of the Republic’s central books (but see her last paragraph, 96) While Adeimantus is acknowledged by Brann as an erisƟc, Glaucon is seen by her in a beƩer light. I agree that Adeimantus is argumentaƟve while Glaucon is a more willing student, and perhaps more capable. (cf. Brann, 51) I have argued that the textual evidence is rather that they are both meant to be contrasted to the careful reader. Cf. chapter one, and later, chapter nine, where I argue Book X as serving Glaucon and Adeimantus’s needs in a ﬁnal answer to Thrasymachus. See note 4 above (regarding Annas). Glaucon may be capable of exercising dianoia, hence having more than opinion in the narrow sense, but not of rising to noēsis. Cf. Brann, Music, 46.

Chapter 4 The Divided Line and the Dynamic of Ascent THE TRUE PHILOSOPHER, THE SUN IMAGE, AND BEGINNING THE ASCENT Plato’s famous image of the Divided Line is too oŌen described in somewhat staƟc terms, as a classiﬁcaƟon of all that is into a set of ontological boxes, stacked in ascending order of truth and degrees of reality. This seems to me not to pay suﬃcient aƩenƟon to both the unity of the Line and the acƟve dynamic of knower and known that Plato sets out in the ever shiŌing progress through it—the Line as the descripƟon of a living process. In our developing story of the interrelaƟon for Plato of soul, world and Ideas, the reading of this image in its dynamic is crucial. Another common view concerns Plato’s denigraƟon of images, as at best less real than their originals, and at worst decepƟve, misleading. And it is certainly easy to ﬁnd the various texts to support this view (including the discussion of poetry and mimesis in Book X). Some have noted with a smile that, paradoxically, Plato himself makes much use of images. Here, too, I wish to suggest in what follows that there is an alternaƟve, or rather parallel, posiƟve Platonic view of images (eidōla, eikones) and of image-making (eidōlopoiikos)—that this role is crucial to an understanding of Plato’s ontology. I shall eventually examine the Line in speciﬁc detail in this chapter, and will return to it again in the next chapter when examining the educaƟon of the ruler (following Plato’s own procedure. Cf. 509d-511e, 517a, ﬀ. esp. 534a). But as in previous chapters, each new topic requires preliminaries for the context. In the previous chapter, I oﬀered an interpretaƟon of just how the Cave image represents the “eﬀects of educaƟon and the lack of it.” Here I will comment on the two archetypal candidates, the true and the false philosopher, for the relaƟon of knower and known that is to be described in the image of the Line. Then, since the Line is an image providing an analogy for the eﬀect of the Good on what is known and on the knower, I will look at the speciﬁc terms in which the

eﬀect is described (the comments in chapter three were rather general). Only then can the Line’s divisions itself be examined. Finally, I suggest just where the interlocutors of the dialogue might be placed on the Line. A central issue in our discussion of the Cave was the nature of the conversaƟons there, and of speech in general. In that scene there was much contending, dispuƟng, and compeƟƟon between those observing the shadows (cf. 514b, 517a-e, 516c). This conversaƟon was contrasted to the dialecƟcal compulsion used in the dialogue that we are to imagine as eventually taking place between the philosopher on his return and that cave dweller whom he seeks to lead towards the light. The same contrast applies to and illustrates the disƟncƟons already discussed between philosophy and erisƟc, the true and the false philosopher, and their respecƟve images in the city. They had been disƟnguished by the nature of the objects that they pursue and by their personal objecƟves in relaƟon to the ciƟzens and the city. This involved preliminary ontological disƟncƟons concerning percepƟon of the one and the many, the principle of idenƟty, and the exclusion of opposites, all of which is called the “spectacle of truth,” as opposed to the “spectacle of sights and sounds”—the sights and sounds of the shadow world and its “echoes.” It was here that the iniƟal disƟncƟons between knowledge and opinion were made. We turn then ﬁrst to the disƟncƟon between the true and false philosophers. Having disƟnguished between the “lovers of knowledge” and the “lovers of opinion” by the end of Book V, the task of ruling the just city is assigned to the “lover of knowledge,” and an account of the “bad reputaƟon of the philosophers” is given. This bad reputaƟon is due in part to those who pretend to philosophy, who “consort with her,” but who do so in such a way as to produce, to give birth to, not the wisdom and just laws that could wisely rule the city, or their own soul, but rather to the fruits of a bad marriage—“So when those unﬁt for educaƟon approach philosophy and consort with her, what kind of thoughts and opinions are we to say they will produce? Will they not be such as to deserve to truly be called sophistry, that is, nothing genuine or partaking of wisdom?”(496a). This imagery of begeƫng will be useful later in analyzing the dynamic of the Line. And so we have on the one hand those who are unﬁt for the labors of the educaƟon for philosophy, but on the other hand, those who, while ﬁt, are seeds that fall on bad soil and are corrupted in their

development, because there is at present “not one of our present consƟtuƟons (which) is worthy of the philosophic nature, and that in consequence this nature is twisted and altered, like a foreign seed which is sown on alien ground” (497b). Thus in the actual situaƟon, though it is possible for the philosophical nature to develop to its full power it is not exactly likely, short of taking root and being nurtured in the city which is ruled by philosophy already, that is, in the city whose consƟtuƟon we have constructed in Books II-V. But as Socrates adds: We said even then that there must always be some people in the city who understand the raƟonal principle on which the consƟtuƟon is based, the same which guided you, the lawgiver, when you made the laws. —We did say that. Yes, but we did not emphasize it suﬃciently, for fear that the proof of it would be long and diﬃcult, as your intervenƟons showed it to be. (497d) What is the basis for the asserƟon that such a raƟonal ciƟzen-soul, a potenƟal arƟst or image maker of true images like that of our city, already exists—and why do the intervenƟons of Glaucon and Adeimantus provide a clue to the obstacles to perceiving this? Now the intervenƟons were, so I have argued, a reﬂecƟon of a misunderstanding, or inability to see the plane on which the consƟtuƟon of the city was being constructed, the level of discourse—that is, to keep in mind the analogical or image-making funcƟon of the whole exercise. The objecƟons are conspicuously raised at the literal level, concerning the diﬃculƟes of actually bringing such a model city into existence, thus seemingly forgeƫng the purpose of the enterprise, which was not to found a city but to discover what jusƟce is, and whether the just person is indeed happier than the unjust, even when suﬀering on the rack, or can we say, living in an unjust state. To hope for more would be, it is suggested, more than what is humanly possible: “If it [the truly philosophical nature] were to ﬁnd the best consƟtuƟon, as it is itself the best, it would be clearly seen to be truly divine while other

natures and pursuits are but human” (497b). For this reason, “taking all this into account, he keeps quiet and minds his own business . . . when they [the philosophical remnant] have fully realized also the madness of the majority, that pracƟcally never does anyone act sanely in public aﬀairs . . .” (496d). But this need not keep the philosopher from pursuing personal jusƟce within his own soul and in that of those few with whom he discourses in private, for though “like a man who has fallen among wild beasts, being unwilling to join in the wrongdoing and not being strong enough to oppose the general savagery alone,” there is sƟll the possibility of taming individual beasts. Thrasymachus is not tamed but rather silenced. The purpose of the Line then, is to aid in our understanding just what the philosophical soul’s raƟonal principles are and their relaƟon to both thinking being and the world(s) that it perceives; and in this way, becoming those “who understand the raƟonal principle on which the consƟtuƟon is based.” The quesƟon then is “How a city can engage in philosophy without being destroyed?” (497d), and one must add, how a soul can engage in philosophy without being destroyed, that is, led astray. The diﬃculty with those who pursue philosophy now is that they do so as a sort of window dressing for the educated young man of culture: “Now, those who study it do so as young men who have just leŌ childhood behind, before they engage in housekeeping and money making.” But the purpose and methods of philosophy proper they never aƩain to, for “just as they approach its most diﬃcult part, they give up and regard themselves as fully trained in philosophy.” It is signiﬁcant that the “most diﬃcult part” is then described as “the study of raƟonal discourse (to peri tous logous),” which study is exempliﬁed and schemaƟzed in the Line. At this point there is perhaps a poke at Cephalus. “In later life they think it much if they are willing to listen by invitaƟon to a lecture on philosophy by others who pracƟce it, but they think one should study it as a sideline. When they reach old age, with a few excepƟons, their eagerness is quenched more thoroughly than the sun of Heracleitus, for it is never rekindled” (498a). Cephalus seems at the beginning of the dialogue to be one of the excepƟons, for he is full of enthusiasm over the chance to converse with Socrates again aŌer such a long Ɵme. But he in fact soon reƟres from the discussion. It is, then, the shining Glaucon, the son (along

with Adeimantus) of Ariston, who, if any one of the interlocutors, is to be “rekindled” (and not the erisƟcal Polemarchus, baƩle-lord, the son of Cephalus). But if we are right about his limitaƟons, then we can only say that it is those who truly parƟcipate in the dialogue of the Republic, the reader who follows the argument, who is rekindled in that very process. Cephalus prefers to look aŌer the ﬁres of the sacriﬁce. “I leave the argument to you [Polemarchus], for I must go back and look aŌer the sacriﬁce” (331d). The ﬁre of philosophy, having never been for him more than a sideline as contrasted to the management of his wealth (cf.330a ﬀ.), while not exactly quenched, is reduced to a ﬂicker, not unlike that of the Cave. Thus, the city and the man in which virtue reigns in both word and deed has never yet been met with, and it is “no wonder that our words do not convince the majority, for they have never yet seen that upon which we are now insisƟng as exisƟng” (498d). Such a perfect city and perfect individual could come to be only under rather special condiƟons: either by chance if philosophers became kings, and if that city were compelled to obey them, or by the collaboraƟon of the gods “if by divine inspiraƟon a genuine passion for true philosophy” possesses kings to become philosophers. But regardless of whether this has ever happened in the past, “or whether it is happening now in some foreign place,” “or will happen in the future,” the crucial thing is to see, once again, that the condiƟon for such possibility is always the rule of philosophy. But furthermore, “we must be ready to struggle to maintain in argument that the city we described has existed, exists now, and will exist whenever the muse of philosophy controls the city” (499c). This would seem to suggest that this city and its best ciƟzen exists whenever and wherever the acƟvity of true philosophy is being pracƟced, and in the poliƟcal wisdom of the conversaƟons of a Socrates, about the governing of oneself, or in concert with others, and discussions about this rule. In these circumstances we should be allowed to say that for the duraƟon of the rule of that Muse, the city can and ought to be said to exist. But even this is only parƟally true, since the pursuit of philosophy, while requiring already the proper ordering of the soul momentarily insofar as reason (not erisƟc) is ruling, is yet not the possession or habit of philosophy considered as aﬀecƟng the well- ordered life which is the consequence of philosophy rightly conceived, i.e.,

its result, or more properly its expression. As in the exchanges of the Symposium, philosophy provisionally rules, regardless of the posiƟons taken, for as long as discourse as a whole is allowed to conƟnue, and as a whole is directed towards and by reasoning about the subject (though individual discourses may be more or less raƟonal). It ceases to exist, both for the individual and for the group, when this acƟvity is interrupted by a “band of revelers,” whose acƟviƟes are inimical to philosophy—they are responsible for the rupture of the discourse in the Symposium, literally a drunken band, and the same image is invoked here: “the intolerance of the many towards philosophy is caused by those outsiders who come to philosophy, where they do not belong, like a band of revelers” (500b). One can only think of the sophists, both oﬀering and consuming a potent brew, reveling in their successes. The many, it is said, will change their opinions about the uselessness of philosophy if they are shown both who we “mean by philosophers” and what their actual object of pursuit is—hence “they will realize that you do not mean the same people as they do” (500a). Now the false philosophers, akin to those who bear aloŌ the images that cast the shadows of the Cave, are precisely those who ulƟmately cause the “intolerance of the many towards philosophy” and whose disputes, and the method itself of dispute, are the shadow images of both the real objects, and of the real methods of discourse which seek not victory but truth. They are that “band of revelers” menƟoned above as responsible for the intolerance of the many towards philosophy, those outsiders who come to it without a sense of its purposes and methods, and for that very reason behave like revelers, in that they “are conƟnually abusing each other and being quarrelsome; they always talk in personaliƟes, which is quite unsuited to philosophy” (500b). The behavior of these pseudo-philosophers is all the more poignant if the references to Socrates are taken with the descripƟon of the source of the intolerance of the many. The true philosopher, by contrast is described as, the man whose thoughts are truly directed to real existences, [and who] does not have the Ɵme to look down upon the aﬀairs of men and by contending with them to be ﬁlled with malice and ill will . . . as he looks upon and contemplates things that are ordered and ever the same, that do no wrong and are not wronged by each other, being all

in a raƟonal order, imitates them and tries to become as like them as he can. Or do you think one can consort with things one admires without imitaƟng them in one’s own person. (500c) Thus the contrast in acƟviƟes and the eﬀect of these acƟviƟes is focused on. The false philosophers are ﬁlled with “malice,” that is, their souls reﬂect both the method, “contending,” and objects of their pracƟces, “wandering,” lacking order. Their contenƟousness reﬂects both the objecƟve of victory (as opposed to knowledge and truth) and the objects of “many sights and sounds,” that is parodied in the random grouping of the shadows and their sequences of the Cave. The true philosopher’s acƟvity, the pursuit of the “things that are ordered and ever the same” with a method that is both suited to this and takes it as its goal, aﬀects the soul in a reﬂecƟon or image of this: “So the philosopher who consorts with what is divine and ordered, himself becomes godlike and ordered, as far as man can” (500d). Each soul, then, is the non-visible image of its acƟvity; this intellectual acƟvity, seemingly epistemological, has ontological consequences in its reﬂected images both in the state and in the acƟvity of the whole soul of the person. It is, then, important to bear this in mind when looking at the Line proper, which occurs but a few pages later in the text—for it is there that we see an image of what these acƟviƟes look like, though in what appears to be in abstracƟon from the beneﬁcial eﬀects just described. The Line describes how knowing works at all levels; the dynamic of the Line is the dynamic of knowing (and of not knowing), but the eﬀects of this on the souls of men as they lead other than strictly noeƟc lives are not given explicitly in the image (i.e., the social context of knowing and not knowing). A dramaƟzaƟon of the struggle between ignorance and knowledge is given life aŌerwards in the psychosocial acƟon of the Cave, as the “eﬀects of educaƟon and the lack of it,” as already discussed. Further, the applicaƟon or pracƟce of especially the highest level is not explicitly directed in the Line to the public or social uses or pracƟces of the philosopher as arƟst-maker, which occurs only in his descent. Rather, the Line focuses on his ascent, that is, on that ontological descripƟon of the world which is the condiƟon for the ascent. The philosopher as arƟst funcƟons in “applying them [the Ideas] to the characters of men both in private and in public life instead of only molding his own [soul]”(500d), and

he does so only as a consequence of, or aŌer, his ascent. Thus there is a contrast between the pure dynamic or dialecƟc of the Line, the ways that we know both more and more truly (though the material is originally from public pracƟces)—and the way in which this knowledge “become(s) beneﬁcial and useful” (cf. 505a; 518e) as the philosopher turned draŌsman “wipes clean the slate,” for example in the struggles with those who have not yet leŌ the Cave, and makes an eﬀort to “compose human life” as the “draŌsman of consƟtuƟons.” But what is this knowing acƟvity on which the designing acƟvity is based, and what is the connecƟon between them? Once having stressed their bond we can now look at the Line itself in this light. For it forms part of the discussion of “how the saviors of our consƟtuƟon will develop, and what studies and pursuits they will follow” (502d).[1] The temperament of the philosopher-ruler is that he must be both quick-wiƩed (but not ﬂighty) and yet stable without being sluggish, and be tested in “those toils, fears and pleasures we menƟoned before.” But also, Socrates now adds, “we omiƩed before . . . [that] it must be exercised in many kinds of studies to see whether it can tolerate the greatest studies.” And the greatest study, to be achieved by the “longer way,” is the study of the Good, which is the “most appropriate study.” Since it is as a further explanaƟon of the Good and its “oﬀspring” that the Line image is oﬀered, we must now again devote a few more pages in explicaƟon of Socrates’s rather sparse comments, before ﬁnally turning to the Line image proper. The discussion had been exploring the analogy of the Sun and the Good. The sun “not only gives to the objects of sight the capacity to be seen, but also provides for their generaƟon, increase and nurture, though it is not itself the process of generaƟon. And say that as for the objects of knowledge, not only is their being known due to the Good, but also their being, though the Good is not being but superior to and beyond being in dignity and power” (509b). This is so extraordinary a statement or claim that even the faithful Glaucon is taken aback: “Glaucon was quite amused, and said: ‘By Apollo, a miraculous superiority.’” To which Socrates replies, “It is your own fault, you forced me to say what I thought about it.” This reminds us that what we are receiving here, ironically, is Socrates’s opinion about these maƩers (506d-e), the dogma of the Ideas and the Good. We

are moved beyond a mere statement of doctrine here only by the suggesƟve elaboraƟon of the Sun-Good analogy, and more concretely by the actual descripƟon of the acƟvity of being and knowing in the Line.[2] To conclude our preparaƟon for the analysis of the Line then, let us look at a few details of this image. The sun, which itself is described in metaphor as the oﬀspring of the Good, is seen as the cause, via its own oﬀspring, light, of a certain feature or quality of things, their capacity (dunamis) to be seen. This is in fact an odd statement. It is true that, as Socrates elaborates above this passage (at 507c-d), we cannot see without light, hence without the presence of the sun. And it would seem to make a kind of common sense to say that the things are not visible (= cannot be seen) in the dark. But to say that the things have a capacity passively to be seen is odd because dunamis is a capacity acƟvely to do something, thus sight as a capacity of the seer, or of the eye. So color is “present” but remains “unseen,” it does not make an appearance unless light is present. “Color is not itself this capacity.” Socrates says that “both the sense of sight and that which is seen do have such a need,” that is, of light, (507d) and yet both sight in the eyes and being visible in the things are themselves described as capaciƟes or powers, “the faculty of seeing and being seen” (Grube trans., 507c). Light, then, yokes together in some strange way the “sense of sight and the power of being seen,” (507e) and frees up the capacity, as it were. The ﬁrst general point which I wish to focus on here is once again the consistent stress on dunamis or capacity, and its presence in both the seer and the thing seen, and thus, according to the analogy, in both the knower and the thing known. The meaning and signiﬁcance of just what a capacity is ontologically, as discussed in chapter two, will become relevant in our examinaƟon of the Line.[3] Socrates says, whenever “the eye of the soul is ﬁxed upon that upon which truth and reality shine, it understands and knows and seems to have intelligence, but whenever it is ﬁxed upon what is mixed with darkness—that which is subject to birth and destrucƟon—it opines and is dimmed, changes its opinions this way and that, and seems to have no intelligence” (508d). In these ways the “eye of the soul” is described as aﬀected by the objects, when, that is, truth and being illumine them. But what is the substance of this image, this metaphor—the

capaciƟes of objects seen and known? The discussion in a previous secƟon had pointed out the crucial role in the argument of the acceptance of capaciƟes as a kind of enƟty, as the presupposiƟon for the theory of Ideas. Where are these represented on the Line and how are we to understand them? Even with regard to sight it is not clear just what kind of thing it is as disƟnct from the eye that sees, as when Socrates says that “sight may be in the eyes . . . and sight is not the sun yet receives from the sun the capacity to see as a kind of ouƞlow” (508b). Thus when it is said that the “many things are the objects of sight but not of thought, while the Forms are the objects of thought but not of sight” this raises the quesƟon equally of what kind of things both sight and thought are. Hence in what sense the former may serve as both analogous and a contrast to the laƩer.[4] The second point concerns the concept of generaƟon, in relaƟon to the realm of the sun, and in relaƟon to being, in the realm of the Good.
