The sun itself is spoken of as the “oﬀspring of the Good, which the Good begot as analogous to itself” (508b). In what sense is the sun the cause of “generaƟon, increase and nurture” (509b), that is, how is this metaphor of the sun as making things grow to be understood? In Socrates’s own explicaƟon of the sun/light relaƟon the focus is primarily on the point just menƟoned, the sun as relates to sight understood as knowing, but there is also the metaphor of generaƟon, in that the sun is the cause of sight, which is “the most sunlike of the organs of sense . . . [And it] receives from the sun the capacity to see as a kind of ouƞlow, the sun is not sight but is it not the cause of it, and is also seen by it?”(508b). The reference here to generaƟon and nurture could be parƟally explicated by analogy to the disƟncƟon of the philosopher as knower versus philosopher as maker- arƟst. The ruler paints the city, makes it. While jusƟce itself is ostensibly uncreated, the model itself is created, if in intellectual imaginaƟon. He thus creates the laws, the consƟtuƟon of soul and city. But this psychical and ethical making occurs within the larger context of the Good as ontological cause of being in general, and that is not explained by this sub-species of creaƟon, taken in isolaƟon, however important it be. The analogy of the sun as cause of becoming and the Good as cause of being is a much stronger and thus more startling sense of cause, as is the ﬁnal asserƟon

that the Good, while a cause, is “not itself being,” is in some sense superior to being and beyond it. It would seem odd to say that something is a cause but lacked being, but equally unsaƟsfactory to say that the Good simply had more being, somehow quanƟtaƟvely. Some suggesƟon, though vague, is oﬀered in the ways in which the Good is said to be “beyond and superior to being,” and the qualiﬁcaƟon will be speciﬁcally of use in our discussion. The Good is said to be beyond and superior to being “in dignity and power,” (presbeia kai dunamei) the laƩer term in the text is again dunamis. This seems to suggest that if we understood what dignity and power were about we might have a clue as to in what sense the Good is beyond being and perhaps also operates as the cause of being. The noƟon of dignity had also been menƟoned in relaƟon to the sun and light, and the “yoke” between things seen and the power of being seen: “they are yoked together by a more honorable yoke than other things . . . unless light is held in no honor” (mē aƟmon 508a). And the sun is invoked as that one of the “gods in heaven . . . responsible for this.” Dignity or honor thus seems to be an acquired quality of something, here of light, a quality which accrues to it because of how it funcƟons—light is rightly “held in honor” because it yokes together the sense of sight and the power of being seen, and this yoking is in turn its power. In the realm of the Good, it is truth that shines like light, yoking the capacity to know and the capacity to be known, not then truth as a characterisƟc of proposiƟons. [5] GeneraƟon raises the quesƟon of the cause of being, as the sight/seeing/knowing metaphor raises the quesƟon of the cause of knowing. But the two, being and knowing, are clearly inƟmately related, as our discussions of dunamis in chapter two have already suggested, and will become more so when we look at capaciƟes in their actual funcƟoning in the descripƟon of the Line. (To explore further the relaƟon of being and knowing, and of Ideas and causes will require that we turn later to a somewhat lengthy examinaƟon of the arguments of the Phaedo).[6] Julia Annas, in An IntroducƟon to Plato’s Republic, is concerned that the ascent is to an impersonal Good (pace Williams), “the ascent out of the Cave oﬀers no personal interest or fulﬁllment.” “The Good that is the supreme object of knowledge has nothing to do with one’s own good; it is the purely impersonal Form of the Good” (260, Annas’ emphasis). Annas

feels that this is contrary to the deﬁniƟon of JusƟce as concern for one’s soul: “ . . . how can the knowledge that produces harmony in my soul, caring for all my concerns, require me to turn away from the world I share with others . . . ” She then goes on to suggest that the problem lies with two diﬀerent “concepƟons of what the philosopher is like,” viz. the pracƟcal versus the contemplaƟve. But Annas misses, I suggest, the link which will make the achieved vision of the ascent both “useful and beneﬁcial.” Annas believes the release from the chains of false values and opinions due to the manipulaƟon of others in no way results from and in any “scruƟny of self.” “The knowledge that the prisoners wake up to is impersonal; individual scruƟny of self plays no role at all. Plato sees no intellectual value in parƟcular facts about parƟcular individuals. The prisoner’s mysterious release from bonds is to be achieved by abstract and impersonal studies like mathemaƟcs. The ascent out of the Cave oﬀers no personal interest or fulﬁllment, nor even the saƟsfacƟon of having shed inauthenƟc roles” (259). (Granted, my analysis of the Cave in the previous chapter is perhaps rather diﬀerent than hers.) But the response to Thrasymachus and the turning of the soul in its educaƟon is, it seems to me, eventually quite a personal examinaƟon of one’s soul and what one ﬁnds aƩracƟve—the basis of such a turning is ulƟmately ontological, but the eﬀects of such ignorance and knowledge are quite individual. The educaƟon may indeed, as she says, be abstract, abstracted from pracƟcal concerns, parƟcularly in the higher educaƟon of the philosopher. But, I argue, both the goal and the result are a change in what one sees as real, an ontological shiŌ, hence in what one values, hence in the way one sees oneself, thus in the way one lives thereaŌer. The arguments of a Thrasymachus are tempƟng, and the choice of the Good and JusƟce is moƟvated by a transformaƟon of what is found desirable, through the experience of other realiƟes. The studies are means, not ends. There is, as she sees, the superior uƟlity of philosophical method in sorƟng out the pracƟcal life, but there is also the necessity of an ontological reorientaƟon if the shiŌ in values is to be aﬀected—and this depends on the results of the upward journey. The very real pracƟcal consequences of not having completed this journey can be seen in the problem of Alcibiades (Cf. Annas, 264-265). Her dilemma is also, once again, the result of losing sight of the analogical level, as her discussion of the return to the Cave issue

reﬂects (266-271). If one returns the analogy to its constant purpose, the compulsion is not of a guardian but of the raƟonal part of the soul in the interests of the whole of the individual soul. In sum, if one is led, it is hardly passively, and certainly not without an “individual scruƟny of self.” And if one considers the journey as a self-leading, then all the more is it of course a self-scruƟny.[7] PRELIMINARY DIVISIONS OF THE DIVIDED LINE We come then to the Line itself (509d ﬀ.). The ﬁrst division made is not of the Line itself, but rather a division of all that is into two realms, each ruled over by its respecƟve ruler (thus immediately conƟnuing the poliƟcal analogy). There is the visible realm ruled over by the sun and the intelligible realm ruled over by the Good. The Line image is then introduced in order to elaborate and explain the nature of each realm, that is, its populaƟon and organizaƟon or structure, and the nature of the ruler- ruled relaƟon. While Socrates does say that “much is omiƩed,” the whole Line image is meant to “conƟnue and explain the similarity to the sun.” Yet the rulers are not themselves in fact present—the sun and the Good are not part of the Line descripƟon and discussion proper. Where then are they to be seen in the image, reﬂected, as it were? We see them in a few ways: I suggest that what we are presented with are the eﬀects of the rule of each, which render them visible, as it were. First, their images are seen in the laws or organizaƟon of the realms over which they rule. Secondly, we see them, again in their images or reﬂecƟons, in the processes described (which we shall be examining in detail), the way in which the phenomena appear at each level and interrelate. Thirdly, as we come to an understanding of these processes, in our coming to understand the image of the Line itself, and hence ourselves and our world, the result is that we come to see ourselves as a conscious subject, and in turn as subject to the uniﬁed reign of each ruler. The Good is present then, in three ways: i) in structure—in the laws and organizaƟon of being, parƟcularly through the greater genē, ii) in process—in the way that phenomena appear, in the process of each stage, and iii) in the subject—in the presence of a knower, ourselves as conscious subjects in relaƟon to a uniﬁed reign. The sun in fact plays liƩle role aŌer the iniƟal analogy, as the literally visible is quickly leŌ

behind, and the visible-intelligible division is replaced with the opinion- knowledge division. There are in fact other ways to see the world, to divide it up, into edible and non-edible for example. The division here into the visible and the intelligible is natural only for the world as subject of the rule of intelligence, or, from the object’s point of view, as subject to intelligibility. And ﬁnally, the present inquiry of the dialogue is meant to give a clearer picture, though sƟll an outline and not a “ﬁnished picture” (504d) of that greatest study of the philosopher in preparaƟon for his own rule, the relaƟon of the heavenly ruler, the Good, to the ontological world; “that the form of the Good is the greatest object of study, and that it is by their relaƟon to it that just acƟons and other things become useful and beneﬁcial” (505a). Though the Line is a skeleton structure of being and knowing in general, it is meant to illustrate just how the world is to be perceived by the philosopher-ruler if he is to be successful in ruling it, and, we must never forget, in ruling himself. He must, then, both understand the world and understand what understanding it is—otherwise it cannot be that in his own image-making “just acƟons and other things become (truly) useful and beneﬁcial.”[8] The ﬁrst division then, is between the visible and the intelligible because without admiƫng of this disƟncƟon in kind, thinking is not even possible. Regardless of what one thinks about the world of one’s experience, as soon as one says something about experience one has made a disƟncƟon between the visible and interpretaƟon, which itself is not visible. For obviously the purely visible, what merely appears, is an epistemological ﬁcƟon; every appearance is already an interpretaƟon, already a meaning or resemblance of something. The boƩom secƟon of the Line begins with a false idenƟﬁcaƟon of an x. This does not require that those who make such primiƟve uƩerances are aware of this—they may be so absorbed in life, or in interpretaƟon, that they are not in fact aware of the disƟncƟon. (Again, supposing that at any given moment one is interested in interpretaƟon. Though this is in some sense natural or inevitable, typical of human being, there are other human acƟviƟes besides speech, but perhaps even these are in a sense interpretaƟons.) Note that though the discussion begins with a division, a separaƟon or disƟncƟon that only intelligence makes, yet the visible itself is also linked

to the noƟon of intelligibility through the occurrence of likenesses (homoiotes) as the iniƟal comparison of the two separate realms suggests. The primary act of interpretaƟon, as we shall see, is idenƟﬁcaƟon of an exemplum, of a kind, a primiƟve (elemental) resemblance, hence the primacy of the visible both in pracƟce and as a metaphor; the primary image of knowing is resemblance (and diﬀerence). We hear two songs of a nighƟngale in succession—or are there two of them? Two nighƟngales may sound alike, for example, but they are not idenƟﬁed as disembodied voices. On the other hand, the primacy of the body in existence as experience is not the same as the asserƟng of the primacy of the body qua visible, which is simply its most accessible form. Also, jusƟce and the just act are out there, in the world as it were, and require embodiment to be visible, though the image of jusƟce is not seen in the visible body of the agent. It is worth noƟng too that the visible-intelligible disƟncƟon is not a staƟc division, it is itself altered in the sense that the visible is itself ruled over by the intelligible in the actual acƟvity of intelligence. In the Line’s detail it is the pathēmata (eikasia, pisƟs, dianoia, noēsis) that generate enƟƟes within the world of the visible per se. Thus we conclude that the original division into two realms is in a sense undercut if one is considering the rule of intelligibility in relaƟon to the visible. The just as of the Sun/Good analogy is intelligible only if the image as image of the sun and the visible world is borne in mind. There are not two realms analyzed but one—the world insofar as it is intelligible, just as the object of knowledge and opinion is in a sense one, seen diﬀerently.[9] Lest I be misunderstood, I argue that “there are not two realms analyzed but one” only in the sense that the world we actually live in is not just undiﬀerenƟated stuﬀ. Rather, it is a world that we always experience as an intelligible collecƟon of objects, albeit with varying degrees of success and with mistakes along the way. This will be the whole point of this chapter—the detailed examinaƟon of the pathēmata of the Divided Line—the capaciƟes that at various levels make the world readable. (This is to be further developed as well in the discussion of RecollecƟon and methexis.) Following the division of the world into visible and non-visible or intelligible, we are then to imagine a “line divided into two unequal parts.” Why a line? Because it can be divided simply and unambiguously into

parts. And these parts then bear a relaƟonship to one another, expressible mathemaƟcally. It seems obvious enough, because a line can be divided, and because the image has become so familiar to us. Yet let us pause over it. The Cave image which follows it is much more natural, a more visible image. But perhaps this is one reason the Line is appropriate, for here we are dealing not with the world as it is experienced directly, subjecƟvely, psychologically, or socio-poliƟcally as in the Cave, but rather as it is structured noeƟcally (though dynamically, both for the knower and the known, as we shall illustrate). If then the world is to be seen in its divisions, we need an image of something which is divisible—albeit two dimensionally, but for that reason perhaps more exactly, at least in representaƟon, thus, as an image, more accurately. We are, with the Line as a whole and in its divisions, taking the measure of the world, and doing so by seeing where measure exists within the world, and what corresponding intellectual tools of measurement we are equipped with, as well as measuring the accuracy of these tools or instruments. The actual pracƟces that reﬂect the ﬁrst and major division of the Line, in which there is a “turning of the soul from a kind of day that is night to the true day, being the upward way to reality (what is, to on) which we say is the true philosophy” (521c), are presented somewhat later in the text, and even then they are but paradigms of the kind of study that “has the power to do so.” There it is clear, as we have seen, that Glaucon has not a clear eye for what these would be, or more importantly, what principles are behind both the studies and the parƟcular way in which they are taken up, that is, in the light of a special purpose, such that they are to result in the desired eﬀect of turning a soul. Though these studies are to provide the upward way and are intellectual in contrast to the tests and training of the earlier educaƟon of the guardian-soldiers (there is a character test for the philosopher-ruler aŌer this sequence, at 535ﬀ.), yet their ﬁnal purpose is to lead to a knowledge of, and experience with, the principles that eventually will result in “the best government of a city.” It would seem rather obvious at ﬁrst glance that the ﬁnal knowledge of the Good should provide just what is needed in this regard. But the studies that lead us up out of the Cave, or upward along the Line, at least those studies which are detailed in the present case, would seem far removed from the vision of an ethical and poliƟcal good such as would seem to be

required. The “highest study” in fact, which is “placed like a coping stone . . . at the top of your studies” (534e) is dialecƟc and not the study or knowledge of the Good. (A more detailed examinaƟon of just what dialecƟc might be is elaborated in the next chapter.) Indeed, the diﬃculƟes that Glaucon has with rightly conceiving of these studies are due to the fact that he constantly seeks an immediately pracƟcal, or at least immediately ethically useful purpose for them. Yet the turning of the soul would seem to be precisely a turning away from this world, from the visible world of generaƟon and decay to a non- visible world of permanence: hence the importance of rightly understanding the iniƟal division of the Line into visible and intelligible. We must ask along with Socrates, “What study would it be, Glaucon, which draws the soul from the world of that which becomes to the world of that which is?”(521d). But such a turning need not imply a two worlds view of reality, and the pracƟces can be seen as propaedeuƟc and prolepƟc. There are other standpoints which would make a disƟncƟon between two worlds (though not visible/intelligible), that of religious faith for example, and would perhaps as well see any studies which turned one’s aƩenƟon away from the physical world to a higher more permanent one as being somehow useful. In such cases the truly just and truly beauƟful are, once one has leŌ the realm of the earthly world, immediately available (God willing), and the studies were merely useful. But in Plato’s case there is a much more inƟmate relaƟon—one cannot simply throw away the ladder of dialecƟc. In the analysis of the Line, and by the end of the whole story, it shall be clear how serious a claim this is with regard to the interpretaƟon of the Ideas. And in the light of such a reading of the Line, the return of the philosopher to the Cave can then be seen as an ontological necessity, rather than a merely narraƟve or ethical one. But this is already implied in a consistent awareness of the analogical nature of the images, that is, in the return as paying a debt to oneself, the beneﬁcial consequence of a turning of the whole soul and the obligaƟon of the raƟonal part to the well-being or happiness of the whole soul, the source of its unity. But to have asserted this as doxa, and even to have shown why the raƟonal part is best suited to this task, is sƟll not to show what the consƟtuƟon of being real is, such that this is both possible and necessary. For the ladder of faith there is the earthly life in imitaƟon of Christ, but that descent (the re-

descent) is not in essence a raƟonal one. While the Platonic ascent is dialecƟkos and this making—because it is also a revealing—is itself transformed, I shall argue, from merely an instrument to the home and life of being. In looking further at the rather condensed and abstract details of the Line I will aƩempt to bring them to life by suggesƟng just of what pracƟces and experiences it is meant to give an account. To this end, let us review the context of the argument in which the Line discussion occurs, parƟcularly as regards the making of images. The purpose of the “greater studies” of the philosopher, who is to be the protector and legislator of our city, was to assist in his vision of the Good. This vision in turn is the basis of that re-descent into the Cave, and of the philosopher-craŌsman’s creaƟon of the ideal in the middle ground of that life which is between pure ideas (and ideals) and that ﬂow of both maƩer and opinions which is the stuﬀ of those wandering images amongst which we ourselves aimlessly wander, like wandering stars without ﬁxed orbits. We are, then, philosopher- craŌsmen who ulƟmately are called upon to subsƟtute a beƩer image for a poorer one. This “draŌsman of consƟtuƟons” it is said, must start with a “slate wiped clean,” both with respect to the city which he models and his own soul. Note that Socrates says that the philosopher-legislator must either have “a clean board or clean it themselves.” The laƩer alternaƟve is the choice that corresponds to the actuality of social dialecƟc. The ﬁrst alternaƟve, starƟng with a clean slate, is saƟrized in the unlikely suggesƟon within the mythical dimension that the cycle of doxa be broken by men and women voluntarily giving up all their children to make a fresh beginning for the city (cf.541a). The phrase “wipe clean the slate” thus needs to be treated with care. One begins, and works with, the social pracƟces, as with the discourse that represents it, and in part forms it. The philosopher-arƟst reorganizes, reinterprets—separaƟng and combining, he creates a new image according to the greater clarity that he has achieved about the real or true meaning of the names of ordinary discourse. As for the consƟtuƟons of which he is the draŌsman, we recall again that they are both his own personal (private) one, his soul, and the public ones, understood both as other souls and, always secondarily, the consƟtuƟon of the polis. It is as a result of his contemplaƟon of Ideas that he creates: “[he] composes human life . . . by looking back and forth, to jusƟce,

moderaƟon, beauty,” etc. And yet he also creates by “mixing and mingling the human likeness from its various pursuits, basing their judgment on what Homer too called the divine and godlike exisƟng in man” (501b). It would seem then, that while in one sense the slate is wiped clean, in another sense, as already noted, Plato allows that there is a potenƟal for the ideal within human being, that the dream state image of our ordinary lives sƟll allows this matching and culƟvaƟng to take place. This is, of course, consistent with the noƟon of recollecƟon, which one must be careful not to forget in focusing on the idea of a clean slate and of some ideal image of the “city laid up in heaven.” The laƩer is described as if the philosopher passively contemplates this image and simply creates it on earth, so to speak, albeit falling short. But if we consider that philosopher as acƟve legislator we are reminded that this image contemplated is one constructed by the philosopher and that its status is like that of a grounded hypothesis of the Line—it is the Ideas alone, the Idea of JusƟce, etc., which remain the Ɵmeless basis for such an image in dialegesthai. And even then, the Ideas are contemplated through the image-making acƟvity of dialegesthai, as we shall see. The image of the ideal city bears an analogous relaƟonship to the Ideas that are its ground as the principles of geometry do to the parƟcular theorems that are its images, and which are, as it were, physically re-presented in the parƟcular instance by the living geometer. (I am not, of course, equaƟng geometric theorems, or methods, and the model of the ideal city and its construcƟon. Both “starƟng points” are taken as “more certain”—but the origins of this certainty are quite diﬀerent.) The status and role of images and image-making are discussed in David Gallop’s arƟcle, “Image and Reality in Plato’s Republic.”[10] Gallop, responding in part to Robinson’s claim that Plato condemns the arƟst while himself using images in the dialogue, especially the Sun, Line, and Cave, stresses the philosophical use of images. Further, he disƟnguishes the “sensible (visual) images of Forms in the similes of Sun, Line and Cave from the extended images of the ideal city and ruler; the laƩer are disƟnguishable from merely postulated images like the former, which are dianoeƟc sketches of the longer way. The images of city and soul of the ruler, are by contrast pictures that “embody a deﬁniƟon of JusƟce and the

State” (119). One who grasps these, Gallop claims, “has thereby aƩained the best vision of these Forms that Plato can give his readers. . . . It reproduces the contents of its author’s intellectual vision.” But Gallop also reminds us that even this is not dialecƟc’s longer way, which would dispense with images altogether in its apprehension of the Forms. While I would agree with most of this, on this last point, as my comments on the philosopher/arƟst/craŌsman here and elsewhere show, I would claim that the Republic’s use of images goes a bit further. For Gallop, the objects represented in the Republic’s images of JusƟce and the State are logoi, made images even as embodying Forms, which are thus limited, being objects of dianoia, “logoi as images” (122). Gallop accepts Glaucon’s view that the philosopher’s own city “exists nowhere on earth but only in a paƩern in heaven. Only in such a city would there be any obligaƟon upon a philosopher to return to the Cave and rule his fellow men” (128), while noƟng that the philosopher will not take part in poliƟcs because “he will be too much preoccupied with watching the consƟtuƟon of his own soul.” But Glaucon’s disappointment, and Gallop’s, is Ɵed to his literalness, and Gallop aƩributes this pessimism to Plato himself: “Thus the painƟng metaphor here signals Plato’s disillusionment and poliƟcal frustraƟon” (130). The best that one can do, under the circumstances, is paint an ideal. But while Plato’s poliƟcal cynicism is well known, and evident in the Republic as elsewhere, Gallop’s reference to it here is, I think, misplaced. In spite of acknowledging that there is this inner city (and implicitly a relaƟon to others, the model of Socrates in conversaƟon as the true and best ciƟzen of Athens), Gallop seems to have let this slip from view in his working up to his concluding remarks. Because the city is only in words, like the poet’s portrait, Gallop feels the need to defend Plato—the response being that, “like the geometer’s so-called ‘construcƟons,’ those of the Republic are undertaken for the sake of knowledge” (125, my emphasis), and of course are images based on the knowledge that “philosophical products in words are closer to the ‘truth’ than an imperfect reality in acƟon.’” But the city is, in fact, potenƟally brought to life in more than words, that is, in the souls that are the true city. (See chapter two above on Plato’s ironic portrayal of the relaƟon of word and deed, and the discussion of the possibility challenge of the Third Wave.) Moreover, the embodying that Gallop rightly points to is not merely in a portrait of moral

and poliƟcal forms, of JusƟce and the State. The working out of these images, including the educaƟon of the ruler, and parƟcularly the principles of their development, represent or embody epistemological pracƟces and ontological claims that underlie the poliƟcal and moral models. To that extent, the Republic is a non-visible image of dialecƟc, though not, I argue, for Glaucon and Adeimantus. Indeed, the funcƟon of the laƩer’s diﬃculƟes, etc. is, I aver, to point just to this other level of the dialogue. Gallop concludes the whole essay lamenƟng that actuality seems to condemn the Republic’s images to remain “only the city in words” (130), beauƟful but sad; Plato’s “demonstraƟon that the city is ‘diﬃcult but not impossible’ (502c) amounts to an admission that it cannot be realized here and now. It is a wry appraisal of the prospects for any approximaƟon to the perfect city in Plato’s own age and society” (130). But, ironically, this is to lose sight of these very models as images of the realiƟes that can be brought to life in the city of the soul and in the human dialogical community. The ontological view embedded in both the sketch of Sun, Line and Cave, and in the broader implicit discussion of the whole dialogue is more opƟmisƟc than Gallop’s view would allow. I am not claiming that the longer way is fully embodied, far from it—the Republic is not interchangeable with the later dialogues—and my own use of the Phaedo is to look for a more explicit account of the realiƟes of Ideas and soul, and of method—though even there oŌen enough cloaked in playful disguises which are themselves revealing images or masks. The studies of the philosopher then, are both a preparaƟon and a set of pracƟces that embody the formal aspects of those principles which had appeared earlier as the basis of the virtues of the auxiliaries, and on which the construcƟon of the image in speech of the ideal consƟtuƟon was based. The philosopher is said to imitate the ideas of the virtues which he sees in their ideal state and “by associaƟon with them becoming like them” to the extent humanly possible, recreaƟng them in dialegesthai and modeling his life on that image in speech. But he is led then ﬁnally to the reality of these Ideas in part by associaƟon with the principles of the greater studies, and ulƟmately of dialecƟc, leading, it is said, to the percepƟon of the Idea of the Good. (The dialecƟcian is “he who rightly conceives one and many in nature” (Phaedrus 266a-b). But this is only a beginning.) First then, the philosopher-arƟst imitates by associaƟon,

somewhat like the auxiliaries earlier. Then, upon his descent, he imitates as the craŌsman of consƟtuƟons, both the personal one and that of others. But this process of reform, both psychological and ontological, is already begun in the turning of the soul that is the ascent. But this process of “consorƟng” and “trying to become as like them as he can” has, it would seem, its ﬁnite limits. For Socrates says that in so doing, while consorƟng “with what is divine and ordered, [he] himself becomes godlike and ordered,” yet he does so only “as far as man can,” a qualiﬁcaƟon that is meant seriously, and which occurs in other contexts whenever the divine aspect of human life is at issue. Thus at 501b human being is represented as being “mixed” and “in between,” both in his being and in even the best of his creaƟons, and the struggle or confrontaƟon with this limitaƟon is reﬂected in the further divisions of the Line. Though we have access to the realm of the non-visible, we live in the realm of the sensible, even once that realm we live in is informed and reformed, and understood as essenƟally dialegesthai, essenƟally always discourse as interpretaƟon. For as dialegesthai our world is always more than the merely literally sensible but less than a postulated complete freedom from limitaƟon. Even the philosopher who has completed the journey (if such could ever be the case—as it is suggested that such a one would be “like a god”) must express that vision in logoi, in something less than the Ideas themselves. As well, in the interpretaƟon of the further divisions of the Line to follow, as has been already pointed to in the interpretaƟon of the Cave, the so-called realm of the visible is meant to include not just what is literally visible or sensible, but all that is normally included in the realm of opinion for Plato. The Line is so readily seen as represenƟng the more literal sense of visible for that part of it, and the discussion of Ideas as originals for sense parƟculars so oŌen focused on as the paradigm case of original and copy, that it oŌen seems to be forgoƩen that the whole is itself an image used to explain the diﬀerence and relaƟon between the stable and unstable, between knowledge and opinion in general, with regard in parƟcular to rather much more important things than beds and tables, and relevant to the immediate themes of the Republic. Otherwise the middle books would be truly no more than an interesƟng philosophical digression. It is with this in mind that we are jusƟﬁed in taking a larger view of the Line, and in having ﬁrst discussed the Cave image, reversing in our

discussion the sequence in the text. Our interpretaƟon will, then, look within the imagery of the further divisions of the Line for both the studies of the philosopher-arƟst and the poliƟcal or social sense of original and image. As in the case of the disƟncƟons concerning the study of astronomy, the noƟon of the turning of the soul “from the world of that which becomes to the world of that which is” (521d) is applicable to the divisions of the Line. The trick is to see the non-visible within the visible (as in the proper study of astronomy),[11] to ﬁnd and work with the non- visible, the intelligible, in the creaƟon of appropriate non-visible images that have more permanence than the transient world whose physical generaƟon and decay is the best image of our transient opinions about it, and of living within it, parƟcularly as regards human excellence and happiness. This negaƟve image of transience is replaced by a gradual construcƟon of the posiƟve image-making processes of the Line. The return of the philosopher must be explained as the re-appropriaƟon of the whole of the world, a return necessitated by intelligence and the things themselves as the ﬁeld of its play, in which Ideas become, and are seen in logoi as, concretely “useful and beneﬁcial,” not merely in a pracƟcal sense but ontologically. Reading the image as image is taken seriously by Richard PaƩerson, in Image and Reality in Plato’s Metaphysics,[12] but with quite diﬀerent results. The diﬀerent senses of image in relaƟon to original F is examined. PaƩerson makes an important disƟncƟon between “being like” and “being a likeness of” (55, cf. 59), resulƟng in the “asymmetry of likeness to original” for a diﬀering group of, say, horses or shuƩles, all having a likeness to F but all with a “diﬀerence in kind, no maƩer how weak, between the Form F and all sensible F’s” (56). For what a “likeness of similariƟes” does not mean, see 40-62. The ﬁnal result is a case for an insistence on diﬀerent kinds or ways of being an “image of F” based on the diﬀerent implicit meanings of the phrase depending on the context or example. See 69-70, parƟcularly on the self-predicaƟon of Forms problem in the Third Man debate. His soluƟon is, “while F itself and its corporeal parƟcipants are F, they are diﬀerent types of F (the corporeal F is not another intelligible, eternal, nature of F at all) and second, the parƟcipant’s being F in the way open to

it is dependent on and related to that of the Form in a speciﬁc way, thus asymmetrical” (70-71). PaƩerson builds on the diﬀerence between, e.g., the horse that we can ride, the painƟng of a horse, and the “abstract nature” in which they both parƟcipate but in diﬀerent ways which we would never be tempted to confuse, though the sharing of the same name points to the sharing in the same Form. Just how the collecƟon under the common name is jusƟﬁed is explained by the similar, but diﬀering and hierarchical, causal relaƟons. “There is a diﬀerence in type between image (sensible) F and model (Form of) F such that the two are not commonly similar with respect to being F” (61). Forms could be viewed as emphaƟcally self-predicaƟonal—in the sense of having their own “onomata predicated of them.” That is, each is truly and essenƟally what it is to be an F without having F quality itself—the Form of horse as an abstract nature could include, for example, able to be ridden but is obviously not something we would ever ride, the Form of F is not a paradigm case. Just as the painƟng of a horse is an image of a horse but diﬀerent in kind from its model, the living horse, so the painƟng and the living horse are images, but diﬀerent in kind, of the Idea in which they parƟcipate. PaƩerson’s thesis is that image relaƟons of the former illuminate the sense of image relaƟon of the laƩer, and one needs to focus on the characterisƟcs of the diﬀerence in kind between image and model. But without appealing to the metaphorical senses of sense and hence of image that I do, the range of the laƩer is more limited for PaƩerson. As a result, dependence and parƟcipaƟon, and the sense of causal relaƟon are diﬀerently explicated, despite similariƟes in the resistance of the image relaƟon to the accusaƟon of being vulnerable to the regress argument. The crux of our diﬀerence is reﬂected in our view of separaƟon. For PaƩerson, Plato’s “aim is not only to establish the reality of intelligible objects as an addiƟon to the already familiar furniture of the world, but also to radically transform our view of the status of worldly things vis a vis these intelligible realiƟes. For this reason, he would not have been happy to refer to the Form only as ‘the abstract nature of F,’ or ‘F-ness.’ That way of speaking would not have been incorrect, but it remains a terminology more appropriate to a moderate Platonism of immanent universals than to an extreme Platonism of separate Forms to which sensibles owe their very being” (71). But Plato is not as extreme as PaƩerson would have him be. I

would certainly agree that Plato wishes to overturn, to upset, our view of the real in everyday experience. And while I also agree, and argue, that Plato’s Ideas are more than “immanent universals,” their status as “abstract Forms over their worldly parƟcipants” is explicated quite diﬀerently. In brief, ontological priority is, on my account (developed in chapters seven and eight), linked to a diﬀerent sense of independence or separateness that requires an interdependence with soul and an interpretable world, hence a more complex relaƟon of image and original.[13] READING THE WORLD: PATHĒMATA AND THE DYNAMIC DIVISIONS OF THE LINE We turn now to the actual internal divisions of the Line and their contents. The two realms ﬁrst are divided as visible and intelligible, about which we have already commented. The Line is further divided at 509d-510b, reproducing in some way the iniƟal division into intelligible and visible, and reproducing in some way the image relaƟon. In looking into the subdivisions we must work out what that way is in each case. The lower subdivision is into “shadows and reﬂecƟons” and objects that are the originals. The iniƟal noƟon of image relaƟon is on the physical model. Thus, when lisƟng the contents of the originals in the visible class of things, only animals, things around us in nature in general, and man-made things, are included. This is, aŌer all, a representaƟon of the realm over which the sun rules—and the relaƟons there are to provide an analogy or image of how things are in the realm of the intelligible. And yet when the faculƟes or capaciƟes, the ways of apprehending or knowing, are divided up and assigned to their respecƟve secƟons of the Line (and to kinds of objects) at 511d-e, opinion, a kind of knowing, is assigned to the secƟon of the visible, and not, what one might have expected, a faculty of physical percepƟon. [14] The proporƟons are represented at 510a-b as follows: “As the opinable [to doxaston] is to the knowable [to gnoston ] so is the likeness [to homiothen] to that of which it is a likeness” (Shorey transl.). At 511e the opinable is represented by eikasia—picture-thinking or imagining—and pisƟs, that is to say, unreﬂecƟve conﬁdence in the solidity or stability of its objects.

There are two observaƟons to be made about this apparent discrepancy or shiŌ from sight to opinion as capacity. First, the original discussion of vision etc. at 507b-c does assign sight, and not opinion, as the capacity responsible for, and acƟve in, the eye-object relaƟon. The disƟncƟon was sight and its world versus intellect and its world. But sight can be wrong a) in darkness, as Socrates suggests (in moonlight, at night) and even b) in daylight, where the judgment or opinion is misled. One could of course insist on making the disƟncƟon that sight itself is never in itself wrong, it just reports what it sees, and intellect judges. But this would not be of much use here, since the same would apply to shadow/reﬂecƟon images, which, when taken in themselves, do not tell sight that they are merely images and not originals. And yet we never see shadows as just dark spots. They are always shadows of something. Of course, eikasia as a mode of percepƟon makes no sense by itself, that is, it is always linked to an implicit awareness of an original, that of which the image is an image, hence an awareness of the image as image. (Similarly, the Cave allegory makes sense only as allegory, as itself an image.) Thus sight as the model capacity of seeing clearly cannot be separated from at least some intellecƟve component. If, then, it makes any sense at all originally to have disƟnguished sight from intellect, it is only in order to provide an image for the larger diﬀerence between kinds of object, the visible and non-visible, and for the noƟon of resemblance that is served by the metaphor of clarity vs. darkness in the applicaƟon of a capacity (sight/intellect). Sight is not the relevant capacity as soon as the Line is discussed, but rather opinion, and then this is subdivided into intellecƟve funcƟons corresponding to the opinable, pisƟs, and eikasia. Secondly, since the original disƟncƟon of knowledge versus opinion did not have to do with the literally visible/intelligible but with opinion versus knowledge in the maƩer of jusƟce, or even craŌ (the navigaƟon/captain example) that is, already with maƩers not literally visible, we would have expected that opinion should be assigned as ruling over those realms where it has its non-visible objects and not just the literally visible—and thus that it would have occurred in the top half of the Line, where the non-visible realm is speciﬁcally located. But this is clearly not the case in Plato’s Line. And this ﬁts with a diﬀerent sense for visible.

One could argue, as some have, that the divisions are merely the result of the “constraints of the image”—of the division into two realms, seeking to explicate further the analogy of Sun to Good, etc. But this explanaƟon seems too trivial. A beƩer one, one with far reaching implicaƟons, and one that ﬁts the Line into the broader discussions of knowledge versus opinion, is that man-made objects of various kinds, the objects of nature, and all the images and reﬂecƟons of the Line, are themselves apt metaphors for all the possible objects of opinion. And that they thus correspond neatly to the images of the Cave as I have discussed them. The emphasis on the physicality or visibility of the primary objects of opinion thus itself becomes a metaphor. The characterisƟc that is constantly stressed by Plato in contrasƟng the physical world with the intelligible, in the Republic and elsewhere, is the generaƟon and decay of the former—its mutability. (Cf. 485b, 490b, 508d, and contrast with generaƟon in the Good/Sun analogy, 509b.) It is not the physicality per se, its solidity, that is suspect or unreliable. To generate and decay are in themselves no sins for Plato; he does not denigrate the body, the senses, the physical etc. as has oŌen been claimed. Rather it is a noƟon of knowledge as governed by principles of relaƟve ﬁxity (idenƟty, etc.) that makes the ﬂux of the physical itself a model or image of the problem of knowing. The primary division of the Line already prepares for the subdivisions, when properly understood. This is not to deny that physical nature is one area where the problemaƟc of knowledge occurs. But one only has to ask what the important issues are for Plato where knowledge versus opinion are concerned to see that the physical/visible- intelligible/knowable disƟncƟon is primarily an image, or at best an example, of the more important claims. In the Republic, it is ulƟmately not “What is this physical object that I see before me?” that maƩers to Plato but rather the dialogue’s central quesƟon, what is jusƟce, and its ontological status. But the argument is, on my interpretaƟon, that ethical diﬀerences, those for example between Socrates and Thrasymachus, ulƟmately reﬂect diﬀerent valuaƟons, ontologically diﬀerent views about what is real, hence of value. And that it is this connecƟon that necessitates, and jusƟﬁes, the ostensible digression of the middle books. In fact, we rarely make mistakes in the realm of the literally visible in our daily lives. Nor for that maƩer does science (the capaciƟes of the

upper half) have much to do with knowledge versus opinion apart from in parƟcipaƟon in popular and public discourse—which is why opinion is located by Plato in the boƩom half; except for quackery, science (dianoeƟc epistēmē etc.) deals with conﬂicƟng arguments and demonstraƟons, though, as we shall see, there is a higher sense of doxa that does apply to the upper half. The ﬂux of generaƟon and decay and the acƟvity of opinion (as pisƟs) and image-making (eikasia) are presented in the Line in the representaƟve form of the physical/visible world. But it seems reasonable to conclude that it is to be taken as an image of the more crucial, and in the Republic certainly more relevant ﬂux of opinions, for example about jusƟce. Let me summarize then the interpretaƟon of the text to this point. Taken literally, the visible ought to have had sight as its corresponding capacity, and not opinion. However, i) this would make no sense as a capacity or faculty of knowing, even in an inferior form, ii) opinion is located by Plato in the boƩom half, iii) sight is not itself a good candidate for a capacity of knowing, even limited to the physical, as it does not judge, iv) opinion has in general a broader range of objects than the physical. Therefore, the divisions of the Line, in this case of the boƩom half, are best taken as images of the larger sense of image-original, opinion-knowledge regarding objects. Either we put opinion in the upper half, corresponding to non-visible objects, which Plato does not do. Or we put non-visible objects among the man-made and natural objects listed for the boƩom half of the Line and take the descripƟons of the Line itself as image or metaphor. The laƩer course, which I am suggesƟng, leaves opinion where Plato places it (which other soluƟons would not do), and gives to opinion the more logical range of broader objects than the strictly physical.[15] We shall return to the lower division of the Line to examine further its subdivisions, but for now we turn to the divisions of the upper half, which had been described as the secƟon of the intelligible. The upper division is divided into the realm of “hypotheses,” which are in some way originals for the objects below them in the upper subdivision of the visible world, and a subdivision higher than the former, which is the original or origin, or source, for the one below it. Note that the ﬁrst, or major division carried out, dividing the visible from the intelligible, is described in terms of its

objects, and a process of imaging within the lower half that occurs naturally, while the division within the realm of the intelligible, is described in terms of how the soul invesƟgates its objects. Secondly, while the iniƟal larger division separated the visible from the intelligible, the subdivision of the intelligible part also immediately links the upper to the lower division, since the soul in the lower level of the upper half “uses as images those very things which at a lower level were models” (511a). The upper subdivision begins in the realm of hypotheses or assumpƟons, and moves again to a source, one that is not a hypothesis, a ﬁnal source not an assumed one, and does so in a way that does not use images but Ideas themselves, by themselves. The ﬁrst secƟon or boƩom of the upper division of the Line is introduced as having the following characterisƟc method: “Using as images what before were models, it is compelled to invesƟgate from hypotheses, proceeding not to ﬁrst principles but to a conclusion” (510b).[16] Our ability to do this is the exercise of dianoia. Our ﬁrst quesƟon is, does the upper half of the Line operate at all in the way the boƩom half, that of the visible, does? Secondly, what is the relaƟonship and interpenetraƟon of the two halves? And ﬁnally, what does “using as images what before were models,” mean, and what kind of image-making does intelligence use? We start by turning to another text concerning the image-making of the producƟon of the Line itself, at the point where the pathēmata of soul corresponding to the divisions are to be arranged in relaƟon to one another: “Place these in the due terms of a proporƟon and consider that each has as much clarity as the content of its parƟcular secƟon shares in truth” (Grube transl., 511e).[17] While of the original geometrical division, Socrates says that, once it is completed, “you will then have secƟons related to each other in proporƟon to their clarity and obscurity” (509d). This shows at least that the four secƟons are arranged in ascending order of the degree of truth each shares in, and that this results in a degree of clarity—that is, the way of knowing appropriate to the objects produces that degree of clarity. But the reason for further dividing the two larger secƟons in the same raƟo must have more relevance than simply to say that in general the original is clearer than the image. It should also be indicaƟng that the relaƟonships work in an analogous or similar, or proporƟonal way, so to speak. In pursuing this analogy, we shall try to use

the passage concerning how knowing by hypothesis and knowing by principles (archē) might work not just in the realm of the intelligible, to which it explicitly applied, but applied to the realm of the visible. The models of the visible secƟon, which are the originals in relaƟon to the lowest secƟon, the source of the shadows and reﬂecƟons, are taken by those operaƟng at the third level, that of hypothesis, now as themselves images. When Glaucon says that he does not quite understand what Socrates means about images and hypotheses, Socrates provides an illustraƟon for this from mathemaƟcs. The geometers “assume the existence” of the odd and even, of ﬁgures, etc. “as if they were known to them.” These mathemaƟcal things are their hypotheses: “These they make their hypotheses and do not deem it necessary to give any account of them either to themselves or to others, as if they were clear to all” (510c).[18] In both cases, in the relaƟon of the higher to the lower secƟon beneath it, what before were models and were taken by the person operaƟng at that level as “originals,” become images when seen from the perspecƟve of the higher level. Again, geometry is oﬀered as but an example with reference to the explicit relaƟonship of hypothesis formaƟon at the level of the capacity for scienƟﬁc knowledge or dianoia to the level of physical representaƟon below it. What is said of knowing at the level of dianoia in relaƟon to the visible level below it now seen as themaƟzed by dianoia, “using as images what before were models,” (510b) thus is analogous to relaƟons between the two lowest levels where we naturally perceive at once the dependence of image and original. Even as concerns the relaƟons between the two highest levels, although this is described as “proceeding from hypothesis without using the images of the other secƟon, by means of the forms themselves and proceeding through these,” there is also a sense in which the image-original relaƟon is true here too, at least iniƟally. When the third secƟon, that of dianoia, is revealed as using hypotheses, they are then seen as less clear (that is, ontologically) than the geometer takes them to be: the laƩer takes the mathemaƟcal objects as not in need of any further account—“they do not deem it necessary to give any account” (510c), while the dialecƟcian/philosopher does, and what were clear models, become less clear, hence more like images—which are both the same yet diﬀerent than the originals now sought for, hypothesized as

the source, as “hypotheses in the true sense of the word,” of what are now less clear images. It is at this point that the truly non-visible becomes itself the subject of inquiry, here as a ground or original for the earlier hypotheses of the geometers, which were taken by them as certain, clear, ﬁrst principles. Thus, dialecƟc “does not consider its hypotheses as ﬁrst principles [as do the geometers] but as hypotheses in the true sense of stepping stones and starƟng points, in order to reach what is beyond hypothesis, the ﬁrst principle of all that exists. . . .” (511b).[19] For the geometer, ﬁrst there are the hypotheses or mathemaƟcal objects that the geometer takes as clear, certain principles (angles, odd and even, ﬁgures): They use visible ﬁgures and talk about them, but they are not thinking about them but about the models of which these are likenesses; they are making points about the square itself, the diameter itself, not about the diameter which they draw and so with others. These ﬁgures, which they fashion and draw, of which shadows and reﬂecƟons in the water are images, they now in turn use as images, in seeking to understand those others in themselves, which one cannot see except in thought. This is what I called the intelligible class, and said that the soul is forced to use hypotheses in its search for it, not travelling up to ﬁrst principles, since it cannot reach beyond its hypotheses, but it uses as images those very things which, in comparison with their images, were thought to be clear and honored as such. (510d-511a) It is obviously true, as Richard Robinson says,[20] that the descripƟon of dianoia’s method, typiﬁed by the mathemaƟcian, is taking its hypothesized beginnings as certain, and that therein lays its mistake. But the unhypothesized beginnings or sources sought for by dialecƟc in its use of hypotheses to rise to what is “beyond hypothesis” does not mean, as Robinson asserts, to certain proposiƟons. It is not higher proposiƟons about Ideas that are “beyond hypothesis” but the ﬁrst principles or archeē or elements, which are seen to be the certainty on which and out of which the true hypotheses are built. (Compare Sallis, 427) The hypotheses or supposiƟons, even when posited by dianoia (that is, as sƟll ungrounded)

are exempliﬁed by “the odd and the even, the various kinds of ﬁgures” (510c) and not represented as proposiƟons. Robinson gives a good argument for understanding Socrates’s descripƟve phrase “destroying hypotheses” in dialecƟc as rightly not to be falsifying or conﬁrming them but rather “the destrucƟon of our aƫtude towards it, which consisted in hypothesizing it” (161). But because he holds “it” to be the proposiƟons rather than the objects, the upward path of dialecƟc is reduced to an epistemological search for indubitable intuiƟve proposiƟons, rather than an ontological one, and his analysis results in a relaƟvely unhappy conclusion. AŌer examining several versions of hypotheƟcal method, he concludes that Platonic certainty, at even the ideal end of Platonic dialecƟc would be really no more than “the establishment of consistency among our standing beliefs” (179). Robinson complains, “destroying the hypotheses turns out to be merely another name for the fact that he does start out with hypotheses and uncertainty, and does end with perfect certainty without hypotheses; but how [R’s emphasis] he does so is said no more here than there” (162)—that is, in the two passages describing dialecƟc explicitly, at 511b and 533c. But the how of dialecƟc is described, and quite diﬀerently, if one takes the objects themselves as what is seen eventually (or alternaƟvely, ideally) as certain. The how is the uncovering of the acƟvity of the Ideas, implicit in our various ways of knowing along the Line, and made more explicit, seen for what they are, in the educaƟon of the philosopher. (A fuller discussion of this is the subject of chapter ﬁve.) About reﬂected images of geometrical ﬁgures only a passing reference is made, since only a non-geometer would be interested in what might be called the purely aestheƟc form of say a triangle. The geometer’s triangles drawn, like those of the slave boy in the Meno, are used as images in that they are not to be studied as parƟculars. About these triangles in the sand, the geometer already knows them, sees them, as images, unlike his relaƟonship to the elements which are his hypotheses. The visual arƟst however, we might note, in a sense somewhat reverses this relaƟonship— for him, the drawing is the (mere) physical original brought to life, of which he had only an aestheƟc image in imaginaƟon, less clear than the fully realized one in the drawing. Of course, this is hardly what Plato has in mind in Book X when discussing the arƟst’s image (Cf. PaƩerson, 49-50, and

especially 69). The arƟst knows, as do we and presumably Plato, that a sculpted horse cannot be ridden, but it may approach the Idea of a good riding horse in ways that an individual physical horse might be said to fall short, to use the Phaedo’s phrase. Consider a poor misshapen horse and the image of a horse in a Delacroix. Again, this of course somewhat reverses Plato’s usual sequence of the image being less real than the original of which it is an image. Yet, what is even more important to Plato, such an image, on the other hand, cannot arƟculate, cannot put in a logos, just what it is portraying as excellent (and certainly not what excellence in general might be—though it could serve as an example for discussion). We cannot carry on a dialogical examinaƟon of the excellence of a riding horse unless and unƟl it is themaƟzed by dianoia. Pisanello’s wonderful drawings are images that may provoke a discourse about the drawings, but the draŌsman qua arƟst cannot parƟcipate in a discourse.[21] Images in imaginaƟon are in this way less real than images in thought (dianoia). Images in nature, in mirrors, reﬂecƟons, shadows, are immediately seen, by human beings that is, as images dependent on an original. It is the dynamic of this dependency that fascinates us, and that we can know with a certain clarity—consider Peter Pan and his shadow, or Narcissus and his reﬂecƟon. The laƩer is tragic precisely because he does not know this to be true for his own image in the pool, and tellingly, tries to carry on a dialogue with the Other. This awareness is also a kind of thinking, a kind of dianoia, but natural, as opposed to the interpretaƟve, scienƟﬁc, construcƟve acƟvity of technical dianoia. But to return to the geometer’s image, it is revealed as less clear because, in pracƟce, a) physical irregulariƟes of the representaƟon are to be ignored, and b) the truths about this one case are to be true about the actual triangle one is looking at through the image of the constructed one. What is a visible original, a model for the reﬂected image when considered non-mathemaƟcally, that is, not as an object of knowledge (here the mathemaƟcal kind), becomes an image when considered mathemaƟcally.[22] Now the geometer funcƟons in two diﬀerent modes. In one, he can pracƟce geometry in analyzing the properƟes of a parƟcular triangle (e.g., calculaƟng the exterior angle)—say a parƟcular isosceles triangle—always with the understanding that any other one with the same angles will have

the same properƟes. In another mode, he is concerned with building geometry itself—with construcƟng or reconstrucƟng the system and proofs that contain, say, the type of triangle called isosceles and its properƟes (or the common properƟes of any triangle, regardless of type). In this mode the geometer is closer to the non-visible form, though the ﬁrst mode, analyzing parƟcular isosceles triangles, is only possible given the second (either explicitly or implicitly—one could generate the system for each individual triangle; and in any case, the noƟon of triangle, or regular shape and angle, straight line, etc. is necessary and implicit in any mode). As regards the change from model to image, the drawn (constructed) triangle is a model in relaƟon to its non-mathemaƟcal image or reﬂecƟon, and becomes an image when considered as the eﬀect or expression of the model in the non-visible realm, which in turn has its place in the hierarchy of generality. So this individual physical ﬁgure before me visibly (if I so constructed one) is now an image of this parƟcular triangle, with a given set of angles, as a mathemaƟcal object. Even this triangle, the model for the individual one but sƟll only a parƟcular, is already one “which one cannot see except in thought.” This parƟcular triangle in turn is an image in relaƟon to the idea or model of triangle in general—and this last is sƟll visible, sƟll barely a percepƟon and product in a sense of a kind of imaginaƟon (eikasia): the next step up is from triangle to the elements of triangle, such as angle, line, and the concept of mathemaƟcal ﬁgure itself, of geometrical or regular ﬁgure, and then to the concept of ﬁgure itself (of bounded extension). It is these elements, called by Socrates “hypotheses,” which are truly non-visible and the object of noēsis. They are the assumed stable basis of all the other, constructed, objects which are to one degree or another visible, either in the physical world or in that of imaginaƟon (mathemaƟcal in this case). Without invesƟgaƟon of these elements, which will take us out of the realm of the geometer per se as representaƟve of the sciences, the soul’s acƟvity of knowing remains essenƟally a downward moƟon; it is “compelled to invesƟgate from hypotheses, proceeding from these not to a ﬁrst principle, but to a conclusion,” that is, a statement and proof (in the geometrical sense). At the point at which one considers the elements themselves, it seems to me that at least two diﬀerent quesƟoning acƟviƟes are possible. Both acƟviƟes take what the geometer treated as stable givens, treated,

Socrates says, as in eﬀect ﬁrst principles, and reveals them in their true idenƟty as hypotheses; at this point what is merely posited for the geometer becomes a quesƟon for the philosopher. Such quesƟoning could take the form of a) quesƟons about the mathemaƟcal nature of the elements, “What is a circle, an angle, a straight line?” or the best way to describe and deﬁne them, or b) quesƟons about the being or nature of such objects—from whence they are derived if they are, their mutability or immutability, their relaƟon or kinship with other enƟƟes, their dependence on something more general sƟll (whether a being or a principle) for which the elements themselves are images. This second kind of quesƟon is in parƟcular the domain of dialecƟc. “DialecƟc does not consider its [geometry, any science] hypotheses as ﬁrst principles, but as hypotheses in the true sense of stepping stones and starƟng oﬀ points, in order to reach that which is beyond hypothesis, the ﬁrst principle of all that exists” (511b). Having thus worked one’s way up to one ﬁrst principle, one supposes the Good (in the Republic), one is then in a posiƟon to see “what follows from it,” and “keeping hold of this” in turn to see the truth of the elements of say, geometry—now “coming down to a conclusion without making use of anything visible at all,” of no images or examples but rather conclusions about the nature of the elements themselves—conclusions about their nature, origin and employment, and our relaƟon to them, answers to the quesƟons in b) above about the status and kinship of the kinds of elements in quesƟon, say of a ﬁgure, or of a virtue. This would be, I suggest, the descripƟon of the ideal compleƟon of the task—the uniﬁed whole. But along the way, as a process, parƟal uniƟes are achieved. This acƟvity then, geometry, is oﬀered as representaƟve—Glaucon says “geometry and kindred sciences,” (511b)—of “how the intelligible class is to be divided.” It is, then, a further elucidaƟon by way of a parƟcular illustraƟon, of the general statement at 510b about the way that the intelligible is divided, with respect to the disƟnguishing of image or model and hypothesis versus ﬁrst principle, an example oﬀered because Glaucon says “I do not quite understand what you mean.” We must see then just how close the example or image can be brought to some other, non- mathemaƟcal examples.[23]

The key is in the noƟons of model and image, hypothesis and principle, which represent the shiŌing percepƟon of relaƟve clarity. The geometer/scienƟst, although he “cannot reach beyond its [the soul’s] hypotheses” and is “forced to use them” in his search for the “intelligible class” in which he operates, does have the use of images. With their aid he can perceive the truth of, or in, examples, such that knowledge is produced. He “uses as images the very things which at a lower level were models, and which in comparison with their images [in turn] were thought to be clear and honored as such.” But even the geometer’s non-visible and intelligible models are images when regarded as the products of, or dependent on, the elements as hypotheses. The clarity of the geometrical proof is stable in relaƟon to the parƟcular case (kind) of dianoia—but it becomes for the moment unclear within the quesƟoning context of ontological interrogaƟon of its elements as a process, and the soul’s capacity to engage in it (noēsis). OUT OF THE CAVE, UP THE LINE: KNOWLEDGE, IMAGE-MAKING, AND DIANOETIC EIKASIA The general “eﬀect of educaƟon and the lack of it” as described in the Cave allegory can now be paralleled to the Line image, and this will assist us in extending the discussion to non-mathemaƟcal examples. The journey of the Cave and its descripƟon mirrors in a general way that of the Line. At each point, as in the ascent of the Line, there is greater clarity (saphēnia, 509d, 511d-e) than lower down; at each level the inhabitants take their mode of knowing and the objects of it as absolute, as clear. Those chained see only images but do not know them as images—they take them for originals. They dispute in arbitrary fashion the names and natures of the shadows—which sounds or voices go with which. They live enƟrely at the level of opinion, as I have argued above, primarily as the receivers of opinion, the cast images of the Cave, and I oﬀered as suitable candidates, poliƟcal and religious opinion (as well as doxai concerning nature, and of course ordinary claims about physical sense percepƟons). Those viewing only shadows, “would believe the truth to be nothing else than the shadows of the arƟfacts” (515c).

The carriers and makers of the objects, the model/originals for the shadows, operate with a limited knowledge of sorts, that the images are only shadows of the clearer reality, the more visible models. But they assume, or do not ask about, the source of what they take to be arbitrary (see earlier discussion, in chapter three). In carrying such a model and in bringing them alive, they construct systems of belief (about both nature and right acƟon—e.g., the beliefs and values of the poets, as reﬂected in their works, and the beliefs of the natural philosophers) for those watching and chained, but they do so arbitrarily. Their only funcƟon seems to be to produce the images for those chained below them, and their knowledge is a negaƟve one, one might say: they can claim that their originals are clearer, and are the cause of what appears below, and that the ones chained are mistaken, misled in taking their own discourse about the sounds and images actually produced by the puppeteers as clear. But such made objects are not coherent systems, they are patched together and have coherence only to the extent that they imitate, more or less unconsciously it seems, more raƟonal originals of which they in turn are images. The pain of deliverance from this and the resistance to seeing each clearer object as more real and the cause of the former ones, is a reminder of just how aƩached the knower is to his place, as it were, to his mode of knowing and the ostensible clarity of his objects. In the case of the Line we were to have knowledge to the extent that truth, like the light of the Cave’s ﬁre, and then the sun, shone on the objects, the Sun giving to objects the capacity to be seen and the Good to the intellect’s objects the capacity to be known. Much Ɵme is spent on the image and analogy of sun-light-sight and the contrasƟng night vision, and this is obviously recalled in the degrees of knowing and relaƟve clarity of the objects in the Cave story. Our explicaƟon has been thus far an aƩempt to indicate how the whole image of the Cave is “related to what we said before” (517b). The socio-poliƟcal epistemic dynamic of the Cave can thus in a general way be ﬁƩed onto the ontological disƟncƟons of the Line, and in a way that accords with the larger themes of the Republic. The world of images of the Line is the domain of the producƟon of human doxa, things for which human beings claim responsibility and use to inform the many. The images of these doxai have their causes both in human agency and in the elements out of which these doxai are made. Fire could reveal things as they are, but

doesn’t. The dogmaƟst of reason, as it were, uƟlizes these doxai as more or less unquesƟoned ﬁrst principles, variously sancƟoned as: the existence and will of the gods, the recƟtude of the laws of the polis as well as the laws themselves, the customs or rites of the community, the canons or convenƟons of beauty, the ﬁrst principles and/or elements of Nature, etcetera—all as objects of belief. All are systems claiming clarity and resƟng on relaƟvely unexamined hypotheses as ﬁrst principles. Thus described, that is, in the relaƟon of their acceptance by people, they best ﬁt in the realm of pisƟs, variously translated as trust, belief or even conﬁdence (Irwin), Socrates’ name for a certain way of thinking about experience. Each subdivision of the Line has a corresponding way of thinking typical of it (given names in a passage somewhat aŌer the describing of the secƟons of the Line). The same doxai or thoughts, or logoi, when considered and developed as explanaƟon, are each the producƟons of a diﬀerent capacity or faculty (not dunameis but patheēmata, stressing their bond to the objects perceived in each case). The capaciƟes of soul, already given some discussion above, are assigned to describe the processes by which souls know the objects of each secƟon and are named at 511d. They are as follows: eikasia (imaginaƟon, imaging, image-making), pisƟs (trust, belief), dianoia (thinking, raƟonal thought), noeēsis (understanding). The many live in relaƟon to these opinions for the most part as passive recipients and thus devoted to “reﬂecƟons and images”—as the chained ones of the cave. Now since the lowest Line secƟon is devoted to images strictly speaking and its faculty is composiƟon or guessing at images, imaginaƟon (eikasia),[24] while the capacity of the secƟon above it is trust or belief (pisƟs), this might seem to reverse the order I am suggesƟng concerning those in chains and the puppeteers, as trust is passive and image-making acƟve. But the technical use of images in what, it has been suggested, is a kind of dianoeƟc eikasia is appropriate to the acƟvity of dianoia in its trusƟng use of the images that, not strictly visible, are used to structure its knowledge, or to mirror the structure that one is trying to explicate with the use of noeƟc elements. As, for example, the double helix image or model of DNA, the structure of which is embedded in the image. The image is not a picture, as it were—it only shows us something, or looks like, physical DNA to the person who knows how to

read the image. And the image is trustworthy both to the extent that the physical DNA is found indeed to reﬂect the structure suggested by the model, and as well that the construcƟon of the model in itself makes raƟonal sense, that is, it inevitably draws upon the elements of intelligibility that make raƟonal image-making possible (in other words, drawn from noēsis). Even the philosopher trusts in the Ideas (and pre- eminently the Good) but with reason supposedly, not at the beginning of his journey but at the end—and creates intelligible images, for example, the Republic itself. In the immediate case the terms are appropriately assigned because the cave dwellers in chains are the primary example of ungrounded blind consumers of images—they are acƟve in that this consumpƟon is their primary epistemic acƟvity and that they also busy themselves with composiƟon or relaƟvely blind interpretaƟons of the image-echoes, etc. The trust or pisƟs of the second level is appropriate to those who carry the puppets, whom I claim to be the makers of these images, because, though they themselves are the creators of dogma for those below them, the models of their own epistemology are based on hypotheses taken on trust as principles. The makers of doxai, inhabiƟng the secƟon of the Line devoted to the models of the images, are content to elaborate or promulgate the systems, either skepƟcally or as true believers. The makers of models here inhabit two realms. As purveyors of doxai about models for the unreﬂecƟve below them they inhabit the realm of doxasƟc pisƟs, the second level of the Line, the puppeteer image of the Cave. But some of these same persons could also be said to inhabit the realm of the capacity or faculty at work outside the Cave, that is, of dianoia or dianoeƟc epistēmē, when pracƟcing their professional experƟse, in which a diﬀerent kind of pisƟs is involved—that corresponding to postulaƟng hypotheses or assumpƟons of a science. In the former case, the pisƟs is that induced in others, the consumers, while in the laƩer case it is the pisƟs necessary for the producers themselves, and of a rather diﬀerent sort. This would be the case for accounts of nature, or for the social sciences and humaniƟes, for that maƩer—but the same would as easily apply to mathemaƟcs if we include the teaching and the study of it. And of course the aƫtude towards its starƟng points or hypotheses is explicitly discussed by Socrates, if brieﬂy. (There is, however, an important diﬀerence between the

hypotheses of mathemaƟcal systems as starƟng points and the empirical hypotheses of the natural sciences subject to the veriﬁcaƟon that will give the system and/or explanaƟon, for example, credibility, or explanatory force.) Both the students of these systems, i.e., those who study their details and structure but not their fundamental assumpƟons, and those who parƟcipate in the actual development of the system have moved somewhat upward. They create or recreate systems, not completely arbitrarily but rather coherently deduced from, and within the bounds of, their starƟng points, which are taken as certain. And which they may indeed be, though ungrounded unƟl, as Plato suggests via Glaucon, these very systems and more parƟcularly their elements or starƟng points are once again encountered on the way down. Students of these sciences “do not go back to a ﬁrst principle . . . although these can be understood if approached from a ﬁrst principle” (511d). In the (physical) sciences a standard of measure is erected, without analysis of the nature of the standard itself. This concerns both the coherence of the knowledge claim (and of the system of which it forms a part), and, where it applies, its empirical validity—its explanatory force in relaƟon to the relevant empirical data and tests. The scienƟﬁc trust, trust at the level of dianoia, is in the reliability, the orderliness and stability, of nature as a whole. (Or, to take an example from a diﬀerent area of study, the case of historiography, in the supposiƟon of a general explanatory hypothesis of historical causaƟon in a preferred hierarchy of causes.) In other words, the imposiƟons of dianoia on nature in a systemaƟc and mathemaƟcal ordering rely both on the extra- scienƟﬁc sense of trust in the regularity of nature and on a corresponding trust in the very noƟon of system, that is, in measurement and the standards that serve as the ulƟmate elements of the system. Thus, the scienƟst to a greater extent sees his images as images, but trusts in the possibility of a correspondence between the order of nature and the order of his measuring standards or laws and explanatory models without usually probing the nature of this possibility, though oŌen with an awareness of this as an issue. While the popular consumpƟon of science, whether in the form of technology or as popularizaƟons in the more usual sense, is prone to take the images and standards as in themselves true, as an absolute reality, and to blindly trust both in them

and in their makers. This can even take the form in popular culture of extending to one domain the supposed truths of another, to parody, something like “Heisenberg proved that everything is uncertain, and Einstein that everything is relaƟve.” Consider another acƟvity, the ﬁne arts. The producers of arƟfacts exercise eikasia. Then there is pisƟs at various levels (again, as in the Cave). There are the consumers of images, and then the shapers of public taste, who trust in their own judgments. At the level of reason as dianoia then there would be the art historian and aestheƟcian and those arƟsts who reﬂect consciously, discursively, on art, e.g., Leonardo da Vinci, Paul Klee, Joachim Quantz, Jean-Phillipe Rameau, Richard Wagner. These last are engaged in the creaƟon of systemaƟc percepƟons and organizaƟons of what is in the realm of art, but here too it is oŌen usual to assume, or leave unquesƟoned, the nature of art itself both as product and human sensibility, either to take this as self-evident or dependably empirical (wholly inducƟve). The art historian/aestheƟcian can of course become involved in the analysis of the starƟng points—in quesƟons that concern both the nature of art and beauty and about the origins and meaning of both the work and the maker, or about the purpose or place of art in human life. As he starts to ask what art (and beauty) is and does, and its kinship with other products of the human spirit perhaps one could say that he passes from dianoia to noēsis—from science in the narrow sense, Socrates calls them “so-called sciences,” to the only true science, dialecƟc, and its objecƟve. Plato’s views on art are controversial, all the more so since he himself rather obviously is a frequent and skilled maker of images. Any account of his view must come to terms with this, and certainly not by simply saying that he could not resist, or that he has a divided nature, as literary arƟst and as philosopher, or even that his use of them is wholly rhetorical or didacƟc. Art is of course taken up explicitly in Book X and I will have more to say at the point of commenƟng on that book. I note here only that what I have said above is consistent with the interpretaƟon there oﬀered, and that those passages must be read in the context in which it is presented, that is, as a discussion of the meaning of imitaƟon in general, and in the light of the speciﬁc purpose of a discussion of imitaƟon at that point. The general issue however, averred to above, might indeed remain the same: To what extent can art contain a logos, some would argue even

do so excellently, and why? But a second quesƟon is always, To what extent does the work provoke, and is it capable of responding to, quesƟoning? (This second condiƟon can as well be applied to discourse in any of its forms, poeƟc or non-poeƟc, spoken or wriƩen.) To conƟnue with our examples, the mechanical engineer and the physicist stand perhaps in a similar relaƟon as the above pairs. The engineer deals with the results or applicaƟons of the models constructed by the physicist.
