The engineer trusts the formulas—he begins there, though some apply them with more skill or experƟse than others. For him, the bridge is constructed on paper. The literal builder of it, the welder, etc. takes the image projected by the designer/engineer and with liƩle or no awareness of even the formulas (e.g., stress formulas) that lie behind it, constructs his image in metal, measuring its success against a model of how it is best done. In each case there is the thought or picture image and the made expression. Finally, there are those of us who merely drive, some expertly, some with average ability, across the bridge every day (excluding the former groups); we know even less than the welder the truth about the bridge—but that does not stop us from wondering (idly) and speculaƟng about just what holds the whole thing together, including someƟmes about why it doesn’t. Discussions amongst non-engineers about why the bridge fell down are more likely to be discussions about the idenƟty and meaning of “shadows and noises.”[25] In the case of the bridge, our speculaƟons have liƩle consequence. Although uninformed speculaƟon can have consequences when the issues of technology interact with the poliƟcal and ethical, as in who gets the contracts, or whether the bridge, the nuclear reactor, etc., is safely constructed, and so on. In the case of other pracƟces, the other sciences and their objects, the objects as it were, that are observable in the social world, the “consequences of an educaƟon or the lack of it” can produce shadows that are at best serviceable, at worst either misleading and dangerous or the object of hopeless squabbles. Finally, with regard to jusƟce, it is operaƟve at the lowest level of the Cave and Line in the habits of the polis. In addiƟon to the general beliefs about jusƟce and its sancƟons suggested above, there are also beliefs about what is the right thing to do in a given situaƟon. There is a general, vague sense of jusƟce underlying this, but on the whole, for the general

public each case is seen as individual, that is, representaƟve of a kind but limited to what we might call a visual sameness: the right thing to do when coming to a stop sign, when an elderly person gets on a crowded bus, desegregaƟon of schools, animal rights, AIDS in Africa, etc., are each mostly treated as separate, unrelated issues, and on the whole the response in each case is a simple right or wrong—a response of the emoƟons (albeit educated in the facts relevant) based on the image presented. This image is never neutral but rather given a voice or coloring —not necessarily the accurate or true measure of it—by either speciﬁc others, or the pracƟces of the society at large. This is not to deny the importance of considering the speciﬁc sameness and diﬀerence of each case with another, but this is conspicuously what is not done or what is lacking—it is not considering but rather the immediacy of the response that is characterisƟc here. This immediacy considers neither the parƟcular diﬀerences of the case on the one hand, nor the similarity with other visually dissimilar kinds in which an important similarity of principle exists. Plato illustrates this piƞall in the discussion of the suitability of women for the Guardian role, where the interlocutors are quick to casually assume, based on the appearance of diﬀerence (whether physical or convenƟonal) that women are not suitable, which gives Socrates the opportunity to develop both the noƟon of soul and that of idenƟty of nature or natural capaciƟes (dunameis, pathēmata). And so the similarity, sameness, or analogy of cases of jusƟce (or other virtues) is not seen, or if it is brought forth, it is more oŌen than not resisted—the most common response heard being “that has nothing to do with it.” There is, then, a dominaƟon of the imaginaƟon (eikasia), the most emoƟonal of the faculƟes of knowing, and opinion oŌen is Ɵed quite literally to the visual, to the visualizaƟon of the situaƟon—an individual visualizes, or pictures, the Muslim as behaving in a certain way, and rightly deserving a certain treatment. The non-visible sameness, e.g., in this case of soul, of human being in essence, which would require the same treatment, is hidden, he cannot see it. The emoƟons, pre-eminently, ontologically, are Ɵed to the visible presence (physical or in imaginaƟon) of things, the emoƟonal response is a shadow image of the things that provoke it and cast it, as it were. It is worth menƟoning here the Meno, where, in the opening passages, Meno’s diﬃculty in deﬁning virtue is illustrated by his reliance on

examples, a collecƟon without a clearly arƟculated common principle. The problem is not so much that he resorts to examples, though Socrates pushes for a deﬁniƟon of virtue itself, but rather Meno’s inability to deduce what the examples have in common, other than giving them the same name, hence jusƟfying the collecƟon, he thinks. Of course the same name issue exists in the Republic, as we have already noted, but here it is used posiƟvely and consciously—we are asked to look at the analogy of city and soul and see if the same name is merited for the same virtues, parƟcularly jusƟce; we are to examine what is oﬀered hypotheƟcally (in this case constructed to match) but in general to quesƟon why and with what jusƟﬁcaƟon the same name is used of diverse images.[26] The general dynamic progression that has been noted here is from blind trust in images as realiƟes, and our discourse about them, to eikasƟc trust in being the creators of the sources of the images, to dianoeƟc knowledge (whether natural and every day, or technical and scienƟﬁc) as the source of the former, to dialecƟc’s reﬂecƟon on the noeƟc sources of the elements of thinking and their role in the images of dianoia. We have considered each of these acƟviƟes, these pracƟces, as representaƟve images of knowing, as capaciƟes exercised at increasingly conscious levels, and reﬂected in the concrete producƟons of each level, their respecƟve pracƟces. That is, the pracƟces which are both their acƟviƟes within their respecƟve sciences and arts and the products which remain as a result, are the concrete forms of their knowledge: the capaciƟes, their exercise, and the end results in the world, correspond to the divisions of the Line and to progress upwards along it. What the ﬁrst ﬁve books of the Republic have to say implicitly about the level of noēsis can be seen in the exhibiƟng of an image of the rule and principles of being and knowing at work in the construcƟon and life of the ideal city and soul, that is, in the soul of the arƟst craŌing the city and in the image of the just soul read in the image. What further can be said about noēsis within the conﬁnes of the Republic, is implicit in the discussion of the educaƟon of the philosopher, to which we turn in the next chapter. What actual argument there is for such truly ﬁrst principles, the Ideas as archai, apart from a showing forth of them, and a claim that only thus is experience intelligible, will take us beyond the Republic, to the Phaedo. As a preliminary formulaƟon of my own posiƟon I

suggest the noƟon of the image in discourse—of the non-visible images of reason at work in a presentaƟon of experience from its standpoint—as somehow the showing forth of the natural noeƟc standpoint for human being. In the Line, and in the Republic in general, logos can present itself to itself as an image in discourse of its own natural world as the workings of discourse. To make and to use images in various ways (and in various senses), is what allows for, in a sense creates, the world that the soul inhabits. To see images as images is seemingly negaƟve—they are revealed as merely images. Yet seen as the general dynamic that drives the soul upward to increasing clarity (511d-e), they are what provides the ladder we must climb.[27] Hugh Benson, in “Plato’s Philosophical Method in the Republic,”[28] though not working with the noƟon of image-making as I do, arrives at somewhat similar conclusions by a much diﬀerent route. He is out to carefully disƟnguish the diﬀerence in method of dianoia and noēsis, that is, of dialecƟc—in parƟcular the diﬀerent role of, and relaƟon to, hypothesis. Both methods employ hypothesis, but in rather diﬀerent ways. The relaƟvely limited results of dianoia as compared to dialecƟc can be traced to the “incorrect applicaƟon” of the “method of hypothesis” (188), to be contrasted with the fully achieved use that it can be put to by dialecƟc. The virtue of dialecƟc, which is producƟve of true knowledge, is that its upward journey through and beyond hypotheses to the forms is completed by a downward journey that searches out both “conﬁrmaƟon” of the truth of the hypothesis and “tesƟng the consequences of the hypothesis to see whether they agree with one another” (191). What is crucial, and the similarity to what I have argued, is the contrast between the tesƟng in applicaƟon of dianoia and that of dialecƟc. The applicaƟon and relaƟve success of “dianoeƟc” is in the applicaƟon of the assumed, unexamined hypothesis to the parƟculars of the relevant set of experiences, or world. “ConﬁrmaƟon” here means tracing out the “conƟngent consequences.” And this could also produce a rather unhappy result, in which the hypothesis is faced with an apparent unsaƟsfactory or contradictory brute fact, e.g., “philosophers are useless and vicious” (Adeimantus, 487b1-d5). But this in eﬀect is an “arƟﬁcial consequence,” the result of a misuse of hypothesis. How so? Because, Benson argues, we were looking at

parƟcular, “conƟngent . . . instanƟaƟons,”—downwards towards parƟculars. “Those philosophers alleged to be vicious are in fact not genuine instanƟaƟons of philosophy . . .” “The nature or being of philosophy is not the cause of these consequences” (202). This is as contrasted to the true, philosophical, hypotheƟcal method, which “examine(s) the consequences of the hypothesis that follow directly from the nature of the Forms involved . . . ”—looking, and tesƟng, downward only aŌer having journeyed upward. “DialecƟc . . . tests those features for consistency and responds to the contrary evidence of the arƟﬁcial or conƟngent consequences. If one can derive the answer to the original quesƟon from a hypothesis which itself is underivable and can conﬁrm that hypothesis by checking its consequences for consistency and against contrary evidence, one can genuinely be said to know the answer to the original quesƟon” (201). But this process, the task of dialegesthai, he too would agree is ongoing, perhaps never complete or completed: “Plato maintains that one cannot rightly claim to know the answer [to the original quesƟon, e.g., concerning virtue, jusƟce, etc.] unƟl this goal has been achieved. Short of conﬁrmaƟon from the unhypotheƟcal archē one’s inquiry remains incomplete. Of course, Plato would concede that few—perhaps none—of us has successfully completed such an inquiry” (194). Benson rejects “incorrigible or certain intuiƟon” of the Ideas or archē as a guarantor of their truth: “viewing the unhypotheƟcal archē does not guarantee its truth, but requires conﬁrmaƟon by avoiding refutaƟon. To know the Form of the Good it is not enough simply to view it, and somehow thereby know it. One must be able to respond in some way successfully to all aƩempts to refute it. One must test it and give an account of it” (199). Or, put another way, one must formulate logoi based on research into the nature of a Form, its features, and armed with that see if such logoi, such noeƟc images, have real explanatory force, truly hold the world together. Finally, let me say that even in my own descripƟon above (and in what follows concerning the interlocutors) the various knowers/souls appear as staƟcally consigned to a given level. The truth rather is more complex. We each more accurately, more realisƟcally, live at one and the same Ɵme at diﬀerent levels depending on the context. Even Socrates is made to admit at one point, perhaps ironically, to a certain self-decepƟon. I can be wise,

knowledgeable about some things, and be sƟll in a shadow world for others—but with a SocraƟc awareness of my ignorance. As well, we each and all are moving upward, as it were—some more, some less. And some few, upon a full ascent, eventually make the journey back downward again in the search for an applicaƟon of the Ideas that will produce true, if parƟal, knowledge. Plato’s Cave and Line images are in this sense invitaƟons to a progressive dialogue, with others and within our own souls, moving towards an ideal—as well as the cost of not doing so. PLACEMENT ON THE LINE Let us now brieﬂy examine how the interlocutors of the Republic might be ﬁƩed to the image of the Line (and Cave) and its levels of image relaƟon. Cephalus, who begins the Republic, has the images of what is right to do in each case in his head, but he cannot talk about it, that is, cannot discuss the sameness and diﬀerence of things in such a way that a workable deﬁniƟon is got at, hence the example of the weapon lent put forward by Socrates, confounds him. For Cephalus, the habit or pracƟce of virtue is more reliable than any one arƟculaƟon he can oﬀer as a guide or rule; hence his inability to handle a new special case of a debt owed where the honoring of it would be dishonorable, and he readily backs away from the unpleasant consequences, preferring what he knows would be right to do to consistency. But of course a thinking interpretaƟon of the maxim he oﬀers—telling the truth and paying one’s debts—is precisely what is presented in the rest of the Republic, in the elaboraƟon of its analogies through images. The issue is the nature of what one owes to others and parƟcularly to oneself, and what ﬁnally is the compulsion to pay the debt, in other words, to return to the Cave. But that vision of jusƟce, of acƟng rightly, requires a turning, again, of the whole soul and its knowing capaciƟes from the visible to the non-visible, from the parƟcular to the general (and back again); thus from jusƟce as an external acƟon to jusƟce as an internal state, comprehended and controlled as the one uniﬁed cause of diverse external acts, and pracƟce discerning its sameness in diﬀerent shapes and guises. For Cephalus etc., jusƟce and the just life is simply the sum of the external right acts, and hence his only reply to Socrates’s challenge is to return to the sacriﬁces. Cephalus relies on what may be

called the set of social pracƟces—but these are reliable only as long as the condiƟons of social pracƟce remain the same, or may also be challenged by a conﬂict arising between the normally separated levels of pracƟces. Or this may be provoked by SocraƟc aporeƟc intervenƟon, to the degree that the interlocutor is perturbable. Such intervenƟons are verbal but the use of images and analogy makes them other than abstract philosophical arguments or conceptual representaƟons. An example of the disrupƟon of the former would be radical social upheaval, revoluƟon, war, economic crises, examples of the laƩer, the clash of religious and poliƟcal values— the dilemma of the AnƟgone, the current aborƟon controversy, etc. Polemarchus and the others present whom he represents, are at the second stage, corresponding to pisƟs. They, along with Cephalus, cite the poets and tradiƟon as the authority for what is right and just, again at the level of accepƟng convenƟonal images (and corresponding deﬁniƟons of what is just)—in x situaƟon, remember Achilles or Orestes or AnƟgone, Simonides or Homer, Lycurgus or Pericles, and do as they do or say one ought to do in such situaƟons. There is, however, some possibility, though not much, of movement here, to the extent that real discourse is possible with them about the convenƟons of trust. But even this is limited by their desire to hang on to their trusted beliefs, like those in the Cave who are disputaƟous. Polemarchus’s argument brings him closer to Thrasymachus’s erisƟc. As late as Book V, Polemarchus and Adeimantus interrupt with a roadblock, and are Ɵed to their inability to rise above the literal or visible level of the analogy, i.e., the visible image constructed of the city of imaginaƟon, as opposed to its funcƟon as an image for the non-visible soul. Perhaps Polemarchus is ranked a liƩle further down than Adeimantus: “He was siƫng a liƩle further away than Adeimantus.” So, Polemarchus’s interrupƟon is suitably physical, i.e., visible, he “extended his hand and took hold of the other’s cloak from above at the shoulder, drew him toward himself while he leaned forward and said something to him” (449a-b). Adeimantus is represented as actually in dialogue with Socrates, though less so than Glaucon (he occupies less of the text as interlocutor), who is in between pisƟs and dianoia. Adeimantus is also presented as at least arriving with the opposite party from the fesƟval at Bendis. Glaucon follows in the dialecƟcal trail/trials but as noted earlier he is too willing a friend of JusƟce, wishing to see it saved and “praised”

rather than analyzed. He would have been saƟsﬁed with a merely verbally persuasive image. He, like most of us, is tempted by the unjust life, at least in the images of imaginaƟon; either fearful perhaps, or for lack of skill, he is someƟmes intellectually lazy, someƟmes painfully struggling. The best descripƟon of him is perhaps that given by Socrates of the one newly freed from the chains of the Cave, whose struggle is partly with seeing rightly, partly with the desire to remain in, or return to, the relaƟve security of each earlier stage (if, that is, he in fact leaves his starƟng point behind—we shall see in our analysis of Book X). At his best, he tries to follow the development of the images and their applicaƟon, duƟfully accepƟng the hypotheses on which they are based “as if they were ﬁrst principles.”At 548e Glaucon is described as a “victory lover,” a philonikias, according to Adeimantus, but this makes sense, given what we have seen he asks for, a “defense” of the just life through encomium.[29] The discussion of “how dictatorship evolves from democracy, and what its nature is when so evolved” is carried on, interesƟngly enough, with Adeimantus and not with Glaucon (from 548e). In turning to Thrasymachus, it is worth recalling again here the opening scene of the Republic where the acƟon and image are somewhat the same as at 449a-b, that of a physical intervenƟon: one group approaches another, somebody is sent ahead and takes hold of Socrates’ cloak. Many issues are implicit in the opening drama—the issues of power, force, compulsion, the physical/rhetorical force versus the compulsion of the Ideas and that of moral obligaƟon, the free eroƟc movement towards the Good, the compelling force of the Good, the chaining of desires and the shackles of ignorance. Finally, consider Thrasymachus’s reliance or trust in force as being both a consequence and a cause of his disbelief or mistrust in the value, hence reality of Ideas. Thrasymachus puts forth verbal images of jusƟce for immediate consumpƟon, not as he believes it actually to be, and brazenly so, even once he is “forced out of hiding.” His sole interest appears to be in winning the argument, brashly maintaining power and control both in the argument and in life, and in preserving the assumpƟon, or hypothesis, which he believes is a solid ﬁrst principle: that might is a higher value than any moral virtue and that, sophisƟcally or perhaps as an actual belief, might makes right. His posiƟon on the Line is

thus ambiguous; also between the second and third levels though unaware of it (as are those who carry the images in the Cave), he uses a technē, hence dianoia, (though less scienƟﬁcally than Protagoras) but in the service of his convicƟon or belief in dominaƟon as a value in itself, thus rooted in the objects of the second level. Speech as erisƟc is a bastard form of dianoia. He ﬁts well the descripƟon of one who abuses both intellect itself, in the form of rhetoric, and his own soul. “The virtue of intelligence belongs above all to something more divine” than the other virtues of the soul, i.e., moderaƟon, self-control, etc. which are “close to those of the body,” because “they do not exist before and are added later by habit and pracƟce,” and intelligence “never loses its capacity but, according to which way it is turned, becomes useful and beneﬁcial or useless and harmful. Have you never noƟced in men who are said to be wicked but clever, how sharply their liƩle soul looks into things to which it turns its aƩenƟon. Its capacity for sight is not inferior, but serves evil ends, so that the more sharply it looks the more evil it works” (518e-519a). Francis SparshoƩ, in “Plato and Thrasymachus,”[30] takes a diﬀerent approach. Thrasymachus merely supposes “that there is no more to jusƟce than obedience. It is precisely this supposiƟon that Plato idenƟﬁes in Book VI (492-3, esp. 493c) as that inevitably made by all sophists. Thrasymachus is here simply succumbing to the occupaƟonal hazard of his profession.” It is “not a symptom of immorality but . . . an eﬀect of ignorance . . . a mistake about what the true interests of the self are” (57). Now these no doubt are his beliefs, and his posiƟons are an expression of them. But to ignore the role of character and epithumia, as this seems to do, is to ignore the source of that ignorance, in part. Thrasymachus’s place on the Line is guaranteed by the interrelated limitaƟons of both character and his views of knowledge and power. SparshoƩ defends Thrasymachus as represenƟng a realisƟc view of the actual polis, and argues for his being a sort of Platonic alter ego. But it is rather a realism limited and distorted by character. His thumos is explained more by his epithumia than by his pisƟs. If Plato is pessimisƟc or “embiƩered” (60) about the actual city that could put Socrates to death, etc., his response is the founding of a beƩer city in a beƩer place, the only place where it is truly possible, and of which Socrates is the model ciƟzen. This is not quite a Platonic anƟthesis, except in the

sense that they live in diﬀerent kinds of city. The opposiƟon is not between the city of Athens and the philosopher’s ideal “city in words,” per SparshoƩ, but rather between the city within the walls and the city within the soul. One certainly would not wish to underesƟmate Thrasymachus’s intelligence or his rhetorical ability, but he is basically an intellectual bully. Perhaps Adeimantus is the beƩer choice of a representaƟve of the limits of the skills of discourse separated from, or at least not ﬁrmly aƩached to, its proper end. (The best representaƟve, though not present in this dialogue, is of course Alcibiades.) Adeimantus is at least presented as a friend (see earlier discussion). He is calmer, more intellectually inclined, yet sƟll presented as contenƟous, raising the obstacles, and as both physically and verbally interrupƟng the argument—albeit with objecƟons which, though misguided (we have argued), are tellingly so. And hence in the end the objecƟons are necessary regarding the problem of the method and level of the discourse, literal versus ﬁguraƟve, keeping sight of the goals and stages of hypothesis/demonstraƟon of the task at hand. For more adept examples of the kind, and references to the misuse of intelligence and argument, we would have to turn to other dialogues.[31] Here I have completed my brief speculaƟon concerning the locaƟon of the various interlocutors on the Line, none of whom, with the possible excepƟon of Glaucon’s halƟng beginning, get much beyond the downward looking technē of dianoia, malevolent in the case of the sophist’s erisƟc, represented by Thrasymachus. Glaucon, and Adeimantus represent a more trusƟng, less reﬂecƟve, less astute or clever type, though the journey upward of the dialogue at least exposes them to a more complex and more raƟonal doxa in the formaƟon and examinaƟon of the ideal city, and of images of the soul in various states. We turn next to some further suggesƟons, rather speculaƟve, for those in public life who might be thought of as examples of souls ﬁrmly, more consciously, rooted in the technē of dianoia than Glaucon and Adeimantus. As ﬁnal brief examples in our parade of character-types, consider the law-maker, lawyer, judge and poliƟcian, who are all more or less aware of the hypotheƟcal nature of their respecƟve arts (though they might not describe it in these terms), but who are content to elaborate the reasoned

consequences of their starƟng points, and even at Ɵmes to speculate about the right starƟng point. So, a lawyer is concerned to discern the common element in (say) two acts in order to bring them under one law. In an adversarial system he does so always in his client’s favor of course—but in erisƟc appeals to what is plausible, as disƟnguished from mere bombast. The laƩer may even win cases, parƟcularly in a jury trial, but by a diﬀerent skill than what the law, the judges, etc. call a good lawyer. Which is not to say that at this level there is not a disƟncƟon sƟll to be made between a clever lawyer and one whose interest in the law is that jusƟce be served, and not merely his client. The judge’s funcƟon is to reason out which of two opposing lawyers makes the beƩer case for subsuming (or not) the individual case under consideraƟon under the general principle set out in the law. The further up the judicial process one goes, the more it is the case that at issue is the correct subsumpƟon of the parƟcular to the general. An appellate court considers (apart from due process) not whether the law is just, which is part of the funcƟon of the legislature, but whether and how the case at hand conforms to the law. There are of course other views of both the judiciary and the legislature which reverse these roles somewhat: the legislators are to seek and express the people’s will, and not to judge what is right to do, and the judiciary is someƟmes seen as ostensible wise men whose interpretaƟon of even the fundamental laws is formaƟve, based on their percepƟon of a higher law and the changing context of civil society. Legislators, and poliƟcians when they are acƟng in that capacity, operate, at least at their best and at certain points in their pracƟce, with some theoreƟcal sophisƟcaƟon and are at the third level when they do so. They, like the scholars and teachers who study the insƟtuƟons the former rule over, have at least some noƟon of consistency and the rule of law, hence of perceiving similarity amongst diversity, and of bringing such order into social life. But as indicated, they lack the skills or interest to quesƟon the fundamental starƟng points. Thus jusƟce, apart from the seeming unity of convenƟon, becomes a maƩer of luck and good will, plus a certain level of intuiƟve insight and an ability to see contradicƟons; that is, when we are considering the contribuƟons of individual consciousnesses, and not their role as a conduit for the collecƟve social will (and the interacƟon of the two). We are concerned here with their degree of self-consciousness, and

this as reﬂected in the degree to which their producƟons, the products of their art as embodied in their pracƟces, can lay claim to knowledge. We have been considering each of these acƟviƟes, these pracƟces, as representaƟve images of knowing, as capaciƟes exercised at increasingly conscious levels, and reﬂected in the concrete producƟons of each level, which we have been calling their respecƟve pracƟces. That is, the pracƟces which are both their acƟviƟes within their respecƟve sciences and arts, and the products which remain as a result, are the concrete forms of their knowledge: the capaciƟes, their exercise, and the end results in the world, correspond to the divisions of the Line and to progress upwards along it. What the Republic has to say about the level of noēsis has been seen thus far primarily in the exhibiƟng of an image of the rule and principles of being and knowing at work in the construcƟon and life of the ideal city and soul, that is, in the soul of the arƟst craŌing the city and in the image of the just soul read in the image. What further can be said about noēsis within the conﬁnes of the Republic, is illustrated in the discussion of the educaƟon of the philosopher, to which we now turn. What argument there is for such truly ﬁrst principles, the Ideas as archai, apart from a showing forth of them, and a claim that only thus is experience intelligible, will take us beyond the Republic, to the Phaedo. As a preliminary formulaƟon of my own posiƟon I suggest the noƟon of the image in discourse, of the non- visible images of reason at work in a presentaƟon of experience from its standpoint, as somehow the showing forth of the natural, noeƟc, standpoint for human being. Before turning to the next chapter, on the educaƟon of the philosopher/ruler, I would like to comment once more on a diﬀerent sense of educaƟon—the issue of the inculcaƟon of implicit values embedded in social pracƟces, and immortalized in dicta in and out of the classroom. Just how deeply embedded are they, what chance is there of freeing ourselves from the Cave, journeying on the upward path? In our most fundamental beliefs and values, are we so educated behind our backs, so immersed in our society, and in our social class, that real educaƟon is not even suscepƟble to meaningful discourse? Apart from progress in knowledge in the natural sciences (and some would say even there), is Plato’s sketch that of an impossible journey, and worse, his sociology of knowledge irrelevant (and, some would say, pernicious)?

Pierre Bourdieu, in DisƟncƟon: A Social CriƟque of the Judgment of Taste,[32] develops a sociologist’s detailed portrait of the process described above. EducaƟon, in the broadest sense, and deepest rooted kind, is viewed as primarily and inescapably the passing on of social pracƟces and values, “hierarchies,” of value and meaning. “In place of pracƟcal schemes of classiﬁcaƟon, which are always parƟal and linked to pracƟcal contexts [formal educaƟon] puts explicit, standardized taxonomies, ﬁxed once and for all in the form of synopƟc schemas or dualisƟc typologies (e.g., ‘classical’/’romanƟc’), which are expressly inculcated and therefore conserved in the memory as knowledge that can be reproduced in virtual idenƟcal form by all the agents subject to its acƟon,” and its eﬀects. It is, of course, just these doxai, someƟmes conscious, oŌen not, that Plato is most concerned to bring to light, and not excluding even the bodily gestures which are an “image of the logic of socializaƟon” (474). But for Bourdieu there is liƩle or no hope of escaping these forms, as we shall see. For Bourdieu, the possibility of escape is dismal. Plato is also, as has been oŌen remarked, someƟmes pessimisƟc, not only about the possibility of poliƟcal change, but even of individual re-consƟtuƟon, both of ontologies and of souls. In DisƟncƟon, Bourdieu is wriƟng primarily about the sources and eﬀects of social classiﬁcaƟons of taste. The term “disƟncƟon” refers to the diﬀerenƟaƟon or disƟncƟon that people make between themselves as belonging to a class, and others, as being themselves “cultured” or “educated” as disƟnct from those who are not. His sociology of taste reveals the dynamics of the imprisoning structures, of the middle class in France in parƟcular, structures of belief (but not of concepts) precisely because they are implicit, in which the social subject is complicit. His introducƟon to the English ediƟon makes the claim that the dynamic and its structure ought to be generally applicable to any society, with a diﬀerent speciﬁc content, each culture being a “parƟcular case of the possible,” (xi) as are its examples. The parallel to Plato’s Cave and its denizens is so striking in one passage that, though he does not make an explicit reference to the Cave (or the rule of doxa in the Line), he seems quite obviously to have had it in mind. It is worth quoƟng at length: Thus, through the diﬀerenƟated and diﬀerenƟaƟng condiƟonings of existence, through exclusions and inclusions, unions (marriages,

aﬀairs, alliances etc.) and divisions (incompaƟbiliƟes, separaƟons, struggles, etc.) which govern the social structure and the structuring force it exerts, through all the hierarchies and classiﬁcaƟons inscribed in its objects (especially cultural products, in insƟtuƟons (for example, the educaƟonal system) or simply in language . . . constantly arising from the meeƟngs and interacƟons of everyday life, the social order is progressively inscribed in people’s minds. … (Our) primary experience of the social world is that of doxa, and adherence to relaƟons of order which, because they structure inseparably both the real world and the thought world, are accepted as self-evident. Primary percepƟon . . . is always an act of cogniƟon, involving principles of construcƟon that are external to the constructed object grasped in its immediacy; but at the same Ɵme it is an act of mis-cogniƟon, implying the most absolute form of recogniƟon of the social order. Dominated agents . . . tend to aƩribute to themselves what the distribuƟon aƩributes to them [the relaƟon of the cave prisoners’ discourse to the puppeteers, and their later anger at the one who has returned from outside the cave], refusing what they are refused . . . adjusƟng their expectaƟons, deﬁning themselves as the established order deﬁnes them . . . in a word, condemning themselves to what is in any case their lot, ta heautou as Plato put it, consenƟng to be what they have to be. (470- 71) This is an apt descripƟon in sociological terms of the sources of the diﬃculty of liberaƟon from doxa. Since this is the deeply embedded source of our behavior and aƫtudes, and of our conscious beliefs per se, it is diﬃcult, but not impossible, for dialegesthai to be eﬀecƟve—and hence the necessity of SocraƟc aporia—that induced state of uncertainty, confusion and discomfort resulƟng from a breakdown of certainty—as well as Plato’s stress on the turning of the whole soul, if such fundamental “knowledge without concepts,” (Bourdieu, 470) to which we have been enslaved is to be challenged and disrupted. But Bourdieu condemns “the logocentrism and intellectualism of intellectuals, combined with the prejudice inherent in the science which takes as its object the psyche, the soul, the mind, consciousness, representaƟons, not to menƟon the peƟt-bourgeois pretension to the

status of ‘person,’ [which] have prevented us from seeing that as Leibniz put it, ‘we are automatons in three quarters of what we do.’” How likely is it, in Bourdieu’s view, that we can break this viselike grip? Not very. “The sense of disƟncƟon, the discreƟo (discriminaƟon) which demands that certain things be brought together and others kept apart,” a parodic dialecƟc, the social dimension of that ignorance of the cave, the blindness of everyday consumpƟon of images, the trust in the substanƟal reality of objects and valuaƟons of them, and the certainty and appeals to self- evidence of the classiﬁcaƟons of those in power and empowered by those below them, is all an intractable structure. Bourdieu concludes, that “this basis of collecƟve and individual idenƟty—responds with visceral, murderous horror, absolute disgust, metaphysical fury, [to that] which, by challenging the principles of the incarnate social order . . . violates the mental order, scandalously ﬂouƟng common sense” (475). Thus results Thrasymachus’s contempt and fury, the friendly doubts and hesitaƟons of Glaucon and Adeimantus, the passive docility of Cephalus and his withdrawal from the argument to aƩend to making a ritual sacriﬁce (331d), the sophistry of the crowds, and Socrates’s trial. Finally, Bourdieu’s own version of the struggle to free oneself from the chains of doxa is as follows: “The individual or collecƟve classiﬁcaƟon struggles aimed at transforming the categories of percepƟon and appreciaƟon of the social world, and through this, the social world itself, are indeed a forgoƩen dimension of the class struggle. But one only has to realize that the classiﬁcatory schemes which underlie agents’ pracƟcal relaƟonship to their condiƟon and the representaƟon they have of it are themselves the product of that condiƟon to see the limits of this autonomy” (483-484).[33] My own response, and that of Plato on my reading, would be the following. The posited autonomy of the philosopher can be framed in a platonic view of discursive pracƟces and both elencƟc and dialecƟc as a clarifying project of those discourses, by accepƟng while criƟcizing from within those pracƟces in dialogue. This places the Ideas in an inescapable human social context of meanings—this tension between acceptance and criƟque (which the sophist rejects) is the ﬁnite limit of transcendence, falling prey neither to an “illusion of the absence of limits” (Bourdieu). In eﬀect, the “embedded social structures” (Bourdieu) have beliefs as implicit

consequences. The platonic task of dialegesthai is to make these explicit and where possible lead in an ascent towards an alternaƟve. This would be precisely a set of alternaƟve pracƟces that embody an alternaƟve interpretaƟon of reality of increasing clarity.[34] NOTES 1. The textual connecƟon of the Line discussion with this passage, i.e., the larger context of the task at hand, does not seem to me to have been suﬃciently clariﬁed. Cf. Klein, Meno, ch.V, especially 112-125, and concluding paragraph of secƟon 3. 2. For two views of analogy as method, compare R. Robinson, Plato’s Earlier DialecƟc, (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1953), 204-22 with Brann “Music” (2004) 56ﬀ. esp. 61-62. For Brann, analogy as a method is to “recognize likenesses,” “in the sense of observing those that are already there by nature, clothing them in ﬁgures and puƫng the ﬁgures into words” (62). Robinson sees analogy in somewhat similar terms, but closer to a weaker form of epagōgē which he equates with an imperfect form of inducƟon (205) as a “method of discovery” and not a “method of proof or argument.” But he is worried about how one chooses the “right case” of analogical comparison, and thus ﬁnds it more suitable a method for leading or teaching another than for “self-teaching”: “Socrates, though he pretends to be making discoveries, is really communicaƟng previous discoveries to others” (221). For ﬁnding likenesses, Robinson thinks that Socrates “seems reduced to blind trial and error” (214) in looking for “co- ordinate cases of the same universal” (213). Brann, on the other hand, does a beƩer job, I would say, of explaining just how and why this is possible—both for the teacher’s ability to lead the learner up to the unknown from the known by a paradeigma, and for the teacher’s own discovery. The possibility of what she terms the “discovering dianoia [that] moves upward by an analogia,” is explicated by appeal to Plato’s development in the dialogue of an image of Being. This philosophical imaging or parsing of Being is reﬂected in the Line and the account of the Good as responsible for “a progression of likenesses [which] is originally responsible for our own ability both to make ourselves like to the highest things by homoiosis (505c5, Theaetetus 176b1) and to recognize likenesses

or to make analogies” (62). But analogia, grounded as it is in ontological reality, is sƟll only “provisional.” Socrates’s true images are “based on analogy” (35) and provoke reﬂecƟon. 3. For an interesƟng aƩempt at mapping the four pathēmata of the Line onto the whole structure of the Republic, see Kenneth Dorter, “The Divided Line and the Structure of Plato’s Republic,” in History of Philosophy Quarterly Volume 21/Number 1 (January 2004). Dorter reads Book One as exemplifying eikasia in that “Socrates … examines only words or images of jusƟce without aƩempƟng to discern jusƟce itself.” So eikasia “looks . . . at words or other images of the physical world . . .” This appears to make some sense, but looking “at” words is odd. As if it was Socrates’s refutaƟons that were the exempliﬁcaƟon? “Eikasia examines words, theories, without invesƟgaƟng the things to which the words refer” (8). But while it is true that the sources are unexamined, the producƟons of eikasia, as doxai, cannot be separated from the object-image pair. Eikasia should be a capacity for seeing images of ‘x’, thus the deﬁniƟons proposed by the interlocutors as imperfectly realized images—and a process engaged in discourse in general, not just in the context of refutaƟon. Eikasia thus does not “look … at words,” but rather produces them in the normal course of things as imperfect images. Dorter also appears to take pisƟs to apply to objects in the visible world, as do most commentators, even though as applied by Dorter to Books Two—Four he ﬁnds it in the pracƟces of jusƟce in acts. Chapter 5 Education and the Mind’s Eye THE TENSIONS OF CONTRADICTION: THE PHILOSOPHER’S STUDIES AND THE NOETIC PRIMACY OF LOGISMOS We turn next to the descripƟons of the actual educaƟon of the philosopher who is desƟned to return to the city as ruler. The exposiƟon of two images in the two previous chapters, The Divided Line and the Cave, suggested just how our interpretaƟon and construcƟon of images both structures and responds to our world. The Cave story depicts how collecƟvely and individually we lose and ﬁnd our way. The Line story gives the structure of a discursive image-world. This is a world of increasing clarity and jusƟﬁable certainty that we make in our moving from opinion through to knowledge. In the present chapter, the descripƟon of educaƟon (as contrasted to the earlier training) will give the details of how individual souls can actually make their way along that journey in a series of pracƟces that are an intellectual training of the soul in the habit of seeing more clearly. At the same Ɵme, it illustrates for the reader what there is to see. It is in this sense an educaƟon in the reading of images. As revelatory as this is, it is sƟll an argument by illustraƟon. Albeit poinƟng to what we actually do, the descripƟon of each stage and of each kind of study is set out in a series of images that will be seen as subtly diﬀerent from their tradiƟonal counterparts. The diﬀerences imbedded in the descripƟve images are to lead the potenƟal philosopher/ruler forward, and are in support of the basis of the knowledge/opinion disƟncƟon. At the same Ɵme, it is an argument for what it is about the consƟtuents of experience that poses an obstacle to this, and how the world can be read diﬀerently. The key, once again, is in the seeing of images for what they are, in reading correctly the image as image. Certain key moments of the interlocutor’s misunderstanding—for example in the discussion of astronomy—reveal the diﬃculty of this and its ontological origin, and the correcƟon in course is instrucƟve. The higher educaƟon of the guardians, that is, the preparaƟon of the philosopher/ruler (521c-535a) is not oŌen given detailed aƩenƟon—

certainly not as much as the similes of Sun, Line and Cave. But this is unfortunate, since the details of the studies, their descripƟon and their sequence, can tell us much about those similes and eventually about dialecƟc and its goal. The studies are, aŌer all, described in such a way as to make them more than just the convenƟonal list of a Greek intellectual’s educaƟon. Though the descripƟon is not the educaƟon itself, and not that vision itself, its descripƟon, and parƟcularly the conversaƟon about it, does shed considerable light. Furthermore, the path “upward to the light” is not a preparaƟon for a sudden illuminaƟon at the end, but rather a gradual upward path along which more and more light is shed through the sequence of studies. They thus deserve more aƩenƟon. Socrates says that the beƩer educated thus is “beƩer able to share in both kinds of life [the public and the private, poliƟcs and philosophy] . . . (they) must each in turn go down to live with the other men and grow accustomed to seeing in the dark. When you are used to it, you will see inﬁnitely beƩer than the dwellers below; you will know what each image is, and of what it is an image, because you have seen the truth of things beauƟful and just and good” (520b-c). So upon his return from his journey out of the Cave and up the Line, the philosopher now sees the truth of each image. He sees it as an image—sees “what each is,” that it is an image, and in what sense in the parƟcular case, and also “of what it is an image.” That is, he sees the original and the relaƟon of image to original for the parƟcular kind of original, which depends on at what level the relaƟon and the objects are being considered. The educaƟon of the philosopher is reviewed as an answer to just how the relaƟvely disinterested ruler can be got for the city. The Line and the Cave sketch what that view of reality entails, i.e., in Socrates’ “opinion”—thus, the Cave gives the “eﬀect of educaƟon and the lack of it,” and the Line image before it gives the world as knowable. The educaƟonal program for the philosopher then gives the parƟcular kind of “studies” that will result in an ontological reorientaƟon that forms the basis for that higher vision. This vision is, in turn, the basis for the rule of the just city, both the city in the visible world and that of the soul itself. It is important to note at the outset that the use of the studies is not necessarily the normal one, the normal way or reason that they are taken up. Just as what we might call the earlier virtues of a visible world, those which require and

result from “training and habit,” were redeﬁned and reoriented to provide the iniƟal training of the guardians, so here, the disciplines of the future philosopher-ruler are redeﬁned and reoriented, aŌer the “excrescencies [have been] knocked oﬀ which belong to the world of becoming [which] have been fastened on the soul by feasƟng, gluƩony and similar pleasures, which like leaden weights draw the soul to look downward” (519c-b). The knocking oﬀ of the “excrescencies” is an external habituaƟon to virtue and corresponds to 1) the earlier educaƟon/training of the guardians, 2) the ﬁrst struggles at the boƩom of the Cave, and 3) the passage in the Line from ImaginaƟon to Trust (eikasia to pisƟs). This is the pre-struggle, that is, the struggle for a reformaƟon and reorientaƟon of values at the level of habit or doxa or that of uncriƟcal philosophy, and is pre-ontological—as contrasted to the educaƟon of the philosopher, where the studies are also a sort of habituaƟon but of the acƟve intellect. Rather than a habit of acƟon (ethical) it is a habit of percepƟon. AŌer this iniƟal turning away, the primary funcƟon of the studies then, is to “draw the soul from the world of that which becomes to the world of that which is” (521d). But this is unintelligible without an awareness of their relaƟon, and a detailed look at just how these studies funcƟon, to which we now turn. Socrates begins the discussion of the educaƟon of the philosopher- ruler, which studies are also to be a test of who is to be ﬁt to rule, by going back to the beginning, that is, by recalling the training studies of the guardians in order to stress their limits—“these men, in youth, must be athletes in war” and “we educated them before this in the arts and physical culture (gymnasƟc).” Now this educaƟon was described iniƟally as a good preparaƟon for the defenders of the city, and it remains so, since those who are to be the leaders of the city are chosen from amongst those who have already been formed. The shortcoming or limitaƟon of these early forms of educaƟon is that they are a result of habit, condiƟoning of the soul, the hammering or tempering of it. Physical training is disqualiﬁed as a higher study because it deals with, or in, “what comes to be and dies” and the turning of the soul is from the world of becoming to that of being. But the training in the arts are disqualiﬁed for the higher studies not because they deal with becoming but because they “educated the guardians through habits; [and] its melodies gave them a certain inner harmony, not knowledge . . . its stories

. . . culƟvated certain habits akin to those [harmony and grace] but there was no knowledge in it which would lead to what you are looking for now” (522a). The link between these two aspects of disqualiﬁcaƟon is important to note: the physicality and exteriority of the objects, the body, music, the arts, corresponds to an exteriority of method—training or habit. This is a learning imposed from without, through imitaƟon on the whole; and especially iniƟally through in some cases quite literally a copying of images (art school, gymnasƟc, rhetorical forms, and the poets, etc.). It does not deal with acƟve intellect except at its lowest level, that of memory, as opposed to recollecƟon which requires comparison and judgment. The link between the two disqualiﬁcaƟons of object and method then is in the nature of our hold on what we have—and not the changeableness of the world of generaƟon and decay per se from which we are said to turn away. [1] For in a sense, nothing is more ﬁxed than habit (the training of the gymnast, the skill of the musician or arƟst) nor for that maƩer anything more reliable, perforce, than the everyday world in which we live—a stability on which we rely.[2] But we operate within this reliability without understanding it, without knowing it. Nor is there a need to understand it, for the most part—though occasionally something goes wrong, something is out of place, or there is a seeming violaƟon of the “laws of nature,” and we are puzzled, disoriented (or someƟmes while the occurrence is a part of the everyday world, it is one from which we are usually hidden, or hide ourselves. Such is the personal experience of death in the death of a loved one). At such a point we either rest with our puzzlement, or it drives us to seek to understand what we see, drives us to a higher level (a fuller discussion of this dynamic is to follow). Apart from these shocks, our trust (pisƟs) in these worlds does change as interpretaƟons either of nature or art change, but the changes of craŌ or habit change passively, so to speak —that is, in response to an external force—the teacher, the culture, etc. and not as a result of the acƟve rethinking of the agent. The ﬂux of nature itself is best taken, as we noted earlier, as a metaphor for the whole realm of doxa, which on the one hand is intractable, on the other, changes, when it does, arbitrarily. One might in fact go so far as to assign the physical training menƟoned to the lowest segment of the Line—since its basis is in a way pure imitaƟon, and then assign the condiƟoning of the soul via the

arts to the second secƟon, where at least the making of images is involved, and where there is the use of intellectual elements (though not their understanding). Again, these new studies are to be disƟnguished from the earlier training because they develop and depend upon the noeƟc capaciƟes inherent in the non-visible soul, as disƟnguished from the skills and habits which are given to the subject, imposed from without. To cast this in terms of our image of the just city—we have been presented with its outer form, the visible city of imaginaƟon with its mirror image in its inner form, the soul, and the larger world as cast or corresponding to that inner form. We are now to look at the acƟviƟes which contain an image of the noeƟc soul at work on its natural objects, just as before the soul was given acƟviƟes that formed in a sense its external nature. The virtues of the laƩer that were called into being—that is, courage, moderaƟon, etc.—are pracƟces that depend for their very existence, if not their meaning, on the embodied soul, on the soul at the level of the desiring/feeling soul that presents us with the baƩleﬁeld of the passions. Even jusƟce, conceived of in its parƟcular applicaƟon to the human situaƟon (as opposed to the bare principle of harmony of parts, unity of a many) might be said to exist as human jusƟce only in the embodied and embaƩled soul (the plan/design laid up in heaven of the just city is not a form—it is an image drawn by the philosopher/arƟst, an ideal not an Idea). Thus though the turning around is of necessity of the whole soul it is “not the art of puƫng the capacity of sight into the soul: the soul possesses that already but it has not turned the right way or looking where it should. This is what the higher educaƟon has to deal with” (518d). The virtue of intelligence is, it seems, not a moral quality acquired with the experience of life, since it may be turned either to good or evil ends, and yet in the laƩer case “its capacity for sight is not inferior” (519a); the capacity to know (diverse in its general sense—all the pathēmata of the Line) is itself an excellence or virtue belonging to something “more divine” simply by virtue of its alignment with what is knowable, what truly is as opposed to what appears to be—or, appears to one to be, in the form of doxa, as opposed to what one knows to be in the form of epistēmē. Having disƟnguished in general what these studies are to be, we may now look at them in parƟcular. Glaucon, not too surprisingly from my point

of view, asks, “Yet what study is there leŌ apart from the arts and physical training and the craŌs” (522b). The answer, Socrates suggests, is something “which bears upon them all … used by all craŌs, all modes of thought and all sciences . . . that triﬂing thing [to phaulon], namely to disƟnguish [diagignōskein] one, two and three, or to give it one name, I call it number and calculaƟon [arithmon, logismon]” (522c).[3] The seriousness and weight aƩached to this beginning is indicated by the playfulness of to phaulon: (pl. hoi phauloi ) meaning 1) slight, light 2) trivial, mean, low or common (of persons), ugly (of persons), mean looking (of outward appearance) 3) careless, thoughtless—hoi phauloi means the vulgar, the common sort, also weak or uneducated, as opposed to hoi sophoi. (Liddell and ScoƩ). It is possibly signiﬁcant that Plato says legō de auto en kephalō translated by Grube as “or to give it one name, I call it. . .” and by Shorey simply as “in sum.” For kephalō is a pun of sorts, meaning, in the daƟve as here, a summary, the sum of the maƩer, but also literally and generally “of or belonging to the head physically—and by obvious extension metaphorically the chief or main point” (Liddell and ScoƩ). If number and calculaƟon are truly the beginning, broadly conceived, of all knowing and the base of all knowability in the things known, then other forms of knowing must all partake of these and these be always “in the head” and “at the head.” This starƟng point is, I believe, so signiﬁcant that I propose to discuss it at length. One is reminded of the Meno and its mathemaƟcal example. One might suppose that the use of a geometrical example there would have predicted a diﬀerent order of studies in the Republic, with geometry preceding arithmeƟc or calculaƟon. The metaphor of sight for knowing and the immediacy of shape as the embodiment of eidos (which is translatable as shape or look) would suggest this, and so with the other examples of idea, such as bed. In the slave boy episode, the ﬁrst quesƟon to Meno about the slave boy is, does he speak Greek, while the ﬁrst quesƟon to the boy himself is, “Do you know that a square ﬁgure is like this?” (the drawn ﬁgure in the sand). “Yes.” “Now a square ﬁgure has these lines, four in number, all equal?” “Certainly” (Meno 82c). And they then go on to compare lines and ﬁgures drawn in diﬀerent ways and the sizes of the spaces delimited, etc. The exercise is indeed one in geometry, or

geometrical reasoning, and does have its beginning with recogniƟon of ﬁgures (what is a square, etc.). But the actual beginning of the analysis, the acƟvity of knowing, is in counƟng, however primiƟvely, the sides of the square, in recognizing, however instantaneously, that the ﬁgure before one (in the sand) is indeed a four-sided equilateral one. The examinaƟon then goes on to logismos or calculaƟon of the divisions of the ﬁgure constructed.[4] There is also the act of comparing, and this might be said to be more basic and more general than calculaƟon. Or, one might say that counƟng and calculaƟon are themselves the images or instances of comparison as the more general dialecƟcal essence. In the Meno too, aŌer all, the slave boy episode is meant to illustrate the general noƟon of recollecƟon. If we consider the ﬁgure as known only as it is idenƟﬁed as a square, and that, only through the ﬁrst implicit and then explicit awareness of its equal four-sidedness, then recollecƟon is only a kind of knowledge when it is acƟve analysis, however primiƟve in awareness, as opposed to an image as precogniƟve or aestheƟc.[5] The adult mind may idenƟfy the object, recognize it as a square, though put to aestheƟc uses; the squares of say, the painƟngs of Joseph Albers, and even more so those of a Renaissance painter, are focused on as such, though in a diﬀerent way, and as means to an end. The very young child lumps preƩy much all ﬁgure together, and only later begins to disƟnguish the famous round from square pegs and holes. But this is at that point primiƟve and instant calculaƟon and counƟng, even in the geometrical modes, as opposed to the more obvious counƟng and calculaƟon of discrete units. The key point is that counƟng and calculaƟon here are oﬀered as fundamental, and that they themselves are, in their literal form (the mathemaƟcal), images of comparison and judgment—they are taken up, aŌer all, as what is in common in all the arts, craŌs and sciences and “all modes of thought.” Even the shoemaker and the pastry cook must count and calculate, and more generally, compare and make judgments. In their literal form as simple counƟng—“to disƟnguish one and two, and three”— they correspond to the simple disƟnguishing of this and that, hence the disƟnguishing of the visible in the lower half of the Line. Recall that those in the Cave in chains pass the Ɵme of day noƟng and counƟng the shadows as they pass before them. It is in disƟnguishing what each one is that they

err. And there is some confusion even in their counƟng as to whether x shadow is diﬀerent or new, or simply passing again—much like children who cannot remember if they have counted this one already before or not. Number and calculaƟon in the higher, limited, more technical sense, as mathemaƟcal per se, is of course to be found in the third highest secƟon, as dianoia. And it is in this form that it is recommended as a study that prepares the ruler, consciously turns his soul. But its introducƟon into the conversaƟon here is as helpful in the second level, that of pisƟs—where the training of athletes in war, the soldier-guardians, is at issue. Again, it is the level at which Glaucon lives, and from which Socrates tries to pry him loose, which is relevant. And so the beginning discussion is of number and calculaƟon in its pracƟcal uƟlity. Glaucon docilely listens to Socrates’s joking story about Palamedes, which is supposedly to illustrate the usefulness of calculaƟon and numbering for the art of war. Socrates says that the ﬁgure of Palamedes in the tragedies “shows up Agamemnon every Ɵme as a quite ridiculous general” because “[Palamedes] says that he invented numbers, which men did not know before, then arranged the companies in the camp in Ilium and counted the ships and everything else.” To which Socrates adds, “Agamemnon apparently did not even know how many feet he had, since he did not know how to count. What sort of general do you think that made him?” Glaucon answers solemnly, “A very strange one, in my opinion, if that was true” (522d). Glaucon may or may not get the joke, depending on the tone of his response—I would tend to think not—but he apparently misses the implicaƟon. Agamemnon may not have been the greatest general but he surely knew how to count—so what is the point of the story? It is, in fact, an indicaƟon of where Glaucon’s mind is, and an implicit comment to the reader about the nature of calculaƟon and counƟng. The point is that Palamedes precisely did not “invent numbers” (another calling to account of the poets, and tradiƟon). CounƟng is a natural capacity of everyone, not a craŌ or art to be “invented”—hence what is ridiculous is not Agamemnon’s generalship but the idea that “Agamemnon did not even know how many feet he had.” Of course he did, and if counƟng is thus natural then Palamedes did not “invent” it. Glaucon’s probable cultural acceptance of the contrary is of unreasonable doxa—signiﬁcantly, embedded in a story of the poets —“Palamedes in the tragedies. . .” He takes the story to grant the authority

of the poets as to the usefulness of calculaƟon in war, but not the signiﬁcance of the quip about Palamedes. The truth of the maƩer comes out of Glaucon’s mouth in spite of himself. When asked whether then this study is “necessary for a warrior,” he replies, “More necessary than anything else, if he is to understand anything about marshalling troops, indeed if he is to be a man at all” (522e). But what then precisely is this study, calculaƟon, which “leads to intelligent thought” but which “no one uses correctly”? Socrates begins Glaucon on a search for a criterion not just for calculaƟon, but to “disƟnguish . . . the studies which lead in the direcƟon menƟoned” and asks Glaucon to “observe them along with me and agree or disagree.” Socrates considers the relaƟon of sense impressions to intelligence. SomeƟmes the “decision of percepƟon is suﬃcient, while others certainly summon the help of intelligence to examine them because the sensaƟon does not achieve a sensible result” (523b). Glaucon takes the disƟncƟon to be between the visually clear and disƟnct and what is fuzzy to sense percepƟon: “You are, he said, obviously referring to things appearing in the distance and to shadow painƟng.” To which Socrates replies, “You are not quite geƫng my meaning.” As usual it is Glaucon’s mistakes that are instrucƟve. There is a test for when we are in need, when a capacity and a kind of knowledge or study is called into play, and in such a way that it is seen to “lead us in the direcƟon we menƟoned”—and this test applies not only in the limited case of calculaƟon but will idenƟfy or characterize the other studies as well. The visually fuzzy, any more than a sharp image, does not acƟvely “call for help,” parakalounta, Plato repeats the word several Ɵmes; their vagueness is not provocaƟve, at least not in the way that is useful here, not thought provoking. “They do not call for help, I said, if they do not at the same Ɵme give a contrary impression; I describe those that do as calling for help whenever the sense impression does not point to one thing rather than its opposite, whether its object be near or far” (523c. Cf. Lesher, Saphēneia, 173). The essence, then, of those experiences that will drive us further along is the tension of contrary impressions—the experience not just of ambiguity or vagueness but of possible opposite judgments about the same percepƟon—eis enanƟan aisthēsin hama. Only these are worthy to be called provocaƟve, or calling forth. A visual example of the merely contradictory or ambiguous would be the drawings of Escher.

Here the visual ﬂip-ﬂops, staircases which can be read either as going up or going down etc., are not provocaƟve in the right way; they are not dialecƟcally opposed such that there is ever a resoluƟon possible, a higher point of view from which intelligence may view the opposites and contain them. The example or image that Socrates now introduces, of the three ﬁngers at diﬀerent heights is, by contrast, of this laƩer sort. It is a basic, non-technical calculaƟon. In the ﬁnger example, the one ﬁnger is both taller and shorter, each in a diﬀerent relaƟon, but in Escher’s staircase, the staircase goes both up and down in alternaƟng percepƟons of the same view. The ﬁrst step in Socrates’s account is the comment that each of the ﬁngers presents itself clearly enough, unambiguously, as what it is, as a ﬁnger, regardless of variaƟons in thickness, color, whether in the middle or at the end, etc. “In all this, the soul of the many is not compelled to ask intelligence (noēsis) what a ﬁnger is, for the sense of sight does not indicate that the ﬁnger is the opposite of a ﬁnger” (523d). This is true only at the level of everyday sight, hence the reference to the “soul of the many.” To a biologist, by contrast, the idenƟty of the ﬁnger—just when something is not a ﬁnger, when it is, and what makes it so—is precisely what is “provoked” by the observaƟon (and framework of quesƟons). For the evoluƟonary biologist, the arƟculaƟon of the ﬁn of the fossil ﬁsh Panderichthys, which it used to lean on in shallow water, counts as a rudimentary ﬁnger. Sight and seeing thus provides iniƟally here an unthinking example. Sight, the very thing that had been used to represent the noblest and highest percepƟons in the Sun/Good analogy, is here used for the simplest and most unambiguous, the presentaƟon of the kind of a thing—at least unƟl further noƟce—hence our trust in the visible world. (Cf. 532c where Socrates repeats the asserƟon of sight as the “clearest sense in the body.”) Each instance of sight is clear, clearly of what it is— taller, shorter—intellect is provoked only when we take the two judgments together. In any event, here we are dealing with the very beginnings of the process of intellect’s probing, again non-mathemaƟcal, responses to the world—the bare physical idenƟty of kinds is leŌ alone as evident. We recall that all in the world of pisƟs, in which a ﬁnger is reliably a ﬁnger, receives eventually a reinterpretaƟon when seen and judged from the standpoint of dianoia—our biologist is an example.

The same object may be judged big or small depending on what it is compared to. The idenƟty of the kind, the ﬁnger, is not at stake, but the idenƟty of relaƟonal qualiƟes in the object may be, e.g., relaƟve bigness. One might be tempted to say that some relaƟonal qualiƟes are subjecƟve as contrasted, for example, to specifying density or length i.e., sense impressions and comparisons of the perceiver. But whatever truth there might be to that is not Plato’s concern here. Rather, each sense, including sight, is capable of presenƟng the tension of contradicƟon that will provoke intelligence. Because each sense is capable of perceiving the opposite quality in a parƟcular instance, for the same thing perceived, unawares it places the perceived object in an ambiguous posiƟon. Every staircase, for example, does in fact go both up and down; the relaƟvely minor tension between them can be resolved and uniﬁed by giving each direcƟon its context (e.g., social rules, signs, etc.) and understanding that the same staircase can serve through both contexts. But in the case of Escher’s staircase the fascinaƟon of it is in our awareness that the tension is permanent—the two contexts are irreconcilable, are in fact the same context—the person walking up is at the same Ɵme walking down (or sideways). For Plato in our present context, the idenƟty or unity of the sense object is not in fact what is at stake here, but rather the intelligibility of the quality applied to it. “Does not each sense behave in the following way: in the ﬁrst place the sense concerned with the hard is of necessity also concerned with the soŌ and it declares to the soul that it perceives the same object to be both hard and soŌ” (524a). The sense personiﬁed is not all that troubled, while thus confronted with conﬂicƟng decisions of percepƟon the soul becomes “puzzled,” Socrates says, not about the thing perceived, but about the “meaning of the light and heavy, if sense percepƟon indicates that what is light is also heavy, and what is heavy is also light. . . . Then, in those cases, the soul is puzzled as to what this percepƟon means by hard, if it says the same thing is also soŌ.” At issue then is the intelligibility of heavy if the same thing can be considered both heavy and light, both hard and soŌ. (The same moƟon, that of seeking the resoluƟon of contradicƟon, is contained in dialecƟc, hence the danger of its perversion in misologos and sophistry.) The point of Plato’s argument is in the direcƟon that it takes here. Obviously there are many ways to

respond to percepƟons. Plato is considering just which experiences of percepƟon will provide the ground for the turning of the soul from becoming towards being, and this because he sees these as parallel to the disƟncƟon between opinion and knowledge. But the sense of becoming is not limited to the sense world—it is the term for the realm of all doxa, of all contradicƟon (actual or potenƟal). It is rather a natural example for this argument to start with a case of supposed opposing sense impressions, hence conﬂicƟng doxai (or rather contradictory judgments provoked in one sense impression). The direcƟon of the argument is to resolve this conﬂict by focusing on the problem of idenƟty, and opƟng for the preservaƟon of the self-idenƟty of the quality, rather than the idenƟty of the object qualiﬁed by opposing predicates. This soluƟon is to provide the “springboard to the Ideas.” The principle that only the self-idenƟcal is ulƟmately intelligible is here presented in a sense as a choice, that is, amounƟng in eﬀect to the denial that the sensible can form an intelligible unity precisely because it is subject to contrary predicates. For there is of course the rejoinder that the contradicƟon “x is taller than y but shorter than z,” is only apparent, since each is in a separate relaƟon. But since Plato actually carefully states the principle of idenƟty with this same qualiﬁcaƟon earlier, at 436e[6] we must ask why he would not employ it here—since the answer cannot be that he was not aware of it.[7] The answer is that the relaƟonal aspect of sensibles holds saƟsfactory for the self-idenƟty of each relaƟon, even while it remains problemaƟc for the unity of the subject that enters into these relaƟons. QualiƟes themselves, and other Ideas, do have relaƟons as part of their own idenƟty, and are thus in a sense a mulƟplicity to be dealt with. But the direcƟon here is to single out Ideas at all, to disƟnguish them from sensibles that are their temporary and ﬂuctuaƟng referents. The Republic does not deal, at least explicitly, with the behavior and complex idenƟty of the Ideas—its topic being the soul in relaƟon to them. We return to the case at hand, the consideraƟon of the funcƟon of calculaƟon and the judgment of qualiƟes: It is likely then that in these cases the soul will aƩempt, by calling upon calculaƟon and intelligence [logismon te kai noēsin], to examine

whether each of the things announced to it is one or two. —Of course. Then if they appear to be two, each appears as diﬀerent and one. —Yes. If each is one, while both are two, it will think of the two as separate, for if they were not separate, it would not be thinking of them as two, but as one. (524b-c) Here, from the last sentence, it is clear that the argument is focused on the disƟncƟon and intelligibility of the two qualiƟes, e.g., tall/short, and that it is the act of thinking of them as separate that demonstrates, at this stage, their independent being or idenƟty—for if they were not indeed separate we would not be able to conceive of them as two—“for if they were not separate, it would not be thinking of them as two, but as one.” The ability to use a name or term at all, and to intend diﬀerent qualiƟes by diﬀerent terms (and the same by the same) is a reﬂecƟon of the intellect’s response to at least the appearance of sameness and diﬀerence in the world (primarily the visible world at this point). It is more an argument about intellect and intenƟonality (though clearly not enƟrely so) at this point. What is important is the one or two of the qualiƟes and not of the subject, which quickly drops out of the picture. The funcƟon of opposites here is to focus the intellect, through their paired opposiƟon in the sensible world in one thing, on precisely the radical separaƟon of them with regard to intelligence, and, it is argued, hence being. The argument, such as it is, is that such tensions of contradicƟon, of opposites, call forth through the puzzlement they provoke the only resoluƟon that intellect is capable of—namely, leaving the sensibles behind for the moment and rising to the self-idenƟcal qualiƟes themselves; that only so can the terms we use in describing have any meaning.[8] Whether we ever return to these sensibles for a resoluƟon at their level (or rather, in their world) is doubƞul. But since the whole enterprise is eventually directed at resolving the conﬂicts of doxa, speciﬁcally about jusƟce and happiness and the soul,

by replacing doxa with knowledge, there must be a return from the Ideas that does deal with these sorts of objects of opinion—the sensibles of doxa in the realm of human acƟon.[9] At any rate, the disƟncƟons here are in terms of the visible as represenƟng the realm of opposiƟon and doxa, as contrasted to the stable world of intelligence, here in isolaƟon or at least in retreat from the sensible. “But we say that the sense of sight saw big and small not as separate but as commingled. Is that not so?” “Yes.” “So in order to clarify this, intelligence is compelled to see big and small not as commingled but as separate, the opposite way from sight” (524c). And from this we are to move from a consideraƟon of the original percepƟon, of an object, to a consideraƟon of the nature of the meaning, and source, of the concepts that percepƟon contradictorily applies: “And it is from some such circumstances that it ﬁrst occurs to us to ask ‘What is the nature of bigness, and again of smallness?’ And so we called the one intelligible and the other visible.” Socrates then shiŌs to a consideraƟon of something a further step removed from the visible (as indicated by Glaucon’s hesitaƟon), that is, to a consideraƟon of “number and unit,” which are, as contrasted to say tall and soŌ, non-visible images. He turns, that is, to our use of these in eideƟc image-making. The earlier quesƟon, whether the qualiƟes are “one or two” implicates number and counƟng, but not yet, as here, in an overt consideraƟon of number itself and its order in itself, i.e., arithmeƟc. In the previous operaƟon we were disƟnguishing the qualiƟes as either one or two, as presented ﬁrst to percepƟon and, as a result of conﬂicƟng judgments, considered in themselves “not as commingled but as separate, the opposite way from sight.” In the consideraƟon of number and unit Socrates urges Glaucon to “reason it out from what was said before.” Unit and number are to be put to the same tests as in the case of the comparison of ﬁngers example of bigness and smallness, i.e., by the provocaƟon of intellect in conﬂicƟng judgments of percepƟon. But unit and number are already somewhat more removed from immediate sensaƟon. The ﬁngers appear immediately fat or thin, taller or shorter; though comparison is necessary, it is more direct, more natural from the point of view of sense experience than counƟng, which employs a device that is

natural in a diﬀerent sense—natural to intellect. Perhaps this accounts for Glaucon’s diﬃculty in extending the previous example of the comparison of ﬁngers. The quesƟon asked is, to which of the two groups do number and the unit belong, those that provoke thought by aﬀecƟng the senses in contrary ways at the same Ɵme or those which do not. In this elencƟc invitaƟon to a dialecƟcal sorƟng, Glaucon is “unable to decide.” Socrates’s explicaƟon is as follows: If the unit in and of itself is adequately seen or perceived by any other sense, then, as we were saying in the case of the ﬁngers, it would not draw one towards reality. If, however, something contrary to it is always seen at the same Ɵme so that it does not appear to be one more than the opposite, it would stand in need of a judge. The soul would then be at a loss, search for an answer, sƟr up intelligence within itself, and ask what is the nature of the unit in itself, and so the study of the unit would be one which leads the soul and turns it toward the contemplaƟon of reality.[10] (524d) Glaucon’s reply is odd, especially considering that he did not know which group to place unit in: “Certainly, he said, the sight of the unit possesses this characterisƟc to a remarkable degree, for we see the same object to be both one and an inﬁnite number [hōs hen . . . hōs apeira to plethōs]” (525a). Probably what Glaucon has in mind is that any physical unit is also inﬁnitely divisible into parts. This is not true of natural parts, like the limbs of a man or the segments of an orange, but perhaps Glaucon is thinking of unit as the unit of spaƟal extension in general, hence not as natural points of division. The framework just given by Socrates was, by extension from the example of the ﬁngers, whether “the unit, in and by itself, is adequately seen or perceived by any other sense . . . (or) something contrary to it is always seen at the same Ɵme so that it does not appear to be more than the opposite.” It would seem then that the percepƟon of the unit itself is a kind of aisthēsis—at least analogously. Glaucon quite literally says the sight of it. The inﬁnite divisibility of sensible units could “provoke” if one thought about it. ConsideraƟon of the tensions of number, the unit per se as concerns arithmeƟc and not the countable of sense, goes on at the level of dianoia,

the third level. But these contraries at the level of dianoia, where one is “at a loss,” result in a movement to “search for an answer, sƟr up intelligence within itself, and ask what the nature of the unit in itself is” at a higher level, that of noēsis, where the nature of unity itself is considered, of which the unit of arithmeƟc is one, rather pure, example. But these consideraƟons can result, it would seem, either directly from a consideraƟon of arithmeƟc or of the one/many composites of the sense and social world. In either case the quesƟon of the nature of the unit is beyond the level of dianoia, of arithmeƟc and poliƟcal science for example, within which the unit is assumed. The higher quesƟon can be conceived either as restricted to the foundaƟons of mathemaƟcs, the unit of arithmeƟc, or, the larger quesƟon in a sense, of the nature of unity such that the uniƟes of the world of appearances can be accounted for, those of the social world, the soul and the city, wherein acƟon is the sensible that results in a unity out of many.[11] Here, Glaucon considers with Socrates only the unity of arithmeƟc and hence the usefulness of it as a study to lead one to the truth—but the applicaƟon is sƟll concrete enough to support Glaucon in his understanding of the ongoing analogy of the inner (personal) and outer ciƟes. “They [calculaƟon and arithmeƟc] would then belong it seems to the studies we seek. The warrior must learn to marshal his troops, and also the philosopher because he must emerge from the world of becoming and grasp reality, or never be a raƟonal thinker. … And our guardian must be both a warrior and a philosopher” (525b). The philosopher must also learn to “marshal his troops” if he is to be able to turn ﬁrst his own soul and then those of others; and the study of arithmeƟc, that is, of counƟng and calculaƟon, is recommended on two grounds.[12] First, it is an acƟvity which in itself turns one from preoccupaƟon and pleasure with the sensible and doxa, to pleasure and preoccupaƟon with the non-visible and knowledge.
