But secondly, and as important if not more so, is the occasion that it gives for intelligence to be forced by the contraries of both arithmeƟc itself and calculaƟon in applicaƟon to the visible world to consider the nature of number and the unit—and it is in this service that it is of parƟcular value. The unit itself is indivisible, but the other numbers are both a unity and each made up of, and divisible into, a sum of ones/units and a sum of parts—a one as the

ﬁŌh numeral yet a many as composed of units. Five is both ﬁve ones and three plus two, etc. (the Greeks did not use fracƟons, rather raƟos). Just as the virtues were considered in a diﬀerent light to the end of reforming or retraining the soul to a new deﬁniƟon of jusƟce, so here, the study of arithmeƟc is appropriated to diﬀerent ends and considered in a diﬀerent light: its ability to train the soul, to turn it, and as a beginning point for dialecƟc in the driving of the soul upward to consider “by pure thought the contemplaƟon of the nature of numbers.” The dynamic of the Line is here illustrated again as a forcing (as in the Cave) of the acƟvity of intellect from one level, that of dianoia, to a higher one, noēsis, when confronted by a contradicƟon, whose resoluƟon is sought perforce at a higher level, in this case, just how the one can be a kind of many. The nature of unity allows for it to be both many and one if the parƟcular kind of manyness that is part-whole is considered. This is not the case with tall-short, which are never a unity though they are a pair. The one ﬁnger is subject to both tall and short, though always in diﬀerent relaƟons; otherwise the intelligibility of each contrary would not be maintained in its self-idenƟty, which was to be the case, hence to lead to the study of the nature of each. But in the case of unit and unity and certainly the other numbers (“every number has it too”) in counƟng, the quality of divisibility is a kind of unity that is co-extensive with the self- idenƟty, and they thus contain the tension within them—and in this way like the ﬁnger—but do so in a way that is essenƟal to the nature of number, and that tallness is not to ﬁnger. A ﬁnger must be of a certain height, while whether it is tall or short depends on the external relaƟon. In one crucial sense the unit must be indivisible in itself, and only that to which it is applied, whether to sensibles or to a number as one speciﬁed aggregate of units, is a one out of many. But one and many, the number two and its divisibility, its composiƟon of units, though co-extensive, are logically disƟnct, and it is the quesƟoning intellect that is forced to go beyond this to consider the nature of number and of unit/unity to see how this can be so. An easing away from the literal level of the discussion of the advantages of the studies is apparent in the irony in Socrates’s tone and the coupling in one sentence: this study will not be pursued “for the sake of buying and selling like merchants, but both for the sake of war and to aƩain ease in turning the soul itself from the world of becoming to truth

and reality” (525c). Yet war is clearly as pracƟcal a use as that of “buying and selling” unless we remind ourselves, as we are meant to here, that the “war” of the guardian who is “both warrior and philosopher” (525b) is only an image, by now well inverted, of the inner war of the soul with itself, hence the real necessity of “turning the soul itself from the world of becoming to truth and reality.”[13] In sum, the soul in this study “does not allow one to discuss them [numbers themselves] by presenƟng numbers with visible and touchable bodies.” The characterisƟc selected to illustrate this prohibiƟon against the introducƟon of “visible and touchable bodies” in the study of calculaƟon, as would be the case in illustraƟons drawn from the “buying and selling like merchants and retailers,” is the indivisibility of the arithmeƟcal unit. Socrates menƟons “experts in these maƩers” as thwarƟng any aƩempt to “divide the unit up in argument”—the experts in logismoi are, then, models in their behavior, which is to preserve the wholeness of the unit. “If someone tries to divide the unit in argument [they] laugh at him and do not allow it; if you divide it, they mulƟply, taking care that the unit should never appear to be many parts and not one” (525e). The ironic use of temnō for “divide” stresses the intended contrast with those physical units that can be physically cut up in pieces, like a butcher cuts up an animal, though through this literal meaning one also arrives at the ﬁguraƟve one, to cut or draw a line. In the Phaedrus the cuƫng up of an argument properly as precisely compared to the butcher’s art in speech is cited as the sign of the proper use of dialecƟc in the pursuit of ontological reality (Phaedr.265e, cf. Parmen. 129ﬀ.). There is a kind of one in many amongst the forms in the idenƟty comprised or composed in their complex relaƟons, and in the operaƟons of dialecƟc in the pursuit of analysis, and at the lowest level in the physical divisibility of bodies. Thus the unit per se (as contrasted to the divisibility of numbers), that of the expert or arithmeƟcian, is an important special case—the unit of numbers, illustrates, as does the zeal of the arithmeƟcian, the indivisibility of a whole; in the case of numbers this means a unit without parts, but in the case of other uniƟes the whole is a complex one, in which what is important is the indivisibility or unity of an Idea in its idenƟty or jusƟﬁable wholeness. In a system like that of Greek mathemaƟcs where there are no

fracƟons, the role being played by whole number raƟos, there is a ready- made contrast available between the physically divisible and the indivisibility of the numerical unit. When a geometrical ﬁgure is constructed and, say, divided or cut up—as in the case of Plato’s Line image —the comparison of lengths is always carried out in terms of the commensurability of the lengths described as raƟos. Hence the incommensurability of the hypotenuse of a (right) triangle can be described by appeal to the raƟo of the (commensurable) opposite sides. The singleness of unity extends beyond the arithmeƟcal form to that of unity itself (the study of which is indicated by the introducƟon of arithmeƟc as the ﬁrst study). The concept of unity itself, which has broader applicaƟon than the unit of arithmeƟc, is of something whole and indivisible, though not in the same sense as arithmeƟcally indivisible—the Idea of unity has no parts itself but is capable of applying to things that do. What it says, or is employed to say, about such things is that they are a whole in some sense, and thus though the whole that partakes of this parƟcular Idea may have other separable parts (even as another Idea) the Idea of wholeness itself does not (though it has relaƟons to other Ideas). Its whole content is ﬁlled up with the idea of unity. Of the applicaƟon or parƟcipaƟon of unity in the sensible this is clear, and we may include other uniƟes that are sensible in the larger sense that we have been arguing for —those in the realm of space, Ɵme and human acƟon and passion—hence the city and the soul. How and whether this applies to Ideas themselves and the relaƟons among them is a more diﬃcult quesƟon. But an organic or natural unity is divisible because of its unity while a merely physical unity is divisible arbitrarily—it can be cut up into arbitrary pieces and is an image of all arbitrary divisions. It is thus the task of dialecƟc to disƟnguish true from false uniƟes, and hence precisely to see just where a unity can be divisible naturally. But we also ought not to confuse arithmeƟcians with dialecƟcians— the former take number, and the unit, and claim or maintain it to be as here described, hence as hypotheses; while these are to be examined and here expanded by the dialecƟcian, who examines the nature of unity, and of the one-many relaƟon, prompted by the tensions of one-many in numbers themselves and in the unit in its applicaƟon. As Grube points out in a note to his translaƟon (178, note 8) the skill of those at issue here,

calculaƟon, or logisƟkos is the same term used “for the highest of the three parts of the soul, the reasoning part,” to logisƟkon at 439ﬀ. Hence Socrates’s statement that “those who are good at calculaƟon are, one might say, naturally sharp in every other study.” But Grube concludes, wrongly I think, that “because of this double meaning the statement that the man who is good at arithmeƟc is good at every other study is less startling in Greek, and this ﬁts in with Plato’s mathemaƟcal approach.” Rather it seems clear (on the basis of the text here at least), that an arithmeƟcian is not yet asking the right quesƟons about the enterprise. He falls short, to use the quasi-mathemaƟcal term that Socrates employs ironically elsewhere. ArithmeƟc in itself only serves as a training and turning of the soul, and then only when properly directed. Secondly, the mathemaƟcal is used here as the clearest image of the more general sense of calculaƟon—of the soul’s ability to take the right measure of something, hence an example of the percepƟon by intellect of the stable non-visible. This is not say that the contents of the other non-visibles, or the method of perceiving them, are themselves mathemaƟcal in any convenƟonal sense, even as objects of dianoia. It is an example, but one with a unique ontological and propaedeuƟc status. If anything, just the reverse is suggested, since the images employed by the arithmeƟcian/expert and his studies are oﬀered here by Socrates precisely as images, examples, and are seen as such by the dialecƟcian, in contrast to the expert—who conƟnues to be saƟsﬁed with life at the level of hypothesis and the limited realm of dianoia and its objects (the Ideas as hypotheses is another story). One such expert is Theodorus in the Theaetetus. Though his hold on his experƟse is of course much more like knowledge than his acquaintance with Heracleitean views of nature, more systemaƟc and explanatory, it is sƟll doxa as regards its starƟng points; and Theodorus is iniƟally both unaware and unperturbed by any contradicƟon or tension between the pracƟce of mathemaƟcs and his views of nature. The complexiƟes of the relaƟon of the dianoeƟc technē of arithmeƟc to its funcƟon as a model for noēsis, and the special signiﬁcance for Plato of numbers, the numerable, and of that singularly human capacity for counƟng, hence for separaƟng and collecƟng—are all dealt with in careful detail by Jacob Klein in Greek MathemaƟcal Thought and the Origin of Algebra (cited above, n.13). My own discussion is in part sƟmulated by his

analysis. The argument of the book goes beyond the central chapters on Plato, since the overall subject is rather the diﬀerence between ancients and moderns, as seen through the ontological shiŌ in the percepƟon of number. The following comment will be seen as more relevant aŌer the issue of separaƟon (chōrismos) is dealt with in the next chapter, on the Phaedo. By arithmeƟc Plato does not mean the skills of addiƟon, subtracƟon, etc. These would hardly be a newly acquired knowledge for the philosopher. But neither is the Greek study of arithmeƟc the theory of numbers in the modern sense. As Klein points out, the convenƟonal Greek understanding of arithmeƟc was the study of numbers themselves—the aƩempt to say what they are—which means in eﬀect to deﬁne them, limit them, as to their kinds. Plato’s advance on this is to examine, as the Line suggests, what are the presupposiƟons or hypotheses of both counƟng (calculaƟon of) things, either in the sense world or units as monads, and the presupposiƟon of number itself and its divisions (e.g., into odd and even). That is, by examining how they are to be deﬁned we are forced to look at what it is about them that makes them knowable—the ontological precondiƟons that are behind their use by the knower, their behavior in their pure relaƟons and in the wholes that are formed. The nature and funcƟon of the unit in parƟcular is fundamental and points the direcƟon for a resoluƟon, or at least the context, of the general problem of the one and the many. Concerning the inƟmate relaƟon between mathemaƟcs and Greek ontology in general, Klein suggests that “mathemaƟcal truths as mathēmata, i.e., as things ‘to be learned’ serves as a model for all teachable and learnable knowledge, and it is knowledge so understood which determines the sphere of Greek ontological inquiry” (61). His study is “an aƩempt to discover the basic presupposiƟons of Greek arithmeƟc and the ontological arguments connected with it within the structure of the arithmos concept itself” (62). He stresses that “Greek scienƟﬁc arithmeƟc and logisƟc are founded on a ‘natural’ aƫtude to everything countable as we meet it in life. . . . The peculiarity of the Greek concept of ‘number’ lies therefore less in an ‘archaic’ [Becker] or ‘intuiƟve’ [Stenzel] character (which is not at all its primary property) than in the kind of relaƟon it has to the ‘thing’ it intends” (63). “For Plato generic idenƟty is the ulƟmate foundaƟon of all possible unity,” and the basis of Aristotle’s

aƩack on the chōrismos thesis as not explaining the relaƟon of eidos to sensibles. (105 ﬀ.) CalculaƟon (logismos) can rely on the natural arƟculaƟon and original source of delimitaƟon, but the pure monads of arithmeƟc are by deﬁniƟon indivisible, thus absolute. “In this sense the ‘one’ (or the one thing subjected to counƟng) makes counƟng and thus ‘counƟng number’ possible: In this sense it takes precedence over number and may be called its archē. The priority of one over number does not follow from a relaƟonship of superiority of genus over species but rather from the character of one as ‘measure.’. . . We comprehend a number as one because we do our counƟng over one and the same thing, because our eyes remain ﬁxed on one and the same thing” (108). But dianoia never considers “single being as such” rather always a “relaƟonal series of beings such that the members of this series are carefully disƟnguished from, and thus simultaneously related to, each other” (76). Dianoia cannot come to face with the one itself, since it is always dealing with it through a mulƟtude, “because, although it is directed to noēta it nevertheless always remains related to that aisthēsis which ﬁrst ‘called upon it’ to clarify an obscure state of aﬀairs,” (78) that is, of contrariety (enanƟon). What dianoia can do is “replace the more and less, which always aƩaches to the realm of aisthēta by the exact relaƟons of numbers, thereby accomplishing the most important step toward gaining that true epistēmē which no longer has any use for aisthēsis and whose object is the realm of those other noēta which ascend to something ‘unsupposed.’ But the dianoia itself is not able to appreciate the full range of signiﬁcance of its accomplishment, because its own noēta, which it ‘supposes’ to underlie the aisthēta, appear altogether lucid and without further need of foundaƟon” (79). There is an opposiƟon in appearances that is provisionally reconciled by the implicit hypothesis of the eidē. But the how of this is beyond the capacity of dianoia. Number, numbering, counƟng provide the pre-eminent example and model that this is possible. It lies between the sensible—to which it can be applied, from which it can be separated and from which it arises (but which is not its cause)—and that which is above it, to which reﬂecƟon on its relaƟons points.[14] TURNING FROM THE VISIBLE: THE PHILOSOPHICAL USE OF THE STUDIES

I have spent so much Ɵme on what is just the ﬁrst of the studies because I think it has far-reaching importance, in spite of the limited and literal context in which calculaƟon is here presented in the text. The funcƟon of arithmeƟc and calculaƟon in the more limited sense is of course itself a preparaƟon—since it reveals itself as presupposing nonsensual monadic units, which turn us, when properly studied or reﬂected on (an issue with all of the preparatory studies), away from the sensible numbers of aggregates to the eidē. But to fully explore the meaning of unity, of calculaƟon as taking the right measure, and the issues here raised, would take us further into the nature of the Ideas than we can go here. I have at this point only wished to stress that we are dealing with an acƟvity as an image. Let us recall that the idea of right measure, the right metron, was to be key to our understanding of the applicaƟon of the ideal city analogy to the healthy soul—and so the capacity for arithmos and logismos, is crucial. The selecƟon of the studies, and to a certain extent the ordering, follows the convenƟons.[15] It is interesƟng however that although calculaƟon is ﬁrst in the studies, it is described as already compelling “the soul to use intelligence alone to discover the truth” (526b) while geometry and astronomy, which follow it, seem more to be linked to visible images, both in their iniƟal objects and to the construcƟons of mathemaƟcal imaginaƟon in the actual pracƟce of their respecƟve calculaƟons, as contrasted to the non-visual ﬁeld of arithmeƟc. The link is misleading of course, as Glaucon’s comments regarding both the study and uƟlity of astronomy in parƟcular show. In a sense, as we shall see, the six studies before dialecƟc—arithmeƟc and calculaƟon (worth keeping separate as number and counƟng), geometry, stereometry, astronomy, and harmonics —are arranged in inverse order with regard to their physicality: from number, which would be by tradiƟon ostensibly the least overtly physical, to harmonics, which is the raƟo of the sensed, that is, observed, vibraƟon of strings. But when seen in their proper perspecƟve, so to speak, we begin with the most concretely linked, the most elemental and consƟtuƟve of our image relaƟon to the world of experience, numbering, and rise to the most abstract study, divine harmonics. The turning of the soul from the visible/sensible to the non-visible/intelligible is the reversing or inverƟng of the convenƟonal percepƟon of each study, if not of their sequence. Thus,

as with the civic virtues earlier, which were taken over from the convenƟonal list, both cases are given a diﬀerent interpretaƟon and a diﬀerent purpose. This may be said to parallel the dual nature of the guardian-philosopher, evident throughout, and represented here by the dual task of the studies, that they be useful in both war and in themselves, i.e., for philosophy. The warrior-philosopher disƟncƟon, as already noted, must also be read as an image, and so we get war as a metaphor for the prevenƟon, or the quelling, of civil strife in both the ideal public polis and the community of the soul itself. The warrior/guardian-philosopher image also serves as an image for the visible/non-visible disƟncƟon, and the division of doxa and epistēmē; the laws as laid down for the polis are doxa, as contrasted to the inner comprehension of their ground and necessity. But doxa and the war is leŌ behind, as Glaucon is with some diﬃculty progressively weaned, at least temporarily, from the pracƟcal-external, i.e., doxasƟc level of his understanding of the uƟlity of these studies. Since the turning of the soul is arduous and the result of the actual pracƟce of the right study of these subjects, and Glaucon gets the point with diﬃculty, if at all, in theory alone, it is thus to be expected that his turning is a halƟng and ﬂeeƟng one. The studies are of course pracƟcal, but not in the sense he aƩributes. Their pracƟcality lies in their ability to turn the soul, and in the superiority of the warrior equipped with knowledge of what is (and what is not) on his return to the world of pracƟcal acƟon. Again, the order of the studies, the ascending order of apparent physicality (from number, through ﬁgure, to the vibraƟons of strings, etc.) of each study must be seen in its true nature as inversely and increasingly not this at all but rather intelligible, and serve in this way to increasingly wean the soul of its doxalogical dependence on the sensible, both by the contents of the studies and the way in which they are taken up, i.e., seen as not what they at ﬁrst appear to be. CounƟng, however, is sƟll ﬁrst as primary, essenƟal in the way we have suggested, and also as the most primiƟve, and in one sense the most physical of intellectual operaƟons— separaƟng and uniƟng the physical thises and thats. Socrates also says of calculaƟon that he does not “think that you will ﬁnd studies which give more trouble to the pracƟcing pupil, or not many of them” (526c). It is hard to know what to make of this unless he means: a) the labors of the beginning young student; b) the larger sense of calculaƟon, when it

becomes in eﬀect dialecƟc, the “right measure” of much more than the nature and objects of number, since “those who are by nature good at calculaƟon are, as one might say, naturally sharp in every other study. . .” (526b, c) that considered rightly in its contrariety (regarding the nature of unit, etc.) it forces the soul upward by necessity (a term repeated oŌen) to use the intellect alone to reach the truth. Preserving the image of calculaƟng and ordering, Socrates then says, “let that then be one of our studies [literally, ‘Let this one be so placed or situated for us’]. In the second place let us look at that which is next to it” (526c). Glaucon, in response, suggests geometry, adding that “In so far as it pertains to war, it is obviously suitable. As regards encampments, occupaƟons of posiƟons . . . etc., being a geometer or not makes all the diﬀerence to a man.” It is clear what level Glaucon is sƟll operaƟng on. Socrates’s rejoinder, with perhaps a slight suggesƟon of impaƟence, is, “Yes, but for those purposes even a small amount of geometry and calculaƟon would suﬃce. We must examine whether the greater porƟon of it which is more advanced tends to make it easier to see the Form of the Good.” The use of “small amount” and “greater porƟon” is perhaps a poke at Glaucon’s literal mindedness for the reader. But it is not only the quanƟty or degree of study that is missing from Glaucon’s vision but rather the purposes of these higher studies. “All things tend in that direcƟon which compel the soul [anankazei] to turn itself towards the place in which the most blessed part [to eudaimonestaton] of reality exists, which the soul must see at any cost. . . . Therefore if it compels the soul to contemplate reality it is suitable, if to see only what comes to be, it is not” (526e). To which Glaucon replies, “So we have said.” Since Glaucon is sƟll not clear on what exactly is going on, Socrates conƟnues by, as in the case of arithmeƟc, poinƟng to a contradicƟon or tension which, when noted and properly considered, will hopefully point Glaucon (and the reader more likely) in the right direcƟon. “No one who has even a liƩle experience of geometry will dispute that the science itself contradicts the expressions used by those who pracƟce it” (527a). This Ɵme the contradicƟon is not in the maƩer itself (though it can also be found there) as was the case with number and the unit, but rather, Socrates says, in the way geometers talk about the acƟvity of geometry, that is, the nature of the discourse they must use in the acƟvity itself.

“They use ridiculous terms, and indeed it must be so. They speak like men of acƟon and all their words point to acƟons. They talk of ‘squaring’ and ‘applying’ and ‘adding’ and do so throughout, whereas the whole study is pursued for the sake of knowledge” (527a). Though a feature of their discourse, contradicƟon is inherent here too since, as Socrates says, it is in the very nature of geometry, in the acƟvity, that they use such terms: “they must do so.” Not that the geometer does not see the diﬀerence between digging a square hole and construcƟng a square on the side of a mathemaƟcal triangle, he knows that his acƟons do not occur in physical space and Ɵme—and that the side contains the square upon it, determines its area absolutely quite independently of the acƟvity of the geometer. But the construcƟon is a necessary acƟvity of the geometer in order for him to see or release this knowledge[16] —and it is combined with the drawing out of the implicaƟons of the relaƟons of the ﬁgure (original and manipulated), which as raƟonal relaƟons are neither visible nor constructed (with the possible excepƟon of congruence, though even here we can disƟnguish between the fact of congruence, the construcƟon of it, and the judgment of it and the consequences (Cf. Theat. 186d-187a). Thus, though the ﬁgures themselves do not possess this contradicƟon, being themselves ﬁxed, there is a necessary contradicƟon between the acƟvity of the geometrical imaginaƟon and the ﬁxity of the ﬁgures.[17] The terminology of acƟon is a verbal image and is “ridiculous” in this context, if necessary. But the reason it is ridiculous yet necessary, the cause and signiﬁcance of this necessity, is hidden from the geometer, who knows perfectly well that his objects are not subject to “birth and destrucƟon.” What he does not know is the ulƟmate signiﬁcance of the diﬀerence, and how the acƟvity of the knowing mind, its dianoeƟc eikasia, its capacity to reconstruct knowledge, in this case geometrical, is itself only an image in acƟvity of the truth of objects themselves. Of course another reason for Socrates’s saying that they “speak like men of acƟon” is that Glaucon has just confounded the true nature of the acƟvity (and its purpose in this context) precisely with the pracƟcal uses of geometry “as it pertains to war.” Hence we are meant to contrast such “men of acƟon” and those who “speak like men of acƟon,” the geometers. The geometer, like the poet/philosopher, creates in words, in images, but

more real ones than those acƟons of the geometer-generals (both more real acƟons and more real ﬁgures created), whose ﬁgures on the baƩleﬁeld “come to birth and [are] destroyed.” Not that the square formaƟon on the baƩleﬁeld is any less a square than that on the geometer’s chalkboard (or the converse)! But the one in the general’s mind is had as doxa (Alexander etc. excepted), put to work in the ﬁeld, while the square in the geometer’s mind is possessed as epistēmē put to work in the theorem. Glaucon mouths the convenƟonal wisdom that the study of geometry is “pursued for the sake of knowledge,” and that this is, as he argues, “knowledge that exists forever,” as contrasted to “knowledge of that which at some Ɵme comes to birth and is destroyed.” But Plato would claim that the laƩer is not, in fact, even suscepƟble to knowledge—and we know from the next discussion that Glaucon does not really understand what is meant by the permanent versus the changeable. Astronomy is praised ﬁrst by Glaucon as useful to the “farmer and navigator, but no less the general.” To which Socrates replies, “You amuse me, you are so like a man who is afraid of appearing to the many to prescribe useless studies” (527d). But clearly this is generous; it is not just that he is “afraid of appearing to the many” etc. but he really does not understand himself the diﬀerence, as the following discussion shows him sƟll struggling. For astronomy is next praised by him as physically turning us towards the “eternals” in the heavens (see earlier discussion). It is only the disƟncƟon between the pracƟcal and the theoreƟcal as rightly understood, between doxa and epistēmē, epistēmē as the image of being and the measure of jusƟce and happiness, that eventually provides the answer to his quesƟon regarding the just and unjust life. Hence this study properly conducted will “draw the soul toward truth and produce philosophic thought”; again, conspicuously it is the awareness of necessary contradicƟon which forces the intellect to a higher level and, so considered, will “make us direct upward those parts of ourselves which we now direct downward when we should not” (527b). Shorey stresses the importance of a “sharp disƟncƟon between mathemaƟcs and dialecƟc,” and that Plato “aﬃrm(s) the general inferiority of the mathemaƟcal method (i.e., that it deals with hypotheses) and the intermediate posiƟon for educaƟon of mathemaƟcs as a propaedeuƟc to dialecƟcs.”[18] But just

how is it “propaedeuƟc”? Here it would seem rather important to see how mathemaƟcs when seen correctly is itself dialecƟcal in its applicaƟon. If it is to be truly propaedeuƟc it must have some essenƟal features in common with dialecƟc and further, as we have shown, be seen as revealing certain tensions or contradicƟons or contraries which drive one to a higher kind of thinking, hence the dynamic of the Line is not only of levels but dynamic interrelaƟon. These tensions or contradicƟons are present but unconsciously so, dianoia lives with them; they only serve as the conscious sƟmulus for upward moƟon when “studied rightly” with this purpose. Concerning astronomy then, we should not confuse its higher purpose with what are its pracƟcal side beneﬁts (from the present standpoint) and even its beneﬁt “with regard to all other studies,” though this helps to recommend it generally. Astronomy properly studied, the science of the laws of heavenly moƟon, turns one’s gaze upward intellectually, inward, and hence the opposite of the “stargazing” (in Socrates’s mocking words) that Glaucon proposes. Here the tension or contradicƟon is between the visible upward gaze at the immediate object of study, the heavenly bodies, and the downward and inward gaze of the mathemaƟcal astronomer whereby “the embroidery of the sky [serves] as models in the study of those other things,” the “moƟons by which true speed and true number and true shapes, both in relaƟon to each other and carrying along what these true shapes contain. These things can be perceived by reason and thought, but not by sight” (529d). The study thus results in a cleansing of the organ of sight, preparatory to dialecƟc, hence not (immediately) for the sake of others, as would be the case with astronomy for the farmer and navigator, who would see the present study as useless in itself; but rather here it is carried out for “one’s own sake.”Thus the “true astronomer” will admire the “beauƟful workmanship” of the “movements of the stars,” but even these “fall far short of true existences” since their moƟons, “the relaƟon of night to day, of these to month, and month to year, and of the other stars to these and each other,” are such that “he will consider it strange to believe that they are ever the same and do not deviate at all anywhere, since they are material and visible, and he will undertake, in every way he can, to understand the real truth of these things” (530a). Thus the “material and visible” nature of these, means that even their moƟons and relaƟons are not “ever the same” and hence provide once

again in their diﬀerences, the contradicƟons that sƟr intellect to search for the “real truth of these things,” that is to say, of the concepts brought to bear on them in the study of their relaƟons and the laws of their moƟons. Hence the true way to conceive of the study of astronomy is analogous to that of geometry, through the study of “problems” with regard to the mathemaƟcal relaƟons and the study of their elements, to which the objects themselves only roughly correspond. The study divides into the exercise of the study itself, of the now mathemaƟzed objects, and that of the study that arises out of this, the study of the nature of its elements and laws. “Let us then study by means of problems as we do in geometry and let the things in the sky go, if the study of astronomy is to make the naturally intelligent part of the soul useful instead of useless” (530b). The study of “problems” may be taken to refer to the mathemaƟcal-astronomical studies themselves or to the higher studies. It is not clear if this must be within the mathemaƟcal study, (not the variaƟon of the physical events, since we are to “let the things in the sky go,”) or if it is the study of the variaƟon in the mathemaƟcal ﬁgures (reﬂecƟng the physical variaƟons of moƟon), since Socrates says that the philosophical astronomer will undertake to “understand the real truth of these things,” where “things” refers to the mathemaƟcal models of the relaƟons of night to day, etc., that is, of the physical of which they are more intelligible images or models. One might also be led to ask what the diﬀerence between geometry and astronomy is, once the laƩer has seemingly been made into the study of problems and having let the things in the sky go. However, astronomy even in its mathemaƟcal form, is sƟll the study of relaƟons of relaƟve posiƟon and of moƟon. MoƟon, it is true, that is formalized and absolutely regular, but moƟon nonetheless. And it is as the study of moƟon that it perhaps has the advantage over geometry to drive intellect further to ask about moƟon and rest per se, as well as about “the equal, the double, or any other raƟo,” and again, about same, other, unit, etc. If the moƟons of the heavens are explained with the use of these, even when turning away from the physical representaƟon of them to the representaƟon of them in thought, i.e., on paper and in imaginaƟon, they themselves can become the object of study precisely in the observaƟon of their paradoxical use, as with the acƟons of the calculaƟng arithmeƟcian and geometer—which can

drive one in each case away from the actual ﬁeld of their use, as hypotheses, to the study of the elements.[19] It is worth noƟng as a result that acƟon and moƟon has been introduced at each stage, for each study, in a diﬀerent form. And that the progress from one study to another, while all within the provenance of dianoia (the studies, not the progression and the study of it) is from apparent stasis (numbers) to increasing degrees of moƟon—but moƟons which are each Ɵme revealed as intelligible, inner images as opposed to their outer shell. So, arithmeƟc is dividing up, counƟng, geometers use acƟon words, astronomers study moƟons of the heavenly bodies. In each case this outward moƟon is a reﬂecƟon of an inner moƟon, raƟonally perceived, ending in dialecƟc, moƟon completely freed of its external context, the moƟon of thought itself. That is, it is moƟon in the study of dialecƟc itself, and of its applicaƟon in the understanding of what might be called its pure objects, the elements themselves. By contrast, in the applicaƟon of pre-ontological dialecƟc in the everyday world, the results of its divisions and collecƟons can be physical, sƟll in only a relaƟve sense: the mule standing over there with the horses can be moved to stand with the other mules, though need not be in order for thought to make the disƟncƟon, and so with the unjust man among the just. So it is that Socrates conƟnues, aŌer ﬁnishing with astronomy, that “moƟon is not of one but of several kinds,” and as astronomy is the image that the eyes are “ﬁxed upon” so the sense of hearing is “ﬁxed upon the movements of harmony” (530d). An external physical moƟon or movement, of the vibraƟng string, is opposed to the actual object of study, which is the non-sensible, non-visible image—that of the laws of the relaƟons of tones—the silent mathemaƟcal raƟos between the sounding tones, which give the isolated physical pitch events their idenƟty as tones. [20] The kinship of these sciences is speciﬁcally menƟoned. In astronomy it is natural to look at the physical images in the sky and it is intellect that must turn downward (the inverted physical moƟon again the image of its true meaning). Harmony has its own physical images which are aƩracƟve for the natural imaginaƟon as explanaƟon; those who literally listen closely place the ear before the mind, and imagine that they are measuring—

imaginaƟon, eikasia, is used to generate doxa about the relaƟons of the tones. But there is a second group of people who study harmony wrongly, or in a limited fashion, though implicitly further along than the ﬁrst. These are those who ﬁnd number in the tones and relaƟons, whose images are thus non-visible as contrasted to the percepƟble images or vibraƟons sought by the former group. They are introduced as representaƟve of dianoia, like the mathemaƟcal astronomers, and thus study the laws of the moƟons of the tones—but only to observe them and produce what might rightly be called dianoeƟc doxa. For though dianoia is systemaƟc by nature, there is the danger of mythologizing the system, of turning it into a cause in itself rather than seeking its cause higher. They do not, as does the ﬁrst group of “harmonists,” study “consonances and sounds which they . . . measure against each other and so labor in vain,” rather, the second group measure or calculate the laws—the raƟos of the string lengths, etc. But they turn these, the raƟos or numbers, into causes: “for they seek for numbers in the consonances they hear but do not make their way up to problems to examine which numbers are consonant and which are not, and what is the reason in each case” (531c). Only when these “consonances” and the laws of their moƟon are studied as images rather than themselves, are they “useful,” “in respect to the search for the BeauƟful and the Good, while pursued in a diﬀerent way they are useless” (531c). IMAGES OF DIALECTIC AND THE PROVOCATIONS OF INTELLECT It is the “kinship” of all these studies (and any others) that they are capable of turning the soul from the visible images to the non-visible images that reﬂect intelligibility.[21] In each case the point is to see the model, law, or term not as a cause in itself but as a non-visible image, having its self- idenƟty, meaning or intelligibility at some other level where it is truly self- idenƟcal and not an image of something like itself. The studies, ending with the “movements of harmony” are but the “prelude to the song that must be learned,” that is, to the exercise of dialecƟc proper. The use of nomos, as Grube points out, puns in Greek on the double meaning of both song and law. But the pun also has the signiﬁcance of establishing a conƟnuity, the series of studies which end with harmony and with the contrast

between a study of the physics of music, the esotericism of the Pythagoreans, and the platonic study of the laws or nomos of harmony, that is, its intelligibility and necessity. The same maƩer, the regularity seen as laws, is seen by the dialecƟcian as images of necessity, so “those who cannot give an exact and reasoned account of what is said [do not] know anything at all of the things we say they must know” (531e). DialecƟc, then, produces the image of discourse as the song of reason, of which the relaƟons of Ideas as a harmony of the whole is the ulƟmate objecƟve content. It is the true noeƟc science that produces the image in speech of the laws that are the song of, for example, musical harmony. The idenƟty of the tones of the literal, musical harmony is inseparable from the relaƟons of the tones, and is expressed in the laws formulated by the dianoeƟc science of harmonics. Analogously, the idenƟty of Ideas, the eideƟc elements reﬂected in the discursive elements that noeƟc imaginaƟon images, is inseparable from the relaƟons of or among the Ideas. These eideƟc relaƟons are expressed in the relaƟons revealed by dialecƟc and formulated as the laws of their moƟon both in their inter- relaƟon, and as the moƟon of the Ideas downward. These two moƟons, the horizontal and the verƟcal, as reﬂected in the Line, are seen in both subject and object. That is to say, it is seen in the medium of visible and non-visible existence, and in the corresponding and co-temporal moƟons of intellect in the reinterpretaƟon of existence as mirroring knowledge. Seen in the light of truth, what before was merely existence and doxa, in both visible things and in human acƟon, becomes knowledge (though even as doxa it is possible only as a melee of images that express and rely, unperceived, on the Ideas). The study of musical harmony parƟcipates in this moƟon, and is the last image of it before dialecƟc, but does so unknowingly. It is the last science, paradigmaƟcally and mythically, that lacks noeƟc self-consciousness. DialecƟc, on the other hand, has as its law precisely the self-awareness of reason—whereas other sciences are images of reason and take their objects as embodying reason objecƟvely. Hence the Line’s forth level, noēsis, is the home of fully self-conscious dialecƟc, arriving at its conclusions “by means of Ideas and through Ideas,” and as the highest form of the hierarchy of capaciƟes. These capaciƟes of the intellecƟve soul, or ways of knowing, are disƟncƟve for each kind of object knowable, but also linked verƟcally as intelligence is driven from a lower to

a higher level of object and corresponding acƟvity. We shall return to a further consideraƟon of dialecƟc momentarily.[22] How literally are we to take Plato’s prescripƟon for just these studies as those which prepare the philosopher for the higher studies of dialecƟc proper? The parƟcular studies chosen can in fact serve to turn the philosophical soul from considering the visible as the real to the non-visible present in the everyday. Similarly, it is important that the image of the city constructed is really possible—though I have argued, only when that possibility is considered as having its locus in the individual soul, the personal city within. These parƟcular studies are chosen partly because, like the virtues of the city and individual, they are both the convenƟonal wisdom of what training in the laƩer case and learning or educaƟon in the former consist in. With the arrival of the sophists on the scene there is of course much controversy over what is to consƟtute a proper curriculum, but at least one tradiƟon, represented by Hippias, is contrasted to that of Protagoras (cf. Prot. 318d-e) and is closer to the one proposed by Socrates. That convenƟonal wisdom has merit in both cases. But in both cases the descripƟon of them in the Republic is seriously altered from what it would be convenƟonally, to enable us to see them in the light of the larger purpose they are made to serve as “useful and beneﬁcial” in the turning or re-educaƟon of the soul. Thus, for the reader they serve to illustrate, are images of, teaching the soul to see rightly. And the arrangement of them in the parƟcular order given is, I have suggested, also meant to illustrate the criteria and methods by which what is real is increasingly revealed. For those who pracƟce the studies, again stressing seen in the right light and conƟnued far enough, the experience of the pracƟce of them is a training of the intellect, a habituaƟon of judgment via the experience of the reality of the non-visible in such studies. But in the Republic and in life they also serve as images, though actually working ones, of both the Ideas and human intellect at work—and other acƟviƟes may serve both as this pracƟcal experience, and as images to be reﬂected on for their ability to lead us further. (This is not to deny that these parƟcular ‘sciences’ are perhaps essenƟal paradigms for insight into the intelligible structure of the natural world, and in parƟcular calculaƟon.)

Furthermore, the ones chosen are described as acƟviƟes in such a way as to bring out, even in their non-technical form, basic truths about knowing, being and human being—such as counƟng “one, two, three” and the divisions of like and unlike, unity, etc. For the percepƟon and study of these acƟviƟes and ideas at work, clearly other studies might serve— biology, for example—though some beƩer than others. On the other hand, arithmeƟc, or more basically, counƟng, is clearly a special case, serving as both fundamental image and primary acƟvity of human calculaƟon or “measuring rightly.” That the studies are not meant to be strictly prescripƟve is parƟcularly clear when one considers the last study, that of harmony, even in its Pythagorean incarnaƟon.[23] The choice of harmony ought to instruct those who would limit insight into knowledge and being to insight into the special, parƟcularly mathemaƟcal, sciences. True, the study of music proposed is with regard to its mathemaƟcal properƟes, etc. yet it is sƟll what is the basis of sensual sound, and of the presence of the BeauƟful. And the placing of music as higher than astronomy and geometry, which could have served as well for the strictly mathemaƟcal aspect to illustrate these, is instrucƟve. (Though there is also the moƟve, as described above, of arranging the studies to illustrate increasingly intellectual kinds of moƟon and the inversion of the physical world.) The choice of the structuring elements of an art as the last study, one designed to bring pleasure, albeit here an intellectual one, is surely signiﬁcant. For it occurs in a discussion whose overall purpose aŌer all is to demonstrate the beauty and ulƟmately the desirability of a unity that is beyond the limited, if pure, one of mathemaƟcs and the sciences—the unity and being of the just soul and its beauty, both within itself and in the world that it knows (astronomy, as well, had a movement from the beauƟful of the starry heavens (530a) to the study of “true speed and true slowness”). Geometry and astronomy could have served if only the percepƟon of the mathemaƟcal intelligibility of Nature were at issue. Harmony, though here as puriﬁed, is signiﬁcantly aestheƟc and eroƟc, as beﬁts a study that prepares the soul for dialecƟc’s approach to the Good. Thus ﬁnally my answer to the quesƟon as to whether these studies in parƟcular are to be taken seriously as the preparaƟon of the philosopher is no, not if taken literally as the only ones capable. And that it is their descripƟon in the

Republic that is ulƟmately important to understand—for it is in understanding this that one would be able to decide “which studies are beneﬁcial and useful and which are not,” and taken up in which way, to what ﬁnal end. Mitchell Miller, in “Beginning the ‘Longer Way’”[24] provides a detailed and careful analysis of the ﬁve studies and their speciﬁc and apt role in preparing for a ﬁnal insight into the Good. Miller disƟnguishes, as do I, between the argument addressed to the interlocutors and that addressed to the careful reader/listener. The studies are both a progression away from aƩachment or immersion in the visible, a “purgaƟon” of the soul, but also a return via the studies to a reinterpretaƟon or “reconsƟtuƟon” of the visible, of the world now seen in terms of its intelligibility. Miller argues that the last of the sequence, “harmony,” takes us to the doorstep of the Good, by introducing us to the noƟon of raƟo contained therein, which unlike the others is “neither visible nor spaƟal” (321). “With the turn from the geometrical disciplines to harmonics, then, we recover in its pure intelligibility the innermost structure of all that becomes, both the corporeal and the incorporeal” (322). Further, “the study of harmonics brings to the fore the complex unity that makes for wholeness and harmony” and provides the philosopher-in-training the basis for appreciaƟng the “normaƟve status of complex unity” and “a keen appreciaƟon for what is whole and harmonious” (333). Miller develops on the basis of this a noƟon of intermediates that are “perfect exemplars” shaped by the “forms they instanƟate,” and in parƟcular the noƟon of “perfecƟon as such” (326-8), which, he argues is “like the forms in having the character of a funcƟon, not an object [my emphasis throughout] . . . providing the context in which the purely intelligible perfect ﬁgure can come to mind. “PerfecƟon as such,” according to Miller, is the very thing that is the “goodness of the Good,” (328) and which is the ground of the ontological funcƟonality of the Good as cause. Miller thus aƩributes, rightly I think, a kind of indeterminancy to the Good, as a kind of richness. Each Form is “an itself determinate way of determining perfecƟon as such,” for example, in triangularity, as prior to its instanƟaƟon in a parƟcular intelligible instanƟaƟon in a perfect triangle. “PerfecƟon as such, on the other hand, is in and of itself indeterminate, hence it both transcends and

lends itself to the host of ways of determining it that the Forms just are and that their intelligible instanƟaƟons exemplify” (327). The Forms themselves are the expression in their “basic nature” of “these diﬀerent ways of determining” perfecƟon as such. That is to say, the Good is an openness out to the world that becomes concrete in the mulƟplicity of its instanƟaƟons. Miller’s understanding of the whole apparatus is much like my own. It is as a dynamic set of funcƟons set in, and seƫng, a context that structures the world, and our soul’s capacity when equipped with the right philosophical educaƟon, for our reading of it in its intelligibility. We have then our rule in this light of both others and ourselves—mirroring the rule of the Good over their Forms and the world in its intelligibility. This is both ontological for the producƟons of being and epistemological for the producƟon of epistēmē. This is very close, I would say, to what I argue. The diﬀerence in our interpretaƟons is that I would not take the educaƟonal program as prescripƟve of the sole route of access but rather more themselves as images, as well as models, albeit singularly apt, actually funcƟoning and producƟve ones. Otherwise, it would seem that one is limited to the reading of the intelligibility of the world as an object of the natural sciences, and the pracƟce in the years spent back down in the Cave if literally only so equipped as somewhat reduced to a preliminary. Miller is led to acknowledge at the end that “the breadth of the longer way” in including the ethical, poliƟcal and other dimensions of human life and virtue, is yet to discover, in the “turning of our soul to all of being.” “The more deeply our path is illuminated by mathemaƟcs, the more urgently we want to understand whether we can extend our insight to, for example, the spheres of the ethical, the poliƟcal, and the religious” (341). I would add, to the ontological ground of these. We turn now to a further consideraƟon of dialecƟc, but it must be said that with regard to dialecƟc as a precise method not much is explicit in the Republic itself. We should note, however, that it is the whole process of the movement from “the deliverance from the bonds and the turning from the shadows” up to the ﬁnal vision of the Good, that is described as dialecƟc (532a). Thus, “the power of sight would be imitaƟng it [be an image of it] when we described it as aƩempƟng to look at actual living creatures, then at the stars, and ﬁnally at the actual sun.” DialecƟc is clearly disƟnguished from the operaƟons of the intellect at each of the ﬁrst

three levels of the Line, since dialecƟc is to operate “without any help from the senses but by means of reason,” and only then and because of this condiƟon, if one does not give up, “does one reach the ﬁnal goal of the intelligible as the prisoner escaping the cave reached the ﬁnal goal of the visible” (532b). The other three levels are in one way or another, as already discussed, Ɵed to the visible—always understood here as comprising not just the physical but all the objects of doxa, and of dianoia insofar as it operates from hypotheses. And yet dialecƟc may also be said to be both present from the beginning in all knowing, as well as being the special technique of the forth secƟon. It is present in the other levels in two ways. First, as the inner tensions of the objects themselves which, in the contradicƟons of their appearances or showing of themselves, have the potenƟal to call forth reason to resolve them—as in the examples of the ﬁngers of diﬀerent lengths, and received doxa about maƩers of piety and jusƟce (shadow idenƟƟes). Secondly, as discourse: each level of discourse is a reﬂecƟon or image of the truer discourse of dialecƟc in its pure self-conscious form. Thus even the blind arguments of the cave dwellers are a dim image of real dialecƟc; their arguments lead nowhere, but at least they reﬂect the ability of human beings to disƟnguish, if not rightly, this from that, to argue about the idenƟty and sequence or relaƟons of the shadows. The turning of the soul away from the shadow wall and towards the cause of the shadows, in the puppets, the parading puppeteers and the ﬁre, is not a complete negaƟng of their earlier discourse but rather a resoluƟon of it (primarily aporeƟc at this level, hence already the danger of misology), a resoluƟon in the light of which their former discourse is seen as mock dialecƟc, yet sƟll having the dialecƟcal features of all discourse and hence prototypic to the keen observer. But the ability of objects of study to call forth intellect in such a way as to drive it upward is dependent on the openness of intelligence to ontological and epistemological tensions at each stage, and thus the necessity for the reformaƟon or turning of the knowing soul towards those tensions which otherwise remain implicit, hidden in ordinary discourse. Once again, it is important to see the several senses in which the journey of dialecƟc is the whole journey, and hence, in the recapitulated image of the Cave journey, at 532b-c, the images of “living creatures and plants and

the light of the sun” are called “divine.” But not the shadows seen in the cave, which are the received images of the doxalogists. The images which the laƩer carry (though including ‘objects’ found in nature) are made images constructed or based on elements that for the makers are sƟll doxa —they do not ask for, and cannot give, an account of their source. In ascent, we are said to be looking “no longer at shadows of images thrown by another source of light [the creaƟons of the doxalogist] which is itself an image as compared to the sun.” Only the last set of images, those that the sciences make or use as dianoia and which correspond to the images and reﬂecƟons outside the cave, approach knowledge closely enough to merit being called divine. “The pracƟce of every study we have described has this power to move the best part of the soul and lead it upward. . .” (532c). So far, the prelude and the surrounding discussion has given but an image of dialecƟc, but when Glaucon asks for the song itself, “the way in which dialecƟc works, what its parts are and what path it follows,” Socrates replies, “Not yet, my dear Glaucon, will you be able to follow—it is not that keenness is lacking on my part,—for you would no longer be seeing an image of what we are discussing but the truth itself, or so it seems to me” (533a). One cannot, then, describe what dialecƟc does to one who does not already have the understanding of its realm of operaƟon and some experience of its method. And Glaucon has just demonstrated in his consistent misunderstanding of the nature and purpose of the higher studies, that he is in fact either incapable or not ready for more than an external image, in the descripƟon of the studies, poorly understood at that. That is, as a friend of the Ideas, he operates sƟll primarily at the level of pisƟs. “It is not worthwhile insisƟng that it is so in fact, but we must maintain [ichuristeon] that one would say something of this kind. Is that not so?” “It surely is.” “And that the power of dialecƟc will only appear to one who is experienced in the studies we have described, and cannot ever appear otherwise” (533a). And then too, one may add, when they are taken up “rightly” and not “as now presently pracƟced.” For the sciences, while they “grasp at reality to some extent,” (533b) as long as they conƟnue as sciences in making use of hypotheses without examining them, are cast as “dreaming about reality, unable to have a waking view of it.” The task of dialecƟc is to be in a posiƟon to do what the sciences themselves cannot do for themselves, which is to “give a reasoned account

of them.” We are not, however, in the same posiƟon as Glaucon, to the extent that we grasp the nature and purpose or use of the studies, and see in their descripƟon, as well as that of the Line etc. the hypothesis of the Ideas that they are built on and point to. In this, we have an iniƟal giving of an account of knowing and being. Though we are not given an immediate example of dialecƟc, we are given an external descripƟon or image of the behavior of dialecƟc. This is given in the descripƟons of the philosopher’s preparatory studies, and in those of the Line and Cave. In other words, we are given images of the world as necessitaƟng and supporƟng dialecƟcal quesƟoning if knowledge is to be possible. Hence the appropriateness of a recapitulaƟon of the Line in the text at just this point, since it is the Line which is an implicit image of dialecƟc, not just as a human endeavor but as a dynamic mapping of knowledge and being in its appearances and images. The Line is a schemaƟc representaƟon of the ways in which the non-visible is available in experience, and the basis of it. It is therefore at this point that the divisions of the object-world presented in the schemata of the Line get matched more concretely to the pathēmata as corresponding ways of knowing (cf. 534a, 511d-e). The Line discussion per se, gave the divisions of the world into objects of knowledge, and a schemaƟc descripƟon of the behavior of the knowing subject, but only gave names at that point to the capaciƟes of the soul that speciﬁcally deal with each segment. What was formerly noēsis becomes here epistēmē, and the former term, noēsis, is reserved for both upper secƟons taken together. There is, further, a signiﬁcant diﬀerence in the characterizaƟon of the seeming repeƟƟon of terms of the two lists. The ﬁrst Ɵme, at 511d, these terms applied to their respecƟve divisions of the object-world of the Line are called pathēmata, and we are “to consider that each has as much clarity as the content of its parƟcular secƟon shares in truth.” Glaucon characterizes them just above this as an “aƫtude of mind.” “You seem to me to call the aƫtude of mind of geometers and such reasoning but not understanding.” On the other hand, at 534a, aŌer the elaboraƟon in detail of the studies and culminaƟng with the descripƟon of dialecƟc, these same acƟviƟes are now seen diﬀerently. First, they have now become visible as the acƟve image-making powers of the soul (dunameis as opposed to pathēmata, though the former term or name does not explicitly occur in the passage, but neither

does pathē). Secondly, they are themselves a prime subject maƩer of dialecƟc, the new science producƟve of true epistēmē. Each of these (eikasia, pisƟs, dianoia, epistēmē ) are in their own way and degree dialecƟcal—but only the ﬁnal pracƟce of dialecƟc as a self- conscious study of being and knowing aƩempts to “apprehend methodically, with regard to each thing, what each really is.” Note that dialecƟc is itself not listed as a kind of knowing or knowledge. In the original descripƟon of the Line, it is the “other [highest] secƟon of the intelligible [as a whole] . . . which reason itself grasps by the power of dialecƟc” and then “having reached this [what is beyond hypothesis, the ﬁrst principle of all that is] . . . it does come down to a conclusion.” The mathemaƟzed objects of reasoning of dianoia are the conclusions via hypothesis; while for the reproducƟon of the Ideas themselves noēsis is the product, and dialecƟc the method. But another reason for not including dialecƟc in the list of ways of knowing is perhaps that, as I have tried to suggest, dialecƟc is implicit in all discourse about experience and only in its explicit form does it (gradually) take leave of the sensible, i.e., the individual. Further, it might be said that the dynamic of discourse has broadly the same implicit features at every stage. This is so even at the lowest level, where it is seen in its saƟric form in the shadow play and dynamic of the Cave, and in the analysis of what calls forth intelligence, beginning as it does with Agamemnon’s feet. Finally, the tension of dialecƟc is implicit in both Being and its appearances—the relaƟon of Ideas as the inner tension in the former and the ﬂux of idenƟty in the laƩer. Thus the dialecƟcal essence of discourse is an image in its moƟon of the dialecƟcal essence of what is in itself and of what appears. In its moƟon it points to reconciliaƟon in the principles of knowing as the principles of any intelligible being. Whether the forms and principles of this knowing are as Plato thought, and hence are the forms of the being that they reveal, is a quesƟon for reﬂecƟon, but even another analysis, say Hegel’s, would be looking for the mapping of intelligible discourse and intelligible being, and discourse would remain in principle sƟll the non-visible and dialecƟcal image of being. At the end of the brief discussion of dialecƟc, Socrates suggests, aŌer lisƟng the powers or capaciƟes that correspond to the levels of knowledge and objects of knowledge, that their relaƟve order, the original order in

which they stand in the descripƟon of the Line, can be alternated, hence their relaƟons: “As being is to generaƟon, so intelligence is to opinion, and as intelligence is to opinion, so knowledge is to belief as reasoning to imaginaƟon” (534a). The main divisions of the Line, and hence the world that it images, is into Being and GeneraƟon, corresponding here to Knowledge (noēsis) and Opinion (doxa). GeneraƟon must obviously, we have argued, be understood as referring not only to the literal world of physical nature and our opinions about it, but to all the realm of the opinable, hence the sphere of human acƟon and judgment, which is the external image of our opinions about jusƟce and the like. We “generate” collecƟvely and individually, our changing opinions about the world—how we take it to be, how we think it ought to be, and how we think we ought to live in it. DialecƟc aƩempts to sort this out, to replace opinion with the broad category of knowledge. But the alternaƟon suggests as well that the same relaƟonship holds between knowledge (epistēmē) and belief (pisƟs) and reasoning (dianoia) and imaginaƟon (eikasia): the second term is less stable, less reliable than the ﬁrst in each case—but we knew that already from their place in the Line, the hierarchical relaƟonship is not changed by the alternaƟon. We are instead asked to focus on the speciﬁc relaƟons of these smaller pairs. As Being is to GeneraƟon so is epistēmē to doxa. The diﬀerence between the two halves of the Line, between noēsis and doxa is one of relaƟve reliability or ﬁrmness, relaƟve absence of change or moƟon. This same diﬀerence holds between the terms of the divisions of each half, and, it is suggested, between the terms in alternaƟon. Dianoia is a kind of Intelligence as contrasted to Opinion, but relies on assumpƟons (hypotheses) while epistēmē characterisƟcally does not. Epistēmē is ﬁrmer than dianoia. A similar comparison is elicited by the alternaƟon Socrates suggests: between the kind and source of the ﬁrmness held by the dialecƟcian and the characterisƟc ﬁrmness of pisƟs, which is ﬁrm belief, tenacious but ungrounded (at least with regard to consciousness, that is, knowledge). The second half of the alternaƟon, “as reasoning (dianoia) is to imaginaƟon (eikasia)” presents, analogous to the ﬁrst pair, the contrast between two kinds of system making: the logical, if hypotheƟcally based, ordering of dianoia, contrasted with the random, baseless (or intuiƟve?), the ordering of imaginaƟon. In each alternaƟon one member is an image of the other, not of their respecƟve objects (as is the case before

alternaƟon) but as to their respecƟve processes or methods—the one being a weaker or defecƟve image of the ﬁrmer method of the other. But these relaƟons of contrast or tension, negaƟve relaƟons, are matched by a more posiƟve relaƟon of the pairs. For the ﬁrst pair, it may be said that the ﬁrmness of belief, while itself ungrounded is not altogether unfounded. Fortunately, much of what we believe is true, or true enough to get along in the world, in both the physical and even the ethical world. The ideas and appearances that we trust get us through the world precisely because they are trustworthy: the physical world is reliably the same, lawlike, and the social world is more oŌen than not, reliably ethical, though wholly convenƟonal. Lest I be misunderstood, I mean only to say that though there is much vice, false virtue, and virtue misconstrued, sƟll, convenƟonal virtue is the cement that held Plato’s world together as much as ours—we do not live for the most part in ethical chaos. This is not, of course, to deny Plato’s challenge, examinaƟon, redeﬁniƟon and transformaƟon of the virtues as already discussed above and elsewhere, for example as we see even in the earlier educaƟon or training of the guardians, and to be further examined in the Phaedo chapter to follow (67b-69e)—let alone in the other SocraƟc dialogues. The funcƟon of philosophy, in Plato of dialecƟc, and hence of recourse to the idea of a necessary relaƟon between true virtue and knowledge (noēsis, epistēmē in the alternaƟon) is not necessarily always to replace this behavior with something else but to ground it. It is to show why it works, when it does, to jusƟfy it, and to provide the grounds for its reinterpretaƟon when it doesn’t. (Then of course there are those elencƟc dialogues where the ﬁnal outcome at least appears to be aporeƟc. Furthermore, Socrates’ redeﬁniƟons in the Republic are, I have argued, in the light of special ends.) Hence, Cephalus makes the right choice, not to return the weapon held in trust, but instead of re-examining his ground, the maxim concerning telling the truth and paying one’s debts that he had oﬀered, he retreats to doxa, the sacriﬁces and the poets, rather than seeking higher ground. The opinions of ﬁrm belief, at least certainly their elements, are reliable, to the extent that they are, because they are a workable arrangement of the elements, albeit unreﬂecƟvely and in unrelated contexts—in short, they are images of noēsis in a much more direct way than dianoia, in that they are reﬂecƟons in the everyday world

of the highest elements of thinking and being. To take Polemarchus’s line, or rather Simonides’s, jusƟce is indeed “giving each his due,”—there is something intuiƟvely right there, and it is what we convenƟonally expect, strive for, etc.—the trick is to ﬁgure out what it is that is due—and what the who is to whom it is owed. Dianoia’s relaƟonship to this world, as sketched earlier in the account of the Line, on the other hand, is in a sense more temporary—as system or theory it is a bridge, or as Socrates says a “springboard” to the Ideas of noēsis. Dianoia is epistemologically more stable of course than anything in the boƩom half. Yet perhaps the ontological link between the Ideas of noēsis and their images in everyday discourse and the experienced world is stronger. The posiƟve link of the second pair, between dianoia and eikasia, Reasoning and ImaginaƟon, is in a sense easier to see. The circle we construct, physically or in imaginaƟon, is an image that feeds and supports the reasoning and is recognized as an image of what dianoia is really talking about, really looking at. The former are the visible circles, whether drawn with our ﬁnger in the sand or with a compass (or again, imagined)— the circle as an object of pisƟs on the other hand, is what common sense believes or unreﬂecƟvely understands as a circle. The court judge in considering the case before him can only judge it as it conforms or not to the law. Dianoia works on the object of common understanding (pisƟs) but works with the image-making that represents the concrete parƟcular. But the individual case is much more than a visual aid. The roughly drawn circle is in fact roughly circular, the man before the judge is in fact roughly either acƟng justly or unjustly, and in both cases the individual is a parƟcular roughly similar to, the same as, other cases—the circle in the sand, the moon, the orbit of the earth. The ability to see these resemblances and also that they are individual and diﬀerent, is the beginning of philosophy, the philosophical capacity par excellence; and the possibility of this acƟvity rests on the general ability or capacity to see sameness and diﬀerence, and the provocaƟve reality of the approximate resemblances and diﬀerences before us. The reason that this faculty is called image-making is that we bring these resemblances together (and exclude the diﬀerent) all the Ɵme —someƟmes wrongly someƟmes rightly, someƟmes well someƟmes badly —but without a criƟcal awareness of what we do, or of how it is possible, which are the quesƟons of philosophy. When eikasia performs this noeƟc

funcƟon for dianoia it is taken up into dianoia as dianoeƟc eikasia. This is contrasted to its normal or everyday natural funcƟoning. The verb eikazō can mean either to represent by a likeness, or to be like or resemble, or to liken, compare: to infer from comparison, to conjecture, guess (Liddell and ScoƩ). Dianoia is directly related to this image-making because it is reason’s ﬁrst aƩempt to get it right, with the aid of hypotheses from above and the use of images, and examples of and for comparison, from below. It is thus in the middle as both temporary and on the way, between. Its relaƟonship to pisƟs is that it is a beƩer sorƟng out of the appearances in image-making. (PisƟs as doxa has more to say than image-making, but it tends to babble rather than explain.) Both of these pairs, then, help to explicate the relaƟon of the non-visible world to its manifestaƟon, appearance, and use in the world of appearing, of acƟon and acƟvity. Both relaƟons are at once aporeƟc or unseƩling and purifying and conﬁrming; and each higher term is in a peculiar way not only an image but a measure of the method or acƟvity of the other term. There is one more topic to take up with regard to both the preparatory studies and dialecƟc itself. Neither leads inevitably to its natural end. Even when studied rightly it is possible to be derailed and misdirected, and this is parƟcularly true, Plato urges, of that early stage of the pracƟce of dialecƟc which involves one in the technique of quesƟoning people and things. It is for this reason that Socrates concludes the brief discussion of dialecƟc in the Republic with a discussion of the dangers of dialecƟc, or what turns out to be a false image of it. In eﬀect, “great evil . . . has now come upon dialecƟc. . . . Those who pracƟce it are ﬁlled with lawlessness” (537e) which is the very opposite of what one would expect. The problem is, that while we cannot assume that with age comes wisdom, as the episode with Cephalus shows, nor can we assume that with youth comes foresight and prudence, in fact the opposite is more likely. Socrates suggests that we consider the image of the vigorous, enthusiasƟc student —a good candidate for further studies. What, he asks, should happen, if the child of rich parents, who had sent their child away to school with “beliefs about just and beauƟful things,” suddenly discovers that “he was not the child of his professed parents … he would honor and care for them less, while his relaƟons with the ﬂaƩerers would become more intense, he would be persuaded by them far more, would now live in the way they

did.” These “ﬂaƩerers” are in fact his teachers, or at least oﬀer themselves as such along the way. “And then a quesƟoner comes along, and asks a man in those circumstances what is the beauƟful. and, when he answers what he has heard from the lawgiver, the argument refutes” both him, his parents, and his spiritual parents, the laws of the lawgiver of the community, from whom he had heard about “beauƟful and just things.” This reduces him to the “belief that this thing is no more beauƟful than it is ugly, and the same with what is just and good and things he honored most” (538d-e). True dialecƟc would have led to “what each thing is,” while false or misused dialecƟc leads to believing that nothing is; that neither of the opposing predicates can be applied with jusƟce. The result is that, when he no longer believes these original values, and has not yet discovered true ones, he will lead the life and adopt the principles of the ﬂaƩering kind. Such youths are aƩracted by the “pleasure” of argument which “ﬂaƩers our soul”—those who resist this absorpƟon in dialecƟc as an end in itself are those “who are at all moderate.” “These honor the principles of their fathers which we menƟoned and obey them;” instead, he “becomes lawless.” This use of dialecƟc, in place of uncovering and conﬁrming order or law, is rather a misuse—resulƟng in lawlessness in both the individual and the realm of acƟvity, whether literally the ethical dimension or as an image represenƟng the object-world. The diﬀerence between an “older man” ready for dialecƟc and “those young puppies” who discredit philosophy, both in the eyes of others and for themselves as a method of arriving at the truth, revolves around a diﬀerence of character. The young have been seduced by the ﬂaƩery of soul, that of the sheer power of reason: “When youths get their ﬁrst taste of reasoned discourse they take it as a game and always use it to contradict. They imitate those who cross-examined them and themselves cross-examine others, rejoicing like puppies to drag along and tear to bits in argument whoever is near them” (539b) The aƫtude, if not the skill, of some of the interlocutors who periodically interrupt, trying to catch Socrates out, and elsewhere in the dialogues, e.g., Meno—in contrast to Socrates’s gentle treatment of Cephalus. Note that Adeimantus arrives on the scene with the opposite party, with Polemarchus. The use of the puppy image is interesƟng since it had just been recalled in a posiƟve light to describe part of the early formaƟon of the guardians: “You remember that

we stated [at 467] the boys were to be led into war, as observers on horseback, and, wherever it is safe to do so, they should be brought close and taste blood, like puppies” (537a). But even there, if we read the present image, which is the metaphor revealed, back on to the earlier discussion, where the image is sƟll veiled heavily, we see the disƟncƟon at work. For although the “future warriors” are allowed, it is said, to “taste blood,” they do so actually only visually, from a distance—they are to be taught to ride early and observe the baƩles “mounted on horseback” to allow for “easy ﬂight.” And so, “We must make opportuniƟes for the children to observe war while contriving to keep them safe.” As future warriors it is worth exposing them somewhat to risk. But precauƟons are taken to minimize it. Fathers will not choose expediƟons that are too dangerous, and more importantly, “they will put in charge of them oﬃcers whose age and experience qualiﬁes them to be leaders and tutors.” And if the unexpected happens, they are mounted on docile horses, “not fond of ﬁghƟng or high spirited … and if the need arises, they will ﬁnd safety in following their older commanders.” Rereading this in the context of the later passage about dialecƟc as educaƟon, the earlier image reveals more of itself as extended metaphor for educaƟon in the later sense, the war between ignorance and knowledge in which dialecƟc assists. Thus the children are put under tutors to “observe warfare”—which one could see as perhaps the reading and discussion of the schools before entry into actual parƟcipaƟon, whether in the actual debates of philosophy or the debates of the city. And the “retreat by horseback” is suggesƟve of the refuge of convenƟonal beliefs, as in the later context—so the horses are docile and not fond of ﬁghƟng and the retreat is to “their older commanders,” the guides of right opinion. The earlier image is a fainter image of the later—i.e., more physical and more disguised an anƟcipaƟon. They are related, as images, as discussion of training (the formaƟon of character by habit, etc.) is to true educaƟon, physical war to the wars of discourse, and as degrees of disclosedness about what truly “is and is not to be feared.” The older man exercises dialecƟc with restraint—“in order to discover the truth rather than one who is merely playing and contradicƟng for play, he will himself be more measured [kai auto metriōteros] and will bring honor rather than discredit to the pursuit of philosophy” (539c). The use of metriōteros here is

signiﬁcant since while it also means moderate, its use in place of sōphrosunē stresses the context of the discussion of dialecƟc, hence the right measure of truth which reﬂects the internally ordered soul, itself both rightly measured by philosophy, and brought into right measure by sōphrosunē, and thus in turn capable of the dialecƟcal right use of its capaciƟes to rightly measure. Moral harmonia is an existenƟal precondiƟon for accessing the harmony of subject and object noeƟcally, the correspondence of knower and known. But the ontological jusƟﬁcaƟon of the harmonia of the soul (jusƟce) and of the construcƟon of its pre-philosophical image in Books II- V, is the philosophical insight into the whole which is the ﬁrmest grounding of this harmonia of soul in the moral sense: Socrates: “The studies that have been indiscriminately taught in the educaƟon of boys must now be brought together for them in order to give them a synopƟc view of their kinship with each other and with the nature of reality.” Glaucon: “Indeed, only the kind of instrucƟon in which this takes place will remain with them.” Socrates: “It is also, I said, the best test of the dialecƟcal nature, for the man who sees things as a whole is a dialecƟcian; the man who does not, is not” (537c). But this vision of the whole is the fruit of hard labor, and the true dialecƟcian is to be disƟnguished from the individual who merely plays at dialecƟc for amusement and the pleasure that is ﬂaƩery of the soul and a destrucƟve mere technique, negaƟve in its results. The ordering of the soul permits its ascent, but is carried out in the light of what is seen, only fully jusƟﬁed at the end of that same ascent.[25] This is the Platonic circle, the image of which is the Republic itself. The ﬁnal end of the journey for the whole soul, as opposed to the raƟonal part alone, is its return to the place where the insight of reason is put to use. It is here where the unity of the whole seen as a reﬂecƟon of the Idea of the Good is “useful and beneﬁcial,” in the return back down the Line to know what each thing is

and “give a reasoned account” i.e., engage in discourse, and in the world of acƟon to “live well,” to “put in order the city and its ciƟzens as well as themselves” (this is not to say, however, that such a return, such a comprehensive vision of the unity of the whole is ever actually fully completed).[26] SƟll, one might have a lingering suspicion that the raƟonal part, albeit not a person, is being treated unjustly. But even here, one might reply, the raƟonal part is deprived only of conƟnuous uninterrupted contemplaƟon, while its work in the city is a deepening insight into the way the forms have an ordering presence. DialecƟc fully formed and put to right use thus produces not a deprivaƟon but a deepening fulﬁllment, in which the rule of the raƟonal part has the opportunity to increasingly mirror image the rule of the Good.[27] To rightly understand the ordering, both of the individual soul/city and that of the reform of the community represented in the Cave, we must understand the soul’s capaciƟes (dunameis), its powers, and what it would mean for these to funcƟon rightly.
