Understanding this ordering is in eﬀect, speaking generally, also to understand the relaƟon of jusƟce and virtue. [28] In the next chapter, we shall take a closer look at the noƟon of soul, and its capaciƟes or powers (dunameis),[29] through examining the noƟon of the separateness of Ideas and the separaƟng and image-making abiliƟes of the soul, as well as the soul’s separateness itself. These are the acƟviƟes that were introduced by Plato in the Republic as the unseen necessary hypotheses that precede the construcƟon of the Line and are embedded in it. Coupled with this will be a further examinaƟon of the noƟon of image. But for a discussion of these topics we turn to the Phaedo, for it is in the context of the Phaedo that we can further clarify the ontological meaning of these concepts, parƟcularly that of separaƟon. This clariﬁcaƟon will ulƟmately also enable us to understand beƩer the philosophical meaning of the descent back down into the Cave, and more generally, the dynamic represented by the Divided Line image; that is, both images as represenƟng an ontological necessity. It is this ontological necessity that will provide an answer to the original quesƟon of why, and from what perspecƟve, the truly just life is happier, and more desirable, than the unjust life, even other things being unequal, as it were.[30]

In both city and soul, disposiƟons and structures are prior to their expression in acƟon. . . . Thus knowing what numbers are concordant, and why, has a very great deal to do with the tasks of government, because concord is an important structural value at the lower level of ethics and poliƟcs” (56). He concludes that “mathemaƟcs and dialecƟc are good for the soul not only because they give you understanding of objecƟve value,” of what truly is, as it is “context invariant,” ordered within each and bound up in a “kinship” that forms a whole, “but also because in so doing they fashion jusƟce and temperance with wisdom in your soul” (77). This direct inﬂuence of mathemaƟcs seems to me a somewhat odd conclusion. Order in the heavens, harmony and order found in the mathemaƟcal studies themselves, while they serve to turn us to the more real from the less real, and thus prepare us for study of the Ideas, does not mean that the order, harmony etc. we would ﬁnd in the laƩer is more than analogous to the former. Secondly, the value found in the stable ordered objects of mathemaƟcs, while beauƟful indeed, is not at all the same kind of value that we mean by ethical value, though both are for Plato certainly Ɵed to

“unqualiﬁed being” (19) and so on. A uniﬁed fascist state could be said to have the requisite qualiƟes of “concord, aƩunement, and proporƟon.” What has gone wrong here? The right ordering of soul and polis is based on knowledge of the objects—hence the details of the Republic—so mathemaƟcal order and value, about which knowledge is gained, since it has rather diﬀerent objects, serves only analogically. There is indeed a kinship—and the Good is responsible for both realms—but part of the turning of the whole soul, and the return of the philosopher to rule well is dependent on seeing that they are kin because they are ontological analogues—an insight that we are helped to see by the study of mathemaƟcs for the ends that Socrates sets out—but not more than that.

Chapter 6 The Phaedo’s Arguments for Immortality THE PHILOSOPHICAL SENSE OF PURIFICATION AND SEPARATION: THE CYCLE OF OPPOSITES ARGUMENT Our interpretaƟon of the Republic thus far has leŌ us with something of a schemaƟc ontology. This was, as noted in the previous chapter, in need of a ﬂeshing out. For this, we turn next to the Phaedo. The Phaedo is a dialogue that is oŌen turned to for a demonstraƟon of Plato’s beliefs concerning two inƟmately related doctrines, the immortality of the soul and the independence of the Ideas. In both cases, the argument turns in part on what is meant by separaƟon—the separaƟon of body from soul and the separateness of the Ideas. But some features of the introducƟon of this term do not seem to me to have received suﬃcient aƩenƟon, parƟcularly with regard to the dramaƟc context. We begin our analysis with the discussion of the separaƟon of body and soul required of the true philosopher for the gaining of wisdom. At 65e Socrates suggests that, the clearest knowledge will surely be aƩained by one who approaches the object so far as possible by thought, and thought alone . . . one who sets himself to track down each consƟtuent of reality purely and simply as it is by means of thought pure and simple: one who gets rid, so far as possible, of eyes and ears and, broadly speaking, of the body altogether, knowing that when the body is the soul’s partner it confuses the soul and prevents it from coming to possess truth and intelligence. (65e-66a) The oŌ-cited apparent epistemological denigraƟon of the senses here had been led up to by an appeal to a Pythagorean (and Theban) moral denigraƟon of the senses to which Simmias and Cebes, the interlocutors, are sympatheƟc (cf. 64d). Our soul is “befouled by this evil admixture” (66b). But we must examine more closely just what sort of separaƟon of

soul from body is meant. The Orphic-Pythagorean context in both the doctrines (epistemological and moral) and the seƫng of the Phaedo, so oŌen noted in its details in the literature, is obvious, beginning of course with the frame context of Phaedo’s narraƟon of the events surrounding Socrates’s last day to Echecrates, in Phlius. Echecrates was apparently a prominent ﬁgure in the Pythagorean tradiƟon centered there. Within the main narraƟon, the central ﬁgures, Simmias and Cebes, have had direct exposure in their home town of Thebes to the teachings of Philolaus (61d), a Pythagorean (the appellaƟon covers a range of views) “of some importance who had seƩled at Thebes aŌer the expulsion of the sect from South Italy about the middle of the ﬁŌh century” (Hackforth, 35). For the purposes of my discussion, it is not necessary to trace the exact genealogy of the views of Simmias and Cebes, who in any event are prone to forgeƞulness and distorƟon, but rather to deal with their views as they are presented in the dialogue, and to note that they are represented either as recounƟng what they have heard on other occasions (including from Socrates). In some cases they repeat this approvingly, as their own view, in some cases with reservaƟons or doubts. Socrates says that, considering the inaccuracy of the senses, there are only two alternaƟves: either knowledge is impossible, or full and absolute knowledge is goƩen only aŌer death (Cf. 66e). He concludes with the admoniƟon, in the language of religious purity, that: While we are alive we shall, it would seem, come nearest to knowledge if we have as liƩle as possible to do with the body . . . keeping ourselves pure and free from bodily infecƟon unƟl such Ɵme as God himself shall release us. And being thus made pure and rid of the body’s follies we may expect to join the company of the puriﬁed, and have direct knowledge of all truth unobscured. (67a) And yet the parƟcular obstacles to knowledge set out just prior to this (66b-d), are not strictly epistemological. That is, they are not in fact limitaƟons of percepƟon due to the bodily nature of the senses per se if we are to “come nearest to knowledge,” as we might have expected, but rather factors of health and sickness, desires and fears, and lastly, external interference with our concentraƟon: so, as Socrates elaborates, the body

“makes demands upon us,” and “any sickness that may befall it hampers our pursuit of true being.” And, we are “ﬁlled with desires and longings and fears and imaginaƟons of all sorts . . . ” These either limit our “leisure for philosophy” or “the worst trouble of all,” once having begun “some invesƟgaƟon,” the body’s demand may “obtrude itself at every point of our inquiries, confusing, disturbing and alarming us, and so prevenƟng us from discerning truth” (66d). All three categories of obstacle are “distracƟons” from the acƟvity of intellect—and the philosophical pracƟce or puriﬁcaƟon involves, in part, aƩempƟng to minimize and/or ignore these—not necessarily quite the same enterprise as the “release to join the company of the puriﬁed” of 67a. But it is his very last remark, immediately aŌer this (quoted in full below), that is revealing. Why is this life of puriﬁcaƟon from “distracƟon,” overlaying the moral, tradiƟonal sense of puriﬁcaƟon for the “company of the puriﬁed,” required here by “the god” as the only correct preparaƟon? Because, he says, “that the impure should apprehend [to lay hold of, ephaptesthai] the pure, heaven will hardly permit” (67b2). Literally, “not lawful” (themiton). Hackforth’s translaƟon relies on the context. The puriﬁed soul, once released by the “god himself,” it is then said, “may expect to join the company of the puriﬁed” (Hackforth transl.) or “shall probably be in like company (to eikos)” (Gallop transl.). This parƟcular god and this parƟcular “heaven,” wherever and whatever it is, require that knowing and being be pure. If the subject is ideally puriﬁed of “distracƟon,” is there a corresponding preparatory puriﬁcaƟon of the object? Hence we return again to the quesƟon of the meaning of separaƟon. Just how, speciﬁcally, can an epistemological puriﬁcaƟon of both knower and known be carried out? In such a strain I think, Simmias, must all those that love knowledge rightly address each other, and such must be their belief. So puriﬁcaƟon turns out, does it not, to consist in just what we have been discussing for some Ɵme past, in separaƟng so far as may be the soul from the body, and habituaƟng it to assemble and gather itself together from every region of the body, so as to dwell alone and apart, so far as possible, both in this present life and in the life to come, released from the body’s feƩers. (67b-c)

But what is this chōrismos, this separaƟng?[1] The corresponding verb chōrizō means to separate, part, sever, divide. Hackforth notes the very physical imagery of gathering the elements of the soul together from the diﬀerent “regions of the body.” This is a separaƟon which results from the gathering together of what belongs together because it is the same kind of stuﬀ, and the result is a separaƟon from a diﬀerent kind of stuﬀ. Hackforth stresses in his notes that this “gathering up” “must not of course be taken literally, but rather as a vivid metaphor.”[2] However, when it comes to the crucial noƟon of separaƟon itself, Hackforth, as others, is all too ready to see this as literal Platonic doctrine. But perhaps the text leads us down a diﬀerent road. The ﬁrst quesƟon to ask is, why use this imagery in the ﬁrst place? The answer is that it is just such a materialisƟc stuﬀ that Simmias, and especially Cebes, vaguely conceive the soul to be, quite explicitly, later on. Striving for this separaƟon then, is pursuing “philosophy aright.” And what before at 64c was deﬁned as death, “simply the departure of soul from body” is now to be “called” or named, onomazetai, a separaƟon. “Then what we call death is a releasing or separaƟon of soul from body . . . Indeed, this and nothing else is the philosopher’s concern, the release and separaƟon of soul from body” (67d4-10). As Hackforth notes, “What at 64c was called an apallagē, a parƟng of the soul from body, has now become a lusis kai chōrismos.” But, he then conƟnues, “the laƩer word does not add much to the noƟon of apallagē and indeed chōris was used at 64c6; the operaƟve word is lusis releasing, which sums up in itself much of what has intervened.”[3] Hackforth thinks that lusis , a releasing, is the governing concept, hence a literal separaƟon of body and soul at death—and that choris means not much diﬀerent than that, i.e., exisƟng apart. Yet, as he himself points out in his note to 64c, Socrates’s deﬁniƟon does not do more than assert that “we can properly think and speak of soul ‘apart’ from body; whether soul conƟnues to exist when thus apart is the quesƟon at issue.” Hackforth thus stresses releasing (lusis) at the expense of separaƟng (chōrismos) as the relevant kind of parƟng of body and soul. But is Hackforth right to insist that the “operaƟve word is lusis”? Only, I would argue, by presupposing a certain reading of separaƟon. As I shall try to

show, Hackforth misses the parallel development of the text’s two voices and the careful development of the vocabulary in this regard. Let us see just how this pair of terms comes to be introduced. Hackforth argues that “chōris was used at 64c6” already—that is, the second term of the pair has really been with us all along, hence the pair of lusis kai chōrismos is really just a hendiadys, and that therefore “the laƩer word does not add much to the noƟon of apallagē.” First, with regard to chōris, let us look at the text to which Hackforth refers: …chōris men apo tēs psuchēs apallagēn auto kath’ auto to sōma gegonenai, chōris de tēn psuchēn [apo] tou sōmatos apallageisan auto kath’ autēn einai (64c5-6) The purpose at hand is the deﬁning of “death” and “being dead,” and separaƟon is carried by apallagē as each of soul and body “come to be by itself” (auto kath’ hauto), whereas chōris is used adverbially (in the coordinaƟon of clauses). In any event, as Gallop points out, and I would agree, “It seems hard to acquit Socrates of pre-judging the issue at this point” (Phaedo 86-87, pace Hackforth, 44 n.1). But is this indeed the philosopher’s kind of death, the one that he has been said to be eager for, and “pracƟcing” all his life? And what is the appropriate philosophical sense of auto kath’hauto? Simmias, at least, had thought that he understood just moments before, and it had provoked both a laugh (64b) and a bit of gallows humor repartee. Socrates conƟnues. At 67c, in the redeﬁniƟon of “puriﬁcaƟon,” in the very sentence in which the language of physical collecƟng is used, Plato employs the inﬁniƟve for separaƟon, chōrizein (as opposed to release). Then, by 67d4-5, in a reprise of the deﬁniƟon of death, chōrismos takes on its full importance. First, it is paired with lusis (a loosening or releasing) in the deﬁniƟon of death as it is to be understood for the philosopher. But then immediately again chōrismos is paired with lusis in the deﬁniƟon of true philosophers, which is given in terms of the right object of study. Now as an explanaƟon of the more general term apallagē (an escape, departure, deliverance from), surely lusis would have been suﬃcient. Thus the addiƟon of chōrismos, which is to be paired with lusis, must be signiﬁcant. Furthermore, it must be signiﬁcant that the new term is introduced just when the dialogue reaches the crucial point of deﬁniƟons. The addiƟon thus suggests to me that the two terms are directed at two diﬀerent audiences: the ﬁrst, literal release, is a muthos or promise and consolaƟon (as in the Apology) for Simmias and

Cebes and the literal-minded reader; the second, the philosophical acƟvity of separaƟon, is directed at the philosophical reader, who can himself separate truth from muthos in deﬁning both death and the proper object, or rather the proper acƟvity, which deﬁnes both philosophy and the philosopher. But more support for this meaning of separaƟon, and for limiƟng the noƟon of immortality to the acƟvity of this capacity, will be seen in our analysis of other passages.[4] The discussion which follows in the text is of virtues as exhibited by the philosopher, virtues which are presented as truer, more authenƟc, than the false versions to which they are contrasted. It seems somewhat of a digression. Here I hope to show that it is directly relevant to the correct understanding of the separaƟon issue. These virtues are deﬁned by an analysis of the diﬀerent ostensible moƟve in each case. We look ﬁrst at courage. What is courage in others, as contrasted to courage in the philosopher? Socrates says, because others count death as a great evil, they must be willing to face it because of some greater evil. He does not actually suggest an example, leaving it at the asserƟon that if death is an evil to be feared, yet faced, it must somehow be because there is an even greater evil to be ostensibly feared—death then being the lesser of two evils supposedly. “[W]hen a brave man faces death he does so through fear of something worse” (68d), dishonor, for example? This produces the paradox that a person apparently is courageous through its opposite, being fearful. The philosopher, on the other hand, simply does not fear death (i.e., in principle, he ought not to), and consequently is “truly courageous.” As an account of either courage or its moƟves, the explanaƟon is rather bogus. For one thing, why assume that what is evil is to be feared, as opposed, say, to hated. For another, even if death were feared, or anything else ostensibly more greatly feared, it preƩy obviously does not simply follow that this is the moƟve for the courageous person’s acts. The normal or obvious thing to say would be that we act courageously because we are aƩached or aƩracted to the act or some value that it represents, rather than repulsed by some fear—we overcome a fear in order to act. Again, we should ask how it is that Simmias agrees so easily, leƫng the above pass unnoƟced—or, as Gallop points out, that the argument hinges partly upon an assumed equivalence between brave and fearless, cowardly and fearful

(Phaedo 100, and see the rest of his comments). A rather diﬀerent explanaƟon is given in the Republic, where the guardians will be courageous because they love their fellow ciƟzens and hate the city’s enemies, and are “more afraid of slavery than death” (Rep.387b). This is a fear more of dishonor or ignominy, righteous fear rather than trembling fear.[5] It seems that in a way the Phaedo’s philosopher is courageous by default, he does not fear death—in fact, he ostensibly welcomes it, both as a release from the body and a union with that which he has sought all his life, wisdom. But even taken thus literally, this is sƟll a mock explanaƟon of courage: behaving in a certain way, because one does not have reasons to fear death, is not the same as an act of courage in the face of death. The philosopher who does not fear death has no need of any courage. In the present dramaƟc context, the retelling of Socrates’s last conversaƟon, it is Simmias and Cebes who think that Socrates needs courage, and believe that he demonstrates it in facing what they take to be a terrible thing, while in fact, Socrates himself is precisely not a “man about to die complaining” as would “what we may call a lover of the body” (68c). Looking at the courage of others, Socrates asks, “Surely it is illogical that a man should be brave through fear and cowardice?” (68d)—brave, that is, through or because of bravery’s opposite, rather than the “simple” courage of the philosopher. Put this way, it does at least strike both the interlocutor and the reader as odd—and yet again, it is not in fact quite through fear that we are convenƟonally courageous. Fear is not the cause of even convenƟonal courage, but rather, we are courageous in the face of fear. It is with a sense of what is worth doing in spite of it, that one summons up courage. Furthermore, while fear of the many as cause of its opposite, bravery or courage in the popular sense, is here rejected as illogical, or at least suspect as not true virtue, yet the very ﬁrst argument for immortality is itself the assumpƟon of a causal cycle of opposites. The obvious ﬂaw, in both cases, is that an empirical pair of supposed opposites is not bound by necessity in a causal cycle. To summarize: the courage of the many is not through fear—even counƟng death “among the greatest evils” will not serve as an accountable moƟve for courage—it not only seems illogical, it is in fact not the case. Nor are the philosopher’s acƟons, for example facing the hemlock, which appear courageous to the many

(represented here by Simmias and Cebes) actually courageous, since qua philosopher, he has no need of it. Of course, his irraƟonal fear as a man is something else again. Thus, while the philosopher qua raƟonal soul has no need of courage, the philosopher as ruler of his soul, of his city, must rule in such a way as to convince the rest of the city to be courageous, and even to be “fearless.” There is that other kind of courage that is evinced by the guardians of the Republic in their training and by the future philosopher- ruler in his studies.[6] Once one discards a false noƟon of cause here, it is clear why the philosopher’s virtues are a product not of a cycle or exchange of emoƟons “small ones for great and great ones for small, as though they were coins” (69a) any more than is the courage of “others” a result of fear, but rather that “true virtue” is caused, in the sense of jusƟﬁed by, phronēsis, intelligence. “And if all our buying and selling is done for intelligence and with its aid (kai meta toutou), then we have real courage, real temperance, real jusƟce, and true virtue in general is that which is accompanied by intelligence, no maƩer whether pleasures and fears and all the rest of such things be added or subtracted” (69b). It is the separaƟng carried out by phronēsis, disƟnguishing what is of value and what is not, the true from the false, or mistaken, that results in “true virtues.” Secondly, phronēsis is able to do this to the extent that it is able by its very nature to separate itself in its acƟvity, from the body, from “pleasures and fears and all the rest of such things.” Socrates then turns to temperance. This is said for the many to spring from a sort of proﬂigacy: “they abstain from one sort of pleasure simply because the longing for another sort and fear of losing it, are too strong for them to resist” (68e). Such a hedonisƟc calculus is then to be contrasted with a measured judgment of the intrinsic worth, or lack of it, of each pleasure. Note again that in both these examples of virtue, courage and temperance, the use of intelligence is contrasted to what we may call a supposed generaƟon from false opposites, or at least of pairs; virtue generated from vice, courage from fear, each springing supposedly from its opposite, or an other. The discussion has once again been couched in the rhetoric of moral terms that Simmias and Cebes so like. The exchange of “pleasures for pleasures, fears for fears” is contrasted with “true virtue,” a

virtue which not only guides the uses of the body, etc. but also, at its best, leaves them behind and takes on the character apparently of an end in itself when “ . . . all our buying and selling is done for intelligence and with its aid,” and even more directly, “no maƩer whether pleasures and fears and all the rest of such things be added or subtracted.” The intensity of the denigraƟon of the body (some other dialogues take a less extreme posiƟon), can be jusƟﬁed by the present context and by its appeal to the interlocutors. Hence ﬁnally, we have the invocaƟon of the puriﬁcatory “mystery rites” which are “not to be despised,” rites in which the “uniniƟated,” those who, in this new version, do not use intelligence rightly, “shall lie in mud,” while those who “have pursued philosophy aright” get to “dwell with the gods.” The irony and perversity of Socrates’s invoking of what “those men who established the mysteries,” and who are called by Socrates the “true philosophers,” cannot be lost on anyone with a sense of humor and an awareness of what he otherwise thinks of BacchanƟc rites and other such enthusiasms. The relevant god to invoke is (or ought to be) rather Apollo than Dionysius. True temperance springs from reﬂecƟon in tranquillity, not the exhausƟon of either proﬂigate or iniƟate. Consider the descripƟon in the Laws, “No creature whatsoever is born with that intelligence, or all that intelligence, which characterizes it in its maturity. Hence, so long as a creature has not yet aƩained its proper level of naƟve sense, it is quite mad, indulging in random cries, and as soon as it has found its feet, in equally random leaps” (Laws 2.672b-d), Or of the lyric poets who are “seized with the Bacchic transport and are possessed” (Ion 534a). This is in contrast to the descripƟon of the transports of the soul of Phaedrus (249d-250d), the vision in which the soul was “iniƟated into that mystery which is rightly accounted blessed among beyond all others,” the contemplaƟon of Beauty itself ﬁnally, so in the Meno: “I believe that you would agree with me [concerning the best method of arriving at a deﬁniƟon] if you had not, as you told me yesterday, to leave before the Mysteries but could stay to be iniƟated” (Meno 76e, cf. 99c). IniƟated, that is, not into the mystery rites of the cult in the city, but rather further conversaƟon with Socrates, to be iniƟated into the cult of dialegesthai. Those fully iniƟated must of course renew the rites from Ɵme to Ɵme in dialogue with others and within themselves.

Socrates, apparently ciƟng a proverbial saying, says that, “Many carry the wand, but Bacchants few are amongst them,” (69c) and concludes, “where by Bacchants I understand them to mean simply those who have pursued philosophy aright”(69c). And certainly it is true that many play at philosophy but few “pursue” it rightly, in Socrates’ view (the quotaƟon can be ironically suggesƟve of the right philosophical concepƟon of the playful use of Eros, as in the upward ascent of the Divided Line through eroƟc dialegesthai). PuriﬁcaƟon then, as I have suggested, is not of knowledge in separaƟon from the contaminaƟons of the evil body. For merely to have turned away from the body towards the soul would sƟll leave many “uniniƟated” in philosophy, as we see before us in Simmias and Cebes. Similarly, in the Republic (Rep. 529), the enthusiast Glaucon, when discussing with Socrates the studies that will prepare the guardians, and the speciﬁc contribuƟon of each study, suggests astronomy, looking “yonder,” as a pracƟce which will turn our “gaze” away from body and towards spirit. He at ﬁrst suggests looking skyward, and is quickly mocked by Socrates for confusing “stargazing” with the mathemaƟcal study of the heavens. What then is the right sense, for the Phaedo of “turning away”? Philosophical puriﬁcaƟon is rather a puriﬁcaƟon of soul in the right and skillful use of “calculaƟon.” In other words, it is a “puriﬁcaƟon” through and of philosophy, hence for example, the ability to disƟnguish true opposites, what makes them so, and crucially, in just what sense they are causes (hence the later arguments of the dialogues). And it is only in that sense that “true virtue is a purging of such things, intelligence itself being a sort of purge” (69c). Since the immediate context is the moral virtue of the philosophers and their puriﬁcaƟon, the related capacity is phronēsis, and the connotaƟon of phronēsis is pracƟcal intelligence, or wisdom. But this is dependent, as we can see in the brief discussion of true and false virtues, on the capacity for deﬁning, hence separaƟng, calculaƟon in the general sense (cf. 65c2, logizesthai, see Burnet’s note) as an epistemological capacity (with ontological consequences) on which authenƟc phronēsis is grounded. We turn next to the arguments for immortality proper, prompted by Cebes’s intervenƟon, in which he avers that “most people,” far from believing that the soul’s fate aŌer death will be either to “lie in mud” or to “dwell with the gods,” (69c) do not even believe that it will conƟnue on

aŌer death—that it will rather be “dispersed like breath or smoke.” The imagery reminds us that we must read the text with an eye to the role of imagisƟc language, and disƟnguishing between what is logos and what is muthos, as we have in the above analyses, for example of what is meant by “puriﬁcaƟon.” Hackforth (58-59, n.2) points to the characterizaƟon of the ﬁrst argument as diamuthologein, but thinks that “here, as in the Apology (Apol. 39e), the word means simply ‘discuss’.” But if my analysis of the text supports the noƟon that we must disƟnguish between what is addressed to Simmias and Cebes and what is addressed to the reader, then the choice of this term once again is likely not accidental. Note as well that what Cebes says that “they” need with regard to immortality will be “no liƩle reassuring [paramuthias] and convincing [pisteōs], that when the man has died, his soul exists, and that it possesses some power and wisdom” (70b2, Gallop transl.) In the Republic it was signiﬁcant that what Glaucon and Adeimantus required was to be “persuaded” that the just life was to be preferred to the unjust, and through a speech that “praised” jusƟce. As Gallop points out, (228, n.15) “the argument from opposites that now follows contains a striking fusion of myth with logic, and the verb diamuthologein may possibly be used with this in mind.” But I will argue that this mixture of logos and muthos can be found in all three arguments for the immortality of the soul, and applies as well to certain aspects of how the Ideas are described. Burger, in The Phaedo: A Platonic Labyrinth, divides the dialogue into a ﬁrst half that fuses muthos and logos and a second half in which there is a “turn to a technē of logos’ that is meant to replace “the genuine philosopher’s understanding of phronēsis as direct contact of the pure psyche with the pure beings” (49-50; see chapter ten, 135-60). But I argue that it is important to see the ﬁguraƟve use of language even in the ﬂight to the logoi. In this regard, it will be instrucƟve to contrast the view of Luc Brisson in Plato the Myth Maker.[7] Brisson traces the development of the muthos/logos disƟncƟon in general in preparaƟon for an analysis of its role for Plato. In parƟcular, he is concerned with the cultural dynamic of myth, analysis of its necessary elements and their social funcƟon, and the evoluƟon of myth in the transiƟon from an oral tradiƟon to a wriƩen one in the cultural transmission and formaƟon of values (see the excellent

detailed appendices for the historical and linguisƟc data and its signiﬁcance). He brings to bear an interesƟng approach that combines cultural anthropology, communicaƟon theory and eventually some philosophical analysis. I ﬁnd the former enlightening but the laƩer problemaƟc. Muthos turns out, not surprisingly, to be platonic rhetoric, a means of achieving speciﬁc community norms through adapƟng the tradiƟonal role of myth to Plato’s chosen ends. The truth of the muthos is ostensibly to be measured against philosophical discourse—a kind of creaƟve co-opƟon. This is as opposed to tradiƟonal myth which is “unfalsiﬁable discourse,” lacking an external referent. (102) Platonic myth is designed to shape and mould the emoƟons of the receivers to good and useful beliefs that will condiƟon their behavior. (74) Brisson starts the philosophical part of his analysis with “the opposiƟon between myth and [Popperian] falsiﬁable discourse” by which he means discourse that is measurable against the facts that are the observable, referenced objects of statements (supported in part by a parƟcular interpretaƟon of passages from the Sophist, contrast Rosen, Plato ’ s Sophist, 291-314). This is followed by “the opposiƟon between myth and argumentaƟve discourse” (These are chapter headings). Of course the noƟons of “falsiﬁability” and of “argumentaƟve discourse” as contrasted to the ﬁcƟons of myth or story do have validity—it is just that they are in my view too limiƟng for the role of myth in Plato. Brisson takes the SocraƟc arguments of the Phaedo for immortality to be “deducƟve” and in his terms “argumentaƟve discourse,” that is, suscepƟble to the test of falsiﬁability and open to logical analysis for internal logical coherence, etc. But I hope to show in detail that it is just here that muthologia at least as metaphorical image-making is already at work. Then, too, the more overtly created myths that Socrates spins in the Republic and Phaedo are valued not merely for their moral contribuƟon to platonic ideals of social cohesion as informed by the philosopher’s vision of the Forms. As Brisson suggests, on the one hand, “the truth or falsity of a [platonic] myth therefore depends on its conformity with the philosopher’s discourse on the intelligible forms in which the individual enƟƟes that are the subjects of this myth parƟcipate” (110). So, for example, “God is perfect and therefore can neither undergo change nor impose any change.” But on the other hand, these are aŌer all for Plato ﬁcƟve enƟƟes—and at

one point it almost seems as if Brisson is not too sure that as culturally alive they are somehow not also then real. So, in the preface to the second ediƟon, Brisson writes that, myth provides reason with the axioms from which it can deduce its most important proposiƟons. A reading of the Meno and the Phaedo shows, in parƟcular how the doctrine of Forms, knowledge of which is re-actualized by the soul, has its origin in what the priests and priestesses relate. (3) This does seem in tension with his main claim that the truth of myth is by reference to the philosopher’s argumentaƟve discourse extrinsic to the myth. The issue then is whether any truth that one wishes to aƩribute to the myth is dependent on extrinsic argument, as Brisson claims, though he also claims that they can be the “source” of “axioms” for that extrinsic argumentaƟve discourse. But certainly for the interlocutors themselves in certain cases, and in the context of the ﬁcƟonal recipients of the ideal city, etc., the measure of what philosophical truth they contain is in the philosophical embodiment of the truths presented in situ —that is, not as dependent on being referenced to “argumentaƟve discourse,” nor to a quasi-religious vision. Consider, for example, Plato’s proposal that the soul is best understood as triparƟte, at war with itself, having a natural kinship with being, etc. It is true that myth in general, considered as a ﬁcƟon, as self-referenƟal is unfalsiﬁable in Brisson’s sense—that is, in contrast to statements that can be referred to fact, or referents outside of the story. By contrast, according to Brisson, the contents of platonic myth have a degree of truth to the extent that they conform to the external philosophical arguments or supposiƟon of the Forms (though again this does not sit well with his claim that they are ﬁnally merely a rhetorical device, a means of persuasion, by contrast to philosophical discourse, cf. 127). But if we consider the image of the triparƟte soul, or the myth of the Cave, etc., as themselves proposing something profound as noeƟc and psychological truth, the noƟon of facts that would ostensibly submit it to potenƟal falsiﬁcaƟon is irrelevant. We may ask, Do these images require an appeal to an external argumentaƟve discourse to evaluate their truth? The problems I think stem in part from two interpretaƟve assumpƟons: 1)

Brisson’s parƟcular epistemological model and a need for a referent for statements based on a certain natural science/proposiƟonal truth concepƟon of knowledge, or 2) when it comes to the knowledge of Forms, an ostensible platonic claim for a direct intuiƟon that underpins the argumentaƟve discourse. In both cases there is an external referent, the ﬁrst Ɵme-bound and inherently unstable, the second stable and outside of Ɵme. I suggest that this is not very useful when applied to Plato, and I have argued against both on textual grounds, as have others. If truth and argument are cashed out in these terms, this really does have the eﬀect of reducing or limiƟng the platonic use of myth to persuasion, which, while it might work for the Myth of Metals, would certainly not ﬁt, for example, the story of the Cave, nor a philosophical reading of the Myth of Er, nor of the many images that are used by Plato that surely are at least intended to contain or illustrate truths without being themselves either deducƟve arguments or referenced to such. If the philosophical sense of puriﬁcaƟon is this capacity for separaƟng, then we must look at the ﬁrst argument for immortality, that of the Cycle of Opposites, in this light. DramaƟcally, this has been prepared for in the dialogue, in part, by the introducƟon of apparent opposites discussed above, and their apparent causal link (e.g., courage resulƟng from fear). Cebes starts: “Most of what you have been saying, Socrates, seems to me excellent, but your view about the soul is one that people ﬁnd it very hard to accept; they suspect that, when it has leŌ the body, it no longer exists anywhere; on the day when a man dies his soul is destroyed and annihilated; immediately upon its departure, its exit, it is dispersed like breath or smoke” (70a). Cebes says that “they” speak so, but he concludes speaking for himself: “ . . . to show that the soul exists when the man has died, and possesses some power and intelligence—well, that, I feel, needs a great deal of persuasive argument.” His later objecƟons at 84c ﬀ., made even aŌer the three arguments for immortality are gone through, concern the possibility that the soul while undergoing successive reincarnaƟons may eventually get “worn out” in the end, and show that he has not in fact assimilated or understood the kind of soul that Socrates has graŌed onto the reincarnaƟon dogma. The main ﬂaw of the ﬁrst argument (oŌen pointed out), which claims that we are caught up in a cycle of Life and

Death, is that it quite obviously presupposes what it sets out to prove. Socrates himself as much as points to both the circularity and hypotheƟcal nature of the argument; “If that is so, if the living are reborn from those that have died, presumably our souls must exist yonder; for they could hardly be born again if they did not exist . . . but if that is not so, we shall need another argument” (70c). What, aŌer all, is meant by “reborn” and “born again”? For something to be born in this sense means for it simply to take on a new form, rather than to come to be. The argument plays on Cebes’s belief in being reborn, that is, in a physical animaƟng at birth by receiving a soul, and simply extends this to the animaƟng soul having “existed” “yonder”—this is introduced as an ancient doctrine and the argument is really just a restaƟng of it, combining the tradiƟon of life aŌer death in Hades, with the “ancient doctrine” of Orphic reincarnaƟon for the ﬁrst half, that is, for life of the soul before death. This is called “good evidence” and yet framed hypotheƟcally, with a further confusion of the inclusion in the premise of what is to be concluded, and a verbal ambiguity concerning gignesthai.[8] Cebes does not pick up on it, and simply responds, “Just so.” However, the posiƟve contribuƟon to the developing thesis comes in the ampliﬁcaƟon that Socrates provides to the introducƟon of opposites as in fact cyclically generaƟng each other. And again, much depends on just how the descripƟon of this generaƟng is heard, on the sense given to it by the interlocutors, as contrasted to the reader. There are, of course, problems with both the examples chosen and the nature of generaƟon or cause, but these are subjects to be taken up again later in the dialogue, and we are meant, I suggest, to see the problems. It is only because Cebes is Ɵed to a more or less physical and literal interpretaƟon of varying doxai, that he does not object to saying: i) that opposites which follow one another in Ɵme cause one another, ii) that they always will follow one another in endless cycle, iii) that things that seem to be natural pairs in whatever ways, will be inextricably caught up in such a cycle. But none of these three is so, and a few negaƟve examples are provided below. It is only because of his ready adherence to the noƟon, or rather the image in an eikasƟc doxa, of the Cycle as an aƩracƟve cosmic principle governing “coming into being (in the) animal and vegetable world,” and his evident

lack of any logical skills, that he is content to apply it to the cycle of Life and Death. Socrates: “Are we saƟsﬁed that all coming to be means the coming to be of an opposite thing from its opposite?” Cebes: “Quite saƟsﬁed” (74a). Indeed, it will turn out, and this is the posiƟve element, that if one chooses the opposites properly, and conceives of them correctly, that is, has an image of them derived by dianoia, a dianoeƟc eikasia, then Socrates is quite prepared to be serious that they always go together, and imply one another. And that such opposites, e.g., odd and even, never being present in the same existent, are in some sense causes, not however in the literal sense of a cause of coming into being and passing away such as Cebes is led to believe. For the idea of one thing to be linked to the idea of another as its opposite, even when done so legiƟmately, does not mean that either is the cause of the physical becoming of the thing so described. Though opposites may be in some sense the cause of what something is in so far as it is intelligible, only the form of the Good is said to be the cause as well of that they are.[9] Smaller does imply bigger, but the smaller thing does not cause the bigger one to become bigger, though if it or something were not so it would make no sense to call the other one smaller. Similarly, that the child outgrows the father is not caused by the opposiƟon of shorter and taller, nor does the cycle conƟnue, obviously. Whatever the historical origin of the concept of a cycle of paired opposites,[10] Socrates simply puts these doxai to work in the present case, subsƟtuƟng coming from for being or coming together, and adding that the coming from goes in either direcƟon. Life and the living is opposite to death and the dead, and being alive follows in a cycle with being dead. Once having introduced the noƟon of processes and the model of going to sleep and waking up, Socrates is able to ask, “Shall we not supply the opposite process to balance dying? Is Nature to be lame on one side . . . ?” (71e) And because Cebes has no clear noƟon of cause and cannot make the disƟncƟon between logical processes and physical processes, between logical necessity (were that the case with a parƟcular pair) and the conƟngency of nature, he is ready to supply the laƩer natural processes as grounding a necessary “coming to life again.” But this cycle will not even provide what Cebes takes it to provide. For, if the argument is to make any sense, by the being dead before and aŌer we

must mean some kind of actual life in Hades—for otherwise we would be stuck with death itself, or the dead bodies, whichever we take the actual opposite of living to be, as that which Living comes from; and so we subsƟtute for being dead, “being in the place for the dead,” where there are souls waiƟng to pass again into being alive. We need to suppose that by “the dead” is meant those who conƟnue to have souls, which is again to have assumed what we set out to prove. Summarizing the errors of the argument in general, we can see how these errors point us in the right direcƟon through what the reader is thus led to infer as, by contrast, replacing them: a) opposites are discussed in terms of becoming, coming to be, generaƟon, hence physical nature is assumed and stressed as the meaning of being, and similarly, a discussion of opposites that begins with comparaƟve terms of quality (taller, greater) is groundlessly extended to include all becoming; b) opposites understood physically do not, as is suggested, always temporally follow one another— colder now need not ever be followed by warmer later, but they do follow one another inexorably ontologically—each is what it is with reference to the possibility and idenƟty of the other; c) sequence is confused with cause; d) not all opposites are so in the same sense or relaƟon; e) all opposites are pairs but not all pairs are opposites (brothers and eyes are pairs but not opposites); f) a logical subject is confounded with an existenƟal one. Some or all of these errors have been pointed out in various places in the literature. But one ought to ask what the unitary cause of such errors is. And rather than ascribing such obvious mistakes to Plato I have suggested that they are rooted in the shortcomings of Simmias and Cebes, and of their spiritual brethren. Further, that there is an alternaƟve view developed at the same Ɵme—a secular view of separaƟon which solely invokes the acƟve capacity of soul to make careful disƟncƟons, unaided and unimpeded by the body, the very thing that the careful reader is brought to do by ﬂaws of the argument at the literal level. Indeed, if we were to imagine the souls of Simmias and Cebes passing to the other world without the insights and developed capacity for separaƟng, that is, sƟll burdened by their current doxai, then it would seem that the mere physical separaƟon of body from soul would not have prepared the unburdened soul to see signiﬁcantly more clearly the unencumbered true objects or beings. The implicit task of the calculaƟon

of just what opposites really are, and how they are both separate yet together, is itself a manifesƟng both of the true separateness of soul itself, and of the separability of opposites, taken together, from their passing instanƟaƟons. The present passages are a ﬁrst indicaƟon of the limits on the meaning of separateness and hence on the immortality of soul and independence of Ideas when stripped of their mythological garb, of and the necessary reassurances provided to Simmias and Cebes. Nicholas Denyer in “The Phaedo’s Final Argument,”[11] thinks that the argument from the cycle of opposites for the immortality of the soul is moderately successful: “weak enough to be plausible, yet strong enough to come surprisingly close to yielding the conclusion that a soul is something immortal and indestrucƟble” (87). But it seems to me that Denyer hedges in linking soul to being alive, which, as the principle of being ensouled, cannot cease to be soul without ceasing to be alive, “soul can never come to be dead, not even by perishing” (95). Cebes is leŌ behind—“as if the immortality which implies eternity were the same as the immortality which is implied by the inability to become dead.” But Denyer think the argument can be patched up by bringing in once more the noƟon of being alive—“So if a soul perishes, it comes to be dead. But no soul, so we have earlier argued, can ever come to be dead, not even at the price of perishing. So no soul ever dies.” But while it may be argued that aliveness is essenƟal to what it is to be a soul, the inextricable link would apply only to logical or deﬁniƟonal possibility—a dead soul would no longer be really a soul. But being essenƟal to the deﬁniƟon is it seems to me confounded with being essenƟal to exisƟng as such? And in any event would apply only to soul in general not to any individual soul. Kenneth Dorter[12] ﬁnds in the ﬁrst argument the beginnings of a resoluƟon to the paradox that “death is beƩer than life and yet suicide is forbidden.” He sees the limitaƟons of the ﬁrst argument if taken to validly lead to personal immortality, but holds that there are in eﬀect three levels to be found therein (see 42-43). First is the level of convenƟonal religion, the comforƟng of Simmias and Cebes and the “child within each of us.” Second, more abstract but not able to saƟsfy the emoƟonal demands of the ﬁrst, is a mere vital principle that animates the cycle of life and death. Third, more abstract sƟll, a “principle of energy” a “world-soul” stuﬀ that

supplies the need in the argument, as Dorter sees it, for an underlying enƟty for the cycle (36), albeit supporƟng only Life in general, a life stuﬀ parallel to a body stuﬀ. The third level is argued for as present in an implicit “argument from moƟon,” and Dorter admits that the term “world-soul” nowhere occurs in the text. An immaterial “world-soul” stuﬀ would seem to me to be lapsing back into muthologia. Dorter is willing to say that the Ideas are “not a separate world but the raƟonal essence of this one,” and I would already ﬁnd this too subjecƟve a view of the Ideas. They are “disƟnguished from conƟngent factors and thus from individuaƟon, so that we transcend the material realm not by ignoring it but by comprehending it—by observing the universal, raƟonal and permanent within parƟcularity and transience” (27-28). Why then is he not willing to say something similar of the soul? And if the “metaphoric” and “incantatory” character of the muthologia is seen for what it is, then one ought not to strain to raƟonalize the muthos as “meant to supplement reason by appealing to our imaginaƟon and emoƟons” (8). Simmias and Cebes need to be “convinced” or assuaged of their fear. As for the child in Socrates or in us, the best medicine is to explicate what disƟnguishes the adult truths about what is worthy of fear from the childish fears, and in that explicaƟon to direct our aƩenƟon away from the immediate circumstances of Socrates’s impending death to the reality of his life. It is for this reason that he refuses the admoniƟon to conserve his energy and talk less, lest he have to drink the poison a second or third Ɵme. Any concepƟon of a “world-soul” is an unnecessary distracƟon (Cf. Burger, 68.) For a more saƟsfactory noƟon of opposites and of the moƟons of both these and of the soul in relaƟon to them we shall have to wait for the following chapters on the Phaedo. (I skip the exhausƟon of souls ampliﬁcaƟon, the simple response being that life may come from what has not yet died, etc.) THE RECOLLECTION ARGUMENT: REALITY, ITS IMAGES, AND THE LIFE OF THE SOUL The second proof is based on the Theory of RecollecƟon or anamnēsis, and is introduced by Cebes. “There is another theory which, if true, points the same way . . . that learning is really just recollecƟon, from which it follows

presumably that what we now call to mind we have learnt at some previous Ɵme” (72e). At which point Simmias intervenes and asks, “But how is that proved?” Cebes’s reply is laughably vague; “When asked some quesƟons they produce right answers to anything of their own accord, providing the quesƟoning is done properly. Secondly, if you confront people with a diagram you have the plainest proof possible” (73a). Cebes’s comments in themselves are certainly not proofs and I take it that the point is precisely to disƟnguish memory from recollecƟon: Cebes has been reminded of what Socrates has in the past been “constantly asserƟng”—he has a memory of the events, and of the dogma, that “learning is just recollecƟon,” and that it somehow follows from this “that what we now call to mind we have learnt at some previous Ɵme; which would not be possible unless our souls existed somewhere before being born in this human frame.” Plato’s reference for the reader is probably to the Meno,[13] but also to what Cebes remembers Socrates’s as “constantly asserƟng.” And these vague memories Cebes calls “excellent argument(s),” and “the plainest proof of the point in quesƟon,” as if the mere menƟoning of the “proof” were itself demonstraƟon. But what is “quesƟoning done properly” and what does “of their own accord” mean, and most importantly, what is the account of these that necessitates “recollecƟon,” and what is the proper understanding of that acƟvity? His second argument and “proof” is even more laughable, more vague, something about just confronƟng people with “anything in the nature of a diagram”— he knows that it has something to do with that, vaguely remembers, but what? Commentators solemnly point out that this surely refers to the Meno, and to the visible shapes and diagrams of the Republic (Rep.510d), and it is true that we the reader are so reminded, but a signiﬁcant dramaƟc point is here to see as well, that Cebes repeats these vague memories just as he would the dogmas of Pythagoreanism, that the reiteraƟon of these are themselves precisely not proofs, and that he oﬀers them as such—in sum, that he doesn’t know what a proof or an argument really is. Hackforth notes[14] that a more literal translaƟon would be “diagrams or something else of that sort” but he fails to see the irony of Cebes’s general vagueness, of his “something else of that sort,” and of his taking this bare

menƟoning of it as “the plainest proof of the point in quesƟon”—this, in response to Simmias having asked, “But how is that proved?” Finally, just to stress the inadequacy of Cebes’s report cum proof, Socrates adds, “And if that doesn’t convince you, Simmias, I will suggest another consideraƟon to which you may perhaps agree,”(73b3-4) and he sets out the argument we are about to look at. But not before Simmias too is unmasked. For Simmias says that he is really “not skepƟcal,” but that what he really needs is “just what we are talking about, namely to recollect” (73a7) (deomai mathein peri hou ho logos, anamnēsthēnai) by which he means remember beƩer. For as he adds, “In point of fact, thanks to Cebes’s seƫng out of the arguments, I do already almost remember [ēdē memnēmai] and am almost convinced; all the same, I should like now to hear how you yourself have set them out” (73b8-10). I make such a fuss about it because once again, as in the Republic, it is important to contrast the level at which the interlocutors are operaƟng, with which they are saƟsﬁed, and that of the reader, which is to be indicated by contrast. The immediate philosophical importance of this disƟncƟon of levels here will be the way in which immortality, and hence the Ideas are to be understood.[15] The ﬁrst example is, when having “seen or heard, or some other sense perceived something, (we) may come to know something other than that, that is, we may think of something else other than that, may think of something else besides that, something that is the object of a diﬀerent knowledge.” And so, in the ﬁrst example, the lyre I now see can remind me of the owner, parƟcularly if I have some vivid feeling for the owner; a man is diﬀerent than a lyre, but “how a lover feels when he sees a lyre or a cloak or some other object commonly used by his beloved,” is a kind of recollecƟon, or an introducƟon to it. Now we note that in the very ﬁrst example, there is a dissimilarity of kind, the lyre does not look like its owner. Secondly, there is an eroƟc moƟve, sƟmulus or natural connecƟon, just as, it will be claimed, there is a natural and acƟve rapport between the knowing soul’s world of its present experiences, even the most elementary of them, and the nonvisible look of what it cognizes. To conƟnue then, a present X, by associaƟon with an absent Y reminds us of that Y, regardless of the fact that it has nothing visibly in common with it. But the result of

this reminding is said to be that the lover “conceives in his mind the form of the boy to whom it belongs.” Now this is in one sense obviously the visible form of the boy. And yet, our recollecƟon of someone is not strictly speaking of their physical appearance, the details of which we oŌen could not be sure of. Rather, it is the total person, their way of being that we remember and are made to call up. There is a marvelous passage in Proust that makes this point beauƟfully.[16] (The reader is forewarned that the following example, though it makes my point, is provocaƟve, not to say perverse.) The central character is describing a young girl of his youth: Ses yeux noirs brillaient et, comme je ne savais pas alors, ni ne l’ai appris depuis, réduire en ses éléments objecƟfs une impression forte, comme je n’avais pas, ainsi qu’on dit, assez‘d’esprit d’observaƟon’pour dégager la noƟon de leur couleur, pendant longtemps, chaque fois que je repensai à elle, le souvenir de leur éclat se présentait aussitôt à moi comme celui d’un vif azur, puisqu’elle était blonde; de sorte que, peut- être si elle n’avait pas eu des yeux aussi noirs—ce qui frappait tant la première fois qu’on la voyait—je n’aurais pas été, comme je le fus, plus parƟculièrement amoureux en elle, de ses yeux bleus. (A la recherche du temps perdu, 186) It is not because she is a blonde that he recalls her eyes as a vivid azure, (though this is why it is recalled as this parƟcular color) but rather because, as he puts it, like most of us, it is the total impression that we remember, and that she had strikingly beauƟful eyes—the very feature of which he found himself “parƟculièrement amoureux.” This feature represents the total “impression forte” which cannot be reduced to “ses éléments objecƟfs.” In one sense, since dialecƟc involves just such a taking apart and puƫng back together again, an analysis of the whole in terms of its parts, this is, one would think, not a good example. The young man made an error; he did not remember the color of the eyes correctly. But in another sense this illustrates well just what Socrates means. The memory of their “éclat” is so vivid, and recalls so well to him the totality of the image of the young girl, that it serves well its purpose—and so the beauƟful irony of Proust’s last sentence: “ . . . si elle n’avait pas eu des yeux

noirs—ce qui frappait tant la première fois qu’on la voyait—je n’aurais pas été, comme je le fus, plus parƟculièrement amoureux, en elle, de ses yeux bleus.” Another, more famous passage in Proust, at the very beginning of the book, has to do with the famous madeleine cake. Every Ɵme the hero sees, and more speciﬁcally, tastes a madeleine, a whole world of his childhood is summoned up, more parƟcularly, the image of his aunt and her world, with whom the cake, its crumbled pieces in a cup of tea served up to him, is associated. And Proust goes on to make the further point, peculiarly Platonic so it seems to me, that the recollecƟon of all this is summoned up quite automaƟcally when he has the present experience of tasƟng once again a madeleine, but that any conscious aƩempt to draw upon his memory has liƩle success by comparison, and produces only a faint image of the past. Just as the lyre or any object associated with a loved one is an experience of something that carries with it the power to summon up the vivid recollecƟon of its owner. This will be parƟcularly important when we come to talk of the relaƟon of the soul to Ideas and of Ideas to parƟculars. This theme is one that Proust returns to Ɵme and again, and one might say that it is the very theme of the whole book—an examinaƟon of the sense in which the world present is constructed around and out of the world past, whether individual or cultural, that is the collecƟve framework for the interpretaƟon of our present reality. Of course, this example is somewhat intenƟonally perverse, given the tradiƟonal interpretaƟon of Plato’s view of sense data, percepƟon and the Ideas. I do not mean to suggest that veriﬁcaƟon of sense percepƟon is not also important, nor to minimize the ﬂux argument in Plato, such as it is. Returning to our text, the next example is that of “seeing a picture” of a horse or lyre and being reminded of the owner, or a picture of Simmias and being reminded of Cebes, or of Simmias and being reminded of Simmias himself. The “picture” is of course the introducƟon of the concept of an image that is indeed less vivid, less real, and an imitaƟon of the original of which it is an image—and this relaƟon is uƟlized as an image when it comes to talking of the sense in which equal things “fall short” of Equality itself. But here, the point is rather our relaƟon to the image, to the list of diﬀering examples of recollecƟon through an image—in all of these cases we “may be reminded of things either by something like them or by

something unlike them” (74a). The picture does not look exactly like its original, but then neither does the lyre look like the young boy, yet we bridge this diﬀerence by our ability to respond to the image as image. The sense of both “like” and “unlike” is in fact mulƟple; it can be both in order of vivacity (picture versus object) and visual resemblance, and of kind (lyre- person). And this is true of relaƟons of the non-visible of “resemblance” and recollecƟon. Thus there are really two points stressed here by Plato— that the picture or image is less in some way less perfect than the original, but equally important, that of an acƟve associaƟon by and through a non- visible relaƟon, that is, being reminded by something of something else that in no way physically resembles it. To use Proust’s example once again, I recollect the girl, I know her inƟmately and accurately in spite of the error I make in my memory, and even, it seems, in my sense percepƟon at the Ɵme of the original experience. Socrates turns next to consider the case of like things, and asks whether “when it is by something like the other thing” that we recollect, a picture is just an example, “are we not certain to ﬁnd ourselves doing something else besides, namely asking ourselves whether the similarity between the object and the thing it reminds us of is defecƟve [elleipei] or not” (74a). Whenever we note the resemblance of two things, Socrates says, we at the same Ɵme wonder about the unlikeness of the two, that is, the parƟcular unlikeness that belongs to things that are like one another, the falling short or defecƟveness of one in comparison to another. This kind of unlikeness of what is similar can be either of kind or degree. The picture of Simmias is like Simmias in that it is an image of him, which serves to remind us of him. But it is at the same Ɵme only a picture, we know it as an image, hence in its diﬀerence in kind, while it is likely that other animals cannot recognize an image as an image. We do not always, in fact probably rarely, consciously say to ourselves this is only an image. [17] But this is just the point—in our ability to use the image, to ignore its immediate features for what it resembles or “reminds us of,” we see the image as image; we show our awareness of its falling short in our ability to ignore it, to see the image as image, though it is not this that we “aƩend” to. Indeed, it is only in this ignoring, which is at the same Ɵme vaguely conscious, that we are able to transcend the image and aƩend to what it is

about. Of course, the quality of the drawing, painƟng or sculpture, etc. its beauty, is itself the form that the meaning takes—and this, far from being ignored, is what contains and conveys the maker’s meaning—but the image as image, in its diﬀerence from what it represents, is what must be ignored or transcended. But because the image does resemble the original, we are led automaƟcally, pre-philosophically as part of everyday human being, to wonder about how good an image it is, about the degree of resemblance. Even when put posiƟvely, when we say for instance that that is a really good picture or image of X, we are always implicitly, and someƟmes consciously, saying that it approaches, and hence falls short, of the original. It is important to note that we say this about many diﬀerent kinds of image, again in pre-philosophical terms—we talk about movies, books, news stories, in short, many diﬀerent kinds of discourse as approaching well or badly the reality of what they are talking about. And even when we think that it is next to impossible to capture the whole truth of the case, yet we somehow hold this out as a standard and a goal. Of course we also talk about things falling short of our expectaƟons, and there we tend to say that we have a picture or an image of how things ought to be by which we measure what is happening before us, being presented before our eyes, so to speak. Now is this “falling short,” whether by our discourse of the way things are, or by the way things are of our standards, a diﬀerence of degree or of kind? Clearly it is meant by Plato to be both. The painƟng is less real than the original, in part just because the laƩer is taken as the standard for the former (insofar as the painƟng is taken to be about its subject). Even if we go beyond verisimilitude, the painƟng is sƟll trying to get at the truth about the person in a good portrait, about his character for example, or the truth about the bowl of fruit, as with Cezanne. (Or a truth—consider two painƟngs with the same subject.) But we may also consider the falling short that results, not from the approximaƟve nature of our images of the truth, but rather the diﬀerence between a painƟng and an original per se— and an indiﬀerent painƟng is as deﬁcient as a great one. That is, there is a larger sense for which Plato intends diﬀerence to be paradigmaƟc of the diﬀerence between any form of discourse and that which it is about, that which it is trying to get at, and get right. Then we are talking not about a diﬀerence in degree but about a diﬀerence of kind—in which a logos is

never an Idea. It is for this reason that Socrates begins with an associaƟon of unlike things, the lyre and the boy. They are in fact like as kinds, in that they are both physical, their unlikeness is that they do not look like one another; the associaƟon is based on something that links them in a non- visible way, and this possibility is representaƟve of the diﬀerence in kind that is gone beyond, transcended, in the associaƟon of equal things with Equality itself. Hence Equality does not look equal the way equal logs do, as a physical appearance judged so in discourse. But at the same Ɵme there is a diﬀerence of degree, hence the judgments of our discourse either about experience or about the discourse itself are measured by a standard, from which they fall short, but which they also approach by degree of truth. Note that Socrates does not say here that the objects are defecƟve or fall short but that the similarity is defecƟve (though later the objects are said to “strive” to overcome their diﬀerence—clearly metaphor). It is not that the equal logs are literally measured against Equality itself and somehow found to be lacking by a bit, but that there is a diﬀerence in kind, represented in our inability to be certain about whether the logs we experience are or are not equal, or in a discourse with someone else with whom we disagree about whether the logs are equal, the statues beauƟful, the city just, but about which we argue in a search for a common measure. But the diﬀerence in kind is also a diﬀerence in degree, and what we argue about or through is which of our discourses is more meaningful; not what our words mean but what they ought to mean, to be a beƩer image of what we are trying, in common, to get at. Diﬀerence in degree is relevant when we compare one approximaƟon to another, a comparison that only makes sense in respect to a noƟon of a standard against which we would wish to measure both, while diﬀerence of kind is relevant when we are comparing each instance to that of which it is a reminder.[18] It is only at this point, aŌer his having goƩen agreement on the idea that in being reminded of the sameness of something we always are implicitly also asking about the diﬀerence or defecƟveness of the similarity, that Socrates brings forth once again the Theory of Ideas. It is against the background of our convenƟonal recollecƟng, our being reminded of one thing that is not present by another thing that is present, whether like or unlike, that the theory is brought up. It is introduced, as before, as

something like a shared belief; “We maintain, do we not, that there is such a thing as equality, not the equality of one log to another, but . . . equality itself” (74a9-11). Simmias answers, for both of them, “Most assuredly we may, not a doubt of it.” And, Socrates asks, “we have knowledge of it, in and by itself?” “Certainly we have.” There are diﬀerent and conﬂicƟng interpretaƟons of what follows as an example at 74b: whether two actual logs are perceived by the same person as someƟmes equal, someƟmes unequal, depending on the Ɵme, or perspecƟve; or is it the disagreement of two people about whether the two logs are of equal length or not; or is it the physical nature of the logs themselves such that they are never quite actually equal, just as the drawn circle is never quite actually round. Is it that the logs remain the same, and provoke diﬀerent percepƟons, or is it that the logs themselves are never quite accurately knowable? Is the deﬁciency in the knower or the known? But for the present purposes I am not sure how much it maƩers (but see Sedley 2007), for in any of these cases the experience we have of equal provokes the thought of equality itself, the standard which we acƟvely employ when we speak of what is presently before us. The quesƟon is not, at this point, whether there is an Idea of Equality itself, that is assumed, but rather “where do we get such knowledge from?” (Two people might very well have the same standard and sƟll disagree, or agree without suﬃcient reason, or agree and be both wrong, etc.) Now in some sense we get this knowledge, as something present to our minds, from the experience that provokes our judgment: “Didn’t they” “the equal logs . . . or whatever they were that we saw” “lead us to conceive of that other something?” But what is it that disƟnguishes the experience itself from that which it provokes? It is the fact that in any of the senses given above the equal things and/or our judgments about them, change. They are the subject of discussion, while the “equals themselves,” what various equals provoke or call to mind in pracƟce, have never, it is asserted, “appeared to you to be unequal, or equality to be inequality.” This is not a claim about their ontological status, that is either assumed or yet to be demonstrated. It is a claim about the diﬀerence between a measure and that which is measured by it—and the phenomenological claim is that we never have the experience, it has never “appeared” to us that “equality be inequality.” Of course only the logs

sensibly appear one way or another. It is to another kind of vision (albeit at the same moment), that of the intellect, that equality appears when provoked by what does visibly appear. And of this experience of the intellect it is true to say that we at least know what we mean, that is, that we cannot think to ourselves or speak intelligibly if we do not mean one thing at a Ɵme by a given term. We can change our minds about what a term means, or mean diﬀerent things by it in diﬀerent senses or diﬀerent contexts, but individually we must and do mean what we say in a given instance; then we can argue, discuss, whether the present case is one of equality or not. Moreover, behind our disagreements is oŌen a diﬀerent use of the same name or term, which at least in principle we would aim to reach agreement on. It is precisely this experience and this capacity to strive for agreement, both intellectual and social (or of agreement of our own diﬀering percepƟons, or of our percepƟon with our logos), which the sophist denies. For the sophist, disagreement is essenƟally negaƟve in its implicaƟons; the diﬀerence is accepted, transformed into nihilism, and discourse serves the only master leŌ, that is, individual desire, power, and the body. While for the philosopher, disagreement is accepted as the basis or beginning and transformed into dialecƟcal search. There may be diﬀerent kinds of equality, diﬀerent kinds of jusƟce, and one may try to determine whether they have enough in common to deserve the common name (so, with courage) but in each case the term in use is itself univocal, and the issue is whether it is correctly applied or not, and where it comes from. To stress this, Socrates again points out that while Equality itself may be “either like those others or unlike . . . that point is immaterial; but so long as the sight of one thing leads you to conceive another, whether like it or unlike, a case of reminder must have occurred” (74e). The unlikeness can be taken in two diﬀerent senses, either that the Idea is unlike its exemplar because it is diﬀerent in kind, or because it does not maƩer as concerns recalling whether the judgment of percepƟon is correct or not. Even if one has made an error, and the logs are in fact not equal, which, say, is what the other person asserts, you sƟll have in mind what the experience has called forth, the idea of equality, and you sƟll understand what you mean by that, as does the other person, or there could in fact be no disagreement. Which is not to say that it is not important to sort out who is correct, or for oneself, to sort out when one is

right. Being wrong about the logs may (or may not) be trivial, but being wrong about whether what is before me is a case of jusƟce (or injusƟce) is surely not. And we do need to get clear about the standards themselves, hence we discuss not only whether this is a case of such and such, but also what we are to mean by, say, jusƟce. The issue at this point in the dialogue, is the contrast between what changes and is disputed and that which we set up, if hypotheƟcally, as the measure of the changing and disputed. The permanence of the Ideas is here not defended, or explained, but is itself taken as given, as, in a sense, itself a hypothesis—the hypothesis of permanence (or Being) as opposed to the hypothesis as the parƟcular Idea at work as standard. It is the contrast between this ﬁrmness and the changeable that is stressed, regardless of whether that changeableness has its source in percepƟon or in objects. Socrates then returns (74d) to the noƟon of deﬁciency, literally a “falling short,” and asks, “Is there some deﬁciency in respect of the likeness of the former to the laƩer, or is there none?” To which the reply is, “Yes, a considerable deﬁciency.” Again, more literally translated, “It falls short by a great deal.” The verb for this is endeō, which means both to be lacking or deﬁcient or to be in want of, the impersonal form being “there is a need or want of.” The physical metaphor of what is measured somehow “falling short” of the measure, equal things of Equality itself, is appealing to Simmias. But just for that reason the metaphorical nature of the language is lost on him. And so he replies, “Falling short by a great amount,” as if the equal things were literally measured against the Equal—which is of course ridiculous, since whatever the diﬀerence is between the two it is not a quanƟtaƟve measure, as if one could say by how much the logs fall short of Equality. This is parƟcularly the case with something like equals, in the literal sense of calculaƟon. Hence the irony of the example points us beyond it to just how not to conceive the Idea-object relaƟon. In the case of jusƟce, there may be some situaƟons etc. that are more just than others, and a standard becomes more interesƟng to the degree that this is so, or arguable. But even here, there is sƟll a qualitaƟve diﬀerence between the most just case and the standard by which it is measured, and it is here that the discrepancy lies. (What this diﬀerence is, is much disputed—whether Ideas are to be thought of as paradigms or as

universals, or as Gallop suggests, someƟmes one, someƟmes the other.)[19] The other aspect of the meaning of this verb, that of to be in need or want, allows Socrates to introduce the noƟon of “striving”: “Then when someone sees a certain object and says to himself ‘The thing I am looking at wants to be like something else, but it can resemble that other thing only defecƟvely, as an inferior copy,’ may we agree that what he is saying necessarily implies a previous knowledge of that which he ﬁnds the object seen to resemble defecƟvely?”(74e) Two ideas are introduced here at the same Ɵme, that of the “striving” of what falls short to be like its original, of which it is an “inferior copy,” and the second idea, that this “necessarily implies previous knowledge,” as an arƟst sees the original before he paints it. But again we note that it is the metaphorical sense that is at work here, that since falling short can also mean “to be in want of” it is a natural extension of the metaphor to characterize the thing that falls short as “striving” to fulﬁll and overcome that lack, to bridge or ﬁll that unﬁllable gap. And it is just as metaphorical to call the defecƟve thing an “inferior copy” (in the way that a painted portrait would be) since in no sense does the equal thing visually look like the original, Equality. If we recall that recollecƟon is to apply to the unlike as well, and in some sense must do so, other problems arise. It obviously would make no sense to say that the lyre of the ﬁrst example strives to be like its owner, the “thing we are reminded of.” Even of the “like,” the portrait does not strive to become in itself like the person—to strive to overcome its deﬁciency would be to strive to lose its two-dimensionality, but then it would cease to be a portrait or image. It resembles, while the striving proper is in the tension of diﬀerence, which we strive to overcome. Taken literally, the metaphor not only is misunderstood but in itself makes no sense. We are thus forewarned about being careful in what follows with regard to where that knowledge comes from and in what sense it is previous, for the only sense in which the ﬁrst part of what is said, about striving and falling short at all implies the second part about previous knowledge is metaphorical—with the arƟst in mind, the process of copying presupposes the pre-existence of the original, a copy comes aŌer the original in a temporal process. But as with the previous argument about the cycle of Life and Death, even were it to make sense as more than a

metaphor, that in any given case an original precedes the copy does not mean that the original cannot have been itself a copy, hence have occurred within the same Ɵme frame (as with Life from Life). To suppose otherwise, one must suppose that all copies come to be at the same Ɵme, as in the previous argument, that all lives come to be at the same Ɵme (and all cease at the same Ɵme, in the case of the “life must come from death or all would cease” argument). Thus while it is clear that the senses provide only the occasion for knowledge, and that while they lead us to it they do not produce it, it follows only that the Equal itself is something other than percepƟon and that we use it as the measure of percepƟon (and so in the case of other judgments of experience). While the individual act of measurement may require that the measuring instrument be had prior to the thing measured (and even this could be challenged), it does not follow that it and all the others are originally got at some temporal moment prior to all experience, as in a pre-natal state. That is, it does not follow that, “before we ever began to see or hear or otherwise perceive things we must, it seems, have possessed knowledge of the equal itself, if we are going to refer the equal things of our sense percepƟons to that standard, conceiving that all such objects are doing their best to resemble it, yet are inferior to it” (75b). It is the animisƟc image of doing their best, of striving to overcome their deﬁciency, which is seducƟve for Simmias and Cebes; as with all mystery religions it is diﬃcult for the adherents to disƟnguish metaphor from literal truth. Which is not to deny the truth of the metaphor. That is, Plato really does believe that the things measured by Ideas really do have less reality, less stability in their natures, are less self-idenƟcal—and he believes that, for many reasons, not the least of which is that they are composite. He also would assert that it makes serious sense to speak of the role of Eros as a kind of moƟon, both of the soul and in a strange way of the things themselves.
