But what he would not permit himself, as is indicated by the simplisƟc errors of the argument at the literal level, is a spaƟo-temporal noƟon of the Ideas or the Soul, hence of a pre-existence or an aŌerlife for either. There are other, posiƟve reasons for what is here obvious only by denial. I note here only that the errors of the argument correspond to the confusion by the interlocutors, and other adherents, of legiƟmate muthos and metaphor taken literally, speciﬁcally with regard to space and Ɵme. It is

perhaps the deepest irony of human belief that those who claim a spiritual credo and to be above this material life in their values are those who place the soul-thing in some other Ɵme and place before and aŌer this Ɵme and place. That Simmias and Cebes, or the child within them, is fearful of death, ironically is the source, or at least the accomplice, of the need for a literal-minded before and aŌer. The best that Socrates can do, as in the Republic, is to soothe the child, in at least a more likely story than that with which they began. To return to the argument, the issue is sƟll just where we get these standards from. The concepƟons arise “from seeing or touching, or some other form of sense percepƟon,” but this is only their occasion. Yet, it is said, these occasions have been with us since birth: “We have been seeing and hearing things, and employing other senses from the very moment we were born,” and so, the argument goes, we must have been employing these standards from that very moment, hence have goƩen them prior to that. Empirically, we do not in fact use our senses well from birth, do not measure or calculate well from the moment of birth, yet we do begin to sort things out from the beginning, and this ability or capacity is applied to experience on the occasion of it, not produced by it. But Simmias and Cebes are convinced that this prior knowledge by which we judge things is got “before we were born.” Socrates extends this knowledge to cover all those things to which we “aﬃx our seal and mark as being ‘the thing itself,’ “signiﬁcantly, “when we put our quesƟons and give our answers.” It is ambiguous, I think, whether we employ these things to which we “aﬃx our seal” in the discussion involving quesƟon and answer, or is it about these things that we put our quesƟons and answers, in determining whether they merit that seal and mark of “the thing itself.” If indeed it is both, then we would give a diﬀerent descripƟon of just how and when the knowledge of these is got. In any event, the claim here is that “we must have possessed the knowledge before we were born.” Socrates then expands the descripƟon to cover other Ideas, those of “the beauƟful itself, the good itself, the just, the holy,” and to everything of which we say “the thing itself,” remembering that Simmias and Cebes began the conversaƟon with an agreement that these exist. These sorts of things clearly are not provoked by the experiences of the senses, and so not since birth. Yet they are

lumped together with those which are provoked by the senses, and it is true that these are used as standards by which we measure the experiences to which they apply. But this does not in itself commit us to an explanaƟon of how they are produced, other than to say that the experiences themselves, since we argue about them, do not produce or resolve the issue, hence the quesƟons and answers. The “recovery of old knowledge” through an associaƟon of either like or unlike, “whether by resemblance or contrast” is the deﬁniƟon of RecollecƟon. This “recovery” (analambanō, to take up again, recover, retrieve) must follow the same paƩern as with qualiƟes of sensibles, being reminded by what presents itself—therefore, since “the argument applies with equal force to the beauƟful itself, good itself, just itself . . . ” etc., “direcƟng our senses to the object” must have for such things either a metaphorical sense or a counterpart. The jusƟﬁcaƟon of the deﬁniƟon of learning as recollecƟon for both kinds of object is then repeated: “The reason being that we found it was possible for a person who had seen or heard or otherwise perceived an object to go on to conceive another object which he had forgoƩen, something with which the ﬁrst object was connected, whether by resemblance or contrast” (76a). The jusƟﬁcaƟon of the deﬁniƟon of recollecƟon as “recovery of old knowledge” is in the suggesƟve experience —the image of recollecƟon by associaƟon through either like or unlike, “it does not maƩer.” This is not memory (as might be the case with like) but an acƟve construcƟon of the intellect. AssociaƟon or “calling up” what has been “forgoƩen,” may be either a new associaƟon or applicaƟon in relaƟon to that which we experience as like the thing that is the occasion for the calling up, or it may be an associaƟon of the “unlike,” either with an unlike kind, or a mistake, that is, a false associaƟon or recollecƟon. Even an error, or a wrong opinion, is in one sense the occasion for recollecƟon—the experience has caused one to recollect an Idea, but the wrong one. Since the claim is that we “have had this knowledge, both before birth and immediately aŌerwards,” that is, we use it but it does not come from experience, Socrates must account for why it is not always ready at hand, present to our consciousness, but must in fact, as we have said, be called up by the relevant occasions. The existence of the Ideas has already been presupposed. The quesƟon is, if we use them, do not get them from experience, and have “had them all along,” then why are they not present

to us all along? The answer given is that we did “learn” them once, we did acquire knowledge of them, but we lost it, yet lost it in such a way that it can be recalled on the occasion of experience of what is connected with the ﬁrst object, “either by resemblance or contrast.” This peculiar kind of losing Socrates calls “forgeƫng.” If “to know means to have acquired knowledge of something and not have lost it,” then “the losing of knowledge is what we mean by forgeƫng” (75d). In order to understand RecollecƟon more fully, it is the sense of this “forgeƫng” that we must look at more closely. The issue is how (and when) exactly do we have this knowledge and how is it lost. Understanding what is meant by losing or forgeƫng will depend on our understanding of having known. Having ﬁrst agreed that knowledge of the equal is got “before we were born,” two alternaƟves are oﬀered to Simmias concerning how we have knowledge. On the one alternaƟve we “must be possessed of it always” and we did not individually, just at the point of acquiring it each before being born, also “forget” what we have acquired before this life. On this account then any forgeƫng is in this life. Literally to be thus possessed of knowledge all our life would be somewhat bizarre, and of course is meant to be a non- alternaƟve, although Simmias says, when asked, that he cannot chose between it and the alternaƟve. The second alternaƟve is that each of us lost at the moment of birth what we had acquired before birth, but aŌerwards by direcƟng our senses to the relevant object recover that “old knowledge” which will mean that “what is called learning will consist in recovering old knowledge which belongs to us; and should we not be right in calling this recollecƟon” (75e). The earlier model of forgeƫng and remembering in the ﬁrst discussion (the lyre/cloak type examples) was that something previously known is brought to mind, though it had been forgoƩen, by associaƟon, “whether by resemblance or contrast.” Such a natural descripƟon is of forgeƫng in this life, of not remembering someone or something. When we are dealing not with the remembering or forgeƫng of parƟcular objects but of a kind (genos) of thing, it is the second, more reasonable alternaƟve that appears to be defended. The argument for discarding the ﬁrst alternaƟve and opƟng for the second alternaƟve, Socrates suggests to Simmias, who is unable to choose between the two alternaƟves, is to be based on the asserƟon that to fully know is to be able to “give an account”: “If a man knows certain things, will

he be able to give an account of them, or will he not?” “UnquesƟonably he will, Socrates” (76b). As for the ﬁrst alternaƟve, not only would it seem to say that we already know everything all the Ɵme, which is patently not the case, but the new criterion, to be able to give an account of the things that we give names to in speech, is a formidable criterion for knowing them, and makes for an easy rejecƟon of the ﬁrst alternaƟve. In eﬀect, once having assumed that we gain the knowledge that we apply before birth, Simmias is at a loss to account not for how we have it but rather how we lost it. What then would be meant by to give an account of Equality? Now for remembering individuals it would be nonsensical to require an account of the mere fact that I remember, for example, the image of the owner of a cloak. To give an account would in this case mean no more than to give a descripƟon of one’s image as remembered. Nor clearly can everybody “give an account” who employs in some rudimentary sense an abstract concept, certainly not babies, who nonetheless, “employ their senses from the very moment” they were born and, quite early at least, ostensibly “refer the equal things of [their] sense percepƟons to that standard [Equality itself],” and ought to qualify as knowing, hence in some sense recollecƟng. Nor is the slave-boy example in the Meno any diﬀerent. He can eventually produce the correct answer, and Socrates stresses that it will be only with some pracƟce that he will understand beƩer how such things are done and will able to do it on his own.[20] SƟll, in this case too, it is not an account of Equality or the relevant Idea that he will be giving, but of how the soluƟon to the speciﬁc mathemaƟcal problem is arrived at. Yet the account to which Socrates refers in the criterion that he oﬀers Simmias for choosing between the two alternaƟves, is just such an account of the terms that they have been discussing, the Ideas themselves, of Equality etc. But, the appeal, one might argue, to RecollecƟon as an explanaƟon of how we have knowledge of such things in this life does not require more than that we are seen to do so when presented with whatever “reminds” us. That is, we are given a descripƟon of the act of recollecƟng in which no giving of an account of the Ideas recollected plays a role. It is certainly true that the quesƟon that Socrates asks, as usual, has a disarmingly simple answer, for it is common sense that someone who knows something can talk sensibly about what he knows, and in this sense could be said to be

able “to give an account” of it. And so Simmias replies readily that this is so. But when he realizes that this is to be applied immediately to the Ideas, he is awe-struck by the prospect. Simmias laments that on the following day, when Socrates is dead, no man alive will be able to give an account. No one truly knows these objects now the way that Socrates does, and he will be gone tomorrow. Since we cannot give an account now, the ﬁrst alternaƟve, “that we are possessed of [knowledge] always” is ruled out, leaving the second alternaƟve, that we once knew, before this life, but lost it and need only to be reminded of it. To be able to give an account is used negaƟvely to eliminate the ﬁrst alternaƟve, but not posiƟvely to validate the second one. But what has happened here to the criterion for knowing as being able to “giv(e) an account” if the instances of it require for knowing only that being reminded occurs? It seems that Simmias has remembered the doctrine of RecollecƟon but has forgoƩen the criterion for knowing as giving an account. And so the second alternaƟve is opted for, that learning is recollecƟon, of what we once learned before this life but have forgoƩen at the moment of birth, to be recovered as old knowledge. But suppose we introduce into this argument the disƟncƟon between knowledge and opinion, parƟcularly right opinion, a disƟncƟon conspicuously missing from the discussion. Then it is possible to say that we both have and do not have knowledge “throughout our whole life”: we have “possessed this knowledge always,” which is the ﬁrst alternaƟve, and yet at the same Ɵme to have “lost” it, and that to know in the sense of right opinion does not require that we be able to “give an account” of it, precisely the lack that deﬁnes right opinion. And so, right opinion being a kind of knowledge without an account, and having “lost” it in this sense, then it is not the case that “to know means to have acquired knowledge of something and not to have lost it,” which is how knowledge is understood in the ﬁrst alternaƟve (to have it always). But this would free us in fact to choose the ﬁrst alternaƟve, that we have knowledge “throughout our whole life,” only that it is also “lost” in a diﬀerent sense. Contrary to what Simmias thinks, in a sense everybody does in fact “know those objects,” and that Socrates is to die does not mean, as Simmias says, that “by this Ɵme tomorrow there will be no man leŌ alive” who has knowledge. Simmias says “capable of giving an account” but even this is contrary to the

noƟon that dialecƟc is a human endeavor and no person has a privileged claim to access to the truth. But in the context of the choice that Simmias is to make between always having knowledge in this life and, alternaƟvely, having learned it in a past life, then forgoƩen it, and now recollecƟng it, it is, as we have said, the fact that not everybody can “give an account” which forces Simmias to accept the second choice. However, that this is in the light of not having availed themselves of the disƟncƟon between kinds of knowledge, between, that is, knowledge that includes an account and knowledge of a sort that we all potenƟally have in the form of right opinion, is suggested by Socrates’s quesƟon: “So you don’t think that everybody knows those objects, Simmias.” “By no means.” “Can they then recollect what they once learnt.” “It must be so.” But if the before and aŌer of learning is the conversion of opinion to knowledge, from a loose sort of having to a secure one, then this could as well be described as recollecƟon of what we have lost. There is also a deeper sense in which this is true. For quite apart from the opinions in which we apply ideas without fully understanding them, there is the broader sense of opinion captured in the rightness of right opinion, in which the Ideas themselves are with us from the beginning, as evidenced by our use of language (and of calculaƟon) at all. The point is that, without commiƫng ourselves to a noƟon of a previous existence or previous experience, one can quite well speak of recollecƟng as the “recovery of old knowledge,” parƟcularly, as Socrates adds, a knowledge which “belongs to us.” Indeed, the two alternaƟves between which Simmias was to choose, on this telling of it, are the same, which is, I think, the point. And neither of them requires a pre-existence. This does not, of course, explain just what is going on in the act of associaƟon that is the model for recollecƟon and hence not what the ontological status of the Ideas is.[21] That Simmias is sƟll on the wrong track, and why, is indicated by his ﬁnal suggesƟon as to just when the Ideas might have been acquired if evidently “not since our birth as human beings.” Simmias suggests “ . . . possibly it was at the actual moment of birth . . . ” to which Socrates retorts, “We are not born with the knowledge: that we agreed a moment ago; do we then lose it at the very moment that we acquire it, or is there some other moment that you can suggest?” “No indeed, Socrates; I see

now that I was talking nonsense” (76d). Simmias is sƟll caught up in Ɵme and space. The conclusion, just before, was that “our souls did exist before they were within this human form, apart from our bodies and possessed of intelligence.” The issue raised by our analysis, and by the dialogue between the reader and Plato, is not whether “our souls did exist before they were within this human form,” for that part of the argument is full of holes, but rather the real meaning of the second part of the phrase, that our souls exist in some sense “apart from our bodies and possessed of intelligence” (76c), which in some sense “belongs to us” (75e). What is meant by apart and how does the acƟvity and possibility of dianoia both depend on and explain this apart?[22] In what sense can an account be given of this acƟvity, and the hypothesis of the Ideas? But that project can and should be separated from the immortality of the soul in the sense of a temporal before and aŌer, and it would then not be true that “all our argument will have gone for nothing” if the temporal, literal sense of immortality is let go. Socrates’s ﬁnal formulaƟon in this secƟon is, “If those objects exist which are always on our lips, a beauƟful and a good and all reality of that sort, and if it is to that that we refer the content of our sense-percepƟons . . . it must follow that as surely as those objects exist so surely do our souls exist before we are born” (76d-e). But one can be sure of and defend the ﬁrst two proposiƟons without being commiƩed to the third, and in fact denying it. Socrates asks Simmias, “Does the existence of our souls before birth stand or fall with the existence of those other objects?” (76e) Simmias replies that he is “uƩerly convinced.” But the existence of those objects as apart does not stand or fall with the “existence of our souls before birth,” or the arguments for it, fortunately. Simmias’s concluding certainty in both cases, that of immortality and that of the eternal Ideas, is equally groundless, as far as an argument having been provided here goes. His now apparently ﬁrm belief in both is yet to be revealed as not immune to doubt, or at least as dependent on an appeal to a rather diﬀerent doxa (the Soul as a Harmony doctrine) with which it will be shown to be in conﬂict. But we should note that while the ﬁrst argument, that of the Cycle of Opposites, had introduced ontological elements, it had done so in a wholly mythological way—the argument was conducted through images. In this,

the second argument, the connecƟon between ontology and epistemology is made, though sƟll inadequately, and thickly clothed in doxa. THE KINSHIP ARGUMENT: MUTHOS, LOGOS, AND THE PHILOSOPHICAL MEANING OF ETERNALITY Socrates now opens the third argument for immortality with the following quesƟon: “What kind of thing is in fact liable to undergo this dispersal that you speak of? For what kind of thing should we fear that it may be dispersed, and for what kind should we not? And next we should consider to which kind the soul belongs . . . ”(78b) The immediate impulse for conƟnuing the argument is to allay their “childish fears” about the soul being scaƩered by the wind upon “dissoluƟon” of the union of body and soul. The conƟnuance of the soul aŌer death, Socrates had said, was already a “complete proof,” combining the present argument regarding RecollecƟon and pre-natal existence with “the principle that everything that lives comes from the dead” i.e., the cyclical argument. But this in fact won’t work: a) it will not provide for personal immortality, which is the concern that generates the childish fears, b) RecollecƟon, given the above account, has not saƟsfactorily been shown to require pre-natal existence, c) life and death are not a necessary causal cycle. The RecollecƟon thesis must be linked instead with a non-material, non-spaƟo-temporal eternality —no before and aŌer—and must be dissociated from a material noƟon of the soul’s existence, which we have seen Simmias and Cebes to have. Hence the need to discuss how both soul and Ideas are—and with that the noƟon of cause. Thus the ﬁrst move in the third argument is to discuss not what soul is but what kinds of things are subject to dispersal at all. Ironically, the terminology with which this discussion begins is sƟll decidedly physical, again accommodaƟng Simmias and Cebes’s beginnings. All that is “compounded or has a composite nature (is) liable to be split up into its component parts.” Only incomposite things “can possibly be exempt for that.” The incomposite is what is “constant and unchanging” while the composite are things that “are diﬀerent at diﬀerent Ɵmes and never constant.” The point is preƩy weak. One might object that neither of these is necessarily the case—as if the fact of being the one or the other were the cause of permanence or dissoluƟon. Something could be

composite, but not necessarily changing over Ɵme, or just never happen to get around to breaking up, or be incomposite and be broken up by force, for example. The terms and deﬁniƟons are couched in language that is readily acceptable to Simmias and Cebes, but ironically so, as we shall see in more detail later. Socrates then asks, “Can the equal itself, the beauƟful itself, the being itself whatever it may be, ever admit any sort of change? Or does each of these real beings, uniform and independent, remain unchanging and constant, never admiƫng of any sort of alteraƟon whatever?” “They must be unchanging and constant, Cebes replied” (78d). The contrast is between, e.g., “the beauƟful itself . . . [which is] uniform and independent, remains unchanging and constant, never admiƫng of any sort of alteraƟon whatever,” and the “many (beauƟful) things, beauƟful human beings, say, or horses or garments . . . the many equal things . . . the things that are called by the same name as those real beings” (78e). The changing is represented by what you can touch and see etc., that is, the visible. The opposite of this is the things that are “constant and unchanging” and these are by contrast not visible. The changing and visible are “never idenƟcal with themselves nor idenƟcally related to each other.” This is familiar doctrine and Cebes readily assents. But it is really rather loose playing. Clearly we could hardly get along if everything were really in absolute and constant ﬂux, and a certain relaƟve physical stability of the visible over a ﬁxed Ɵme frame is evident. This applies as well to the relaƟve stability of the relaƟonal qualiƟes, that my father yesterday is my father today would not be possible without a certain form of existenƟal, hence visible conƟnuity. Nor does it follow simply from something’s being visible per se that it is changeable. And the fact that all ideas are invisible does not mean that all invisibles are like ideas or concepts, let alone Platonic Ideas or Forms, that is, that they have the quality of being unchangeable and constant. For example, my feelings are not visible, but they change. The government is not visible, but it changes. And even the noeƟc acƟvity of soul is a kind of change. This is the basic and obvious ﬂaw in the third argument from kinship. The soul does indeed have a kinship with the Ideas and is itself invisible, but it does not follow that it shares with its kin all of the qualiƟes of the laƩer, that it is of the same nature or kind (genos) as its kin. And so it is not in fact true that “the invisible (is)

always constant, the visible never,” a weak link and supposiƟon on which the argument at this point is based. And yet, there is a link between the soul as knower and the relaƟve constancy of ideas as standards in pracƟce, both ontologically (or to use Heidegger’s term, pre-ontologically,[23] in our use of discourse), and in the search for greater stability that dialecƟc both witnesses to and allows. It is clear to all commentators but those who think anamnēsis is dependent on proving immortality, that the Ideas are assumed in the argument, but one needs to understand just why the assumpƟon is implemented in just the way that it is: if Simmias and Cebes, who clearly have only a vague and literal noƟon of the Ideas and how they work and are, need primarily to be reassured that the soul does not dissipate at death, then we might as well use their belief in the Ideas, and the way that they believe in them, combined with an assortment of rather general Pythagorean, Orphic and possibly Empedoclean doctrines[24] to reassure them. But Plato does so in such a way that is so patently false in argument that we are led to ask just what the “unchanging and constant” nature of the Ideas really is, what sense of the term eternal does make sense, and then to see how and when the soul is anything like this. This accounts for the extremity of the argument, the polarizaƟon of the senses and the soul as invesƟgator of what is. Elsewhere the senses are given a role, and here too, if one recalls that it is on the occasion of the presentaƟon of sensible equals that one is to recollect the equal itself. That was just a few lines earlier, at 74b. But here, when Simmias and Cebes are to be led to a hopeful conclusion, the senses are completely useless: “Now were we not saying some Ɵme ago that when the soul makes use of the body to invesƟgate something through vision or hearing or some other sense—of course invesƟgaƟng by means of the body is the same as invesƟgaƟng by sense—it is dragged by the body towards objects that are never constant, and itself wanders in a sort of dizzy drunken confusion, inasmuch as it is apprehending confused objects” (79c). By contrast, “when it invesƟgates by itself alone, it passes to that other world of pure, everlasƟng, immortal, constant being, and by reason of its kinship thereto abides ever therewith . . . and then it has rest from wandering . . . and is not this the experience which it has called intelligence” (or wisdom, phronēsis). The mythic-poeƟc language, the

depicƟon of a living individual soul’s experience, is obvious enough. But how then are we to take the passage, just how much of it is metaphor or image? What is directed at the literal-minded and dogmaƟc, unreﬂecƟve Simmias and Cebes, and what at us? Not only is the denigraƟon of the senses misleading, but this parƟcular descripƟon of the “soul when it invesƟgates by itself alone” is so as well. For without an explanaƟon and understanding of just what that invesƟgaƟng is, of the nature of dialecƟc and of its objects and objecƟves, an understanding which Simmias and Cebes as trusƟng in the existence of the Ideas certainly do not have, the image could as well be of a soul contemplaƟng, meditaƟng on supposed invisible eternal objects and truths, a sort of mysƟcal and non-discursive experience which is far from what Plato would grant as phronēsis.[25] Yet it is close enough to what Simmias and Cebes would understand in Pythagorean rites etc. But with diﬀerent understandings of meaningful discourse come radically diﬀerent understandings of immortal and unchanging. What makes something unchanging is indeed in one sense that it is incomposite or at least an indissoluable unity. But that indivisible unity is not a physical one, rather the unity of the Idea. That such a unity does not come to be or pass away, is not because it is some immutable stuﬀ, as Simmias and Cebes take the soul to be, but because it is not in space and Ɵme at all. To the extent that the soul is like this, it parƟcipates in that form of eternality, and no other. When the soul is doing what it does most typically and best, engaging in discourse, it does so outside of space and Ɵme—although a man and his acƟon in equity are spaƟo-temporal, the discussion or judgment they provoke are not. That a discussion or judgment occurs at a given Ɵme does not make its meaning or content temporal, any more than that it occurs at a given place makes it spaƟal, which does not, however, commit one to an unchanging logos. Indeed, it is not clear that the soul as an enƟty is perhaps any more than this acƟvity. And since the ﬁeld of its acƟvity is itself spaƟo-temporal as regards individual discourse, which is occasioned by individual experience, it is not clear what either a pre-natal or aŌer-death knowledge or experience of Ideas could possibly mean. It is not so much that we need a body but that we need a world of experience in which Ideas are “useful and beneﬁcial,” as is our discourse about them.

Socrates puts icing on the cake by adding ﬁnally that the body relates to the soul as subject to ruler, which implies that the soul is thus like the divine, to which it “naturally belongs” to “rule and lead;” the “soul is like the divine (the god) and the body like the mortal.” Thus the soul is as immortal as the gods and the body as mortal as slaves. Since the proof is already completed, here too we have a double message. The soul is indeed godlike and deserves to rule, but the veiled skepƟcism of the Apology[26] is surely not forgoƩen. Plato and Socrates have their own divinity and they need not look up in the skies to see the divine, like Glaucon’s star-gazing astronomer; they see the divine, since the Ideas are both in everyday discourse, our experience of the world as intelligible, and the distant background in which we search for a fuller understanding, in dialecƟc. In order to stress these rather diﬀerent noƟons of the divine, Socrates ends the third argument for immortality with a mocking absurdity: “Well then, that being so, isn’t it right and proper for the body to be quickly destroyed but for the soul to be altogether indestrucƟble, or nearly so” (80b). What, in heaven’s name, could be “nearly so,” nearly indestrucƟble? Let us review the dramaƟc development of the language and its signiﬁcance, how that language aﬀects and reﬂects the argument. Why are the disƟncƟons composite/incomposite, changeable/unchangeable introduced at 78b and then not speciﬁcally menƟoned again, relying rather on kinship with the invisible? In looking for a reason for this we must have in mind the basic ﬂaw of the Kinship argument; that what have some qualiƟes in common, may not share others. The categories that Socrates suggests have a certain immediate appeal, and apparently a certain familiarity for Cebes as a descripƟon of a division into kinds of things: i.e., a noƟon of changing versus unchanging drawn from a naturalisƟc dogma of the opposiƟon of composite versus incomposite, the laƩer being indissoluble. The Ideas, the equal itself, etc. ﬁrst are said “never to admit of change” and one would think that Socrates would follow this up immediately with the conclusion that they are “like” the other unchanging things (whatever those might be?) and indissoluble, then that the soul is like the Ideas and it too is indissoluble, or immortal. But this is not quite what happens. The next move is rather to disƟnguish the visible from the invisible, and through the kinship of the invisible, of the invisibility of both

Ideas and Soul, to conclude that the soul, like the invisible Ideas, is constant, and thus as essenƟally unchanging and eternal as its kin. This, as we have seen, is not a legiƟmate argument: having certain qualiƟes in common does not mean that other qualiƟes are shared. The sense of eternal ﬁnally reached in the conclusion of the argument, as understood by Cebes, is stubbornly material in its imagery. At the beginning, Cebes had recounted how some people “suspect that, when it has leŌ the body, it no longer exists anywhere . . . it is dispersed like breath or smoke, vanishing into thin air . . . ” (70a) In the end, it is simply a beƩer, stronger, somehow indissoluble stuﬀ. What kind of constancy is invoked? When the soul is described ﬁnally by Cebes at 87a, he conƟnues to maintain that it is both constant and incomposite. The laƩer is the only basis for constancy that he can envision, which is why this material image of constancy is introduced. But earlier, Cebes, who is superﬁcially familiar with the doctrine of Ideas, might have balked at calling Ideas incomposite, as indeed they are not, since though unitary, as self-idenƟcal, they may sƟll be complex. For example, whatever JusƟce “itself by itself” may be, it is certainly complex as contrasted to the model of physical homogeneity implied in the contrast of composite and incomposite. So the noƟon of visible versus invisible as the disƟncƟve feature is brought in instead, a noƟon with which he is equally, if not much more, at home. Thus only in the conclusion is Cebes’s understanding of soul as materially incomposite brought back into play as the implicit kind of indissolubility he can accept. It is reintroduced in the ﬁnal list of qualiƟes aƩributable to what the soul is very like: “divine, immortal, intelligible, uniform (simple, of one kind), indissoluble, unvarying, and constant in relaƟon to itself” (80b, Gallop).[27] What is signiﬁcant here is the re-inclusion of “indissoluble” (adialutō), not menƟoned since the beginning of the argument at 78b where the quesƟon was what things can suﬀer dispersion, and what things cannot. For leaving this oﬀ the list (but it is always on Cebes’s list) would allow that the soul’s kind of immortality is atemporal but temporally bounded and corresponds to the qualiƟes, and perhaps even the mode of existence, of the objects of its acƟvity in knowing. Each Ɵme that I am engaged in knowing, the soul, like its objects, is not spaƟo-temporal in its acƟvity. But for this, conƟnued existence is not required upon dissoluƟon of the body.

The next passage, 80c-82d, conƟnues the same development. Increasingly mythic, it describes the aŌerlife of souls in the same language. But there is always the other, philosophical voice to be heard as well. The body, falling to pieces, sƟll survives a “considerable Ɵme.” The soul lasƟng even longer, “passes to an invisible region” and “‘the soul that has dissociated itself as much as possible from the body in life,” as the philosopher does in “pracƟcing death and dying,” having trained to be by itself, will “depart into the world of the invisible which it resembles … (and) there aƩain(s) happiness, released from its wanderings and follies and fears” This is in contrast to any soul which departs polluted, “one which had always associated with the body and tended it, ﬁlled with its lusts and so bewitched by its passions and pleasures as to think nothing real save what is bodily, what can be touched and seen and eaten and made to serve sexual enjoyment . . . to hate and shun with terror the things that are invisible” (81b). Such a soul cannot depart unsullied, and because it is “interspersed with a bodily element that had been worked into its substance by unceasing commerce,” is bound to return again to this life in some degraded form. This says in eﬀect that all those souls that have not undergone the puriﬁcaƟon of philosophy, that is to say most, apparently depart this life with some sort of mixture of body and soul, weighted down by the remainder of material body stuﬀ. Granted, the language is poeƟcal, mythic, but it is the speciﬁc kind of image that is of importance, always remembering that Simmias and Cebes tend to take the image literally. For here, obviously soul is not radically diﬀerent in kind, as was to be supposed, if it can allow of being interspersed—again working on Cebes’s soul stuﬀ, “the bodily residue we must think of as a ponderous . . . earthy and visible substance.” Cebes accepts that such weighted down souls haunt tombs, in “dread of the invisible that is called Hades” and “sƟll retain some visible substance, which is just why they can be seen” (81d). Thus it is not only their “substance” that prevents them from entering Hades, but Socrates aƩributes to these ghosts an eﬀect that is somewhat original and clearly ontological in intent, “dread of the invisible.” Thus the wandering souls must await reincarnaƟon, being “chained up again in a body” for not having made the right judgment about what is more real, what is less so: the moral dogma of what is a bad life in its aƩachment to bodily pleasures

is here turned into an epistemological-ontological one, the soul must learn what are its natural objects. The wicked now are those who “think nothing real save the body” and did not pracƟce dying, that is, focusing the soul on the acƟvity of knowing, and what can be known, the speciﬁcally human acƟvity of discourse. This is as opposed to those whose training is “gluƩony, unchasƟty and drunkenness,” which naturally prepares such souls to “join the company of donkeys or some such creatures”—that is, they have pracƟced being not-human. Even the merely virtuous, having pracƟced “virtues which spring from habit and training, devoid of philosophic wisdom” (82b) become “bees” or “ants,” and while they thus are the “happiest,” and pass to the “most favored region,” yet the “company of the gods” is reserved for those “who have sought wisdom” and “only the lover of knowledge may go thither” (82b-c).[28] The laƩer’s “absƟnence is not due to fear of . . . an evil life” but his insight into the “divine,” that is, “the direcƟon whither philosophy points him.” Note that the ghost-souls that haunt tombs act out of “fear of the invisible” while the philosopher’s soul acts “not out of fear” but out of a posiƟve aƩracƟon, one might add, aƩracƟon to the invisible. Although Cebes’s moral and religious beliefs are called into play here, there is a crucial shiŌ in blame, the reasons why the souls deserve such a lowly, or at least non-human, reincarnaƟon: in Socrates’s formulaƟon, it is not moral disapprobaƟon that condemns them but their implicit ontology. Suﬃce it to say that materialism is a natural ontology for the embodied soul (I would oﬀer Thrasymachus as an example). The greatest danger, and the “greatest evil” upon feeling “intense pleasure or intense pain in anything” is not moral but ontological, leading one “at the same Ɵme [to] believing that the chief object of these his emoƟons is transparently clear and uƩerly real, though in fact it is not; this is especially the case with visible objects” (83c). One is reminded of Phaedo’s puzzlement at the beginning of the dialogue about “a strange sort of blend of pleasure and pain” that came upon him when he realized that Socrates was to die. This is followed immediately by the opening scene in the prison cell, in which, on feeling the pleasure of release from the shackles, and recalling the previous pain, Socrates begins a discussion with Phaedo on the subject. A poeƟc image is

provided as part of the discussion, the pleasure and pain are like “two creatures aƩached to a single head.” This is quickly interrupted by Cebes’s query, not about the subject at hand, nor the image, but about poetry in the common sense of the term, about Socrates’s “versifying,” “when you had never produced any composiƟon before” (60d). But in eﬀect, the conƟnuous dialogue between Plato and the reader—the ontological discussion of what is real, what is independent and separate, truly released, as contrasted to a poeƟc mixture of mysƟcal image-making and a natural, materialisƟc ontology of substance-things—has been going on all the Ɵme, behind the scene, as it were. As contrasted to a kind of quasi- materialisƟc naturalism, our soul is naturally linked through our fundamental interpretaƟve acƟvity of image-making to the invisible in the everyday—an unreﬂecƟve relaƟon without which we could hardly get along. But precisely because it is unreﬂecƟve, we do not draw the natural inferences from it—which is precisely what philosophy, dialecƟc and the Republic’s turning of the whole soul, must do. In sum, my interpretaƟon above and in the following chapters accords on the whole with Fine’s examinaƟon of separaƟon and her conclusions (see n.1), but makes a stronger claim. Fine shows that Plato’s theory of Forms in the middle dialogues (hence the Phaedo and the Republic, with which we are concerned here) does not require that Forms have separaƟon as a deﬁning feature, nor do the texts ever explicitly claim that they are separate. In other words, Fine is not saying that Plato did not believe that the Forms were separate, only that the texts and arguments do not acƟvely support or require this. My own claim is somewhat stronger, that the text of the Phaedo can be shown to be making the claim that the Forms are substances separable only in the deﬁniƟonal sense (though this phrase does not reﬂect their ontological status in my interpretaƟon) and to be in part directed against an interpretaƟon of the Forms as independently exisƟng substances. As for the soul, the immediate object here, I have been concerned to show that chōrismos as it applies to the soul is carefully limited to the same sense. Fine is willing to take the soul’s separateness in this life and its being autē kath’ hautēn in this sense (60), but in passing seems to be willing to take the separaƟon of the soul in a pre-existence and an aŌerlife as a literal claim (72-73). Of course, her main concern is with the supposed

separaƟon of Forms. But as I show here, aƩenƟon to the use of chōris and its cognates in relaƟon to the soul has a direct bearing on interpretaƟon of the Forms, and is in eﬀect in support of Fine’s basic interpretaƟon. I will argue that the existenƟal sense of exist separately is always a muthos, that this is to be deduced from the dramaƟc reading of the text. Most importantly, I argue that the move from the argument regarding Forms and parƟcipants to the argument regarding Soul and body and the independence of each, hence to immortality for the former, is all based on a subtle play on just this diﬀerence between the two senses of separaƟon. The rest of the dialogue must, then, both maintain Simmias and Cebes’s “hope” and yet also give an intelligible account of the invisible, the “path” and “direcƟon whither philosophy points.”[29] The “sustenance” on which the soul is said to feed is got in “contemplaƟng the uƩer certainty of divine reality.” And “surely if that be the manner of its sustenance, my friends, we need not be alarmed about its having to fear that on its release from the body it may be dissipated, blown to pieces by the winds” (84b). But Simmias and Cebes, not having understood the nature of this relaƟon of sustenance and sustained, are sƟll worried, and raise objecƟons that reveal the more clearly their starƟng point. Like the unmasking of Thrasymachus, and the objecƟons of Glaucon and Adeimantus concerning the literal or visible possibility of the ideal city, their conƟnuing material model or image of soul as a more durable stuﬀ or, in Simmias’s case, the name for the relaƟons of stuﬀ, is brought out in the dramaƟc acƟon. In all three cases, their implicit ontologies are revealed as based in the acceptance of the sensible/visible as by far more concretely real, and directly known, protestaƟons apart. It is their very trust in the literal visible image that is to be uƟlized by Socrates to achieve what “turning” of their souls they are capable of.[30] But, ironically, this very use of images, both in the “proofs” of the immortality of the soul in the Phaedo, and in the account of “possibility” for the ideal city in the Republic, reveal the limits of these interlocutors, as contrasted to the reader. This limitaƟon is precisely in their inability to see an image as an image. They are prevented from seeing image as image, from considering image-making in all its implicaƟons, by the very ontology from which they implicitly operate as hypotheses concerning what is real.

Thus, though they are moved ahead in their caring for the aﬀairs of the soul, it is only at the level of doxa—their “turning” is an incomplete one. Yet their very shortcomings, as played out before us in the dialogues, are meant to be our own gain. What is invisible to them, both their own doxa as image and what it is an image of, is made visible to us, in our acƟvity of “quesƟon and answer” about the image in discourse before us.[31] Rather than taking Simmias and Cebes as seriously parƟcipaƟng in the conversaƟon with Socrates at a philosophical level, their importance in the argument of the dialogue is as dramaƟc foils.
